docs.title: 1.12 Yoga as a Living Tradition
docs.text:
What distinguishes Yoga from a mere philosophical system or historical curiosity is that it remains a living tradition. Millions of practitioners across the globe continue to practise it, although most modern practice — centred on postures and largely pursued for health — differs considerably from the meditative and renunciant Yoga of the classical texts (Chapter 11).

In December 2014 the United Nations General Assembly, on India’s initiative, declared 21 June the International Day of Yoga. Clinical research suggests that yoga can modestly help with conditions such as chronic low-back pain and anxiety, but the evidence is uneven in quality and many popular health claims remain unproven (see Section 11.11).

In the classical sources, however, the aim of Yoga lies beyond health and well-being: it is liberation, whether understood as the kaivalya of Sāṃkhya-Yoga, the mokṣa of Vedānta or the nirvāṇa of the Buddhists.

docs.title: 1.13 Structure of This Volume
docs.text: The chapters follow the currents of yoga roughly in the order in which they arose, so that each technique is met after the ideas from which it grew. Chapter 2 treats Patañjali’s Yoga Sūtra: its four parts, its eight limbs, its theory of mind and the commentators who interpreted it for fifteen centuries. Chapter 3 turns to the Gītā’s yogas of action and devotion and to their later history, and Chapter 4 asks how the Advaita Vedāntins, for whom liberation came by knowledge alone, used and criticised yoga. Chapters 5 and 6 describe the yoga of the Tantras and the subtle body of channels, centres and kuṇḍalinī that the Tantras devised. Chapter 7 follows Haṭha Yoga, which inherited that body, from the Amṛtasiddhi to the Mysore court, together with the ascetic orders that carried it and its life in Tamil, Marathi, Persian and the Sikh scriptures. Chapters 8 to 10 take up three practices that run through all these traditions: breath-control, meditation (with its Buddhist and Jain forms) and the yogas of mantra, dissolution and inner sound. Chapter 11 traces modern yoga from Vivekānanda to the International Day of Yoga, including its politics, its scandals and the clinical evidence. A chronology, a glossary and a select bibliography close the volume.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Patañjali’s Yoga Sūtra and the Eight Limbs
docs.text:
Traditional invocation to Patañjali (a late verse, found in an 18th-century work by Śivarāma)

yogena cittasya padena vācāṃ malaṃ śarīrasya ca vaidyakena yo'pākarot taṃ pravaraṃ munīnāṃ patañjaliṃ prāñjalir ānato'smi I bow with folded hands to Patañjali, the foremost among sages, who removed impurities of the mind through Yoga, of speech through Grammar, and of the body through Medicine.

docs.title: 2.1 Patañjali and His Work
docs.text:
Patañjali did not invent Yoga. He systematised existing yogic teachings — Brahmanical, and in part Buddhist in vocabulary — into a compact work of 195 or 196 aphorisms (sūtras), whose terseness invites comparison with Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī. Later tradition, in the invocation above, made him the author of three works that purify mind, speech and body: the Yoga Sūtra, the Mahābhāṣya on grammar and a lost medical treatise. Modern scholarship does not accept this attribution.

The dating of Patañjali has long been debated. The identification of the author of the Yoga Sūtras with Patañjali the grammarian (c. 150 BCE) would place him in the 2nd century BCE, but most modern scholars reject it on grounds of language and doctrine. Philipp Maas, who produced the first critical edition of the work’s first chapter (Maas 2006), has shown from the manuscript tradition that the sūtras and the Bhāṣya ascribed to “Vyāsa” were transmitted as one work, the Pātañjalayogaśāstra, which he dates to c. 325–425 CE; he argues that Patañjali compiled the sūtras and wrote the explanatory prose himself (Maas 2013). Not all scholars accept single authorship, but a date around the 4th–5th century CE for the work in its present form is now widely accepted. The text shows considerable familiarity with Sarvāstivāda and Yogācāra Buddhist ideas, and Karen O’Brien-Kop has argued that “classical” Yoga is best read as one participant in a shared Brahmanical and Buddhist discourse of meditation rather than as a self-contained system (Bryant 2009; White 2014; O’Brien-Kop 2021).

docs.title: 2.2 Structure of the Yoga Sūtras
docs.text:
The sūtras are divided into four chapters (pādas), each addressing a distinct aspect of the yogic path. (The count of 55 or 56 sūtras in the third chapter varies between editions; sūtra numbers cited below follow the common numbering of Woods’s translation (Woods 1914).) Table 2.1 gives the subject of each pāda. This chapter follows the four parts in turn, but treats the eight limbs, which run from the end of the second part into the third, together (Section 2.5).

Table 2.1. The Four Pādas of the Yoga Sūtras Pāda Name Sūtras Subject Matter I Samādhi Pāda 51 Nature of Yoga; states of samādhi; obstacles II Sādhana Pāda 55 Practice; kleśas; Kriyā Yoga; first five limbs III Vibhūti Pāda 56 Supernatural powers (siddhis); last three limbs IV Kaivalya Pāda 34 Absolute liberation; nature of consciousness

docs.title: 2.3 Pāda I: Samādhi Pāda — The Chapter on Absorption
docs.text: Later commentators held that the first chapter is addressed to the student who is already advanced in practice. It defines Yoga, describes the modifications of the mind, names the obstacles and their remedies, and presents the stages of samādhi.

docs.title: 2.3.1 The Opening Sūtras: Definition of Yoga
docs.text:
Sūtra 1.1

atha yogānuśāsanam Now begins the authoritative instruction on Yoga.

Vyāsa’s Bhāṣya explains that atha (“now”) marks the beginning of a topic (adhikāra), and glosses the word yoga as concentration (samādhi).

Sūtra 1.2 — The Definition

yogaś citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind-stuff.

This is the defining sūtra (lakṣaṇa sūtra). Citta is the whole mental apparatus — in the commentators’ terms, the Sāṃkhya mind, intellect and ego-sense together (Section 2.9); its vṛttis are its fluctuations or modifications; nirodha is their cessation or restraint.

Sūtra 1.3 — The Result

tadā draṣṭuḥ svarūpe'vasthānam Then the Seer abides in its own true nature.

When the fluctuations of the mind cease, the Puruṣa (the Seer, draṣṭā) rests in its own nature; when they do not, it seems to take on their form (vṛtti-sārūpyam itaratra, 1.4).

docs.title: 2.3.2 The Five Vṛttis
docs.text:
Sūtra 1.5–1.6

vṛttayaḥ pañcatayyaḥ kliṣṭākliṣṭāḥ pramāṇa-viparyaya-vikalpa-nidrā-smṛtayaḥ The fluctuations are fivefold, and may be painful (kliṣṭa) or non-painful (akliṣṭa). They are: valid cognition, error, imagination, sleep, and memory.

Each of the five may be painful or not; Table 2.2 gives the sūtra that defines each.

Table 2.2. The Five Vṛttis and Their Characteristics Vṛtti English Description Sūtra Pramāṇa Valid cognition Correct knowledge through perception, inference, or testimony 1.7 Viparyaya Error Misconception; knowledge not based on the real form of the object 1.8 Vikalpa Imagination Verbal cognition without a corresponding object 1.9 Nidrā Sleep The modification based on the absence of content 1.10 Smṛti Memory Retention of experienced objects 1.11

docs.title: 2.3.3 Abhyāsa and Vairāgya
docs.text:
Sūtra 1.12

abhyāsa-vairāgyābhyāṃ tan-nirodhaḥ The cessation of the fluctuations is achieved through practice (abhyāsa) and dispassion (vairāgya).

Sūtra 1.13–1.14

tatra sthitau yatno'bhyāsaḥ sa tu dīrgha-kāla-nairantarya-satkārāsevito dṛḍha-bhūmiḥ Of these, abhyāsa is the effort to maintain steadiness. That practice becomes firmly grounded when pursued for a long time, without interruption, and with devotion.

The three conditions of firm practice — long duration (dīrgha-kāla), continuity (nairantarya) and care or reverence (satkāra) — are the nearest the sūtras come to a programme of training. Dispassion is defined next (1.15–1.16): the lower kind is mastery over craving for things seen or heard of; the higher (para-vairāgya) is indifference even to the qualities of nature, which comes from knowledge of the Puruṣa.

docs.title: 2.3.4 Īśvara Praṇidhāna
docs.text:
One of the most distinctive features of Patañjali’s Yoga, compared with classical Sāṃkhya, is the inclusion of Īśvara (the Lord) as a special Puruṣa. Īśvara is not a creator; he is a self who has never been bound and who serves as teacher and object of meditation:

Sūtras 1.23–1.27

īśvara-praṇidhānād vā kleśa-karma-vipākāśayair aparāmṛṣṭaḥ puruṣa-viśeṣa īśvaraḥ tatra niratiśayaṃ sarva-jña-bījam pūrveṣām api guruḥ kālenānavacchedāt tasya vācakaḥ praṇavaḥ Or, (samādhi is attained) by devotion to Īśvara. Īśvara is a special Puruṣa, untouched by afflictions, actions, results, or latent impressions. In Him is the unsurpassed seed of omniscience. He is the Guru even of the ancients, being not limited by time. His designator (name) is the Praṇava (Oṃ).

The next sūtra prescribes the repetition of this syllable together with contemplation of its meaning (1.28; Chapter 10).

docs.title: 2.3.5 The Obstacles and Their Remedies
docs.text:
The first chapter also analyses what stands in the way of practice:

Sūtra 1.30

vyādhi-styāna-saṃśaya-pramādālāsyāvirati- bhrānti-darśanālabdha-bhūmikatvānavasthitatvāni citta-vikṣepās te'ntarāyāḥ Disease, dullness, doubt, carelessness, laziness, worldliness, erroneous perception, failure to attain a stage, and instability — these are the distractions of the mind that are the obstacles.

Pain, dejection, trembling of the limbs and irregular breathing accompany these distractions (1.31). Table 2.3 gives Vyāsa’s explanation of each obstacle.

Table 2.3. The Nine Obstacles (Antarāyas), YS 1.30 Obstacle English Description (following Vyāsa) Vyādhi Disease Imbalance of the bodily humours, fluids and senses Styāna Dullness Mental inertia; unwillingness to act Saṃśaya Doubt Wavering between alternatives Pramāda Carelessness Failure to cultivate the means to samādhi Ālasya Laziness Heaviness of body and mind Avirati Worldliness Craving for sense objects Bhrānti-darśana False perception Mistaken understanding Alabdha-bhūmikatva Non-attainment Failure to reach a stage of concentration Anavasthitatva Instability Inability to hold an attained stage

Patañjali’s own remedy is practice on a single principle (eka-tattvābhyāsa, 1.32). He then offers a series of alternatives for steadying the mind: cultivating friendliness, compassion, joy and equanimity towards the happy, the suffering, the virtuous and the wicked (1.33, discussed as a meditation practice in Chapter 9); the expulsion and retention of breath (1.34); engagement of the mind with a subtle sense-experience (1.35); a luminous state free of sorrow (1.36); a mind free from passion, such as that of a saint (1.37); the knowledge of dream or deep sleep (1.38); and, finally, meditation on any object one likes (1.39). The list is notably open: no single technique is required, and a range of supports is offered for people of different temperaments.

docs.title: 2.3.6 The Stages of Samādhi
docs.text:
This is the book’s one full treatment of the stages of samādhi; the chapters on Haṭha Yoga and on meditation refer back to it. Patañjali distinguishes two kinds of absorption. Cognitive (samprajñāta) absorption is accompanied by gross thought (vitarka), subtle reflection (vicāra), bliss (ānanda) and the bare sense “I am” (asmitā) (1.17); the other kind, reached through supreme dispassion (para-vairāgya, 1.16) and the practice of the idea of cessation, retains only latent impressions (1.18).

Sūtras 1.41–1.51 analyse cognitive absorption as a series of “coalescences” (samāpatti) of the mind with its object, which become progressively simpler. In savitarka absorption the object is still mixed with its name and with the idea of it (1.42); when memory is purified, the object alone shines forth (nirvitarka, 1.43). The same two steps are then repeated with subtle objects (savicāra, nirvicāra, 1.44). All of these are “with seed” (sabīja, 1.46). At the highest of them the mind becomes so clear that its insight is called “truth-bearing” (ṛtaṃbharā prajñā, 1.48), and the impression left by that insight blocks all other impressions (1.50). When even this impression is stopped, the absorption is “seedless” (nirbīja, 1.51). The commentators, from Vyāsa onwards, built these sūtras into a ladder of six cognitive stages leading to the non-cognitive state; Vācaspati Miśra’s systematisation of that ladder is the one usually taught today (Figure 2.1; Table 2.4). The final stage before liberation, the “cloud of dharma” (dharmamegha), is described in the fourth chapter (Section 2.7).

Figure 2.1. Classification of Samādhi in Patañjali’s Yoga System. All cognitive (samprajñāta) samādhis are “with seed” (1.46); the seedless state is the cessation of even the final impression (1.51). The finer subdivision and the placement of dharmamegha follow the commentators. Table 2.4. Stages of Samādhi as Systematised by the Commentators Stage Type Object Characteristics Savitarka Cognitive Gross Absorption with name, form, and knowledge mixed Nirvitarka Cognitive Gross Only the object’s essential nature shines Savicāra Cognitive Subtle Absorption on subtle elements with reflection Nirvicāra Cognitive Subtle Truth-bearing insight (ṛtaṃbharā prajñā) Sānanda Cognitive Sattvic joy Absorption in pure bliss Sāsmitā Cognitive Pure ego Only the sense of “I am” remains Asamprajñāta Non-cognitive None Cessation of all mental activity; seedless

docs.title: 2.4 Pāda II: Sādhana Pāda — The Chapter on Practice
docs.text: According to the commentators, the second chapter is addressed to the student of intermediate qualification who requires practical guidance. It introduces Kriyā Yoga, analyses the causes of suffering (kleśas), and begins the account of the eight limbs.

docs.title: 2.4.1 Kriyā Yoga: The Yoga of Action
docs.text:
Sūtra 2.1

tapaḥ-svādhyāyeśvara-praṇidhānāni kriyā-yogaḥ Austerity (tapas), self-study (svādhyāya), and surrender to Īśvara (īśvara-praṇidhāna) constitute Kriyā Yoga.

Kriyā Yoga is practised, the next sūtra says, to cultivate samādhi and to weaken the afflictions (2.2). The same three practices reappear as the last three observances (niyama) of the eight-limbed path (Section 2.5.2), and the commentators read Kriyā Yoga as the yoga of those not yet fit for the higher practices of the first chapter.

docs.title: 2.4.2 The Five Kleśas (Afflictions)
docs.text:
Sūtra 2.3

avidyāsmitā-rāga-dveṣābhiniveśāḥ kleśāḥ The afflictions are: ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and clinging to life.

Table 2.5 summarises the five.

Table 2.5. The Pañca Kleśas (Five Afflictions) Kleśa English Description Sūtra Avidyā Ignorance Mistaking the non-eternal for eternal, impure for pure, painful for pleasant, non-Self for Self 2.5 Asmitā Egoism Identification of the Seer with the instrument of seeing 2.6 Rāga Attachment Clinging to pleasure 2.7 Dveṣa Aversion Recoiling from pain 2.8 Abhiniveśa Fear of death Clinging to life, present even in the wise 2.9

Sūtra 2.4 — Avidyā as the Root

avidyā kṣetram uttareṣāṃ prasupta-tanu-vicchinnōdārāṇām Ignorance is the field for the others, whether they be dormant, attenuated, alternating, or fully active.

Because ignorance is the field in which the others grow, the analysis has a single point of attack. Egoism arises because the instrument of seeing is mistaken for the seer; attachment and aversion follow the pleasant and the painful; and the fear of death comes from identifying the self with the mortal body. Remove ignorance, and the other afflictions lose their ground. The means of removing it is named a little later:

Sūtra 2.26

viveka-khyātir aviplavā hānopāyaḥ The means of liberation (hāna-upāya) is unbroken discriminative discernment (viveka-khyāti).

Viveka-khyāti is not intellectual analysis but a direct perception of the difference between the Seer (Puruṣa) and the seen (Prakṛti), the fruit of the truth-bearing insight of the higher samādhis. The eight limbs, to which the sūtras now turn, are presented as the practice that destroys impurity until this discernment shines forth (2.28).

docs.title: 2.5 The Eight Limbs (YS 2.28–3.8)
docs.text:
Yoga Sūtra 2.29

yama-niyamāsana-prāṇāyāma-pratyāhāra-dhāraṇā-dhyāna-samādhayo'ṣṭāv aṅgāni Restraint, observance, posture, breath regulation, sense withdrawal, concentration, meditation, and absorption — these are the eight limbs.

The aṣṭāṅga or eight-limbed yoga is the best-known framework of yogic practice in the Brahmanical tradition, and the one most often taken as normative in modern times. Aṅga means “limb” or “auxiliary”, not “step”: the eight are parts of a single discipline, and the ethical limbs are meant to be kept throughout. Patañjali himself divides them into two groups (YS 3.7–3.8). The first five are “external” (bahiraṅga); the last three are “internal” (antaraṅga), though they are in turn external in relation to seedless samādhi (Figure 2.2). B.K.S. Iyengar’s image of the limbs as the parts of a tree, from the root of yama to the fruit of samādhi, makes the same point for modern readers (Iyengar 1988).

Figure 2.2. The Eight Limbs of Aṣṭāṅga Yoga, from external discipline to inner absorption, with Patañjali’s division into external and internal limbs (YS 3.7–3.8).

docs.title: 2.5.1 Yama: The Restraints
docs.text:
Sūtra 2.30

ahiṃsā-satyāsteya-brahmacaryāparigrahā yamāḥ Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, continence, and non-possessiveness are the restraints.

When the restraints are kept without limitation of birth, place, time or circumstance, Patañjali calls them the “great vow” (mahāvrata, 2.31); Vyāsa’s example of a limited vow is the fisherman who harms only fish. Ahiṃsā comes first, and Vyāsa makes the others depend on it. He defines it as sarvathā sarvadā sarvabhūtānām anabhidrohaḥ, “the absence of injurious intent towards all living beings, in every way, at all times”, and adds that the other restraints and observances are practised to perfect it. Satya is speech and thought that accord with what has been seen, inferred or heard, spoken for the good of others; asteya is the absence of the wish to take what belongs to another; aparigraha is freedom from acquisitiveness.

Brahmacarya originally meant the life of a Vedic student (“one who moves in brahman”, that is, in Vedic study), which required chastity. In the Yoga Sūtra it means sexual continence: Vyāsa defines it as restraint of the sexual organ together with the other senses, and Patañjali was writing for renunciants. The Yoga Upaniṣads (for example the Śāṇḍilya) extend the definition to thought and word, and the Haṭha texts add a physiological reason, the preservation of semen (bindu). For the householder Dharmaśāstra prescribes not celibacy but marital fidelity. Many modern teachers reinterpret brahmacarya as moderation in general; that is a reading for lay practitioners, distinct from the ascetic meaning of the classical sources.

The sūtras then state what each restraint brings when it is firmly established (2.35–2.39): hostility ceases in the yogin’s presence; his words come true; jewels present themselves to him; he gains vigour (vīrya); and he knows the circumstances of his births. These are claims of the tradition; Vyāsa illustrates the first with natural enemies living peacefully near the sage.

docs.title: 2.5.2 Niyama: The Observances
docs.text:
Sūtra 2.32

śauca-saṃtoṣa-tapaḥ-svādhyāyeśvara-praṇidhānāni niyamāḥ Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and surrender to the Lord are the observances.

Where the restraints govern the yogin’s dealings with others, the observances govern his own discipline. Śauca is both external purity, of the body and of food, and internal purity of mind; the first is said to bring disgust for one’s own body and disinclination for contact with others, the second cheerfulness, one-pointedness, mastery of the senses and fitness for the vision of the self (2.40–2.41). Santoṣa, contentment, yields unsurpassed happiness (2.42). Tapas, literally “heat”, is the endurance of the pairs of opposites — heat and cold, hunger and thirst — by which impurity is destroyed and the body and senses are perfected (2.43); the Bhagavad Gītā (17.14–16) distinguishes austerity of body, of speech and of mind. Svādhyāya is, for Vyāsa, the study of texts that lead to liberation or the repetition of Oṃ, and it brings contact with one’s chosen deity (2.44); the modern gloss “study of the self” extends the etymology (sva, “own”) rather than the classical meaning. Īśvara-praṇidhāna is, in Vyāsa’s words, the offering of all actions to the supreme teacher, and through it samādhi is perfected (2.45).

docs.title: 2.5.3 Āsana: The Seat
docs.text:
Sūtra 2.46

sthira-sukham āsanam The posture should be steady and comfortable.

The word āsana literally means “seat” (from ās, “to sit”). In the Yoga Sūtra it is the seated posture in which the yogin remains for long periods of breath-control and meditation. Vyāsa names about a dozen such seats (lotus, hero, auspicious, staff and others); none is a standing or athletic posture (Figure 2.3). Perfection in posture comes from relaxing effort and from absorption in the infinite (2.47), and then the yogin is no longer troubled by the pairs of opposites (2.48). The very different āsana of Haṭha Yoga, and the long history by which “seat” became “posture”, are traced in Chapter 7.

Figure 2.3. Ascetics in yogic and austere postures, including seated lotus-type postures; South Indian gouache, c. 1820 (Musée Guimet, Paris). Photo: Jean-Pierre Dalbéra, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 2.5.4 Prāṇāyāma: Regulation of the Breath
docs.text:
Sūtra 2.49

tasmin sati śvāsa-praśvāsayor gati-vicchedaḥ prāṇāyāmaḥ That (āsana) being established, prāṇāyāma is the interruption of the flow of inhalation and exhalation.

For Patañjali, prāṇāyāma is not a set of breathing exercises but the stopping of breath movement. Sūtra 2.50 distinguishes three forms of this cessation, each to be measured by place, time and number until it becomes “long and subtle”; 2.51 adds a “fourth” that goes beyond the external and internal spheres; and 2.52–2.53 state its fruits: the covering of the inner light wears away and the mind becomes fit for concentration. These sūtras, Vyāsa’s explanation of them and the very different techniques of Haṭha Yoga are discussed in Chapter 8 (Section 8.9).

docs.title: 2.5.5 Pratyāhāra: Withdrawal of the Senses
docs.text:
Sūtra 2.54

sva-viṣayāsaṃprayoge citta-svarūpānukāra ivendriyāṇāṃ pratyāhāraḥ Pratyāhāra is, as it were, the imitation by the senses of the mind’s own nature, when they withdraw from their objects.

Pratyāhāra is the hinge between the external and the internal limbs. Vyāsa compares the senses to bees that rise and settle with their king: when the mind is restrained, the senses follow it. The older image is the tortoise withdrawing its limbs into its shell (Bhagavad Gītā 2.58). From withdrawal comes supreme mastery over the senses (tataḥ paramā vaśyatendriyāṇām, 2.55). It is the limb least discussed in modern posture practice. Some Brahmanical and Haṭha yoga texts, such as the Yogayājñavalkya, give it a technical sense of their own, as the withdrawal of the breath from a series of vital points in the body.

docs.title: 2.5.6 Dhāraṇā, Dhyāna and Samādhi
docs.text:
The third chapter of the sūtras opens by defining the three internal limbs:

Sūtras 3.1–3.3

deśa-bandhaś cittasya dhāraṇā tatra pratyayaikatānatā dhyānam tad evārtha-mātra-nirbhāsaṃ svarūpa-śūnyam iva samādhiḥ Dhāraṇā is the binding of the mind to a single location. Dhyāna is the unbroken flow of cognition towards that object. When that same (meditation) shines forth as the object alone, as if devoid of its own form — that is Samādhi.

In dhāraṇā the mind, withdrawn from external objects, is fixed on a chosen place (deśa). Vyāsa lists places in the body — the navel circle, the lotus of the heart, the light in the head, the tip of the nose and the tip of the tongue — and external objects; later traditions added images of the deity, flames, yantras and mantras. The mind still wanders and must be brought back. When the stream of attention (pratyaya) towards the object becomes continuous (ekatānatā), dhāraṇā has become dhyāna; later commentators compare it to oil poured in an unbroken stream from one vessel to another. The difference between the two is one of degree. (Some later Haṭha texts and Yoga Upaniṣads quantify it, making one unit of dhyāna equal to twelve of dhāraṇā; this is not found in Patañjali or Vyāsa.) In samādhi, finally, the object alone shines forth, and the mind is so absorbed in it that it seems empty of its own form. The texts do not describe this as unconsciousness or blankness: the sūtras compare the purified mind to a flawless jewel that takes on the colour of whatever is placed beside it (1.41), and the higher samādhis are states of heightened clarity in which the truth-bearing insight arises (Section 2.3.6). Meditation as a practice, with its objects and its Buddhist and Jain forms, is the subject of Chapter 9.

docs.title: 2.5.7 Saṃyama
docs.text:
Sūtras 3.4–3.5

trayam ekatra saṃyamaḥ taj-jayāt prajñālokaḥ The three (dhāraṇā, dhyāna, samādhi) together form Saṃyama. By mastery of saṃyama, the light of wisdom dawns.

Practised together on a single object, the three internal limbs are called saṃyama. In Patañjali’s account saṃyama is the yogin’s instrument of knowledge: directed at any object, gross or subtle, it is said to reveal that object completely, and the powers of the third chapter arise from applying it to different objects (Section 2.6).

docs.title: 2.5.8 Other Schemes of Limbs
docs.text:
The eight-limbed system of Patañjali is not the only multi-limbed classification of Yoga in the Bhāratīya tradition. Several other texts present alternative schemes (Table 2.6).

Table 2.6. Comparative Analysis of Multi-Limbed Yoga Systems Limbs Source Period Limbs Listed 6 Maitrī Upaniṣad last centuries BCE (debated) Prāṇāyāma, Pratyāhāra, Dhyāna, Dhāraṇā, Tarka, Samādhi 8 Yoga Sūtras c. 325–425 CE Yama, Niyama, Āsana, Prāṇāyāma, Pratyāhāra, Dhāraṇā, Dhyāna, Samādhi 6 Vivekamārtaṇḍa / Gorakṣaśataka 13th–14th c. CE Āsana, Prāṇāyāma, Pratyāhāra, Dhāraṇā, Dhyāna, Samādhi 4 Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā c. 1450 CE Āsana, Kumbhaka (Prāṇāyāma), Mudrā, Nādānusandhāna (as its four chapters) 15 Aparōkṣānubhūti (attrib. Śaṅkara) medieval Vedāntic reinterpretation: yama, niyama, tyāga, mauna, deśa, kāla, āsana, mūlabandha, dehasāmya, dṛk-sthiti, prāṇasaṃyamana, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, ātmadhyāna, samādhi 7 Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā c. 1700 CE Ṣaṭkarma, Āsana, Mudrā, Pratyāhāra, Prāṇāyāma, Dhyāna, Samādhi

The differences are instructive. The Maitrī Upaniṣad’s six-limbed system, which reappears in the Śaiva Tantras (Chapter 5), omits yama, niyama and āsana. The Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā replaces the ethical limbs with ṣaṭkarma and mudrā, reflecting the Haṭha emphasis on physical purification. The Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā’s four chapters treat āsana, prāṇāyāma, mudrā and nāda as the pillars of practice; the six-limbed Haṭha texts drop yama and niyama altogether, and the Dattātreyayogaśāstra declares that anyone who practises — brahmin, ascetic, Buddhist, Jain, Kāpālika or materialist — will attain success (Mallinson and Singleton 2017). The Advaita Aparōkṣānubhūti turns each limb into an aspect of the knowledge of Brahman (Chapter 4). Patañjali’s eight limbs were thus widely known and constantly reinterpreted: kept in name, they were filled with Tantric, Haṭha or Vedāntic content.

docs.title: 2.6 Pāda III: Vibhūti Pāda — The Chapter on Powers
docs.text: After defining the three internal limbs and saṃyama, the third chapter analyses the transformations of the mind and the extraordinary powers (vibhūtis or siddhis) said to arise from saṃyama.

docs.title: 2.6.1 The Three Transformations of the Mind
docs.text:
Sūtras 3.9–3.12

vyutthāna-nirodha-saṃskārayor abhibhava-prādurbhāvau nirodha-kṣaṇa-cittānvayo nirodha-pariṇāmaḥ tasya praśānta-vāhitā saṃskārāt sarvārthataikāgratayoḥ kṣayodayau cittasya samādhi-pariṇāmaḥ tataḥ punaḥ śāntoditau tulya-pratyayau cittasyaikāgratā-pariṇāmaḥ Nirodha-pariṇāma: The suppression of the rising impressions and the arising of the impressions of restraint. Samādhi-pariṇāma: The decline of all-pointedness and the rise of one-pointedness. Ekāgratā-pariṇāma: When the subsiding and arising cognitions are identical — one-pointed transformation.

The three transformations describe the deepening of practice from the side of the mind: first the impressions of restraint overcome the impressions of outward activity, so that the mind flows calmly; then many-pointedness gives way to one-pointedness; finally the cognition that fades and the cognition that arises are the same. The next sūtra (3.13) extends the analysis to all things, distinguishing change of property (dharma), of temporal character (lakṣaṇa: past, present, future) and of condition (avasthā); Vyāsa’s commentary here engages directly with Sarvāstivāda Buddhist debates on time and change.

docs.title: 2.6.2 The Siddhis
docs.text:
Patañjali describes numerous siddhis that, according to the text, arise from saṃyama on various objects (Table 2.7). These are claims of the tradition, not demonstrated abilities; scholars have noted that the chapter places Yoga within a wider Indian culture of ascetic power (White 2009).

Table 2.7. Selected Siddhis from the Vibhūti Pāda Object of Saṃyama Resultant Siddhi Sūtra Three transformations (of citta) Knowledge of past and future 3.16 Sounds of living beings Understanding of all languages 3.17 Saṃskāras (latent impressions) Knowledge of previous births 3.18 The form of one’s body Invisibility (antardhāna) 3.21 Strengths (bala) The strength of an elephant and the like 3.24 The Sun Knowledge of the worlds (bhuvana-jñāna) 3.26 The Moon Knowledge of the stars 3.27 The pole star (Dhruva) Knowledge of the movement of stars 3.28 The navel centre Knowledge of the body’s arrangement 3.29 The throat pit Cessation of hunger and thirst 3.30 Kūrma Nāḍī Steadiness (sthairya) 3.31 The light in the head Vision of perfected beings (siddhas) 3.32 Pratībha (intuitive flash) Knowledge of everything 3.33

Patañjali himself issues a caution regarding these powers:

Sūtra 3.37

te samādhāv upasargā vyutthāne siddhayaḥ These (siddhis) are obstacles to samādhi, though they are powers in the externalized state.

Whatever their status, the text treats the siddhis as obstacles (upasarga) to the goal of kaivalya; the yogin is to renounce them and continue towards liberation (cf. 3.50).

docs.title: 2.7 Pāda IV: Kaivalya Pāda — The Chapter on Liberation
docs.text: The final chapter addresses the subtlest questions of the system: the sources of the powers, the mechanism of karma, the relation between mind and object, and liberation.

docs.title: 2.7.1 Powers, Karma and Impressions
docs.text:
Powers, the chapter begins, arise from birth, herbs, mantras, austerity or samādhi (janmāuṣadhi-mantra-tapaḥ-samādhi-jāḥ siddhayaḥ, 4.1). It then analyses karma:

Sūtra 4.7–4.8

karmāśuklākṛṣṇaṃ yoginas tri-vidham itareṣām tatas tad-vipākānuguṇānām evābhivyaktir vāsanānām The karma of the yogi is neither white nor black; for others, it is threefold. From that, only those latent impressions corresponding to the fruits of karma manifest.

Every experience leaves a trace (saṃskāra) in the mind, and accumulated impressions form latent tendencies (vāsanā) that shape later perception and action. They survive even across births: there is continuity of memory and impressions “even when separated by birth, place, and time, because they are identical in form” (jāti-deśa-kāla-vyavahitānām apy ānantaryaṃ smṛti-saṃskārayor eka-rūpatvāt, 4.9). Yoga interrupts the cycle of action, impression, tendency and desire by destroying the impressions themselves (Figure 2.4). Modern readers often compare this with the psychology of habit and implicit memory; the comparison is illuminating, but Patañjali should not be read as anticipating modern psychology.

Figure 2.4. The Saṃskāra Cycle and How Yoga Breaks It: Actions create impressions, which form tendencies, which generate desires, which motivate further actions. Yoga interrupts this cycle through abhyāsa and vairāgya.

docs.title: 2.7.2 The Cloud of Dharma and Liberation
docs.text:
The last stage before liberation is called the “cloud of dharma”:

Yoga Sūtra 4.29

prasaṃkhyāne'py akusīdasya sarvathā viveka-khyāter dharma-meghaḥ samādhiḥ For one who has no interest even in the highest meditation, and who possesses constant discriminative discernment, there arises the samādhi known as “the Cloud of Dharma.”

From it, the sūtras continue, comes the cessation of the afflictions and of karma (4.30). The work ends with a definition of liberation:

Sūtra 4.34 — The Concluding Sūtra

puruṣārtha-śūnyānāṃ guṇānāṃ pratiprasavaḥ kaivalyaṃ svarūpa-pratiṣṭhā vā citi-śaktir iti Kaivalya is the counter-involution of the guṇas, which are devoid of purpose for the Puruṣa; or it is the establishment of the power of consciousness (citi-śakti) in its own nature.

When discriminative knowledge is firmly established, nature has done all it can for the Puruṣa: its constituents resolve back into their source (pratiprasava), and consciousness stands alone in its own nature. “Isolation” (kaivalya) is the Sāṃkhya-Yoga name for this freedom.

docs.title: 2.8 The Commentarial Tradition
docs.text:
The Yoga Sūtras have inspired a commentarial tradition spanning some fifteen centuries (Table 2.8), surveyed work by work in the Yoga volume of the Encyclopedia of Indian Philosophies (Larson and Bhattacharya 2008). The commentaries are not only aids to reading the sūtras; they are the record of how Patañjali’s yoga was understood, argued over and adapted to the dominant philosophies of each period, and most of what is now taught as “the meaning” of a sūtra comes from one of them.

Table 2.8. Major Commentaries on the Yoga Sūtras Commentary Author Period Significance Yoga Bhāṣya Vyāsa c. 4th–5th c. Earliest; foundational; inseparable from the Sūtras Vivaraṇa attributed to Śaṅkara 8th c. or later (disputed) Sub-commentary on the Bhāṣya; authorship debated Tattvavaiśāradī Vācaspati Miśra c. 950 Sub-commentary on Vyāsa’s Bhāṣya Rājamārtaṇḍa Bhoja of Dhārā c. 1040 Royal commentary on the sūtras alone Yoga Vārttika Vijñānabhikṣu after c. 1550 Reconciles Yoga with Vedānta Maṇiprabhā Rāmānanda Sarasvatī 16th–17th c. Advaitic interpretation Yogasiddhāntacandrikā Nārāyaṇatīrtha probably 17th c. Places other yogas, including Haṭha and bhakti, within the eight limbs Bhāsvatī Hariharānanda Āraṇya 20th c. Modern Sāṃkhya-Yoga sub-commentary

docs.title: 2.8.1 One Book or Two? The Sūtras and the Bhāṣya
docs.text:
Section 2.1 noted Philipp Maas’s argument that the sūtras and the Bhāṣya were composed and transmitted as one work. The commentarial tradition is itself part of the evidence. The chapter colophons of the printed text call the whole “Patañjali’s treatise on yoga, the exposition of Sāṃkhya” (pātañjale sāṃkhyapravacane yogaśāstre); the further words “in the commentary of the venerable Vyāsa” that follow in the printed colophons come, Maas notes, from comparatively recent paper manuscripts. Al-Bīrūnī, around 1030, took the work to be a single book of Patañjali consisting of text and explanation (Section 2.8.5). King Bhoja of Mālava, who wrote his own commentary on the sūtras alone around 1040, compares himself in a benedictory verse to the serpent-king, that is, to Patañjali in his mythical form as Śeṣa, who removed the impurities of speech, mind and body by writing on grammar, yoga and medicine — the same triple legacy that the later invocation at the head of this chapter celebrates. The attribution of the Bhāṣya to Vyāsa appears in the introductory verses of Vācaspati Miśra’s sub-commentary of about 950, although Vācaspati’s works are not consistent on the point, and the oldest unambiguous statement that sūtra and Bhāṣya had different authors that Maas could find is in Mādhava’s fourteenth-century survey of the systems, the Sarvadarśanasaṁgraha. The modern habit of speaking of “Patañjali and Vyāsa” as two authors therefore rests on a late and uncertain tradition (Maas 2013).

The question matters for interpretation. If the prose is Patañjali’s own, it is the author’s explanation of his sūtras, not the first of many possible readings, and the frequent modern practice of reading the sūtras without the Bhāṣya, or against it, loses its main justification. Many scholars still prefer to leave authorship open, but there is broad agreement that the sūtras cannot be understood apart from the Bhāṣya, and that the later commentators, from the Vivaraṇa onwards, comment on the two together.

docs.title: 2.8.2 The Vivaraṇa and the Śaṅkara Question
docs.text:
In 1952 the Government Oriental Manuscripts Library in Madras published, from South Indian manuscripts, a commentary on the sūtras and Bhāṣya called the Pātañjalayogaśāstravivaraṇa. Its chapter colophons name its author with the formal title used for Śaṅkara, the Advaita Vedāntin (c. 700–750 CE; the traditional date, 788–820, rests on later sources and long served as the conventional date in scholarship): pupil of Govinda, wandering ascetic of the highest order, Śaṅkarabhagavat. The editors accepted the attribution, and for more than half a century the Vivaraṇa has been at the centre of a debate.

Paul Hacker had noticed features of Śaṅkara’s Vedānta that suggested an early familiarity with Yoga, and in 1968 he proposed that Śaṅkara had been a follower of Yoga in his youth before he became an Advaitin, a hypothesis that presupposed rather than proved the identity of the two authors. Trevor Leggett translated the whole work as Śaṅkara’s (1990). Wilhelm Halbfass pointed to striking parallels between arguments in the Vivaraṇa and in Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, but also showed that Śaṅkara’s attitude to Sāṃkhya metaphysics and to Yoga as a path to liberation, as stated in his major works, is very hard to reconcile with the Vivaraṇa’s commitment to Patañjali. T. S. Rukmani, who also translated the work, argued that it was much later, between the eleventh and fourteenth centuries, and that it knew Vācaspati’s commentary; Kengo Harimoto and Maas have answered that the passages she cited do not show this (Maas 2013).

Whoever its author was, the Vivaraṇa matters. The latest author it clearly refers to is the Mīmāṃsā philosopher Kumārila (7th century); the text of the Bhāṣya on which it comments preserves old readings lost from most manuscripts; and it explains many difficult passages on which Vācaspati is silent. It is therefore probably the oldest surviving commentary on the Pātañjalayogaśāstra, and it records debates between Sāṃkhya-Yoga and the Buddhist and Brahmanical schools of the second half of the first millennium. Its treatment of Īśvara is notable: in commenting on YS 1.23–1.28 its author goes to great lengths to establish the existence of God by reasoning. Harimoto has edited that section critically (2014), and a full critical edition is still awaited (Harimoto 2014). The question of authorship can only be settled, as Maas puts it, by systematic comparison of style once reliable editions of both the Vivaraṇa and Śaṅkara’s works exist.

docs.title: 2.8.3 Vācaspati Miśra and King Bhoja
docs.text:
Vācaspati Miśra of Mithilā (mid-10th century) wrote standard commentaries on almost every Brahmanical system: on Nyāya, on Sāṃkhya (the Tattvakaumudī on the Sāṃkhyakārikā), on Mīmāṃsā, and on Śaṅkara’s Brahmasūtrabhāṣya (the Bhāmatī). His Tattvavaiśāradī on the Yoga Bhāṣya expounds the text from inside the system, as a Sāṃkhya-Yoga śāstra among others, and it became the most widely copied and printed of the sub-commentaries; much of the standard modern explanation of the Yoga Sūtras, such as the systematic classification of the stages of samādhi, reaches modern readers through it. It was printed with the Bhāṣya in Calcutta in 1874 and in the Ānandāśrama edition of 1904, and James Haughton Woods’s English translation of 1914 rendered the sūtras, the Bhāṣya and Vācaspati’s commentary together (Maas 2013; Woods 1914).

Bhoja, the Paramāra king of Dhārā in Mālava (r. c. 1010–1055), a celebrated patron and the author of works on poetics, architecture and medicine, wrote the Rājamārtaṇḍa (also called the Bhojavṛtti) around 1040. Unlike Vācaspati he comments on the sūtras alone, briefly and in his own words, and in his introductory verses he criticises earlier commentators for passing over what is difficult and dwelling at length on what is plain. Its brevity made it popular: the early English translations, James Ballantyne’s (1852) and Rājendralāl Mitra’s Yoga Aphorisms of Patanjali (1883), both followed Bhoja (Maas 2013; White 2014).

docs.title: 2.8.4 Vijñānabhikṣu and the Late Commentators
docs.text:
The most ambitious later commentator was Vijñānabhikṣu, who worked in North India some time after 1550. His Yogavārttika, a long sub-commentary on the Bhāṣya, his digest the Yogasārasaṁgraha, and his works on Sāṃkhya and on the Brahmasūtra together argue that Sāṃkhya, Yoga and Vedānta, rightly understood, teach a single doctrine, in which the selves are both different from and non-different from Brahman (a form of bhedābheda that he called “non-separation”, avibhāga). He criticised Śaṅkara’s Advaita as a “crypto-Buddhist” doctrine of illusion, and he read Patañjali’s Īśvara in a strongly theistic way. Andrew Nicholson has argued that this project of reading the orthodox systems as one philosophy, of which Vijñānabhikṣu was an important early representative, prepared the ground for the modern presentation of the orthodox systems as branches of a single “Hindu philosophy” (Nicholson 2010). Vijñānabhikṣu is also, on several points, a bold interpreter rather than a faithful one: Maas shows, for example, that his reading of YS 2.27 contradicts the explanation the Bhāṣya itself gives in the next sentence (Maas 2013).

After him the commentaries multiply. Rāmānanda Sarasvatī’s Maṇiprabhā and the grammarian Nāgeśabhaṭṭa’s Vṛtti (early 18th century) are short explanations of the sūtras; Bhāvāgaṇeśa, a pupil of Vijñānabhikṣu, condensed his teacher’s views; and Nārāyaṇatīrtha, who commented on the sūtras twice, in the Yogasiddhāntacandrikā and the shorter Sūtrārthabodhinī, presented the sūtras as a framework into which the other recognised yogas, including Haṭha Yoga and the yoga of devotion, could be fitted. That last move shows how far the tradition had travelled. By the early modern period the Yoga Sūtra was being read alongside the Haṭha texts and the Bhāgavata, and Haṭha authors in turn borrowed Patañjali’s eight limbs (Chapter 7). In the nineteenth century the Bhāṣya with Vācaspati’s and Bhoja’s commentaries was printed in Calcutta, Benares and Poona, and these printed editions, rather than living teaching lineages, became the basis of the European translations and of Vivekānanda’s Rāja Yoga (1896). The last major commentary in the classical manner is the Bhāsvatī of Hariharānanda Āraṇya (1869–1947), the founder of the Kāpil Maṭh at Madhupur in Jharkhand, which continues to teach Sāṃkhya-Yoga as a monastic tradition.

docs.title: 2.8.5 The Yoga Sūtra in Arabic: al-Bīrūnī’s Kitāb Pātanjal
docs.text:
All the commentaries in Table 2.8 were written in Sanskrit. The earliest known rendering of the Yoga Sūtra into another language was made in Arabic in the early eleventh century by Abū Rayḥān al-Bīrūnī (973–after 1050), the Central Asian scholar who came to north-western India in the train of Maḥmūd of Ghazna, learned Sanskrit from Indian pandits, and wrote the most searching account of Indian learning produced by any outsider before modern times (his work on Indian mathematics and astronomy is discussed in Volume 11, Gaṇita, and Volume 12, Khagola Jyotiṣa). In the preface to that survey, the Taḥqīq mā li-l-Hind (“Inquiry into what belongs to India”, c. 1030), he says that he had already translated two Indian books into Arabic, one on the origin and nature of created things, that is, a Sāṃkhya work, and one by Patañjali on the release of the soul from its bondage to the body. The second, the Kitāb Pātanjal, survives in a single manuscript in Istanbul, which was identified and published by Hellmut Ritter only in 1956; Shlomo Pines and Tuvia Gelblum later translated it into English, chapter by chapter, in a series of articles beginning in 1966 (Pines and Gelblum 1966).

The Kitāb Pātanjal is not a word-for-word translation. Al-Bīrūnī recast the sūtras, together with explanations drawn from a commentary, as a dialogue in which an ascetic asks questions and a sage answers them, and he rephrased Indian technical terms in the vocabulary of Arabic philosophy so that a Muslim reader could follow the argument. The explanations do not simply reproduce Vyāsa’s Bhāṣya, and which commentary he used, or whether he combined several, is still debated. His treatment of Īśvara (YS 1.23–1.29) leans towards a monotheistic reading, in line with his general view, stated in the Taḥqīq, that the learned among the Hindus believed in one God, while the polytheism he saw around him belonged to the common people. In the same work he quotes Patañjali repeatedly beside the Bhagavad Gītā and Sāṃkhya, and compares the yogic path to release with the teachings of the Sufis (White 2014).

The translation matters to the history of Yoga in two ways. First, it is the earliest witness to the text from outside the Sanskrit commentarial tradition, and it shows that in the early eleventh century Patañjali’s work was regarded in India as a leading authority on liberation — which supports the view that any eclipse of the text came later (Section 2.10). Secondly, its later influence was slight: there is little evidence that the Kitāb Pātanjal circulated widely in the Islamic world. When Muslims in India took a sustained interest in yoga in the following centuries, they met it as the practice of living Nāth and other yogis, through texts such as the Amṛtakuṇḍa, rather than through Patañjali (Chapter 7, Section 7.17).

docs.title: 2.8.6 Patañjali in Java: the Dharma Pātañjala
docs.text: A second witness from outside the Sanskrit commentaries comes from Indonesia. Among the Old Javanese and Sanskrit scriptures of the Śaiva religion of pre-Islamic Java is a text called the Dharma Pātañjala, preserved in a single fifteenth-century palm-leaf manuscript from West Java. Its first part sets out a Śaiva theology close to the Śaiva Siddhānta; its long second part is a yoga section that follows the first three chapters of the Yoga Sūtra and explains them in Old Javanese prose. Andrea Acri, who edited and translated the text, has shown that this prose often resembles the Bhāṣya but departs from it in places, and that some of its doctrinal details agree with other commentaries and with al-Bīrūnī’s Arabic version. Where most Old Javanese works teach the six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga) of the Śaiva scriptures, the Dharma Pātañjala keeps Patañjali’s eight limbs, recast within a Śaiva framework (Acri 2011). Like the Kitāb Pātanjal, it shows that Patañjali’s work travelled with its explanations and was read by people who understood it in their own theological terms; unlike al-Bīrūnī’s translation, it was the scripture of a living religious community.

docs.title: 2.9 Citta: Patañjali’s Theory of Mind
docs.text:
Citta is not simply “mind” in the modern sense but the whole field of mental activity through which Puruṣa (pure awareness) experiences the world. Patañjali does not himself define it in these terms. The commentators equate it with the Sāṃkhya “inner instrument” (antaḥkaraṇa), which later Vedāntic works analyse into three or four functions: manas, the sensory-motor mind that receives impressions and co-ordinates action; buddhi, the intellect that determines and discriminates; and ahaṃkāra, the “I-maker” that appropriates experience as one’s own. Vyāsa’s Bhāṣya also classifies the states of citta by the predominance of the three guṇas (Table 2.9).

Table 2.9. The Five States (Bhūmis) of Citta According to Vyāsa State Sanskrit Dominant Guṇa Characteristics Scattered Kṣipta Rajas Restless; agitated; unable to concentrate Dull Mūḍha Tamas Heavy; lethargic; prone to sleep and delusion Oscillating Vikṣipta Rajas-Sattva Occasionally focused but easily distracted One-pointed Ekāgra Sattva Concentrated; capable of sustained attention Restrained Niruddha Sattva (transcended) All vṛttis ceased; Yoga is achieved

Vyāsa adds that the first three states are not yoga. Even the oscillating mind, with its moments of focus, is unstable; yoga properly begins with the one-pointed mind and is complete in the restrained one.

docs.title: 2.9.1 Patañjali and Modern Psychology
docs.text:
The Yoga Sūtras contain a detailed psychology of attention, memory and affliction (Indian theories of mind are treated more fully in Volume 22, Manas and Śikṣā), and modern readers often set it beside clinical psychology. Patañjali’s analysis of the kleśas, for example, is read today as an account of the roots of psychological suffering, with ignorance as cognitive distortion, egoism as a rigid self-image and clinging to life as existential anxiety. Such comparisons are heuristic. Unlike modern clinical psychology, which is oriented to health and adaptation, Patañjali’s system begins from a soteriological goal and analyses the mind in terms of what obstructs it (Table 2.10).

Table 2.10. Comparative Framework: Patañjali and Modern Psychology Aspect Patañjali’s System Modern Western Psychology Goal Liberation of consciousness (kaivalya) Adaptation, well-being, symptom reduction Model of mind Citta as instrument of Puruṣa; mind is not the self Mind as emergent property of brain; self is mental construct Unconscious Saṃskāras and vāsanās: latent impressions accumulated across lifetimes Unconscious drives (Freud); implicit memory (cognitive science) Suffering Kleśas: five root afflictions rooted in ignorance Psychological disorders rooted in maladaptive patterns Method Systematic sādhana: ethical conduct, posture, breath, meditation Talk therapy, pharmacology, behavioural modification Evidence First-person experiential verification through samādhi Third-person empirical measurement

docs.title: 2.10 The Fortunes of the Yoga Sūtra
docs.text:
How much the Yoga Sūtra mattered in India between the commentators and the moderns is debated. David Gordon White has argued that the text was little read between roughly the twelfth and the nineteenth centuries, and that it owes its present status as “the” scripture of Yoga largely to colonial-era Indologists, to Vivekānanda’s Rāja Yoga (1896) and to later modern teachers (White 2014). The second half of the thesis is widely accepted: the nineteenth-century printed editions and translations, not living teaching lineages, made the sūtras the canonical text of modern yoga. The first half is contested. The commentaries of Vijñānabhikṣu, Rāmānanda Sarasvatī, Nārāyaṇatīrtha and Nāgeśa (Section 2.8.4) show that the sūtras continued to be studied and argued over by Sanskrit scholars in the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries; Haṭha and Vedānta authors borrowed their eight limbs; and Advaitins such as Vidyāraṇya quoted them as an authority on stilling the mind (Chapter 4). What seems to have declined in the second millennium is not scholarly attention but the text’s place as a guide to practice, which passed largely to the Haṭha and Tantric manuals (Maas 2013; Larson and Bhattacharya 2008).

The sūtras’ central claims — about samādhi, the separateness of puruṣa and the attainment of kaivalya — are metaphysical and experiential claims that lie beyond the reach of empirical investigation; the tradition grounds them in the testimony of accomplished practitioners. Their analysis of attention and of the afflictions invites comparison with modern research on attention and mindfulness, but such comparisons are analogies rather than confirmations.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Karma Yoga and Bhakti Yoga
docs.text:
Bhagavad Gītā 3.19

tasmād asaktaḥ satataṃ kāryaṃ karma samācara asakto hy ācaran karma param āpnoti pūruṣaḥ Therefore, always perform action that must be done, without attachment. For by performing action without attachment, one attains the Supreme.

Part A: Karma Yoga — The Path of Selfless Action

docs.title: 3.1 The Meaning of Karma Yoga
docs.text:
Karma Yoga is the discipline of acting without attachment to results (phala): one performs one’s duties (svadharma) and offers the action to God, so that ordinary activity becomes a means of liberation rather than a cause of bondage. The word karma, from the root kṛ (“to do”), means action and, by extension, ritual action and the consequences of action. The idea answered a problem that the renunciant traditions had made acute. If action binds the self to rebirth, as Buddhists, Jains and the Upaniṣadic renouncers taught, must the seeker of liberation abandon the world? The Gītā’s answer is that bondage comes not from action but from desire for its fruits.

Definition: Karma Yoga

Karma Yoga is the discipline of performing all actions as an offering to the Divine, without attachment to their fruits, maintaining equanimity in success and failure, and thereby purifying the mind and attaining liberation through action itself.

docs.title: 3.2 The Bhagavad Gītā and Karma Yoga
docs.text: The Bhagavad Gītā, part of the Bhīṣma Parva of the Mahābhārata and probably composed between the 2nd century BCE and the 2nd century CE (Malinar 2007), is the foremost scripture of Karma Yoga. Kṛṣṇa’s teaching to Arjuna on the battlefield of Kurukṣetra is the classic exposition of selfless action in Indian thought, and every major school of Vedānta commented on it; Śaṅkara’s commentary, the oldest to survive, is available in Gambhirananda’s translation (Śaṅkarācārya 1997).

docs.title: 3.2.1 The Dilemma of Arjuna
docs.text:
The Gītā opens with Arjuna’s crisis: faced with the prospect of fighting against his own kinsmen, teachers, and elders, the great warrior is overwhelmed with grief and confusion. He throws down his bow and declares that he will not fight. It is in response to this existential crisis that Kṛṣṇa unfolds the teaching of Karma Yoga (Figure 3.1).

Figure 3.1. Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna in the chariot, with Hanumān on the banner (Indian miniature painting, British Museum). Painting: unknown artist, British Museum; public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 3.2.2 Key Teachings on Karma Yoga
docs.text:
Gītā 2.47 — The Cardinal Verse of Karma Yoga

karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadā cana mā karma-phala-hetur bhūr mā te saṅgo'stv akarmaṇi Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits. Let not the fruit of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction.

This is perhaps the most quoted verse of the Gītā. It is built of negations: the agent has no claim to the fruits, must not let them be his motive, and must not, for all that, fall back on inaction. The next verse defines yoga itself in these terms, as equanimity:

Gītā 2.48 — Yoga as Equanimity

yoga-sthaḥ kuru karmāṇi saṅgaṃ tyaktvā dhanaṃjaya siddhy-asiddhyoḥ samo bhūtvā samatvaṃ yoga ucyate Established in Yoga, perform actions, O Dhanañjaya, abandoning attachment, remaining equal in success and failure. This equanimity is called Yoga.

Gītā 3.9 — Action as Sacrifice

yajñārthāt karmaṇo'nyatra loko'yaṃ karma-bandhanaḥ tad-arthaṃ karma kaunteya mukta-saṅgaḥ samācara The world is bound by actions other than those performed as sacrifice. Therefore, O son of Kuntī, perform action for that purpose, free from attachment.

docs.title: 3.2.3 Niṣkāma Karma: Desireless Action
docs.text: The later tradition summed up this teaching as niṣkāma karma, action without desire for personal gain, and contrasted it with sakāma karma, action driven by desire. The first is done as duty, service or an offering to God; its agent regards himself as an instrument rather than the doer and stays equal in success and failure; and it leads to liberation. The second is done for reward, binds its agent to the outcome, breeds anxiety and leads to further rebirth. The Gītā’s own image for desireless action is sacrifice: action done as an offering does not bind.

docs.title: 3.2.4 Lokasaṃgraha: Action for the Welfare of the World
docs.text:
Kṛṣṇa introduces another powerful motivation for action: lokasaṃgraha — action performed for the welfare and cohesion of the world:

Gītā 3.20–3.21

karmaṇaiva hi saṃsiddhim āsthitā janakādayaḥ loka-saṃgraham evāpi saṃpaśyan kartum arhasi yad yad ācarati śreṣṭhas tat tad evetaro janaḥ sa yat pramāṇaṃ kurute lokas tad anuvartate By action alone, Janaka and others attained perfection. You should act with a view to the welfare of the world. Whatever a great person does, common people follow. Whatever standard he sets, the world follows.

docs.title: 3.3 The Philosophy of Action and Non-Action
docs.text:
The Gītā contains a subtle and profound analysis of the nature of action:

Gītā 4.18

karmaṇy akarma yaḥ paśyed akarmaṇi ca karma yaḥ sa buddhimān manuṣyeṣu sa yuktaḥ kṛtsna-karma-kṛt One who sees inaction in action and action in inaction — that person is wise among human beings, a yogi, a doer of all actions.

The commentators read this verse in the light of the Gītā’s Sāṃkhya: the self is never an agent (akartā), all action belongs to nature (prakṛti) and its constituents, and the wise person acts in the world while knowing that he does not act. For Śaṅkara the verse shows why action can never itself be the means of liberation (Chapter 4); for theistic commentators it shows how action offered to God ceases to bind.

Gītā 5.8–5.9

naiva kiṃ cit karomīti yukto manyeta tattva-vit paśyañ śṛṇvan spṛśañ jighrann aśnan gacchan svapañ śvasan pralapan visṛjan gṛhṇann unmiṣan nimiṣann api indriyāṇīndriyārtheṣu vartanta iti dhārayan The one who knows the truth thinks “I do nothing at all” — while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, breathing, speaking, releasing, grasping, opening and closing the eyes — knowing that it is only the senses interacting with their objects.

docs.title: 3.4 Karma, Duty and the Gītā’s Social Setting
docs.text: Karma Yoga presupposes the doctrine of karma, which is treated with the darśanas in Volume 3, Darśana Darpaṇa. Later Vedāntic texts divide karma into three stores: the karma accumulated in past lives (sañcita); the portion of it that has begun to bear fruit in the present body (prārabdha); and the karma now being made, which will bear fruit in future (āgāmin, also called kriyamāṇa, “what is being done”). Advaita texts such as the Vivekacūḍāmaṇi teach that knowledge burns the first and the third, while the second must be exhausted by experience even by the liberated person (Chapter 4). In these terms the Karma Yogin’s desireless action adds nothing to the future store, and his equanimity lets the fructifying karma run out without new entanglement. The Gītā itself analyses every action into five factors — the body as its seat, the agent, the various instruments, the various efforts and, fifth, the unseen or divine (daiva) (18.14) — so that the self, which is none of these, is not the doer.

docs.title: 3.4.1 Svadharma: One’s Own Duty
docs.text:
Central to the Gītā’s teaching on action is svadharma, the duty that falls to a person by nature (svabhāva) and station:

Gītā 3.35

śreyān sva-dharmo viguṇaḥ para-dharmāt sv-anuṣṭhitāt sva-dharme nidhanaṃ śreyaḥ para-dharmo bhayāvahaḥ Better is one’s own dharma, though imperfectly performed, than the dharma of another well performed. Death in one’s own dharma is better; the dharma of another is fraught with danger.

In the Gītā’s own context, svadharma is the duty of one’s varṇa: Arjuna must fight because he is a kṣatriya, and the text states that the four varṇas were created by Kṛṣṇa according to quality and action (4.13) and lists the duties proper to each (18.41–48). This aspect of the text has been read in sharply different ways. B.R. Ambedkar saw the Gītā as a defence of the caste order and of brahmanical orthodoxy (Ambedkar 1987). Modern Hindu interpreters such as Tilak, Aurobindo and Gandhi instead read svadharma as one’s individual nature and vocation (Section 3.13), and many devotional traditions stressed the verse that opens the highest goal to women, vaiśyas and śūdras who take refuge in Kṛṣṇa (9.32). The same verse contains the compound pāpayonayaḥ, “of sinful birth”. On one construal, which many translators follow, it describes the women, vaiśyas and śūdras; on another, it names a further group, “even those of sinful birth”, alongside them (Malinar 2007). Either way, the verse opens the path while reflecting the hierarchy it addressed, and a reader should recognise both the social setting of the teaching and the universalising readings it has inspired. Read in the second way, the Karma Yogin is called to perform the duties that fall to him or her — as parent, teacher, farmer, artist or official — with skill and without selfish motive.

Part B: Bhakti Yoga — The Path of Divine Love

docs.title: 3.5 The Meaning of Bhakti
docs.text:
Bhakti is derived from the Sanskrit root bhaj, “to share in”, “to partake”, and hence “to serve, worship, love”. Bhakti Yoga is the discipline of devotion to a personal God, cultivated until it becomes complete surrender. In the Gītā it is one of the forms that yoga takes; in the later devotional traditions the relation was often reversed, and yoga became one of the forms, or one of the rivals, of devotion.

Nārada Bhakti Sūtra 2

sā tv asmin para-prema-rūpā That (Bhakti) is of the nature of supreme love for God.

Nārada Bhakti Sūtra 3–4

amṛta-svarūpā ca yal labdhvā pumān siddho bhavaty amṛto bhavati tṛpto bhavati It is of the nature of immortal bliss. Having obtained it, a person becomes perfected, immortal, and completely satisfied.

docs.title: 3.6 Bhakti in the Bhagavad Gītā
docs.text:
The Bhagavad Gītā, particularly Chapters 9 and 12, contains some of the most moving teachings on Bhakti Yoga:

Gītā 9.26

patraṃ puṣpaṃ phalaṃ toyaṃ yo me bhaktyā prayacchati tad ahaṃ bhakty-upahṛtam aśnāmi prayatātmanaḥ Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water — that offering of devotion from the pure-hearted I accept.

Gītā 9.34

man-manā bhava mad-bhakto mad-yājī māṃ namaskuru mām evaiṣyasi yuktvaivam ātmānaṃ mat-parāyaṇaḥ Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, bow to Me. Absorbed in Me, with Me as your supreme goal, you shall come to Me.

Gītā 18.65–18.66 — The Supreme Secret

man-manā bhava mad-bhakto mad-yājī māṃ namaskuru mām evaiṣyasi satyaṃ te pratijāne priyo'si me sarva-dharmān parityajya mām ekaṃ śaraṇaṃ vraja ahaṃ tvāṃ sarva-pāpebhyo mokṣayiṣyāmi mā śucaḥ Fix your mind on Me, be My devotee, sacrifice to Me, bow to Me. Truly I promise you: you are dear to Me. Abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in Me alone. I shall liberate you from all sins; do not grieve.

docs.title: 3.7 The Navadhā Bhakti: Nine Forms of Devotion
docs.text:
The Bhāgavata Purāṇa (c. 9th–10th century CE) presents the celebrated nine-fold path of devotion (navadhā bhakti), spoken by the child-devotee Prahlāda to his father Hiraṇyakaśipu (Table 3.1):

Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.5.23

śravaṇaṃ kīrtanaṃ viṣṇoḥ smaraṇaṃ pāda-sevanam arcanaṃ vandanaṃ dāsyaṃ sakhyam ātma-nivedanam Hearing, chanting, remembering, serving the feet, worshipping, saluting, servitude, friendship, and complete self-surrender — these are the nine forms of Bhakti to Lord Viṣṇu.

Table 3.1. The Nine Forms of Bhakti (Navadhā Bhakti), with the exemplars named in later tradition No. Form English Description Exemplar 1 Śravaṇa Hearing Listening to the Lord’s name, glories, and deeds Parīkṣit 2 Kīrtana Chanting Singing the praises and names of the Lord Śuka 3 Smaraṇa Remembering Constant remembrance of the Lord Prahlāda 4 Pāda-sevana Serving the feet Humble service to the Lord’s lotus feet Lakṣmī 5 Arcana Worship Ritual worship with offerings Pṛthu 6 Vandana Salutation Prostration and prayer Akrūra 7 Dāsya Servitude Regarding oneself as the Lord’s servant Hanumān 8 Sakhya Friendship Relating to the Lord as an intimate friend Arjuna 9 Ātma-nivedana Self-surrender Complete offering of oneself to the Lord Bali

docs.title: 3.8 The Nārada Bhakti Sūtra
docs.text: The Nārada Bhakti Sūtra is a celebrated treatise on the philosophy and practice of Bhakti, attributed to the celestial sage Nārada. It consists of 84 aphorisms that define, describe, and extol the path of divine love (Nārada 1943). Its date is uncertain; it draws on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa and is generally regarded as a medieval work.

docs.title: 3.8.1 Characteristics of Supreme Bhakti
docs.text:
Nārada Bhakti Sūtra 6–7

yaj jñātvā matto bhavati stabdho bhavaty ātmārāmo bhavati sā na kāmay­amānā nirodha-rūpat­vāt Having known which, one becomes intoxicated, stunned, and delights in the Self. It (Bhakti) is not of the nature of desire, being of the nature of cessation (of all desires).

docs.title: 3.8.2 Parā and Aparā Bhakti
docs.text: The devotional treatises distinguish a lower, preparatory devotion (aparā or gauṇī bhakti) from the supreme devotion (parā bhakti) of the Nārada Sūtra’s definition. The first is mixed with desire and expressed through ritual, vows and pilgrimage; it seeks boons and protection and fluctuates with circumstance. The second is love for its own sake, steady and spontaneous; the tradition’s examples are the cowherd women (gopīs) of Vṛndāvana and, among the saints, Mīrābāī.

docs.title: 3.9 The Philosophy of Divine Love in Bhakti Yoga
3.9.1 Rasa Theory and Bhakti
docs.text:
The Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava tradition, following Rūpa Gosvāmī’s Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu, developed an elaborate classification of devotional emotions (rasas) that the devotee can experience in relation to the Divine (Table 3.2).

Table 3.2. The Five Primary Rasas (Devotional Relationships) in Bhakti Rasa Relationship Exemplar Character Śānta Peaceful contemplation Sanatkumāras Tranquil awareness of God’s presence Dāsya Servitude Hanumān Devoted, selfless service to the Lord Sakhya Friendship Arjuna; Sudāmā Intimate, playful companionship Vātsalya Parental love Yaśodā; Nanda Protective, nurturing affection Mādhurya Conjugal love Rādhā; Gopīs Intense, all-consuming divine love

Each rasa represents a distinct mode of relating to the Divine, and the tradition holds that the devotee is naturally drawn to the rasa that corresponds to their innermost spiritual temperament. The mādhurya rasa (the mood of conjugal love) is considered the highest, as exemplified by the Gopīs of Vṛndāvana, whose love for Kṛṣṇa was so intense that it transcended all worldly attachments.

docs.title: 3.9.2 The Concept of Prapatti (Śaraṇāgati): Total Surrender
docs.text:
The highest expression of Bhakti is prapatti or śaraṇāgati — total, unconditional surrender to the Divine. The Śrī Vaiṣṇava tradition, drawing on the Pāñcarātra Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā and Lakṣmī Tantra and as systematised by Vedānta Deśika (14th century), describes six components of śaraṇāgati (Table 3.3).

Table 3.3. The Six Components of Śaraṇāgati (Prapatti) Component Sanskrit Description Resolve to please Ānukūlya Saṃkalpa Determination to do what is pleasing to the Lord Avoidance of displeasure Prātikūlya Varjanam Avoidance of what is displeasing to the Lord Faith in protection Mahāviśvāsa Firm faith that the Lord will protect Prayer for protection Goptṛtva Varaṇam Active supplication for the Lord’s protection Surrender of self Ātma-nikṣepa Placing oneself entirely in the Lord’s hands Humility Kārpaṇya Awareness of one’s own helplessness

Stotraratna of Yāmuna (Āḷavantār), 22

na dharma-niṣṭho'smi na cātma-vedī na bhaktimāṃs tvac-caraṇāravinde ak­iñcano'nanya-gatiḥ śaraṇya tvat-pāda-mūlaṃ śaraṇaṃ prapadye I am not established in dharma, nor do I know the Self. I have no devotion to Your lotus feet. Helpless and with no other refuge, O Lord, I surrender at Your feet.

docs.title: 3.10 Devotion and Yoga in the Bhakti Movements
docs.text:
From the sixth century onwards devotional poetry in the regional languages transformed Indian religion: the Tamil Āḻvārs and Nāyaṉārs (6th–9th centuries), the Vīraśaiva vacana poets of twelfth-century Karnataka, the Vārkārīs of Maharashtra from Jñāneśvar and Nāmdev to Tukārām, the Sants of North India such as Kabīr and Ravidās, the Kṛṣṇa devotion of Sūrdās, Mīrābāī and Caitanya, and Śaṅkaradeva in Assam. Their literature is treated in Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā; what matters here is how they related to yoga.

Three attitudes can be distinguished. The first subordinated yoga to devotion. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa keeps the eight limbs but turns meditation into loving remembrance, and in its eleventh book Kṛṣṇa calls the yogic powers distractions (Chapter 1, Section 1.5.3); the Gauḍīya theologians went further and held that the pure devotee does not even desire liberation. The second absorbed yoga into devotion. Jñāneśvar (13th century), who traced his lineage to the Nāth gurus, wrote a famous account of kuṇḍalinī in Marathi inside his commentary on the Gītā (Chapter 7, Section 7.16), and the Sants of North India, like the Sikh Gurus, used the vocabulary of Nāth yoga — the unstruck sound, the tenth door, the state of natural ease (sahaj) — for the fruits of devotion to the divine name. The third treated the yogi as a rival. Kabīr mocks the yogi’s earrings, ashes and matted hair as outward show. Patton Burchett has argued that the rise of Rāmānandī and Kṛṣṇa devotion in early modern North India was shaped by its competition with Tantric and Nāth yoga: devotional authors from Nābhādās, whose Bhaktamāl (c. 1600) is the great hagiography of the movement, onwards presented bhakti as respectable, open to all and morally superior to the power-seeking yogi and the Tantric worshipper (Burchett 2019). In the Tamil country, by contrast, the Śaiva devotional canon itself came to include a great yoga text, Tirumūlar’s Tirumantiram (Chapter 5, Section 5.8).

docs.title: 3.11 Bhakti and Society
docs.text:
Bhakti as a Universal Path — and Its Limits

Bhakti teachers repeatedly declared that devotion is open to all, regardless of caste, gender or learning. The Gītā (9.32) already promises the highest goal to women, vaiśyas and śūdras who take refuge in Kṛṣṇa (on a common reading, while still calling them “of sinful birth”; Section 3.4), and the vernacular saint-poets — among them women such as Āṇṭāḷ, Akka Mahādevi and Mīrābāī, and low-caste or untouchable saints such as Cokhāmeḷā and Ravidās — composed in the languages of ordinary people rather than Sanskrit.

Historians caution, however, against treating Bhakti as a straightforward social revolution. The equality proclaimed in devotion often coexisted with caste practice in daily life: Cokhāmeḷā was revered as a saint yet barred from the Paṇḍharpur temple, and his poems lament this exclusion. Some movements, notably the Vīraśaivas of 12th-century Karnāṭaka, did attack caste directly; others reinforced brahmanical norms. The radical voices of Bhakti are best read as a sustained protest within the caste order rather than as its abolition (Hawley 2015).

docs.title: 3.12 The Integration of Karma and Bhakti
docs.text:
Karma Yoga and Bhakti Yoga are complementary rather than separate disciplines. The Gītā teaches that the highest form of Karma Yoga is Bhakti — action performed as an offering to God, motivated not by duty alone but by love:

Gītā 9.27

yat karoṣi yad aśnāsi yaj juhoṣi dadāsi yat yat tapasyasi kaunteya tat kuruṣva mad-arpaṇam Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give, whatever austerity you perform, O son of Kuntī — do that as an offering to Me.

Action offered in love loses its power to bind, and devotion expressed as service becomes action. The theistic commentators, above all Rāmānuja, read the Gītā as teaching that both culminate in a devotion that is itself a form of knowledge, a steady and loving remembrance of God (Chapter 4).

docs.title: 3.13 Modern Readings of Karma Yoga
docs.text: In the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries Karma Yoga became the most politically consequential of the yogas. Vivekānanda’s Karma Yoga (1896) made selfless work, and service of the poor as service of God, the spiritual practice of the householder; the Ramakrishna Mission’s relief work was its institutional form. Bal Gangadhar Tilak, writing in Mandalay jail, argued in his Gītā Rahasya (1915) that the Gītā teaches energetic action in the world, not renunciation, and he rejected the Advaita reading that subordinated action to knowledge. Aurobindo’s Essays on the Gita, serialised between 1916 and 1920, read it as a synthesis of works, knowledge and devotion, the germ of his own integral yoga (Chapter 11, Section 11.4.3). Gandhi, who called his Gujarati rendering of the Gītā Anāsaktiyoga, “the yoga of non-attachment”, made desireless action the basis of a politics of non-violence and read the battle of Kurukṣetra as an allegory of the inner struggle. These readings were contested in their turn: Ambedkar’s criticism of the Gītā’s defence of varṇa (Section 3.4) was aimed partly at them. They show that the Gītā’s yoga of action, like Patañjali’s yoga of stillness, has been reinterpreted in every age.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Jñāna Yoga: Advaita Vedānta and Yoga
docs.text:
Bhagavad Gītā 3.3

loke'smin dvividhā niṣṭhā purā proktā mayānagha jñānayogena sāṃkhyānāṃ karmayogena yoginām In this world, O blameless one, a twofold path was taught by me of old: the yoga of knowledge for the Sāṃkhyas, the yoga of action for the yogins.

docs.title: 4.1 A Name and Its History
docs.text:
“Jñāna Yoga”, the yoga of knowledge, is an old phrase with a modern career. The Gītā uses it in the verse above for the path of the Sāṃkhyas, those who seek liberation through discriminating knowledge, and sets it beside the yoga of action. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa names three yogas, of knowledge, action and devotion (11.20). But the idea that “Jñāna Yoga” is one of four parallel paths, alongside Rāja, Karma and Bhakti Yoga, is largely Vivekānanda’s: his lectures published as Jñāna Yoga (1899) presented Advaita Vedānta under that name, and modern teaching has followed him (Chapter 1, Section 1.9).

For the classical Advaitins themselves, knowledge was not one yoga among others. It was the only direct means of liberation, and their relation to yoga — to Patañjali’s system, to meditative technique, to the Haṭha practices of their own renunciant order — was complex: they rejected yoga as a philosophy, used it as a discipline, and argued about how far it could help. That relation is the subject of this chapter. The doctrines of Advaita (the unreality of difference, superimposition, the levels of reality, the theory of māyā) are treated in Volume 3, Darśana Darpaṇa, and are recalled here only as far as the argument requires.

docs.title: 4.2 Knowledge Alone: The Advaita Position
docs.text:
Advaita Vedānta’s classical exponent is Śaṅkara (c. 700–750 CE; the traditional date, 788–820, rests on later sources and long served as the conventional date in scholarship). His authentic works include commentaries on the principal Upaniṣads, the Brahmasūtra and the Bhagavad Gītā, and the independent Upadeśasāhasrī; hundreds of other works, including the Vivekacūḍāmaṇi and the Ātmabodha, are attributed to him by tradition, but most scholars doubt that he wrote them (Mayeda 1979). His central claim is that the self (ātman) is identical with the absolute (brahman), and that bondage is nothing but ignorance of this identity. It follows that liberation cannot be produced by any action, ritual or meditative, since whatever is produced by action is impermanent. It can only be revealed by knowledge, which removes the ignorance as light removes the appearance of a snake in a rope.

The means to that knowledge is the study of scripture under a teacher. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad’s injunction that the self “is to be seen, heard, reflected upon and meditated upon” (ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyo maitreyi, 2.4.5) gave the Advaitins their triad of hearing (śravaṇa) the great sayings of the Upaniṣads, such as tat tvam asi (“That thou art”, in the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad), reflecting on them (manana) to remove doubt, and contemplating them (nididhyāsana) until the knowledge is firm. At the opening of his Brahmasūtra commentary Śaṅkara lists the qualifications of the student: discrimination between the eternal and the transient, dispassion, a group of six virtues beginning with calm and self-control, and the desire for liberation. Advaita was above all a tradition of renunciants, and it was socially restricted: following the Dharmaśāstra, Śaṅkara held that only twice-born men were entitled to study the Veda, and in his Brahmasūtra commentary (1.3.34–38) he denied śūdras access to Vedic knowledge, although he allowed that they might attain liberation through the epics and Purāṇas. Modern Advaita teachers have generally abandoned these restrictions.

docs.title: 4.3 Śaṅkara and Yoga
docs.text:
Śaṅkara’s attitude to yoga has two sides. As a philosophy, Patañjala Yoga was for him a rival. The Brahmasūtra itself, after refuting Sāṃkhya, adds that “by this, Yoga is refuted” (etena yogaḥ pratyuktaḥ, 2.1.3). Śaṅkara explains that the yoga tradition is rejected in so far as it teaches, with Sāṃkhya, an independent primal matter as the cause of the world and a plurality of selves liberated by discriminating them from matter. Liberation does not come, he insists, from knowing the self as separate from nature, but from knowing it as Brahman.

As a discipline, however, yoga was indispensable to him. His commentary on the sixth chapter of the Gītā, which teaches the yoga of meditation (dhyānayoga), treats posture, the steadying of the mind and the withdrawal of the senses as an aid to knowledge, the means by which the mind of the renunciant is made fit to receive it. In the Brahmasūtra commentary he accepts those parts of the yoga tradition that do not contradict the Veda, and he does not doubt that the yogin’s concentration can be real. What he denies is that any such state, however exalted, is liberation in itself. This placed him in a long dispute with other Vedāntins. Maṇḍana Miśra and others held that knowledge of Brahman must be made effective by repeated meditation (prasaṅkhyāna); Śaṅkara, in the Upadeśasāhasrī, rejects the idea that meditation produces a liberation that knowledge has not already given (Mayeda 1979).

Whether Śaṅkara also wrote a commentary on the Yoga Sūtra itself, the Vivaraṇa, is still debated (Chapter 2, Section 2.8.2). Paul Hacker’s suggestion that Śaṅkara had been a follower of Yoga before he became an Advaitin would explain both the commentary and the yogic flavour of some of his early works; it would also explain why the later Advaita order took yoga so readily into its practice.

docs.title: 4.4 Before and Around Śaṅkara: Gauḍapāda’s “Yoga of No Contact”
docs.text: The oldest surviving Advaita work, the verses on the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad ascribed to Gauḍapāda (Māṇḍūkyakārikā, probably 6th–7th century), already has a yoga of its own. In its third book it calls the realisation of non-duality the “yoga of no contact” (asparśayoga, 3.39), a yoga that, it says, the yogins themselves find hard to see and fear, since they mistake its fearlessness for annihilation. The same book describes the discipline of the mind with a famous image: the mind is to be restrained tirelessly, like a man emptying the ocean drop by drop with the tip of a blade of grass (3.41).
