Birch’s count of the āsanas they actually describe is telling: none in the Amaraughaprabodha and the Yogabīja, one (the lotus) in the Dattātreyayogaśāstra, two in the Vivekamārtaṇḍa, four in the Śivasaṃhitā. The Brahmanical Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā describes ten, among them non-seated postures such as the peacock (mayūrāsana), balanced horizontally on the hands, and the cock (kukkuṭāsana). The Haṭhapradīpikā’s fifteen (Table 7.5) were thus already a considerable expansion, and Svātmārāma justifies them as the āsanas “accepted by” sages such as Vasiṣṭha and yogis such as Matsyendra (HYP 1.18) (Birch 2018). Throughout this period the texts give āsanas a modest place: they are the first auxiliary of Haṭha, valued for steadiness and for preparing the body for breath-control and the mudrās, while a few are credited with specific effects, such as kindling the digestive fire — claims that are part of the texts’ physiology, not tested medical findings.

docs.title: 7.12.2 The Proliferation of Āsanas
docs.text:
The number eighty-four, which the Haṭhapradīpikā (1.33) attributes to Śiva’s teaching, was a traditional figure before it was a real repertoire; lists of eighty-four āsanas, which do not agree with one another, became common only later (Bühnemann 2007). From the sixteenth century the texts began to describe many more postures (Table 7.11). Many of the new postures are complex, involving binding, inversion, balancing on the hands or repeated movement, yet they were added to the older framework rather than replacing it: in these texts āsana remains the first auxiliary of Haṭha Yoga, preparing for breath-control, the mudrās and samādhi (Birch 2018).

Table 7.11. Number of Āsanas Described in Selected Pre-modern Texts Text Date Āsanas Remarks Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā 12th–13th c. 10 Includes mayūra and kukkuṭa Dattātreyayogaśāstra c. 1200 1 The lotus only Vivekamārtaṇḍa 13th c. 2 Siddhāsana and padmāsana Śivasaṃhitā 15th c. 4 Seated postures Haṭhapradīpikā c. 1450 15 Says Śiva taught 84 Yogacintāmaṇi 16th–17th c. 34 One manuscript (1659) lists 118 Haṭharatnāvalī 17th c. 36 Names 84 Gheraṇḍasaṃhitā c. 1700 32 “Useful in the world of mortals” Jogapradīpakā 1737 84 Brajbhāṣā Haṭhābhyāsapaddhati 18th c. 112 Six groups, practised in sequence Śrītattvanidhi c. 1810–1868 122 80 “principal”, 42 “additional”

Counts after Birch (2018), Mallinson and Singleton (2017), Bühnemann (2007) and Birch and Singleton (2019); they refer to postures described, not merely named.

Illustration followed description. Some of the earliest surviving pictures of yogic postures are the paintings in the Persian Baḥr al-ḥayāt made for the Mughal prince Salīm around 1600 (Section 7.17); illustrated manuscripts of the Jogapradīpakā depict its eighty-four āsanas (Bühnemann 2007); and in the nineteenth century the Mysore court produced the most elaborate illustrated collection of all, discussed below.

docs.title: 7.12.3 The Haṭhābhyāsapaddhati
docs.text:
The richest pre-modern account of āsana practice is found in a little-known text, the Haṭhābhyāsapaddhati (“Manual on the Practice of Haṭha”), first studied in detail by Jason Birch and Mark Singleton in 2019 and edited in 2025 (Birch and Singleton 2019; Mallinson et al. 2025). It is written in a rough, unpolished Sanskrit and survives in a notebook-like manuscript in Pune, apparently written for personal use, and in a related manuscript in the Mysore Palace. It names its author as Kapālakuraṇṭaka, a siddha otherwise unknown. Its preference for Vaiṣṇava mantras and practices suggests a Vaiṣṇava author, though it also professes faith in the scriptures of Matsyendra and Gorakṣa and requires no initiation; a Marathi plant name in its text points to Maharashtra; and it was probably composed in the eighteenth century.

The work covers the yogin’s hut, twenty-five yamas and niyamas (introduced by two verses from the Bhāgavata Purāṇa), āsana, the cleansing practices, breath-control and the mudrās. Its hut is unusually specific: different huts, with walls of different materials, are prescribed for different practices, and one, for the most dynamic postures, is to be three bow-lengths (about five and a half metres) high. Its section on āsana describes 112 postures in six groups: supine, prone, “stationary”, standing, postures using a rope, and postures said to pierce the sun and the moon. Many are unattested elsewhere; several involve repeated or sequential movement; and in many the instruction begins from the posture before, so that each group forms a sequence to be practised in order — the only known pre-modern text to arrange āsanas in this way. Among its ten rope postures is “the pose leading to heaven” (svargāsana), in which the yogin, seated in the lotus, climbs a hanging rope with his hands. Ropes appear in yoga texts only from the seventeenth or eighteenth century, and earlier probably belonged to ascetic austerities such as the “bat penance”, in which the ascetic hangs upside down; the Haṭhābhyāsapaddhati’s account of them is the fullest before modern times (Birch and Singleton 2019).

docs.title: 7.12.4 The Śrītattvanidhi and the Road to Mysore
docs.text:
The Śrītattvanidhi (“Treasury of Glorious Principles”) is a vast illustrated compendium of iconography commissioned by Mummaḍi Kṛṣṇarāja Woḍeyar III of Mysore (1794–1868; on the throne from 1799, though without administrative powers after 1831). It contains some 1,888 painted miniatures in nine “treasuries”, and its seventh, the Śaivanidhi, includes 122 illustrated āsanas. It was compiled between 1810 and 1868, probably after 1850. Norman Sjoman, who published its āsana section, showed that it represents an older, pre-Krishnamacharya tradition of posture practice at the Mysore court (Sjoman 1996). Birch and Singleton then found that the descriptions of all but one of the Haṭhābhyāsapaddhati’s 112 āsanas recur word for word in the Śrītattvanidhi, rearranged and supplemented by a few postures from elsewhere, so that the Mysore compiler must have worked from a manuscript of that text (Birch and Singleton 2019).

These findings bear directly on the history of modern yoga (Chapter 11, Section 11.7). A manuscript of the Haṭhābhyāsapaddhati was in the palace collection where T. Krishnamacharya taught from 1933, and it is likely that he knew it; its sequences offer a pre-modern precedent for linking postures in series. But the continuity should not be exaggerated. Only eight of the text’s 112 postures are identical in name and form to postures in the systems derived from Krishnamacharya, and no pre-modern yoga text teaches the sun salutation sequences with which Ashtanga Vinyasa practice begins. The text was one source among several, alongside the exercise manuals of the period, for an innovative modern synthesis (Birch and Singleton 2019; Singleton 2010).

docs.title: 7.13 The Theory of Bindu and Amṛta in Haṭha Yoga
docs.text:
A distinctive teaching of Haṭha Yoga is the concept of bindu (the vital essence) and amṛta (the nectar of immortality). According to the HYP and related texts, a nectar (amṛta) continuously drips from the “moon” in the head and is consumed by the “sun”, the digestive fire in the belly. This process is held responsible for ageing and death. Viparīta Karaṇī (in which the yogi inverts the body so that the sun is above the moon) and Khecarī Mudrā are designed to reverse or block this flow and conserve the amṛta. In the earliest Haṭha texts the substance to be preserved is bindu, semen; the techniques were meant to stop its loss, whether through ejaculation or through the dripping of the nectar (Mallinson and Singleton 2017).

This is a pre-modern physiology of the subtle body. Attempts to map the “moon” and “sun” onto the pineal, pituitary or adrenal glands are modern speculations with no basis in the texts or in physiology.

docs.title: 7.14 Khecarī Mudrā: The Royal Seal
docs.text:
Khecarī Mudrā is considered one of the most important mudrās in the Haṭha Yoga tradition, and a whole text, the Khecarīvidyā, is devoted to it (Mallinson 2007a). The word khecarī means “moving in space” (kha = space, carī = moving).

In its full form, Khecarī involves turning the tongue backwards above the soft palate into the nasal cavity, where it is said to block or drink the descending amṛta. The HYP (3.33–36) describes lengthening the tongue by gradually cutting the frenulum and rubbing it with rock salt and myrobalan powder over many months. Some ascetics still do this; many modern teachers teach only a “soft” version in which the tongue is curled back against the palate.

Health and Safety Note

Cutting the frenulum of the tongue, urethral techniques such as vajrolī, and prolonged breath retention are described here only as part of the historical record. They can cause serious injury and must not be attempted on the basis of this book.

Scholarly Note: Texts Attributed to Gorakṣa

Many works are attributed to Gorakṣanātha. The oldest, the Vivekamārtaṇḍa and an early Gorakṣaśataka, date from roughly the 13th–14th centuries; others, such as the Gorakṣapaddhati and the Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati, are considerably later. Attribution to Gorakṣa is a mark of lineage authority rather than evidence of authorship. Svātmārāma drew heavily on the early texts in compiling the Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā.

docs.title: 7.15 Yogis and Ascetic Orders in Early Modern India
docs.text: Between the Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā and the colonial period, Haṭha Yoga was carried less by texts than by people: organised orders of ascetics who learned its techniques from their gurus, travelled the pilgrimage routes, and lived in monasteries supported by kings and landholders. Persian chronicles, European travel accounts, Mughal and Rajput paintings and the land-grant documents of monasteries show yogis as numerous, mobile, sometimes armed and often courted by rulers (White 2009; Pinch 2006). Three groups matter most for the history of Yoga: the Nāth yogis, the Daśanāmī saṃnyāsīs and the Rāmānandī vairāgīs.

docs.title: 7.15.1 The Nāth Yogis
docs.text:
The Nāths (Section 7.1.1) are known in North India as jogīs and, from their most visible mark, as Kānphaṭas, “split-eared”: at initiation the cartilage of the ears is cut and large rings (mudrā or kuṇḍala) are later inserted. A Nāth also wears a small horn whistle on a woollen thread, and greets others with the word ādes. George Weston Briggs’s study, based on fieldwork in the early twentieth century, remains the fullest description of the order’s customs, its tradition of twelve sub-orders (bārah panth) and its sacred sites (Briggs 1938). Not all Nāths were celibate renouncers. In Punjab, Rajasthan and Bengal there are householder communities of jogīs who trace their descent to the order; their singers carried the vernacular epics of King Gopīcand and King Bhartharī, rulers who renounced their thrones to become Nāth yogis (Gold 1992). For most people, these songs, rather than Sanskrit manuals, were what Nāth yoga meant.

The order’s monasteries were important institutions. Besides Gorakhpur, its principal centres included Gorakh Ṭillā (Tilla Jogian) in the Salt Range of Punjab, for centuries one of the order’s chief seats, abandoned at Partition in 1947; Kadri at Mangalore; Dhinodhar in Kutch; and Caughera in western Nepal. Persian documents preserved at the Nāth monastery of Jakhbar, near Pathankot, record grants of revenue-free land and other favours from Mughal officials from the reign of Akbar onwards, showing that the Mughal state treated Nāth establishments much as it treated other religious foundations (Goswamy and Grewal 1967). Some kings went further. The Shāh rulers of Gorkha, who unified Nepal in the eighteenth century, honoured Gorakhnāth as their tutelary saint. In Jodhpur, Mahārājā Mān Singh (r. 1803–1843) made the Nāth guru Āyas Devnāth his preceptor, built the Mahāmandir for him, and had court artists illustrate Nāth texts and lineages on a grand scale; resentment of the Nāths’ power at court was a source of conflict with the nobility, and their influence did not survive the king’s death (Diamond et al. 2008).

docs.title: 7.15.2 Daśanāmī and Rāmānandī Ascetics
docs.text:
The Daśanāmī (“ten-named”) saṃnyāsīs are, according to their tradition, the order founded by Śaṅkara, with four principal monasteries at Śṛṅgerī, Dvārakā, Purī and Jyotirmaṭh and ten lineage names (Giri, Purī, Bhāratī, Sarasvatī and others). Matthew Clark has argued that the order as it now exists took shape gradually, by the integration of diverse ascetic lineages, some of them with older Śaiva yogic affiliations, and that its familiar organisation is largely a product of the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries (Clark 2006). The Rāmānandīs, who trace themselves to Rāmānanda (traditionally of the fourteenth or fifteenth century), are Vaiṣṇava devotees of Rāma; their renunciant wing, the vairāgīs, became the largest ascetic order of North India.

Both orders developed nāgā (“naked”) sections organised in akhāṛās, regiments of ascetics who trained in arms. In 1567 Akbar watched two rival bands of ascetics fight at Thanesar over the right to collect pilgrims’ alms, an episode illustrated in the imperial Akbarnāma; in the eighteenth century armed ascetics served as soldiers and military entrepreneurs, and the Daśanāmī and Rāmānandī akhāṛās clashed over precedence at the great bathing festivals. William Pinch’s Warrior Ascetics and Indian Empires traces this history, which is told from the military side in Volume 20, Yuddha and Dhanurveda (Pinch 2006). The akhāṛās’ processions still lead the principal bathing days of the Kumbh Melā.

For the history of Yoga the point is that these orders were the main bearers of Haṭha practice. Their ascetics combined the techniques of the Haṭha texts with older austerities (tapas) that travellers from the seventeenth century onwards described with astonishment: holding one arm aloft until it withered, standing day and night for years, sitting in the summer sun surrounded by fires (pañcadhūnī), a practice still performed by Rāmānandī renouncers. Texts were also produced in these milieux. The Brajbhāṣā Jogapradīpakā (1737), which teaches eighty-four āsanas, was written by Jayatarāma, apparently a Rāmānandī; and in South India the Advaita renunciant Upaniṣadbrahmayogin, in the eighteenth century, transmitted and commented on the expanded Yoga Upaniṣads, into which verses of the Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā had been incorporated (Chapter 1) (Bouy 1994). As noted above (Section 7.1.1), the identification of Haṭha Yoga with the Nāths alone is a simplification: Daśanāmī and Rāmānandī ascetics were practitioners too, and much of what is known about how the techniques were actually taught comes from observing their living traditions (Mallinson 2011; Mallinson and Singleton 2017).

docs.title: 7.15.3 The Yogi’s Reputation
docs.text: Outside the orders, yogis inspired both reverence and fear. David Gordon White has shown that in Sanskrit story literature, Persian chronicles and European travel writing the “yogi” is often a man of power rather than a contemplative: a sorcerer who can enter other bodies, a healer and alchemist, a spy, a soldier, a trader, or a king’s adviser (White 2009). Under Company rule armed ascetics were disarmed and wandering mendicants were increasingly treated as vagrants, while photographs and descriptions of “fakirs” performing extreme austerities came to stand, for many Western and Western-educated observers, for Indian religion at its most irrational. The reformers of the late nineteenth century distanced themselves from this figure and from Haṭha Yoga with it — one of the starting points for the modern reshaping of yoga described in Chapter 11 (Singleton 2010).

docs.title: 7.16 Yoga in Tamil and Marathi: The Cittars and Jñāneśvar
docs.text: Haṭha Yoga was codified in Sanskrit, but from the twelfth century it was also sung, preached and argued over in the regional languages, and for most practitioners it was the vernacular songs, not the Sanskrit manuals, that defined it. The Nāth songs of North India and Bengal have been mentioned above, and the Hindi verses of the Sants in Chapter 3; two other bodies of literature deserve notice in their own right.

docs.title: 7.16.1 The Tamil Cittars
docs.text:
The Tamil Cittars (from Sanskrit siddha, “accomplished one”) are a loose tradition of poet-yogins, conventionally numbered eighteen, whose verses survive in popular collections. They include Civavākkiyar, Pattirakiriyār, Pāmpāṭṭi Cittar, Iṭaikkāṭṭu Cittar and Akappēy Cittar, and the tradition also claims Tirumūlar (Chapter 5, Section 5.8), Akattiyar (Agastya) and Pōkar (Bhoga), to whom large medical and alchemical corpora are attributed. Most of the poems cannot be dated with confidence; Kamil Zvelebil, whose The Poets of the Powers remains the standard introduction in English, placed the bulk of them between about the fifteenth and the eighteenth centuries (Zvelebil 1973). Their yoga is close to the Haṭha and Nāth yoga of the north: breath-control (Tamil vāci), the raising of the coiled power through the centres, the nectar dripping from the head, and the cultivation of an incorruptible body (kāyakaṟpam). The refrain of Pāmpāṭṭi Cittar, the “snake-charmer” poet, bids the snake to dance; the snake is the awakened kuṇḍalinī.

The Cittars are as remarkable for what they rejected as for what they taught. Many of their verses mock the worship of a stone set up as a god, temple ritual, pilgrimage, the authority of Brahmins and the distinctions of caste, and insist that the god is to be found within the body. T. N. Ganapathy has argued that this is not mere iconoclasm but a coherent mysticism of the body (Ganapathy 1993). The tradition lived on in Siddha medicine (cittar maruttuvam), whose practitioners still trace their knowledge to the Cittars; Richard Weiss has shown how, in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, Siddha physicians presented this inheritance as a distinctively Tamil science (Weiss 2009). Siddha medicine itself is treated in Volume 13, Āyurveda.

docs.title: 7.16.2 Jñāneśvar and the Marathi Nāths
docs.text:
In Maharashtra the Nāth tradition entered vernacular literature through Jñāneśvar or Jñānadev (traditionally 1275–1296). His Jñāneśvarī, also called Bhāvārthadīpikā, is a Marathi verse commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā in about nine thousand stanzas, completed according to its colophon in 1290 at Nevase on the Godavari. At its close Jñāneśvar names his lineage: Ādinātha (Śiva) taught Matsyendranātha, who taught Gorakṣanātha, who taught Gahīnīnātha, who taught Nivṛttinātha, Jñāneśvar’s elder brother and guru. His commentary on the sixth chapter of the Gītā, the chapter on the yoga of meditation, expands its few verses on posture into the most celebrated account of kuṇḍalinī in Marathi: the yogin presses the root of the body with his heel, the coiled power wakes like a young serpent, rises through the centres, and finally merges with Śiva in the space at the crown of the head (Jñāneśvara 1967).

What is distinctive is the setting. Jñāneśvar put Nāth yoga inside a commentary on a text of action and devotion, in a language that ordinary people could understand, and he is remembered as a founder of the Vārkārī devotion to Viṭṭhala at Paṇḍharpur, whose later saints, from Nāmdev to Tukārām, sang of bhakti rather than of yoga. Catharina Kiehnle’s edition and study of songs on yoga attributed to Jñāndev and other Marathi Nāths shows how fully the vocabulary of the Haṭha subtle body was absorbed into this devotional world (Kiehnle 1997). The Amṛtānubhava, also attributed to Jñāneśvar, is a treatise on non-dual experience; and the Mahānubhāvas, a rival Marathi sect, also revered Dattātreya, the patron deity of yogis (Chapter 1, Section 1.5.3). Like the Cittars in the south and the Sikh Gurus in the north (Section 7.17), the Marathi poets took Haṭha Yoga out of the ascetic orders and into the songs of householders.

docs.title: 7.17 Yoga among Sufis, Mughals and Sikhs
docs.text:
Haṭha Yoga took shape in a North India much of which was ruled by Muslim dynasties, and its practitioners were seen, described, painted and argued with by Muslims and, from the sixteenth century, by the Sikh Gurus. This history is not a footnote. Some of the earliest surviving illustrations of yogic postures were made for a Mughal prince; Sufi authors wrote some of the most detailed pre-modern descriptions of yogic practice outside Sanskrit; and Guru Nānak’s dialogue with the Nāth siddhas is one of the classic critiques of Haṭha Yoga in Indian religious literature. Volume 6, Tantra–Āgama, summarises these exchanges in a paragraph, and Volume 24, Samanvaya, places Sufism and Sikhism in the wider history of religious encounter; this section treats them from the side of Yoga. Table 7.12 lists the principal works.

Table 7.12. Yoga in Arabic and Persian: Principal Works Work Author Date Character Kitāb Pātanjal (Arabic) al-Bīrūnī before c. 1030 Free rendering of the Yoga Sūtra with commentary (Section 2.8.5) Ḥawḍ mā’ al-ḥayāt (Arabic) anonymous; ascribed to Rukn al-Dīn Samarqandī uncertain; frame story set in 13th-c. Bengal Translation of the lost Amṛtakuṇḍa; breath, subtle body, mantras Rushdnāma (Persian, with Hindavī verse) ‘Abd al-Quddūs Gangohī early 16th c. Nāth vocabulary in Chishtī teaching Baḥr al-ḥayāt (Persian) Muḥammad Ghawth Gwāliyārī before 1563 Expanded Amṛtakuṇḍa; postures, breath and Sufi dhikr Ā’īn-i Akbarī, section on Indian learning Abū al-Faẓl c. 1595–1600 Includes an account of the Pātañjala school Jōg Bāsishṭ (Persian) Niẓām al-Dīn Pānīpatī 1597 Translation of the Laghu Yogavāsiṣṭha for Prince Salīm Dialogue with Bābā Lāl Dārā Shikoh c. 1653 Questions to a Vaiṣṇava ascetic on the ascetic life and meditation

docs.title: 7.17.1 The Amṛtakuṇḍa and Its Translations
docs.text:
The most widely read Islamic work on yoga was a translation of a lost text called the Amṛtakuṇḍa (“Pool of Nectar”). Its Arabic version, the Ḥawḍ mā’ al-ḥayāt (“The Pool of the Water of Life”), opens with a story: in Bengal, soon after its conquest in the early thirteenth century, a Muslim judge, Rukn al-Dīn Samarqandī, met a learned yogi who accepted Islam and taught him the book. Carl Ernst, who has studied the many manuscripts, regards this frame as a later legend, but the content is genuinely yogic. The text presents the body as a microcosm of the universe; teaches breath control and the art of predicting events from the flow of breath through the two nostrils; describes centres in the body, each with its mantra; and gives practices for summoning a group of female spirits who correspond to the yoginīs of Tantric tradition (Ernst 2003). Its yoga resembles that of the Nāth texts.

Ernst calls what the translators did the “Islamization” of yoga. They did not simply copy the material: they glossed Indian deities as angels or spirits, paired or replaced mantras with Arabic names of God, and fitted the whole into the Islamic and Neoplatonic science of the microcosm. The Arabic version was later ascribed to the great Andalusian mystic Ibn ‘Arabī, and under that name it was copied and read in the Ottoman lands, far from India. In India the Persian Baḥr al-ḥayāt (“Ocean of Life”) of Muḥammad Ghawth Gwāliyārī (d. 1563), a master of the Shaṭṭārī Sufi order who had spent years in ascetic retreat in the hills near Chunar, expanded the text and added a set of postures, each combined with breath control and with recitation (dhikr) of Islamic formulas (Ernst 2003, 2005).

docs.title: 7.17.2 Sufis and Yogis
docs.text:
The meeting between Sufis and yogis was not only a matter of books. Sufi and yogi lived side by side at shrines, on pilgrimage routes and in the countryside, and Sufi conversation records describe encounters and debates with jogīs. The Chishtī master ‘Abd al-Quddūs Gangohī (1456–1537) composed Hindavī verses, under the pen-name Alakh, that use the language of the Nāths — Gorakh, the stainless one (nirañjan), the void — to express Sufi teaching on the unity of being. Sufi manuals of the period describe holding the breath (ḥabs-i dam) during dhikr; whether this was learned from yogis was debated among Sufis themselves. In Hindavī literature the Sufi romances of the sixteenth century — Qutban’s Mirigāvatī (1503), Jāyasī’s Padmāvat (1540), Manjhan’s Madhumālatī (1545) — repeatedly send their prince in search of his beloved disguised as a jogī, with earrings, ashes and horn; Aditya Behl has shown that these poems use the Nāth yogi’s quest as an image of the Sufi’s path to God (Behl 2012).

Ernst warns against two easy readings of this material (Ernst 2005). It is not evidence that Sufism derived from yoga; Sufi practice has its own roots in the Qur’ān and in the early mystics of Iraq and Iran. Nor is it “syncretism” in the sense of a merging of two religions: Sufi authors placed yoga within an Islamic framework, valued it as a technique or as a science of the subtle body, and subordinated it to Islamic goals, while some Sufis rejected it altogether. The material shows a sustained, selective and intelligent engagement with yogic practice by people who remained, in their own eyes, fully Muslim.

docs.title: 7.17.3 The Mughal Court and the Painted Yogi
docs.text:
Akbar (r. 1556–1605) took a personal interest in yogis. The hostile chronicler Badā’ūnī reports that the emperor received jogīs privately at night, learned from them, and set apart a quarter for them, and Abū al-Faẓl’s Ā’īn-i Akbarī includes the Pātañjala system in its survey of Indian learning. At Prince Salīm’s court in Allahabad, around 1600, Niẓām al-Dīn Pānīpatī’s Persian version of the Laghu Yogavāsiṣṭha was illustrated, and a copy of Ghawth’s Baḥr al-ḥayāt was painted with a series of yogis in postures; this manuscript, now in the Chester Beatty Library in Dublin, contains some of the earliest surviving illustrations of āsanas. As emperor, Salīm (Jahāṅgīr) visited the ascetic Jadrūp at Ujjain and recorded his admiration in his memoirs. Dārā Shikoh (Volume 24) questioned the Vaiṣṇava ascetic Bābā Lāl at Lahore, and the Persian record of their conversations covers the ascetic life, meditation and the relation of the soul to God (Gandhi 2020).

Yogis became a favourite subject of Mughal, Deccani and Rajput painters, from the battle at Thanesar in the Akbarnāma to studies of ascetics gathered round a fire and the large Nāth paintings of Mān Singh’s Jodhpur. Debra Diamond’s exhibition Yoga: The Art of Transformation (Arthur M. Sackler Gallery, Washington, 2013–14), the first major exhibition on the visual history of yoga, and its catalogue brought this material together and showed how much it tells us about practice: postures, the ascetics’ insignia, their camps and their patrons (Diamond 2013). Paintings follow artistic conventions and cannot be read as photographs, but they are an important source for a period from which few practical manuals survive.

docs.title: 7.17.4 Guru Nānak and the Nāths
docs.text:
The Nāth yogis were among the religious specialists most often encountered by Guru Nānak (1469–1539), and Sikh scripture records his response. The longest statement is the Siddh Goṣṭ (“Discourse with the Siddhas”), a composition of seventy-three stanzas in Rāg Rāmkalī in the Guru Granth Sāhib, in which Nānak answers the questions of Nāth siddhas about his path. The yogis ask why he does not renounce the world; he answers that liberation comes through the Guru’s word (sabad) and meditation on the divine name (nām), received by grace, not through the yogi’s techniques or the yogi’s withdrawal from society. In the Japjī (stanzas 28–31) Nānak addresses the yogi directly, turning the emblems of the order — the earrings, the begging bag, the ashes, the patched cloak — into inner virtues such as contentment, modesty and meditation, and each stanza ends with the Nāth salutation ādes redirected to the one God. Later Sikh tradition, especially the first vār of Bhāī Gurdās (d. 1636), narrates Nānak’s debates with the siddhas on Mount Sumeru and at the Śivarātri fair at Achal near Batala; W. H. McLeod treats these narratives as later hagiography, while regarding the hymns themselves as Nānak’s own (McLeod 1968).

The vocabulary of Haṭha and Nāth yoga — the unstruck sound (anahad), the tenth door at the crown of the head (dasam duār), the state of natural ease (sahaj), nectar (amrit) — runs through the Guru Granth Sāhib, as it does through the songs of Kabīr and other Sants. The Gurus use it, however, for the fruits of devotion to the name and of the Guru’s grace, attained by householders living honestly in the world, not for the results of bodily technique. In Sikh understanding, therefore, Nānak’s teaching is not a form of yoga but a distinct revelation (bāṇī), which took up the religious language of its time in order to redirect it (Volume 24 discusses the debate over “synthesis”). The renunciant impulse did not vanish entirely: the Udāsī order, which traces itself to Nānak’s son Śrī Cand, kept an ascetic way of life, was later recognised among the ascetic akhāṛās, and managed many Sikh shrines until the Gurdwara reform movement of the 1920s (Oberoi 1994).

docs.title: 7.18 The Haṭha Yoga Tradition in Historical Context
docs.text:
Haṭha Yoga changed the place of the body in Indian religion. Where the classical Yoga of Patañjali and the early Buddhist and Jain contemplative paths treated the body chiefly as something to be stilled, Haṭha Yoga made it the primary instrument of liberation. The Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā calls the body a ghaṭa (pot), and compares it to an unbaked clay pot that dissolves in water: it must be “baked” in the fire of yoga (Mallinson 2004).

The Haṭha texts also have a social dimension that is often overlooked. Unlike Vedic learning, Haṭha practice was not restricted by caste or sect: several texts insist that anyone who practises will succeed. Haṭha Yoga was nonetheless an ascetic discipline, taught in secret and in person by a guru, and its techniques were meant for renunciants seeking siddhis and liberation, not for general health.

Its influence on the modern global yoga movement is real but indirect: modern posture practice took names and some techniques from Haṭha Yoga, but combined them with Western physical culture and gymnastics (Chapter 11).

docs.title: Chapter 8: Prāṇāyāma: Breath and Its Regulation
docs.text:
Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā 2.2

cale vāte calaṃ cittaṃ niścale niścalaṃ bhavet yogī sthāṇutvam āpnoti tato vāyuṃ nirodhayet When the breath is unsteady, the mind is unsteady. When the breath is steady, the mind is steady, and the yogi attains stillness. Therefore, one should restrain the breath.

docs.title: 8.1 The Meaning of Prāṇāyāma
docs.text:
The word prāṇāyāma is composed of two Sanskrit terms: prāṇa (vital life force, breath) and āyāma (extension, expansion, regulation). Thus, prāṇāyāma literally means “the extension or regulation of the vital life force.” It is the fourth limb of Patañjali’s Aṣṭāṅga Yoga and occupies a central position in the entire Haṭha Yoga tradition.

Definition: Prāṇa

Prāṇa is not merely the physical breath but the universal vital energy that pervades all creation. In the individual, it manifests as the life force that sustains the body, mind, and senses. The breath is the gross manifestation of this subtle energy.

docs.title: 8.2 The Five Prāṇas (Pañca Prāṇa)
docs.text:
The Yoga tradition teaches that prāṇa operates in the body through five principal functions (pañca prāṇa) and five subsidiary functions (pañca upa-prāṇa) (Tables 8.1 and 8.2; Figure 8.1).

Table 8.1. The Five Principal Prāṇas Prāṇa Direction Region Function Prāṇa Inward Heart, chest Respiration; intake of food and experience Apāna Downward Below navel Elimination; excretion; childbirth Samāna Equalising Navel region Digestion; assimilation; metabolism Udāna Upward Throat, head Speech; growth; at death, departure of soul Vyāna Pervading Entire body Circulation; distribution of energy Table 8.2. The Five Subsidiary Prāṇas (Upa-Prāṇa) Upa-Prāṇa Function Nāga Belching; hiccupping Kūrma Blinking; opening and closing of the eyes Kṛkara Sneezing; causing hunger Devadatta Yawning Dhanañjaya Pervading the entire body; remains after death (decomposition) Figure 8.1. The Pañca Prāṇa and their locations in the body.

docs.title: 8.3 The Three Phases of Prāṇāyāma
docs.text:
In the Haṭha texts every prāṇāyāma has three phases: inhalation (pūraka, “filling”), retention (kumbhaka, from kumbha, “pot”, the body being filled like a pot) and exhalation (recaka, “emptying”). Retention is the heart of the practice, and the texts distinguish two kinds: sahita kumbhaka, deliberate retention “accompanied” by inhalation and exhalation, and kevala kumbhaka, “isolated” retention, in which the breath stops of itself. The second is the goal; the HYP says that for one who has mastered it nothing in the three worlds is hard to attain. Because retention is dangerous, the texts insist on gradual progress:

HYP 2.15

yathā siṃho gajo vyāghro bhaved vaśyaḥ śanaiḥ śanaiḥ tathaiva sevito vāyur anyathā hanti sādhakam Just as lions, elephants, and tigers are tamed gradually, so the breath must be brought under control step by step. Otherwise it destroys the practitioner.

docs.title: 8.4 Classical Prāṇāyāma Techniques
docs.text:
After alternate-nostril purification of the channels, the HYP teaches eight kumbhakas (2.44): sūryabhedana, ujjāyī, sītkārī, śītalī, bhastrikā, bhrāmarī, mūrcchā and plāvinī. The techniques below, with kapālabhāti, are described for historical understanding; the benefits listed are those claimed by the texts or by modern teachers unless a study is cited.

Health and Safety Note

Breath retention and forceful breathing (kapālabhāti, bhastrikā) can cause dizziness, fainting and hyperventilation, and are unsuitable in pregnancy and for people with high blood pressure, heart disease, epilepsy, glaucoma, hernia or recent surgery. The HYP itself (2.16–17) warns that improper practice causes hiccups, asthma, cough, headache and pain in the ears and eyes. Learn from a qualified teacher and seek medical advice if you have any health condition.

docs.title: 8.4.1 Nāḍī Śodhana (Alternate Nostril Breathing)
docs.text:
Nāḍī Śodhana is the foundational prāṇāyāma practice, designed to purify the subtle energy channels (nāḍīs) and balance the solar and lunar energies.

HYP 2.7

baddha-padmāsano yogī prāṇaṃ candreṇa pūrayet dhārayitvā yathā-śakti bhūyaḥ sūryeṇa recayet Seated in Padmāsana, the yogi should inhale through the left (lunar) nostril, retain as long as he is able, then exhale through the right (solar) nostril. (The following verses reverse the sequence: inhale through the right, retain, and exhale through the left.)

Technique:

  1. Close the right nostril with the thumb; inhale through the left nostril (Pūraka)

  2. Close both nostrils; retain the breath (Kumbhaka)

  3. Release the right nostril; exhale through it (Recaka)

  4. Inhale through the right nostril (Pūraka)

  5. Close both nostrils; retain (Kumbhaka)

  6. Release the left nostril; exhale through it (Recaka)

  7. This completes one round

Ratio: Later texts such as the Śāṇḍilya Upaniṣad prescribe a ratio of 1:4:2 (inhalation : retention : exhalation), measured in syllabic units (mātrā). Modern teachers start beginners with retention-free, equal breathing (Figure 8.2).

Figure 8.2. Participants at a group session practising alternate-nostril breathing (Nāḍī Śodhana). The man in the foreground closes one nostril with the right thumb and rests two fingers between the eyebrows, a common modern variant of the hand position. Photo: Biswarup Ganguly, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 8.4.2 Kapālabhāti (Skull-Shining Breath)
docs.text:
Kapālabhāti is technically classified as a ṣaṭkarma (purificatory practice) rather than a prāṇāyāma, though it is often included in prāṇāyāma sequences.

Technique: Rapid, forceful exhalations through the nose with passive, automatic inhalations. The abdominal muscles are vigorously contracted during each exhalation.

Claimed benefits: The HYP (2.35) says it destroys disorders of phlegm (kapha). Modern claims that it “purifies the frontal lobes” have no basis.

docs.title: 8.4.3 Bhastrikā (Bellows Breath)
docs.text:
The HYP compares this practice to the working of a blacksmith’s bellows.

Technique: Vigorous, forceful inhalations and exhalations through the nose, like the pumping of bellows. Both inhalation and exhalation are active and forceful.

Claimed benefits (HYP): Stokes the digestive fire (jaṭharāgni), removes disorders of all three humours, breaks the three granthis, awakens kuṇḍalinī.

docs.title: 8.4.4 Ujjāyī (Victorious Breath)
docs.text:
Technique: Inhalation through both nostrils with a slight constriction of the glottis, producing a soft, ocean-like sound in the throat. Exhalation may be through the left nostril or through both nostrils.

HYP 2.51

mukhaṃ saṃyamya nāḍībhyām ākṛṣya pavanaṃ śanaiḥ yathā lagati kaṇṭhāt tu hṛdayāvadhi sasvanam Closing the mouth, draw in the air slowly through both nostrils so that it produces a sound from the throat to the heart.

Claimed benefits (HYP): Removes phlegm in the throat, increases the digestive fire, and cures disorders of the channels.

docs.title: 8.4.5 Śītalī (Cooling Breath)
docs.text:
Technique: Roll the tongue into a tube; inhale through the rolled tongue with a cooling sensation; retain; exhale through the nostrils.

Claimed benefits (HYP 2.57–58): Cools the body; cures disorders of the spleen, fever and bile; counteracts hunger, thirst and poison.

docs.title: 8.4.6 Sītkārī (Hissing Breath)
docs.text:
Technique: Inhale through the clenched teeth with a hissing sound (sīt); retain; exhale through the nostrils.

Claimed benefits: Similar to Śītalī; often taught to those who cannot roll the tongue.

docs.title: 8.4.7 Bhrāmarī (Humming Bee Breath)
docs.text:
Technique: Inhale through both nostrils; during exhalation, produce a deep humming sound like a male bee (bhrāmara). The sound should resonate in the head.

Claimed benefits: The HYP says it brings an indescribable joy to the mind; modern teachers use it to prepare for meditation on inner sound (Chapter 10).

docs.title: 8.4.8 Sūryabhedana, Mūrcchā and Plāvinī
docs.text: The remaining three kumbhakas of the HYP are less often taught. In sūryabhedana (“piercing the sun”) the yogin inhales through the right, solar nostril, holds the breath and exhales through the left; the text says it purifies the skull and destroys intestinal worms and disorders of wind. In mūrcchā (“swooning”) the breath is held with the chin lock until the mind faints into a pleasant stillness. In plāvinī (“floating”) the belly is filled with air, and the yogin, the text claims, floats on water like a lotus leaf.

docs.title: 8.5 Signs of Progress in Prāṇāyāma
docs.text: The Haṭha texts describe progressive signs of success. The HYP (2.12) says that at the lowest level the practitioner sweats, at the middle level trembles, and at the highest the breath “reaches its place”. The Śiva Saṃhitā describes four stages of practice — beginning (ārambha), the “pot” (ghaṭa), familiarity (paricaya) and consummation (niṣpatti) — in which the body first sweats and grows lean and bright, then trembles and may hop “like a frog”, then becomes light enough, the text claims, to rise from the ground, and finally attains Rāja Yoga. The same four names are given in the HYP to the stages of inner sound (Chapter 10). These are textual claims, not observed results.

docs.title: 8.6 Precautions and Guidelines
docs.text:
Key Point: Essential Precautions for Prāṇāyāma

  1. Guru’s guidance — Always learn from a qualified teacher

  2. Gradual progression — Never force the breath; increase duration slowly

  3. Empty stomach — Practise on an empty stomach (several hours after a meal)

  4. Clean environment — A well-ventilated, quiet, clean space

  5. Moderate diet — Mita-āhāra (moderate, sāttvika food)

  6. Regular timing — Best times: brāhma muhūrta (pre-dawn), sunset

  7. Steady posture — Must be seated in a firm, comfortable āsana

  8. No strain — If dizziness, nausea, or headache occurs, stop and rest

docs.title: 8.7 The Relationship Between Breath and Mind
docs.text:
One of the most profound insights of Yoga is the intimate connection between breath and mind. As the HYP declares (2.2): “When the breath is unsteady, the mind is unsteady. When the breath is steady, the mind becomes steady.” This bi-directional relationship means that by controlling the breath, one gains control over the mind, and vice versa.

Modern research supports a more limited version of this insight. Slow, controlled breathing shifts autonomic balance towards parasympathetic activity and can reduce subjective anxiety; evidence for effects on cortisol and on EEG rhythms is less consistent, and many studies are small (Zaccaro et al. 2018).

HYP 4.29

indriyāṇāṃ mano nātho mano-nāthas tu mārutaḥ mārutasya layo nāthaḥ sa layo nādam āśritaḥ The mind is lord of the senses; the breath is lord of the mind; absorption (laya) is lord of the breath, and that absorption rests on the inner sound (nāda).

docs.title: 8.8 Prāṇāyāma in the Textual Tradition
docs.text:
The oldest description of breath-control as a technique of meditation is in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, in the verse that follows its instruction on posture (Chapter 1):

Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.9

prāṇān prapīḍyeha sa yukta-ceṣṭaḥ kṣīṇe prāṇe nāsikayocchvasīta duṣṭāśva-yuktam iva vāham enaṃ vidvān mano dhārayetāpramattaḥ Restraining his breaths here, with his movements controlled, he should breathe out through the nose when the breath is diminished. The wise one should hold the mind attentively, as one holds a chariot yoked to unruly horses.

Here, as in Patañjali, the restraint of the breath serves the restraint of the mind. Table 8.3 summarises how later texts developed the practice.

Table 8.3. Prāṇāyāma in the Major Yoga Texts Text Period Key Teachings on Prāṇāyāma Bhagavad Gītā c. 2nd c. BCE–2nd c. CE Prāṇa-apāna offerings; prāṇāyāma as sacrifice (yajña) (4.29) Yoga Sūtras c. 325–425 CE Fourth limb; external, internal and suspended movements regulated by place, time and number; a “fourth” beyond these Yogayājñavalkya c. 13th–14th c. CE Prāṇāyāma with fixation of the breath on the elements in the body; therapeutic applications Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā c. 1450 CE Eight kumbhakas detailed; emphasis on nāḍī purification; signs of success; mitāhāra Śiva Saṃhitā c. 15th c. CE Four stages of practice; retention with bandhas; kuṇḍalinī Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā c. 1700 CE Eight kumbhakas, including sahita and kevala; breathing combined with mantra (sagarbha)

docs.title: 8.9 Patañjali’s Analysis of Prāṇāyāma
docs.text:
Patañjali devotes five sūtras (2.49–2.53) to prāṇāyāma. His definition (2.49, quoted in Section 2.5.4) is striking: once posture is mastered, prāṇāyāma is the interruption (gati-viccheda) of the movement of in-breath and out-breath — a cessation, not a technique of breathing. The next sūtra classifies that cessation:

Yoga Sūtra 2.50

bāhyābhyantara-stambha-vṛttir deśa-kāla-saṃkhyābhiḥ paridṛṣṭo dīrgha-sūkṣmaḥ Prāṇāyāma has external, internal, and suspended movements, regulated by place, time, and number, becoming prolonged and subtle.

Following Vyāsa’s commentary, the three movements are explained in Table 8.4. Note that all three are forms of retention; Vyāsa does not equate bāhya and ābhyantara with exhalation and inhalation, as some modern manuals do.

Table 8.4. Patañjali’s Three Types of Prāṇāyāma Type Sanskrit Description External Bāhya Vṛtti Retention after exhalation; the breath is held outside Internal Ābhyantara Vṛtti Retention after inhalation; the breath is held inside Suspended Stambha Vṛtti Suspension of both movements at once, by a single effort, wherever the breath happens to be

The fourth type of prāṇāyāma described in Sūtra 2.51 is the most significant:

Yoga Sūtra 2.51

bāhyābhyantara-viṣayākṣepī caturthaḥ The fourth (type of prāṇāyāma) transcends the domain of the external and the internal.

Scholarly Note

This enigmatic “fourth prāṇāyāma” has been interpreted by commentators in various ways. Vyāsa understands it as a state that transcends the deliberate regulation of breath entirely — a spontaneous cessation that occurs in deep meditation. It is often compared to the kevala kumbhaka of the Haṭha Yoga tradition. The result of this mastery, Patañjali states in Sūtra 2.52, is that “the covering of light is dissolved” (tataḥ kṣīyate prakāśāvaraṇam) — the veil of ignorance is thinned, and the inner light of the Self becomes visible.

docs.title: 8.10 The Role of Bandhas in Prāṇāyāma
docs.text: The three bandhas or “locks” — the root lock at the perineum (mūla), the abdominal lock that makes the “great bird” of the breath fly up (uḍḍīyāna) and the chin lock (jālandhara) — are described with the other mudrās in Chapter 7 (Table 7.6). In the Haṭha texts they are integral to kumbhaka. The HYP prescribes jālandhara at the end of inhalation and uḍḍīyāna at the end of retention; applied together during kumbhaka (modern teachers call this bandha-traya), the locks are said to force the breath into the suṣumnā and awaken kuṇḍalinī.

docs.title: 8.11 Prāṇāyāma Ratios and Progressive Training
docs.text:
Later texts prescribe ratios of inhalation, retention and exhalation, measured in units (mātrā), and the Śāṇḍilya Upaniṣad’s 1:4:2 is the best known. Modern teachers usually begin with equal breathing without retention and lengthen the exhalation and then the retention by stages; such schemes are not a training programme, and long retentions should not be attempted without supervision.

Key Point: The Principle of Gradualism (Krama)

All traditional texts emphasise that prāṇāyāma must be developed gradually (śanaiḥ śanaiḥ). Just as a lion tamer gradually tames a wild animal, the yogi must gradually bring the breath under control. Forcing the breath leads to illness, mental disturbance, and even danger. The hallmark of correct practice is that it produces feelings of lightness, clarity, and joy — never strain, dizziness, or agitation.

docs.title: 8.12 Modern Scientific Understanding of Prāṇāyāma
docs.text:
Contemporary research has begun to investigate the physiological effects of controlled breathing. The diagram shows mechanisms that are proposed and partly supported; the outcomes in the top box are hypotheses under study, not established effects of prāṇāyāma (Figure 8.3).

Figure 8.3. Proposed physiological pathways for the effects of slow, controlled breathing.

Key research findings include:

  • Slow breathing (about 6 breaths/minute): Engages the baroreflex and increases heart rate variability (a marker of healthy autonomic regulation); this rate is close to the resonant frequency of the cardiovascular system and is the basis of HRV biofeedback (Lehrer and Gevirtz 2014; Zaccaro et al. 2018).

  • Alternate nostril breathing (Nāḍī Śodhana): Small trials report short-term reductions in blood pressure and anxiety; popular claims that it “balances the hemispheres” of the brain are not established.

  • Humming (as in Bhrāmarī): Weitzberg and Lundberg found that humming increases nasal nitric oxide about fifteen-fold compared with quiet exhalation, probably by improving ventilation of the paranasal sinuses (Weitzberg and Lundberg 2002). Claims of wider cardiovascular benefit do not follow from this finding.

  • Kumbhaka (Breath Retention): Breath-holding produces falling blood oxygen and rising carbon dioxide; it has measurable effects on cerebral blood flow, but prolonged retention carries risks and its long-term effects are poorly studied.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Dhyāna: Meditation and the Stages of Samādhi
docs.text:
Bhagavad Gītā 6.10

yogī yuñjīta satatam ātmānaṃ rahasi sthitaḥ ekākī yata-cittātmā nirāśīr aparigrahaḥ The yogi should constantly engage the mind in meditation, dwelling in solitude, alone, with mind and body controlled, free from expectations and possessiveness.

docs.title: 9.1 The Meaning of Dhyāna
docs.text:
Dhyāna (meditation) is the seventh limb of Patañjali’s Aṣṭāṅga Yoga and a practice common to almost every form of yoga. The word is derived from the Sanskrit root dhyai (to contemplate, to think deeply, to meditate). Patañjali defines it as the unbroken extension of a single cognition towards the object (tatra pratyayaikatānatā dhyānam, YS 3.2), a definition discussed with the other limbs in Chapter 2 (Section 2.5.6). This chapter looks at meditation as a practice: its stages, objects, methods and obstacles, and its place in the Upaniṣadic, Buddhist and Jain traditions.

Through Buddhism, the word dhyāna (Pali jhāna) gave rise to the Chinese Ch'an, the Japanese Zen, and the Korean Sŏn — a measure of how widely Indian meditative vocabulary travelled.

docs.title: 9.2 The Progressive Stages: Dhāraṇā, Dhyāna, Samādhi
docs.text: Patañjali treats concentration, meditation and absorption as one continuum, the three “internal” limbs that together form saṃyama (Chapter 2, Sections 2.5.6–2.5.7). Seen from the side of practice, the difference between them is the steadiness of attention. In concentration the mind is fixed on one point but still wanders and must be brought back; in meditation the stream of attention flows without interruption; in absorption the object alone remains and the sense of a separate meditator fades. Most meditation manuals, Hindu, Buddhist and Jain, describe some such progression from effortful focus to effortless absorption, and most warn that the later stages cannot be forced.

docs.title: 9.3 Meditation in the Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā
docs.text:
The Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā describes three types of meditation (Table 9.1).

Table 9.1. Three Types of Dhyāna (Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā) Type Name Description Gross (sthūla) Sthūla Dhyāna Meditation on a concrete form (deity, Guru, image) Luminous (jyotis) Jyotir Dhyāna Meditation on inner light; the flame of consciousness Subtle (sūkṣma) Sūkṣma Dhyāna Meditation on kuṇḍalinī, bindu, or formless Brahman

docs.title: 9.4 The Stages of Samādhi
docs.text: The stages of absorption that lie beyond meditation — the cognitive absorptions with and without gross and subtle thought, the truth-bearing insight, the seedless absorption and the “cloud of dharma” that precedes liberation — are set out once, with Patañjali’s sūtras and the commentators’ classification, in Chapter 2 (Section 2.3.6; Figure 2.1). The Haṭha texts, for their part, use samādhi as a synonym of Rāja Yoga, of the “no-mind” state (amanaska) and of the dissolution of the mind in inner sound (Chapters 7 and 10); the Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā, which closes its sevenfold path with six kinds of samādhi reached through different techniques, shows how far the term had moved from Patañjali’s analysis.

docs.title: 9.5 Meditation Posture and Environment
docs.text:
The Bhagavad Gītā provides precise instructions for the meditation posture:

Gītā 6.11–6.13

śucau deśe pratiṣṭhāpya sthiram āsanam ātmanaḥ nāty-ucchritaṃ nāti-nīcaṃ cailājina-kuśottaram tatraikāgraṃ manaḥ kṛtvā yata-cittēndriya-kriyaḥ upaviśyāsane yuñjyād yogam ātma-viśuddhaye samaṃ kāya-śiro-grīvaṃ dhārayann acalaṃ sthiraḥ saṃprekṣya nāsikāgraṃ svaṃ diśaś cānavalokayan In a clean spot, having established a firm seat for oneself, neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, deerskin, and kuśa grass; thereon, making the mind one-pointed, with thoughts and senses controlled, one should practise Yoga for self-purification, holding the body, head, and neck erect and still, gazing at the tip of the nose, not looking in any direction.

docs.title: 9.6 Yoga Nidrā: Yogic Sleep
docs.text:
Yoga Nidrā (“yogic sleep”) is a state of conscious deep sleep — a systematic method of inducing complete physical, mental, and emotional relaxation while maintaining awareness. It is often described as the state between waking and sleeping, where the body is in deep rest but the mind remains fully alert.

In pre-modern texts yoganidrā denotes either the cosmic sleep of Viṣṇu or, in some Haṭha works, a state of samādhi. The modern guided-relaxation practice of that name was created in the 1960s–70s by Swāmī Satyānanda Sarasvatī of the Bihar School of Yoga, who said he drew upon the Tantric practice of nyāsa (the ritual placing of mantras on different parts of the body) as well as modern relaxation methods.

Key Point: The Practice of Yoga Nidrā

A typical Yoga Nidrā session includes the following stages:

  1. Preparation: Lying in Śavāsana; setting a saṃkalpa (resolve)

  2. Rotation of consciousness: Awareness is guided systematically through each part of the body

  3. Breath awareness: Observation of the natural breath

  4. Opposite sensations: Experience of pairs of opposites (heavy-light, hot-cold)

  5. Visualisation: Guided imagery (nature scenes, symbols, cakras)

  6. Saṃkalpa: Repetition of the resolve

  7. Return: Gradual return to external awareness

Research on Yoga Nidrā is limited. A small brain-imaging study found increased dopamine release in the striatum during the practice (Kjaer et al. 2002), and some trials report reduced anxiety, but larger and better-controlled studies are needed.

docs.title: 9.7 The Four Attitudes (Bhāvanās)
docs.text:
Among Patañjali’s remedies for the obstacles that scatter the mind (Chapter 2, Section 2.3.5), one became a meditation practice in its own right in several traditions: the cultivation of four attitudes (bhāvanās) towards others (Table 9.2):

Yoga Sūtra 1.33

maitrī-karuṇā-muditōpekṣāṇāṃ sukha-duḥkha-puṇyāpuṇya-viṣayāṇāṃ bhāvanātaś citta-prasādanam By cultivating friendliness towards the happy, compassion towards the suffering, joy towards the virtuous, and equanimity towards the non-virtuous — the mind becomes serene.

Table 9.2. The Four Bhāvanās (Attitudes for Mental Serenity), with effects as explained by commentators. The same four are the Buddhist brahmavihāras. Attitude Towards Effect Maitrī (Friendliness) Happy people Removes jealousy Karuṇā (Compassion) Suffering people Removes callousness Muditā (Joy) Virtuous people Removes envy Upekṣā (Equanimity) Non-virtuous people Removes contempt and agitation

docs.title: 9.8 Classification of Meditation Objects in the Yoga Tradition
docs.text:
The Yoga, Tantric and Vedāntic traditions offer a wide range of meditation objects (ālambana), suited to different temperaments and usually graded from gross to subtle; Patañjali himself allows meditation on “whatever one likes” (YS 1.39). Table 9.3 groups the principal objects with their sources.

Table 9.3. Hierarchy of Meditation Objects from Gross to Subtle Category Examples Tradition and Textual Source Places in the body (deśa) Navel circle; heart lotus; light in the head; tip of the nose; tip of the tongue Vyāsa on Yoga Sūtra 3.1 Physical form (Sthūla) Mūrti of the chosen deity (Viṣṇu, Śiva, Devī); the guru; flame; yantra; lotus Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.28; Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā 6; Āgama texts Elements and cakras The five elements with their shapes and colours; the cakras with their bījas and deities Tantric and Haṭha texts; Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa Breath (Prāṇa) Inhalation-exhalation cycle; pause between breaths Yoga Sūtras 1.34; Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā Mantra Oṃ; so'ham; personal mantra from Guru Yoga Sūtras 1.27–28; Tantra texts Inner light (Jyotis) Luminous point in the heart or between the eyebrows Yoga Sūtras 1.36; Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad Sound (Nāda) Inner sounds heard in meditation; anāhata nāda Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā 4.65–102 Formless awareness Pure consciousness without object; the witness (sākṣin); the enquiry “Who am I?” Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad; Yoga Sūtras 1.51; Advaita (Chapter 4)

docs.title: 9.8.1 The Practice of Antar Trāṭaka — Internal Gazing
docs.text: The Haṭha Yoga tradition describes Trāṭaka (steady gazing) as a powerful bridge between external practice and internal meditation. After gazing steadily at an external object (typically a small mark or, in modern practice, a candle flame) until the eyes water (HYP 2.31), the practitioner closes the eyes; modern teachers add visualisation of the after-image at the ājñā cakra (the point between the eyebrows). This practice develops Ekāgratā (one-pointedness) and prepares the mind for deeper, objectless meditation.

docs.title: 9.9 Dhyāna in the Upaniṣadic Tradition
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads contain some of the earliest and most profound instructions on meditation in any tradition. The progression from the older to the younger Upaniṣads reveals an increasingly systematic understanding of contemplative practice (Table 9.4).

Table 9.4. Meditation Teachings in Major Upaniṣads Upaniṣad Key Meditation Teaching Bṛhadāraṇyaka Neti Neti — the via negativa: meditation by progressively negating all that is not the Self Chāndogya Dāhara Vidyā — meditation on the tiny space within the heart, which contains the entire universe Kaṭha The chariot metaphor: the Ātman as the rider, buddhi as the charioteer, manas as the reins, senses as the horses — meditation as the mastery of this inner vehicle Śvetāśvatara Detailed meditation posture, breath regulation, and visualisation of inner fire and light Māṇḍūkya The four states of consciousness (waking, dreaming, deep sleep, Turīya) as progressive stages of meditative realisation

The Śvetāśvatara’s instruction on posture (2.8) is quoted in Chapter 1.

The Dāhara Vidyā — Meditation on the Inner Space

The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (8.1.3) declares: “As vast as this external space is the space within the heart. Within it are contained both heaven and earth, both fire and wind, both sun and moon, lightning and stars. Whatever is here in the world and whatever is not — all that is contained within the heart.” This Dāhara Vidyā (meditation on the tiny inner space) represents one of the most ancient and profound meditation techniques in the Indian tradition. The practitioner is instructed to contemplate the space within the heart as identical with infinite Brahman — discovering that the microcosm of the individual self contains the entirety of the macrocosm.

docs.title: 9.10 Buddhist and Jain Yoga
docs.text: Brahmanical Yoga was never the only Indian science of meditation. Buddhist and Jain renunciants developed their own disciplines from the time of the Buddha and Mahāvīra, and the three traditions borrowed from, argued with and redefined one another for well over a thousand years (Bronkhorst 1993; Samuel 2008). Their doctrines and institutions are treated in Volume 4, Buddha–Jina Prabhā; this section outlines their contribution to the history of yoga.

docs.title: 9.10.1 Buddhist Meditation
docs.text:
The early Buddhist discourses (the Pali Nikāyas and their parallels in other languages) describe four meditative absorptions, the jhānas (Sanskrit dhyāna). The first is accompanied by applied and sustained thought (vitakka, vicāra) and by the rapture and happiness born of seclusion; in the second, thought falls away and the mind becomes unified; in the third, rapture fades into equanimity and mindfulness; the fourth is beyond pleasure and pain, purified by equanimity. Beyond these lie four formless attainments, from the sphere of infinite space to the sphere of “neither perception nor non-perception”. According to the discourses, the future Buddha learnt the last two from his teachers Āḷāra Kālāma and Uddaka Rāmaputta and found them insufficient; liberation required insight (vipassanā, Sanskrit vipaśyanā) into impermanence, unsatisfactoriness and not-self, joined to calm (samatha, śamatha) (Gethin 1998; Wynne 2007). The Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta organises mindfulness under four headings — body (beginning with the breath), feelings, mind and mental phenomena — and became the charter of later insight meditation.

The parallels with Patañjali are close and long recognised. The first two stages of cognitive samādhi in YS 1.17 bear the Buddhist names vitarka and vicāra; the five qualities that lead to samādhi in YS 1.20 (faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration and insight) are the Buddhist five “faculties”; and the four attitudes of YS 1.33 (Table 9.2) are the Buddhist brahmavihāras. Buddhist scholasticism produced its own manuals of yoga. Buddhaghosa’s Visuddhimagga (5th century) lists forty meditation subjects — coloured and elemental discs (kasiṇa), the foulness of the body, recollections, the four divine abidings and others — and matches them to the temperaments of different students. In North India the school known as Yogācāra (“practitioners of yoga”) took its name from meditative practice, and its vast Yogācārabhūmi maps the stages of the path. The late Buddhist Tantras taught subtle-body practices of their own: the Kālacakra Tantra (early 11th century) teaches a six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga) of withdrawal, meditation, breath control, retention, recollection and absorption, and the earliest Haṭha text, the Amṛtasiddhi, comes from a Buddhist milieu (Chapter 7). The Tantras of this class divide practice into a “generation stage” (utpattikrama), in which the practitioner visualises himself as the deity in its maṇḍala, and a “completion stage” (sampannakrama or niṣpannakrama), in which he works directly with the channels, winds and drops (nāḍī, prāṇa, bindu) to bring the winds into the central channel. The completion-stage yogas — among them the “inner heat” (caṇḍālī, Tibetan gtum mo) of the Hevajra Tantra and the cycle later known in Tibet as the Six Yogas of Nāropa — were carried to Tibet from the eleventh century and are still practised there; they are the closest Buddhist relatives of Haṭha Yoga’s aim of forcing the breath into the central channel (Samuel 2008). In the 20th century the Burmese revival of insight meditation, carried to India by S.N. Goenka from 1969, and the secular “mindfulness” programmes derived from it, made Buddhist meditation as global as postural yoga.

docs.title: 9.10.2 Jain Meditation and Jain Yoga
docs.text:
Jain usage is distinctive. In Jain doctrine yoga first means the activity of body, speech and mind through which karmic matter flows into the soul (kāya-vāṅ-manaḥ-karma yogaḥ, Tattvārthasūtra 6.1); the ascetic’s aim is to bring this “yoga” to rest. The early ideal is the motionless standing posture of “abandoning the body” (kāyotsarga) in which Mahāvīra and the Tīrthaṅkaras are portrayed. Umāsvāti’s Tattvārthasūtra defines meditation (dhyāna) as the restraint of thought on a single object (9.27) and distinguishes four kinds: “sorrowful” and “cruel” meditation, which bind, and “virtuous” (dharma) and “pure” (śukla) meditation, which lead to liberation (Dundas 2002).

From the 8th century Jain authors engaged directly with Patañjala Yoga. Haribhadra Sūri wrote several works on yoga, among them the Yogabindu and the Yogadṛṣṭisamuccaya, which arranges the path in eight “views” (dṛṣṭi) correlated with Patañjali’s eight limbs and discusses the yogas of other schools with notable generosity (Chapple 2003). Śubhacandra’s Jñānārṇava (11th century) and Hemacandra’s Yogaśāstra (12th century), written for the Caulukya king Kumārapāla, combine the ethics of the Jain layman and monk with breath control and four graded objects of virtuous meditation — the body, syllables and mantras, the form of the Jina, and the formless — while warning that breath control is not needed for liberation and may disturb the mind (Qvarnström 2002). In the 1970s Ācārya Mahāprajña of the Terāpanth order developed Prekṣā Dhyāna, a modern Jain meditation system that draws on these sources.

docs.title: 9.10.3 Shared Ground
docs.text: Across the three traditions the vocabulary of practice — dhyāna, samādhi, bhāvanā, the breath, the four divine attitudes — is largely shared, while the goal is understood differently: the isolation of the self (puruṣa) in Sāṃkhya-Yoga, the extinction of craving and ignorance (nirvāṇa) in Buddhism, and the release of the soul (jīva) from karmic matter in Jainism. Christian contemplative prayer, Sufi murāqaba and Daoist inner alchemy also cultivate inner stillness, and interpret it in their own terms.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Mantra Yoga, Laya Yoga, and Nāda Yoga
docs.text: Part A: Mantra Yoga — The Path of Sacred Sound

docs.title: 10.1 Mantra
docs.text:
Mantra Yoga is the spiritual discipline based on the repetitive chanting or mental recitation of sacred sound formulas (mantras). Grammatically, mantra is formed from the root man (to think) with the instrumental suffix -tra: “an instrument of thought”. Tantric texts add a traditional etymology, mananāt trāyate, “that which protects when it is meditated upon”.

Definition: Mantra

A mantra is a sacred syllable, word, or phrase believed to be endowed with spiritual power (śakti). According to the tradition, when it is repeated with faith, concentration, and proper intonation, it transforms the consciousness of the practitioner, purifies the mind, and leads to the direct experience of the deity or principle that the mantra embodies.

Several Indian traditions treat sound (śabda) as a primordial creative force. The Upaniṣads speak of a “sound-Brahman” (śabda-brahman) to be known before the supreme Brahman (Maitrī Upaniṣad 6.22); the grammarian Bhartṛhari (5th century) identified Brahman with the eternal Word; and the Tantras describe the universe as unfolding from the Goddess as Speech (vāk) through the letters of the alphabet (see Volume 10, Śabda Vidyā). The Vedic tradition is fundamentally an oral tradition, in which the sacred sounds of the Vedas are transmitted with extraordinary precision from Guru to disciple.

docs.title: 10.2 Types of Mantras
docs.text:
Table 10.1 lists the principal kinds of mantra.

Table 10.1. Classification of Mantras Type Description and Examples Bīja Mantras (Seed) Single-syllable mantras containing the essence of a deity or element: Oṃ, Hrīṃ, Klīṃ, Śrīṃ, Aiṃ Vedic Mantras Mantras from the Vedas: Gāyatrī Mantra, Mahāmṛtyuñjaya Mantra (ṚV 7.59.12), Śānti Mantras Purāṇic and Āgamic Mantras Formulas of devotional and sectarian worship: Om Namaḥ Śivāya, Om Namo Nārāyaṇāya Tāntric Mantras Complex formulas from the Tantra traditions, often with specific nyāsa rituals Nāma Mantras Divine names: Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Hari, Devī

docs.title: 10.2.1 The Praṇava: Oṃ
docs.text:
The supreme mantra of the Yoga tradition is Oṃ (also written AUM), known as the Praṇava. It is the primordial sound from which all creation emerges and into which it dissolves.

Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 1

oṃ ity etad akṣaram idaṃ sarvaṃ tasyopavyākhyānaṃ bhūtaṃ bhavad bhaviṣyad iti sarvam oṃkāra eva yac cānyat trikālātītaṃ tad apy oṃkāra eva Oṃ — this syllable is all this. All that is past, present, and future is Oṃ. And whatever transcends the three times — that too is Oṃ.

The Upaniṣad goes on (verses 8–12) to equate the three constituent sounds A, U and M with the waking, dreaming and deep-sleep states of the self — named Vaiśvānara, Taijasa and Prājña — and the soundless “measureless” syllable with the fourth state, Turīya (see Table 1.5 in Chapter 1). Repetition of Oṃ is thus also a contemplation of the whole range of consciousness.

docs.title: 10.2.2 The Gāyatrī Mantra
docs.text:
The Gāyatrī Mantra (also called the Sāvitrī) is considered the most sacred mantra of the Vedic tradition. The verse itself is Ṛg Veda 3.62.10; the opening om bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ (the syllable Oṃ and the three “utterances”, vyāhṛtis) is prefixed in ritual use. Traditionally its recitation was restricted to initiated twice-born men; in the 19th and 20th centuries reform movements such as the Ārya Samāj and many modern teachers opened it to all.

Gāyatrī Mantra — Ṛg Veda 3.62.10, with the ritual prefix

om bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt We meditate upon the glorious splendour of the Divine Light (Savitṛ). May that Light illuminate our intellects.

docs.title: 10.3 Methods of Japa (Mantra Repetition)
docs.text:
Japa is the systematic repetition of a mantra. The tradition distinguishes three modes: aloud (vācika), whispered so that the lips move but no sound is heard (upāṃśu), and mental (mānasa). The Manusmṛti (2.85) already ranks them, declaring the sacrifice of muttered prayer ten times better than the prescribed rites, the whispered form a hundred times and the mental a thousand times better; mental japa is accordingly held by the tradition to be the most powerful. Repetitions are usually counted on a rosary (mālā) of 108 beads, and modern devotional practice adds the writing of a mantra many times over (likhita japa). Patañjali’s own instruction on the praṇava concerns meaning as much as sound:

Yoga Sūtra 1.28

taj-japas tad-artha-bhāvanam The repetition of that (Praṇava) and meditation on its meaning (is the practice).

Patañjali emphasises that japa must be accompanied by artha-bhāvanam — deep contemplation of the meaning. Mechanical repetition without awareness yields limited results; it is the union of sound and meaning that produces the transformative power of mantra.

docs.title: 10.4 The Bīja Mantras and the Cakras
docs.text:
In the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa each of the six cakras carries the seed syllable (bīja) of its element — laṃ (earth), vaṃ (water), raṃ (fire), yaṃ (air) and haṃ (space) — with Oṃ at the ājñā; the syllables are installed and meditated upon in the cakras, together with the letters on the petals of each lotus (Table 6.3 in Chapter 6). The psychological “effects” that modern teachers attach to each bīja (grounding, creativity, confidence and so on) are not found in the classical texts.

Part B: Laya Yoga — The Yoga of Dissolution

docs.title: 10.5 The Meaning of Laya
docs.text:
Laya means “dissolution”, “absorption” or “merging”, and layayoga is the yoga in which the mind is dissolved in its object until no separate mind remains. The Haṭha texts define the state precisely:

HYP 4.34

layo laya iti prāhuḥ kīdṛśaṃ laya-lakṣaṇam apunar-vāsanotthānāl layo viṣaya-vismṛtiḥ People say “laya, laya” — but what is the mark of laya? Laya is the forgetting of sense-objects, because latent impressions no longer arise.

In the medieval yoga texts layayoga is one of four yogas, with mantra, haṭha and rāja. The Dattātreyayogaśāstra and the Amaraughaprabodha arrange the four in a hierarchy of practitioners, in which laya stands above mantra and below haṭha and rāja (Chapter 7, Section 7.3.1), and the Yogabīja makes them successive stages of one “great yoga”. The methods the texts group under laya are varied: fixing the mind on points inside or outside the body, gazes such as the śāmbhavī mudrā, in which the eyes are open but attention is turned inward, and above all listening to the inner sound. The Haṭhapradīpikā says that Ādinātha taught a vast number of methods of laya, but that attention to the inner sound (nādānusandhāna) is the foremost of them (4.66), and it treats laya, the “no-mind” state (amanaska), Rāja Yoga and samādhi as names for one goal (4.3–4) (Birch 2011; Mallinson and Singleton 2017).

docs.title: 10.5.1 The Dissolution of the Elements
docs.text:
A second meaning of laya comes from Tantric ritual. In the rite of purifying the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), which precedes worship in many Tantras, the practitioner dissolves the elements of his body in imagination, each into its subtler source — earth into water, water into fire, fire into air, air into ether, ether into mind and mind into pure consciousness — and then rebuilds a divine body in which the deity can be worshipped. The ascent of kuṇḍalinī through the cakras, each the seat of an element, was read in the same terms (Chapter 6). The modern presentation of “Laya Yoga” as a systematic dissolution of the elements through the cakras combines this Tantric rite with the medieval yoga of absorption; the classical sources keep them apart.

Part C: Nāda Yoga — The Yoga of Inner Sound

docs.title: 10.6 The Meaning of Nāda
docs.text:
Nāda literally means “sound” or “vibration.” Nāda Yoga is the discipline of attuning to the inner, mystical sound (anāhata nāda — the “unstruck sound”) that arises spontaneously within the body, without any external cause. By following this inner sound deeper and deeper, the mind is drawn inward and eventually dissolves in the supreme silence.

HYP 4.93

sarva-cintāṃ parityajya sāvadhānena cetasā nāda evānusandheyo yoga-sāmrājyam icchatā Abandoning all thoughts, with an attentive mind, one who desires the kingdom of Yoga should concentrate solely on Nāda.

docs.title: 10.7 The Four Stages of Nāda
docs.text:
The Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā (4.69–76) describes four progressive stages as the breath pierces the three knots, each marked by a characteristic inner sound (Table 10.2).

Table 10.2. The Four Stages of Nāda (Inner Sound) Stage Name Description of the Sound 1 Ārambha (Beginning) Brahma granthi pierced; tinkling of ornaments heard in the space of the heart 2 Ghaṭa (Pot) Viṣṇu granthi pierced; the breath enters the middle channel; the sound of a kettledrum in the throat 3 Paricaya (Familiarity) The sound of a drum (mardala) in the space between the eyebrows 4 Niṣpatti (Consummation) Rudra granthi pierced; sounds of flute and vīṇā; the state of Rāja Yoga

Elsewhere in the same chapter (4.85–86) the HYP describes the sounds heard as practice deepens: at first loud sounds like the ocean, thunder and kettledrums; in the middle, drums, conch and bells; at the end, tinkling bells, flute, vīṇā and the humming of bees.

docs.title: 10.8 The Practice of Nāda Yoga
docs.text:
The HYP’s instructions are brief. The yogin sits in the “liberated” posture (muktāsana), adopts the inward gaze of śāmbhavī mudrā and listens to the sound in the right ear (4.67); later teachers add the closing of the ears, eyes and mouth with the fingers (ṣaṇmukhī mudrā). At first loud, external-seeming sounds are heard, then subtler ones; the mind, the text says, is drawn to the subtlest sound as a bee to nectar and dissolves in it, and when even that sound ceases the yogin is in samādhi.

The doctrine of inner sound did not stay within the yoga texts. The Sants and the Sikh Gurus spoke of the “unstruck” sound (anahad) as the sign of the divine name realised within (Chapter 7, Section 7.17). Musicians took it over too. Śārṅgadeva’s Saṅgītaratnākara (13th century), the most influential Sanskrit treatise on music, opens its account of musical sound with a description of the body and its centres and derives audible sound (āhata) from the meeting of breath and the body’s fire, beside the unstruck sound (anāhata) of the yogins; “Nāda Yoga” is still the name by which Indian musicians describe their discipline (Volume 9, Saṅgīta–Nāṭya).

docs.title: 10.9 The Principal Bīja Mantras
docs.text:
The Bīja Mantras (seed syllables) represent the most concentrated form of sacred sound. Each Bīja is understood not as a word with lexical meaning but as a sonic essence — a vibrational pattern that directly embodies the energy of a specific cosmic principle or deity (Table 10.3).

Table 10.3. Major Bīja Mantras and Their Deities (the cakra assignments reflect modern teaching and vary between sources) Bīja Deity/Principle Cakra Significance Oṃ Brahman (the Absolute) Sahasrāra The source of all mantras; the praṇava Hrīṃ Māyā Śakti Anāhata The heart bīja; veiling and revealing power Śrīṃ Lakṣmī Maṇipūra Abundance, auspiciousness, prosperity Klīṃ Kāmadeva / Kṛṣṇa Svādhiṣṭhāna Desire, attraction, creative energy Aiṃ Sarasvatī Viśuddha Knowledge, speech, learning Hūṃ Śiva / Agni Maṇipūra Destruction of obstacles; fierce protective energy Krīṃ Kālī Mūlādhāra Transformative power; dissolution of bondage Gaṃ Gaṇeśa Mūlādhāra Removal of obstacles; auspicious beginnings

Tantric texts give many of these syllables traditional names. Oṃ is the praṇava, regarded as the seed from which all others emerge; Hrīṃ is the “seed of Māyā” or of Bhuvaneśvarī; Klīṃ the “seed of desire” (kāmabīja); Śrīṃ the seed of Śrī or Lakṣmī; and Aiṃ the “seed of speech” (vāgbīja), sacred to Sarasvatī.

In the ritual use of a mantra, the kīlaka (“pin”) is a component said to “lock” its power, which is released by proper initiation. The ending in nasal resonance (anusvāra, ṃ) is interpreted in Tantric theory as the bindu; claims that bījas have been shown to have specific physiological effects are not supported by research.

docs.title: 10.10 Mantra and the Guru-Śiṣya Paramparā
docs.text:
In the traditional understanding, a mantra is not effective merely by being read from a book or heard casually. It must be received through Dīkṣā (initiation) from a qualified Guru who stands in an unbroken lineage (Paramparā) of transmission. The Guru imparts not merely the sound but the caitanya (consciousness-energy) of the mantra, awakened through his or her own practice (Table 10.4).

Table 10.4. Stages of Mantra Transmission and Practice Stage Sanskrit Term Description Initiation Dīkṣā The Guru transmits the mantra with its specific svara (intonation), nyāsa (ritual placement), and dhyāna-śloka (meditation verse) Preliminary practice Puraścaraṇa The practitioner completes the prescribed number of repetitions (often 100,000 per syllable of the mantra) to “awaken” the mantra Matured practice Mantra Siddhi Through sustained practice, the mantra becomes spontaneously active in the practitioner’s consciousness, arising without effort Integration Ajāpā Japa The mantra merges with the breath and continues spontaneously, even during sleep

Scholarly Note: The Concept of Mantra Caitanya

The concept of Mantra Caitanya — the “aliveness” or “awakened consciousness” of a mantra — is central to the Tantric understanding of sacred sound. A mantra without Caitanya is compared to a seed that has been roasted: it retains its external form but has lost the capacity to sprout. The Guru’s role in Dīkṣā is held to be precisely to transmit this living energy, which has been maintained through an unbroken chain of teacher-to-student transmission extending, in principle, back to the original Ṛṣi who first “heard” the mantra in deep meditation.

docs.title: 10.11 The Integration of Mantra, Laya, and Nāda
docs.text: Mantra Yoga, Laya Yoga, and Nāda Yoga are intimately related. Mantra provides the external vehicle of sound; Laya provides the process of progressive dissolution; and Nāda provides the inner guide that leads the mind to its final dissolution in the Absolute. Together, they constitute a path of liberation through sound — from the grossest audible chant to the subtlest inaudible vibration, and finally, in the tradition’s own terms, to the silence beyond all sound, which is Brahman itself (compare HYP 4.5, quoted in Chapter 7).

docs.title: Chapter 11: Yoga in the Modern World: Global Spread and Contemporary Debates
docs.text:
Bhagavad Gītā 6.46

tapasvibhyo'dhiko yogī jñānibhyo'pi mato'dhikaḥ karmibhyaś cādhiko yogī tasmād yogī bhavārjuna The yogi is superior to the ascetic, superior even to the person of knowledge, and superior to the one who performs ritual action. Therefore, O Arjuna, be a yogi.

docs.title: 11.1 Introduction: Yoga’s Journey Across the World
docs.text:
In the last 130 years Yoga has travelled further than at any time in its long history. Practised in some form on every continent, taught in studios, hospitals, schools and prisons, and promoted by the Government of India and the United Nations, it has become one of India’s most visible contributions to world culture.

This success raises questions that this chapter tries to answer honestly. What exactly travelled? Modern “yoga” — for most people a class of postures and breathing — differs greatly from the meditative discipline of Patañjali and from the secret ascetic techniques of medieval Haṭha Yoga. How did the modern form come about? What does scientific research actually show about its health effects? And what has been the cost of the guru model when it has been transplanted into commercial settings?
