docs.title: 13.11 The Tamil Country: The Tirumantiram and the Siddhas
docs.text:
The Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta, the Nāyaṉmārs and the later Siddha poets are treated in Chapter 2 and below. One text, however, stands between Sanskrit Tantra and Tamil devotion and deserves separate notice: the Tirumantiram (“Sacred Mantra”), ascribed to Tirumūlar and placed as the tenth book of the Śaiva canon, the Tirumuṟai (Zvelebil 1975).

The legend and the date. According to the Periyapurāṇam, Tirumūlar was a yogi from Kailāsa who, travelling in the Tamil country, entered the body of a dead cowherd named Mūlaṉ out of pity for his grieving cows, and remained in it to compose the work, at the rate of one verse a year. Tradition therefore makes the text very old. Modern estimates range from about the sixth to the twelfth century. The work’s familiarity with developed Tantric doctrine — the Āgamas by name, the categories of the Siddhānta, a yoga of cakras and kuṇḍalinī, diagrams made of syllables, and the worship of a goddess in forms close to those of the Śākta Tantras — has led many scholars to favour a date late in this range, and the text as we have it may be composite (Zvelebil 1975).

Contents. The Tirumantiram consists of about three thousand quatrains in nine books (tantiram), a structure that itself recalls the Sanskrit scriptures. It treats Śiva, souls and bonds; morality and the dangers of attachment; a yoga of eight limbs that includes breath control and the raising of inner power; mantras and their diagrams (cakkaram); the grace of Śiva and the guru; and the states of the liberated. Several of its verses are among the most quoted in Tamil religious literature. One declares that love and Śiva are not two; another, that those who let the body perish lose the soul as well, and that the poet learnt to preserve the body and so preserved the soul; another, that the heart is the great shrine and the body of flesh the temple; and a much-quoted line proclaims that humanity is one family and God is one.

Significance. The Tirumantiram shows that the Sanskrit Tantric world view — initiation, mantra, yoga of the subtle body, the identification of body and temple — was rendered into Tamil verse and absorbed into the Tamil Śaiva canon. It became an authority both for the Siddhānta theologians and for the Siddha poets who rejected temple ritual, and it remains a point of reference for modern Tamil Śaivism.

docs.title: 13.11.1 The Tamil Siddhas
docs.text:
The Tamil country has its own tradition of cittar (from Sanskrit siddha), poet-yogis whose verses are among the most radical in Indian religious literature. Tradition counts eighteen Siddhas (patiṉeṇ cittar), but the lists differ, and the poems collected under the names of figures such as Civavākkiyar, Pāmpāṭṭi Cittar, Iṭaikkāṭar, Akappēy Cittar and Paṭṭiṉattār are difficult to date; most are probably late medieval or early modern, though Tirumūlar’s Tirumantiram is often regarded as their precursor (Zvelebil 1973).

Written in plain, colloquial Tamil, the Siddha poems ridicule image worship, temple ritual, pilgrimage, the authority of the Vedas and the claims of caste and of the Brahmin priesthood, and they locate the divine within the body, to be realised through yoga, breath control and the raising of kuṇḍalinī. Many Siddhas are also credited with alchemy and medicine. The Tamil Siddha system of medicine (citta maruttuvam), now one of the officially recognised systems of medicine in India, traces itself to them and uses mineral and metallic as well as herbal preparations, and legend credits the Siddha Pōkar with making the image of Murukaṉ at Paḻaṉi. The Siddhas thus share the Nāthas’ concern with the perfected body, while their critique of caste and ritual recalls that of the Vīraśaiva poets (Section 2.10). The safety note in Section 13.12.2 applies equally to Siddha mineral preparations.

docs.title: 13.12 Orders across the Regions: The Nātha Yogis
docs.text: The Nātha or Kānphatā yogis, who trace their lineage to Matsyendranātha and Gorakṣanātha (probably 11th–13th centuries), are an order of Śaiva ascetics whose traditions bridge Kaula Tantra and haṭha yoga. Matsyendranātha is honoured as the founder of a Kaula tradition, and a Kaulajñānanirṇaya is ascribed to him. The Nāthas became the principal exponents of haṭha yoga, with its techniques of posture, breath control, “seals” (mudrās) and “locks” (bandhas) aimed at the raising of kuṇḍalinī and the preservation of vital fluid, and with a goal of bodily immortality and powers. Recent research has shown, however, that the earliest haṭha texts, such as the Amṛtasiddhi (11th century) and the Dattātreyayogaśāstra (13th century), arose in Buddhist and Vaiṣṇava as well as Śaiva milieus; the Haṭhapradīpikā of Svātmārāma (15th century) compiled these earlier teachings (Mallinson and Singleton 2017); see Volume 5, Yoga Taraṅgiṇī, for haṭha yoga itself. The Nāthas were open to men of all castes and attracted a large popular following, and the lists of the “nine Nāthas” vary from region to region.

docs.title: 13.12.1 Nāthas, Sufis and Sants
docs.text:
From the thirteenth century the Nāthas were among the most visible religious figures of North India, and their ideas crossed religious boundaries. A treatise on yoga called the Amṛtakuṇḍa (“Pool of Nectar”), now lost in its original form, was translated into Arabic and Persian; the Persian version, the Baḥr al-ḥayāt (“Ocean of Life”) of the Shaṭṭārī Sufi Muḥammad Ghawth Gwāliyārī (d. 1563), describes yogic postures, breath control and the recitation of mantras alongside the Sufi practice of remembrance (dhikr). Carl Ernst has shown how these translations recast yoga in Islamic terms while preserving much of its technical content (Ernst 2003). In the same milieu the songs of Kabīr and other Sants drew on Nātha vocabulary — the “unstruck” sound, the central channel, the inner nectar — while rejecting the ritual of both Hindus and Muslims, and Nāth yogis appear frequently in Persian chronicles and in Mughal painting. These exchanges are a reminder that the yogic and Tantric traditions were never confined to a single religious community.

The Sikh scripture preserves the most direct record of such an exchange. The Siddh Goṣṭ (“Discourse with the Siddhas”), a long composition of Guru Nānak (1469–1539) in the section of the Ādi Granth devoted to the rāga Rāmkalī, presents a dialogue in verse between Nānak and Nāth yogis, in which the yogis question him about his path and he answers that liberation comes not from the yogi’s earrings, ash, patched coat and bodily disciplines, nor from withdrawal from the world, but from the divine Name and the Word received through the Guru, by one who lives as a householder. Nānak’s hymns elsewhere take over and reinterpret Nāth vocabulary — the “unstruck” sound, the “tenth door” at the crown of the head, the “innate” state (sahaj). W.H. McLeod showed how the Nāth tradition formed both the background and the foil of Nānak’s teaching (McLeod 1968); the Sikh tradition as a whole lies outside the scope of this volume.

docs.title: 13.12.2 Tantra and Alchemy
docs.text:
Indian alchemy (rasaśāstra, “the science of mercury”) developed in close association with the Tantric and Nātha traditions from about the tenth century. Works such as the Rasahṛdayatantra of Govinda and the Rasārṇava present alchemy as a path to liberation in a perfected, immortal body: mercury is identified with the semen of Śiva and sulphur with the menstrual blood of the Goddess, and the alchemist’s “killing” and “binding” of mercury parallels the yogin’s mastery of breath and seed. David Gordon White has described this “alchemical body” as a meeting point of Tantra, haṭha yoga and medicine (White 1996). Rasaśāstra later became part of Āyurvedic pharmacy, where mercurial and other metallic preparations (bhasmas) are still made.

Health and Safety Note

Classical alchemical and rasaśāstra preparations contain mercury, lead, arsenic and other toxic metals. Studies of Āyurvedic products sold in the United States and over the internet found detectable heavy metals in about a fifth of those tested, in some cases at levels exceeding safety limits, and products containing rasa ingredients were especially likely to be contaminated (Saper et al. 2004, 2008). No recipe in the alchemical texts should be prepared or taken; the account here is historical only.

docs.title: 13.13 Regional Patterns
docs.text:
Table 13.1 compares the regional traditions surveyed in this chapter.

Four patterns stand out. First, everywhere the Sanskrit Tantric system was adapted to a regional priesthood and to regional kings: the Nampūtiri tantrī, the Bengali digest-writer, the Kāmākhyā priest and the Newar Rājopādhyāya are all local specialists in a pan-Indian discipline. Second, in every region learned Tantric ritual coexists with non-Brahmin performers and local deities — teyyam and muṭiyēṟṟu dancers, the daitās of Purī, the masked Navadurgā — who embody the gods in ways the Sanskrit texts only partly control. Third, regional traditions generated their own critics: the Ekasaraṇa movement of Assam, the Bengali Vaiṣṇavas, the Tamil Siddhas and the modern temple-entry movements of Kerala all contested the claims of Tantric ritual specialists. Fourth, the regions were never sealed off from each other: Nātha yogis, Siddhas, Śaiva preceptors and Bengali priests carried texts, practices and deities between them, and a goddess or a lineage could travel from one end of the subcontinent to the other.

docs.title: Chapter 14: Interpreting Tantra: Ethics, Reception and Scholarship
14.1 Introduction
docs.text: The Tantric traditions have seldom been described without being judged. Their own authors ranked them above the Veda; Brahmanical critics called them heretical; colonial missionaries saw in them the worst of Hinduism; Indian reformers disowned them or reinterpreted them; and modern Western readers have made them, by turns, a scandal, a philosophy and a technique of pleasure. The preceding chapters have described the traditions themselves. This one turns to the questions that their judges have asked. It considers first what the traditions prescribe about conduct and how they justified their transgressions; then the history of how “Tantra” has been condemned, defended, marketed and studied since the late eighteenth century; and finally how scholars now define the subject, and what remains of the traditions as living religions.

docs.title: 14.2 The Ethics of Tantra
docs.text:
The Āgamas bind their initiates with detailed rules (samayas): devotion to the guru and the deity, regular worship, truthfulness, purity, secrecy and the avoidance of harm, with expiations for every breach (Section 9.8). The Siddhānta, the most widely followed form of Tantric Śaivism, largely accepted the norms of Brahmanical society, and its manuals read in many places like codes of householder discipline. The Bhairava and Kaula traditions, and the Buddhist Yoginītantras, prescribed rites that deliberately violated those norms: the consumption of meat and alcohol, sexual ritual and the use of impure substances (Chapter 4). Their stated rationale was that the conventional distinction of pure and impure is itself a form of bondage, and that its ritual transcendence frees the initiate from the limited self (Sanderson 1988; White 2003). The same texts confined these rites to qualified initiates and condemned those who used them for indulgence, and the Buddhist vows required the practitioner never to abandon compassion for beings (Section 10.7.1).

Two further elements belong to the historical record as much as the philosophy does. The manuals contain rites for subjugating, paralysing, driving away and even killing enemies, the “six acts” (Section 7.3.3), whose ethics troubled the traditions themselves; and many Āgamic and Śākta traditions practised animal sacrifice (Section 4.12). On caste and gender, the earlier chapters have shown that Tantric openness to initiates of all castes and to women was real but limited: caste distinctions were often suspended in the ritual and retained in social life, priesthood became hereditary and caste-bound, and texts composed by men frequently treated women as means to male attainment (Sections 1.8 and 4.14). The debates over temple priesthood discussed in Section 11.10 show that these questions remain open.

docs.title: 14.3 Tantra in Modern Hindu Movements
docs.text:
Modern Hindu attitudes to Tantra have been ambivalent. Rāmakṛṣṇa (1836–1886) practised a series of Tantric disciplines under a female teacher at Dakṣiṇeśvar (Section 4.14.3), yet his disciple Vivekānanda, while revering the Goddess, criticised the left-hand rites and presented Vedānta as the core of Hinduism. In Bengal, scholars such as Atal Bihari Ghose worked with Woodroffe on the Tantrik Texts, and Gopinath Kaviraj (1887–1976) devoted a lifetime of scholarship and practice to Tantric traditions. Sri Aurobindo drew on the Tantric affirmation of the world and of Śakti in his integral yoga. In Kashmir, Svāmī Lakṣmaṇ Jū taught the Trika, and in South India Śrīvidyā gurus initiated growing circles of urban disciples (Urban 2003; Brooks 1992).

At the same time, the word “tāntrik” retains, in much of India, connotations of black magic, and self-styled tantriks offering exorcism, love charms or cures have been prosecuted under laws against superstition and fraud, such as Maharashtra’s anti-superstition act of 2013. The gap between the learned traditions described in this volume and the popular image of the “tantrik” remains wide.

docs.title: 14.4 “Tantra” in Colonial and Modern Perception
docs.text: The modern image of Tantra was made in two stages. In the nineteenth century missionaries, orientalists and many Hindu reformers described “Tantrism” as the degenerate underside of Hinduism, and Sir John Woodroffe (Arthur Avalon) and his Indian collaborators answered by presenting it as a profound and ethically respectable philosophy. In the twentieth century Western teachers and writers reinvented it as a technique of sexual fulfilment and spiritual self-development. Hugh Urban has shown how the condemnation, the rehabilitation and the reinvention each constructed “Tantra” as a category in response to the concerns of its own time (Urban 2003). Each stage left its mark on how the traditions are still perceived.

docs.title: 14.4.1 Missionaries, Orientalists and Reformers
docs.text: The first detailed European accounts of Tantric worship came from Bengal, where missionaries and East India Company scholars met the Śākta religion of the region at first hand. The Baptist missionary William Ward of Serampore, whose account of the Hindus (first published in 1811 and enlarged in later editions) was widely read in Britain, described the left-hand rites as the extreme point of Hindu idolatry and moral corruption; Horace Hayman Wilson’s survey of the Hindu sects (1828–1832) treated the Śāktas more soberly but still as a degenerate late development, and Monier Monier-Williams later wrote in the same vein. Urban has shown how such accounts made “Tantrism” the convenient image of everything that colonial rule claimed to reform: secret, sexual, irrational and, through blood sacrifice, violent (Urban 2003). Many Bengali reformers accepted the diagnosis. Some, as the case of the Mahānirvāṇa Tantra shows (Section 4.5), sought a purified Tantra compatible with monotheism and law; others, like the Brāhmo leaders, rejected Tantric worship altogether, and the word “tāntrik” acquired the pejorative sense that it still has in much of India.

docs.title: 14.4.2 Woodroffe and His Collaborators
docs.text: The rehabilitation of Tantra in English is associated above all with Sir John Woodroffe (1865–1936), a judge of the Calcutta High Court who published, under the name Arthur Avalon, translations and studies that included The Serpent Power (1919), the work that introduced the six-cakra system of Pūrṇānanda to Western readers (Avalon 1913, 1919). Kathleen Taylor’s study has shown that “Arthur Avalon” was in large part a collaborative identity: much of the Sanskrit work was done by Woodroffe’s Bengali associates, above all Atal Bihari Ghose, whose role was obscured by the pseudonym (Taylor 2001). Woodroffe’s own contribution was to present Tantra as a coherent, philosophically serious Śāstra, continuous with the Veda and suited to the present age, and to explain its transgressive rites as symbolic or as reserved for a small qualified elite. This apologetic reading answered the missionary caricature, but it also gave the late Bengali Tantras, and the Mahānirvāṇa above all, a representative status that historical scholarship has since qualified (Chapter 4).

docs.title: 14.4.3 The Goddess and Bengali Nationalism
docs.text: In the decades around 1900 the Goddess of the Bengali Śāktas became a symbol of the nation. Bankimcandra Chattopadhyay’s novel Ānandamaṭh (1882), with its hymn Vande Mātaram, presented the motherland as a goddess to be served by ascetic warriors, and the pamphlet Bhavānī Mandir (1905), associated with Aurobindo Ghose, proposed a temple to the Goddess as the power (śakti) of India, served by a dedicated order. Some members of the revolutionary societies of Bengal took vows before images of Kālī. Colonial officials, for their part, read the revolutionary violence of these years through the old image of Tantric blood sacrifice. Urban has traced how the Goddess and the language of sacrifice served both as a nationalist idiom and as a colonial explanation of “terrorism” (Urban 2003). The episode shows that the meanings attached to Tantra were never only religious.

docs.title: 14.4.4 Pierre Bernard and the American “Tantriks”
docs.text: In the United States the word “Tantra” was first popularised by Pierre Arnold Bernard (born Perry Baker, 1875 or 1876–1955), who founded a “Tantrik Order” in the first decade of the twentieth century, attracted newspaper notoriety as “Oom the Omnipotent”, and later ran a country club at Nyack, New York, where wealthy clients practised haṭha yoga. Bernard had some genuine knowledge of yoga, and his nephew Theos Bernard became a serious student of Tibetan Buddhism; but the “Tantra” he offered combined physical culture, secret initiation and sexual frankness in a form that had little to do with the Indian traditions (Love 2010; Urban 2003). The pattern of a Western teacher presenting himself as the holder of an exotic secret, and of a press presenting Tantra as scandal, was set for the rest of the century.

docs.title: 14.4.5 Neo-Tantra
docs.text:
From the 1960s Tantra became, in Western popular culture, a name for sacred sexuality. Mircea Eliade’s influential studies of yoga had already presented it as an archaic Indian spirituality of the body, and the counter-culture, popular writers and teachers such as Rajneesh (Osho) promoted it as sexual liberation and self-realisation. Urban has shown that this “neo-Tantra” drew less on Indian sources than on a Western tradition of sexual magic and erotic mysticism, which he traces from Paschal Beverly Randolph in nineteenth-century America through Aleister Crowley and Julius Evola, and which was later merged with Indian vocabulary by Rajneesh and by a large self-help literature (Urban 2006). Its themes — liberation through pleasure, the body as sacred, the rejection of repression — were those of the counter-culture, not of the medieval texts, whose sexual rites served the production of ritual substances, the gaining of powers or the realisation of non-duality within a demanding discipline of initiation (Chapter 4). White’s Kiss of the Yoginī was written in part to correct this picture (White 2003). Tibetan teachers in exile, meanwhile, introduced Buddhist Tantric practice to Western students in more traditional forms. The global market for “Tantra” workshops nevertheless continues to shape what many people, in India as well as abroad, imagine the word to mean, and Western ideas in turn influence how Tantra is presented in India today.

The secrecy of the teaching, the authority of the guru and the sexual elements of some traditions have also, in modern times, been used to justify abuse, in India and abroad, by teachers who claimed Tantric legitimacy. Traditional authorities and scholars alike have condemned such misuse, and the medieval texts themselves warn against teachers who exploit their pupils (Section 1.6).

docs.title: 14.4.6 Rāmakṛṣṇa and the Kālī’s Child Controversy
docs.text: The tensions between academic and devotional readings came to a head in the debate over Jeffrey Kripal’s Kālī’s Child (1995), a study of Rāmakṛṣṇa that read the saint’s mystical experiences, and his ambivalence towards the Tantric rites in which a woman ascetic had trained him, in terms of homoerotic desire (Kripal 1995). The book was praised by some reviewers and strongly contested by others, especially within the Rāmakṛṣṇa Order. Swami Tyagananda and Pravrajika Vrajaprana later published a detailed critique arguing that the book’s argument depended on mistranslations and selective readings of the Bengali sources (Swami Tyagananda and Pravrajika Vrajaprana 2010). The controversy raised questions that remain central to the study of Tantra: who may interpret a living tradition’s saints and secrets, what weight psychoanalytic readings can bear, and how the sexual elements of Tantric practice can be discussed in a way that both scholars and practitioners can recognise as accurate.

docs.title: 14.5 Tantra and Modern Science
docs.text: Modern presentations of Tantra often claim that its doctrines anticipated modern science: that spanda is the vibration of quantum fields, that mantras work through acoustic “frequencies”, that the cakras are endocrine glands, or that yantras channel measurable “energy”. Such claims find no support in the Sanskrit sources, which speak in the categories of their own theology, and they misrepresent both the texts and modern science. The Kashmiri doctrine of consciousness can be compared with modern philosophy of mind as a philosophical position, and contemplative practices derived from Tantric and Buddhist traditions have been studied by psychologists and neuroscientists; but such research concerns meditation as a human practice, not the truth of the cosmological claims of the texts. The traditions deserve to be understood on their own terms, as religious and philosophical systems, without being made to borrow authority from physics or medicine.

docs.title: 14.6 The Academic Study of Tantra
docs.text:
The academic study of Tantra has passed through four overlapping phases. The colonial period offered condemnation and selective description. The first half of the twentieth century brought rehabilitation: Woodroffe and his collaborators, Gopinath Kaviraj in Varanasi, the editors of the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies, K.C. Pandey’s study of Abhinavagupta (Pandey 1963) and Lilian Silburn’s translations and studies (Silburn 1988). From the 1960s philology and history took the lead: the editions of N.R. Bhatt and Hélène Brunner at Pondicherry, André Padoux’s studies of the Word, the surveys of Teun Goudriaan and Sanjukta Gupta, the dictionary of technical terms begun in Vienna (Brunner et al. 2000), Alexis Sanderson’s reconstruction of the history of Śaivism, and the editions of early scriptures by Dominic Goodall and his colleagues (Gupta et al. 1979; Goudriaan and Gupta 1981; Padoux 1990; Goodall et al. 2015). Alongside them, ethnographers and social historians have studied living temple priesthoods, goddess worship and Tantric practitioners (Fuller, McDaniel) and the social history of Tantra (Davidson, White, Urban, Samuel) (Fuller 2003; McDaniel 2004; Davidson 2002; Samuel 2008).

Of these, Sanderson’s work has done most to set the present agenda. His thesis of a “Śaiva Age” (Chapter 12), his demonstration that the Buddhist Yoginītantras borrowed from Śaiva scriptures, and his tracing of Śaiva ritual forms in Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist, Jain and Smārta practice place the Tantric traditions at the centre, not the margin, of medieval Indian religion (Sanderson 1988, 2009). This volume follows his framework in many places, and the reader should bear in mind that much of it rests on one scholar’s reading of a vast and still largely unpublished body of sources, which younger scholars are now testing text by text.

docs.title: 14.7 What Is “Tantrism”?
docs.text: The reception history has also made scholars cautious about the category itself. The Sanskrit sources speak of tantras as texts and distinguish what is tāntrika from what is vaidika, but “Tantrism” as the name of a single religious phenomenon is a nineteenth-century Western coinage. André Padoux argued that it is best treated as a scholarly construct, useful for grouping traditions that share features such as initiation, mantra, ritual diagrams, the deification of the body and the pursuit of both liberation and power, but not to be mistaken for an indigenous self-description (Padoux 2002). Douglas Brooks proposed a list of characteristics none of which is necessary on its own (Brooks 1990), and Urban has emphasised how the category was formed in exchanges between Indian and Western authors (Urban 2003). The approach of Sanderson and his colleagues, followed in this volume, sidesteps the problem by starting from the scriptures: a tradition is “Tantric” when it takes the Tantras or Āgamas as its authority (Section 1.1).

docs.title: 14.8 The Living Traditions Today
docs.text: The traditions described in this volume are not only objects of study. The great Āgamic temples of South India draw very large numbers of pilgrims and remain centres of ritual, music and community life, and traditional schools and state-run Āgama schools train their priests; the opening of that training to non-Brahmins, and debates over the participation of women, are changing the priesthood. Tibetan Buddhism, in exile communities in India and worldwide, maintains Indian Buddhist Tantric lineages, and the Kālacakra initiation has been given by the Dalai Lama to very large audiences. Goddess worship, from Kāmākhyā to the village shrines of the Tamil country, continues in forms that the Sanskrit texts only partly describe. Thousands of Āgamic and Tantric manuscripts remain unedited, and digitisation projects in India, Nepal and Europe are making them more accessible; and the collaboration of traditional scholars with academic researchers, as at Pondicherry, has brought priests and philologists to the same texts.

docs.title: 14.9 Conclusion
docs.text:
What emerges from this volume is not a single “Tantra” but a family of traditions that, from about the fifth century CE, transformed Indian religion. They created the temple liturgies that still govern much Hindu worship and much of the ritual of Buddhists and Jains; they offered initiation, at least in principle, beyond the limits of the Vedic order; they produced philosophies of consciousness, language and aesthetic experience of lasting importance; and, in some lineages, they pursued liberation and power through the deliberate transgression of social and ritual norms.

These elements belong together. The philosopher Abhinavagupta was also the author of a ritual handbook that included the secret Kaula rites; the temple priest who performs the daily worship of Śiva follows manuals that also prescribe rites for kings; and the traditions that opened initiation to women and to the low-born also reproduced the hierarchies of their world. The living temples of South India, the Tibetan monastic traditions and the many lineages of goddess worship show that this inheritance remains a living and contested part of the present.

docs.title: Chronology of Texts and Authors
docs.text:
Dates are approximate and follow mainstream scholarship; traditional dates, where they differ, are noted. Many Āgamic and Tantric texts cannot be dated more closely than to a range of centuries.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Meaning Abhiṣeka Consecration by sprinkling or bathing; in Buddhism, Tantric initiation Ācāra “Conduct”; in Śākta texts, a mode of practice (Vedic, Dakṣiṇa, Vāma, Kaula etc.) Ācārya Preceptor; in Śaivism, an initiate consecrated to initiate others and perform consecrations Adhikāra Entitlement or qualification for a practice Adhvan “Path”; the six levels of the cosmos purified in Śaiva initiation Ādiśaiva Hereditary priest of Tamil Śaiva Āgamic temples Āgaṃ Newar secret shrine of a lineage’s Tantric deity, open only to initiates Āgama “That which has come down”; revealed scripture, especially of the Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava traditions Ajapā The “unrecited” mantra haṃsa, identified with the breath Āmnāya “Transmission”; one of the directional families (eastern, northern, western, southern and upper) into which later Kaula and Śākta traditions group their cults Āṇavamala Innate impurity that limits the soul (Śaiva Siddhānta) Anugraha Grace; the fifth of Śiva’s five acts Arcā The consecrated image as a mode of the deity’s presence Atimārga The early ascetic Śaiva orders (Pāśupata, Lākula, Kāpālika) Āvaraṇa Enclosure of a maṇḍala or yantra, with its deities Bhūtaśuddhi Ritual purification of the elements of the worshipper’s body Bhūta Tantra Scripture of the western stream of the Mantramārga, on possessing spirits and their exorcism Bīja “Seed”; a monosyllabic mantra Bindu “Point”; the centre of a yantra; a drop of vital essence Cakra “Wheel”; a centre in the subtle body; a ritual circle; a diagram Caryāpāda Section of an Āgama on conduct Ḍākinī In Buddhist Tantra, a female deity or human practitioner who embodies wisdom and grants or guards the teaching; in Hindu sources, a class of dangerous female spirits Dakṣiṇācāra “Right-hand” practice conforming to purity rules Dhāraṇā “Fixation”; a limb of yoga; in the Śaiva scriptures, especially the fixation of the mind on the elements and the levels of the cosmos Dhāraṇī Buddhist protective or mnemonic formula Dhruva The fixed principal image in the sanctum of a Vaikhānasa temple Dīkṣā Initiation Dūtī Female ritual partner in Kaula rites Gāruḍa Tantra Scripture of the eastern stream of the Mantramārga, on the treatment of snakebite and poison Heruka Fierce male deity of the Buddhist Yoginītantras, such as Cakrasaṃvara or Hevajra Homa Fire offering Japa Repeated recitation of a mantra Jñānapāda Doctrinal section of an Āgama (also vidyāpāda) Kaḷameḻuttu Kerala floor drawing of a deity, especially Bhadrakālī, in coloured powders Kālasaṁkarṣaṇī “She who draws in time”; the supreme Kālī of the Jayadrathayāmala and the Krama Kālīkula The Kālī-centred scriptures and lineages of the Vidyāpīṭha, including the Krama Kañcuka The five “coverings” that limit the soul’s powers Kapāla Skull; the skull-bowl of Kāpālika ascetics and fierce deities Kaula Tantric traditions of the kula, the clan of goddesses; associated with transgressive ritual Kautuka The small “power” image of a Vaikhānasa temple, used for daily worship Khaṭvāṅga Skull-topped staff carried by skull-bearing ascetics and fierce deities Krama “Sequence”; the Kālī-centred non-dual tradition of Kashmir Kriyāpāda Ritual section of an Āgama Kubjikā “The hunchbacked one”; goddess of the western transmission of the Kaula traditions, whose cult survives among the Newars Kuladevī Lineage goddess of a clan or royal house Kumārīpūjā Worship of a young girl as the Goddess Kumbhābhiṣeka Consecration of a temple with water from consecrated pots Kuṇḍa Fire-pit for homa Kuṇḍalinī The coiled power in the subtle body Mahāsiddha “Great adept”; Buddhist (and Śaiva) Tantric master Mahāvidyā One of ten goddesses forming a late Śākta group Mahāvrata “Great observance”; the skull observance of the Lākula and Kāpālika ascetics Mala Impurity or bond of the soul Maṇḍala Circle; diagram in which a deity and retinue are installed Mantra Formula of sacred speech; the deity’s form in sound Mantramārga The Tantric Śaivism of initiation and mantra Mantrapīṭha “Seat of mantras”; the branch of the Bhairava Tantras centred on Svacchandabhairava Maṭha Monastery, often endowed with land and attached to a temple Mātṛkā The phonemes of the alphabet as the matrix of mantras and cosmos Māyā In Śaivism, the real material cause of the impure worlds; a tattva Melaka “Meeting”; the adept’s encounter with the yoginīs that confers power Mudrā Ritual gesture; also parched grain or the female partner in Kaula usage Nāḍī Channel of the subtle body Nātha Order of Śaiva yogis associated with haṭha yoga Nirbījadīkṣā “Seedless” initiation that frees the initiate (e.g. a king) from post-initiatory rules Nirvāṇadīkṣā Liberating initiation Nyāsa Ritual placing of mantras on the body or an image Paddhati Ritual manual setting out the procedure of worship, initiation or consecration step by step Pañcabera The set of five images (fixed, power, bathing, festival and offering) of a Vaikhānasa temple Pañcamakāra The “five Ms” of Kaula ritual: wine, meat, fish, parched grain, sexual union Pāñcarātra Tantric Vaiṣṇava tradition and its scriptures (saṃhitās) Paśu, Pati, Pāśa Soul, Lord and bond: the three categories of the Śaiva Siddhānta Pīṭha Seat; a sacred site of the Goddess Prakāśa, Vimarśa The light of consciousness and its reflexive self-awareness Prapatti Surrender to the Lord (Śrīvaiṣṇava) Pratiṣṭhā Consecration of an image or temple Pratyabhijñā “Recognition”; the Kashmiri non-dual philosophy Pūjā Worship Rājaguru Royal preceptor; in the Śaiva Age often the king’s initiating guru Rasa Aesthetic savour Sādhaka Initiate who propitiates a mantra to gain powers Sādhakī Female practitioner; in early Śākta scriptures, a woman fully initiated to practise for powers Sahaja “Innate”; the natural state of awakened mind (Buddhist) or of divine love (Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyā) Śakti Power; the Goddess Śaktipāta “Descent of power”; grace Samaya Rule or vow of initiates Siddhi Supernatural power or accomplishment Spanda “Vibration”; the dynamism of consciousness Śrīcakra The diagram of the goddess Tripurasundarī Śrīvidyā The tradition and mantra of Tripurasundarī Srotas “Stream”; one of the five classes of Śaiva scripture said to issue from the five faces of Sadāśiva Sūrimantra Secret mantra conferred on a Śvetāmbara Jain monk raised to the rank of ācārya Svātantrya The absolute freedom of consciousness Tantra “Loom”; system; a class of revealed scripture Tantrī In Kerala, the hereditary Nampūtiri ritual authority of a temple Tattva Principle or level of reality (thirty-six in Śaivism) Trika “Triad”; the Kashmiri Śaiva tradition of three goddesses Upāya “Means”; in Kashmiri Śaivism, one of the graded ways to liberation (of the individual, of Śakti, of Śiva, and “no means”); in Buddhism, compassionate skill in means Upacāra An offering or service in worship Utsava image Movable festival image carried in procession Vāc Speech; the Word Vaikhānasa Hereditary Vaiṣṇava priestly tradition claiming Vedic authority Vaikuṇṭha Four-faced image of Viṣṇu with human, lion, boar and fierce faces, prominent in Kashmir Vajrayāna “Vehicle of the vajra”; Buddhist Tantra Vāmācāra “Left-hand” practice involving the five Ms Vāma Tantra Scripture of the northern stream of the Mantramārga, centred on Tumburu and his four sisters Vāstupuruṣamaṇḍala The grid diagram underlying temple plans Vidyāpīṭha “Seat of female mantras”; the goddess-centred branch of the Bhairava Tantras, including the Trika and Kālī-centred scriptures Vimāna Sanctum with its superstructure (South Indian temples) Vyūha “Emanation”; one of the four forms (Vāsudeva, Saṁkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha) of the Lord in Pāñcarātra theology Yantra Diagram, often metal, serving as the seat of a deity Yoginī Powerful female deity of the Kaula and Vidyāpīṭha cults

docs.title: Guide to Further Reading
docs.text:
The following works, all listed in the bibliography, are recommended starting points. For the technical vocabulary of the Hindu Tantras, the Tāntrikābhidhānakośa (Brunner et al. 2000), a dictionary of terms with references to the sources, is the standard reference work.

Editions and translations of primary texts. Among the primary sources discussed in this volume, the following are available in editions or translations listed in the bibliography: the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā (Goodall et al. 2015); the Brahmayāmala (Hatley 2018); the Kiraṇavṛtti of Rāmakaṇṭha (Goodall 1998); the Rauravāgama (Bhatt 1961–1988); Somaśambhu’s manual (Brunner-Lachaux 1963–1998); the yogic chapters of the Mālinīvijayottara (Vasudeva 2004); the Vīṇāśikhatantra (Goudriaan 1985); the Kubjikāmata (Goudriaan and Schoterman 1988) and the opening chapters of the Ṣaṭsāhasrasaṃhitā (Schoterman 1982); the early Pāñcarātra works edited by Acharya (Acharya 2015); Yāmuna’s Āgamaprāmāṇya (van Buitenen 1971); the Haribhaktivilāsa (Broo 2023); the Kulārṇava Tantra (Vidyāratna 1917); the Mahānirvāṇa Tantra in translation (Avalon 1913); the Saundaryalaharī with Lakṣmīdhara’s commentary (Sastri and Ayyangar 1937); the Tantrāloka with Jayaratha’s commentary (Abhinavagupta 1918–1938); Utpaladeva’s Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā (Torella 2002); Somānanda’s Śivadṛṣṭi, chapters 1–3 (Nemec 2011); the Śivasūtra, Spandakārikā and Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya in translation (Singh 1979, 1980, 1963); and the Hevajra Tantra (Snellgrove 1959).

General introductions. André Padoux’s The Hindu Tantric World (Padoux 2017) and Gavin Flood’s The Tantric Body (Flood 2006) are reliable overviews. Teun Goudriaan and Sanjukta Gupta’s Hindu Tantric and Śākta Literature (Goudriaan and Gupta 1981) and Hindu Tantrism (Gupta et al. 1979) survey the texts. David Gordon White’s anthology Tantra in Practice (White 2000) offers translations with introductions.

History. Alexis Sanderson’s “Śaivism and the Tantric Traditions” (Sanderson 1988) is the classic short history; his “The Śaiva Age” (Sanderson 2009) presents the evidence for royal patronage in detail. Geoffrey Samuel’s The Origins of Yoga and Tantra (Samuel 2008) sets Tantra in a long history of Indic religion; Ronald Davidson’s Indian Esoteric Buddhism (Davidson 2002) gives a social history of Buddhist Tantra.

Śaiva Siddhānta and temple ritual. Richard Davis’s Ritual in an Oscillating Universe (Davis 1991) and A Priest’s Guide for the Great Festival (Davis 2010); Hélène Brunner’s edition of Somaśambhu’s manual (Brunner-Lachaux 1963–1998); C.J. Fuller’s Servants of the Goddess (Fuller 1984) and The Renewal of the Priesthood (Fuller 2003); Stella Kramrisch’s The Hindu Temple (Kramrisch 1946). For the early scriptures, Goodall’s editions of the Kiraṇa commentary and the Niśvāsa (Goodall 1998; Goodall et al. 2015).

Vaiṣṇava traditions. Schrader’s Introduction to the Pāñcarātra (Schrader 1916), Matsubara’s Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās and Early Vaiṣṇava Theology (Matsubara 1994) and van Buitenen’s translation of Yāmuna (van Buitenen 1971). Acharya’s edition of the earliest Pāñcarātra texts (Acharya 2015), Rastelli on the Pārameśvara (Rastelli 2006), Colas on Vaikhānasa images and fires (Colas 1996) and Broo’s edition of the Haribhaktivilāsa (Broo 2023) take the subject further. On the Tantric Vaiṣṇavism of Bengal, Dimock’s The Place of the Hidden Moon (Dimock 1966), Openshaw’s Seeking Bāuls of Bengal (Openshaw 2002) and Urban’s The Economics of Ecstasy (Urban 2001).

Śākta traditions. Thomas Coburn on the Devīmāhātmya (Coburn 1984); David Kinsley on the Mahāvidyās (Kinsley 1997); Douglas Brooks on Śrīvidyā (Brooks 1990, 1992); June McDaniel on Bengal (McDaniel 2004); Vidya Dehejia on yoginī temples (Dehejia 1986); and, on the Kaula traditions and their interpretation, David Gordon White’s Kiss of the Yoginī (White 2003) and Hugh Urban’s Tantra (Urban 2003). On women in the Tantric traditions, Törzsök on the early Śākta scriptures (Törzsök 2014), Biernacki on the late Kaula texts (Biernacki 2007), Gupta’s survey (Gupta 1992) and McDaniel on women tāntrikās in Bengal (McDaniel 2007).

Healing, possession and the lesser streams. Slouber’s Early Tantric Medicine (Slouber 2017); Goudriaan’s edition of the Vīṇāśikhatantra (Goudriaan 1985); Frederick Smith’s The Self Possessed (Smith 2006).

Kingship and the Śaiva Age. Sanderson’s “The Śaiva Age” (Sanderson 2009) with his studies of the Khmers and of inscriptions (Sanderson 2003–2004, 2013); Hermann Kulke’s Kings and Cults (Kulke 1993); B.D. Chattopadhyaya’s The Making of Early Medieval India (Chattopadhyaya 1994); Hans Bakker’s The World of the Skandapurāṇa (Bakker 2014); Florinda De Simini’s Of Gods and Books (De Simini 2016); and, for wider perspectives, Davis’s Lives of Indian Images (Davis 1997), Pollock’s The Language of the Gods in the World of Men (Pollock 2006), Talbot on medieval Andhra (Talbot 2001), Fuller on Navarātri and royal ritual (Fuller 1992) and Sarkar on the royal cult of Durgā (Sarkar 2017). On ascetic orders, Lorenzen’s The Kāpālikas and Kālāmukhas (Lorenzen 1972); on the yoginīs, Hatley’s study and edition of the Brahmayāmala (Hatley 2007, 2018) and the essays edited by Keul (Keul 2013).

Regional traditions. For Kerala, Tarabout (Tarabout 1986) and Caldwell (Caldwell 1999); for Bengal, McDermott (McDermott 2001) and Sircar on the pīṭhas (Sircar 1973); for Assam, Urban (Urban 2010); for Odisha, Eschmann, Kulke and Tripathi (Eschmann et al. 1978); for Nepal, Levy’s Mesocosm (Levy 1990) and Dyczkowski on Kubjikā (Dyczkowski 1988); for the goddesses of the north-western hills, Erndl (Erndl 1993); for Rajasthan, Harlan (Harlan 1992) and the Jodhpur catalogue Garden and Cosmos (Diamond et al. 2008); for the Tamil Tirumantiram, Zvelebil (Zvelebil 1975); for Bali, Hooykaas (Hooykaas 1966).

Jain, Saura and Gāṇapatya traditions. Dundas’s The Jains (Dundas 2002) and his essay on the sūrimantra (Dundas 1998); Gough’s Making a Mantra (Gough 2021); Cort’s Jains in the World (Cort 2001); Laidlaw’s Riches and Renunciation (Laidlaw 1995); von Stietencron on the Sun priests (Stietencron 1966); Courtright on Gaṇeśa (Courtright 1985).

Kashmiri Śaivism. Mark Dyczkowski’s The Doctrine of Vibration (Dyczkowski 1987); Paul Muller-Ortega’s The Triadic Heart of Śiva (Muller-Ortega 1989); Jaideva Singh’s translations of the Śivasūtra and Spandakārikā (Singh 1979, 1980). For the Pratyabhijñā, Torella’s edition of Utpaladeva (Torella 2002), Nemec on Somānanda (Nemec 2011) and Ratié on the self (Ratié 2011); for the older scholarship, Pandey’s Abhinavagupta (Pandey 1963) and Silburn (Silburn 1988). For the Krama, Rastogi’s The Krama Tantricism of Kashmir (Rastogi 1979), and for the history of Kashmiri exegesis, Sanderson’s “The Śaiva Exegesis of Kashmir” (Sanderson 2007). On the yoga of the Śaiva scriptures, Vasudeva’s study of the Mālinīvijayottara (Vasudeva 2004).

Reception. Taylor on Woodroffe and his collaborators (Taylor 2001); Urban on colonial and Western constructions of Tantra and on modern sexual magic (Urban 2003, 2006); Love on Pierre Bernard (Love 2010); Padoux on the category “Tantrism” (Padoux 2002); and, for the Kālī’s Child debate, Kripal and his critics (Kripal 1995; Swami Tyagananda and Pravrajika Vrajaprana 2010).

Mantra, yantra and the Word. Padoux’s Vāc (Padoux 1990); Alper’s Understanding Mantras (Alper 1989); Bühnemann’s Maṇḍalas and Yantras (Bühnemann 2003) and Pūjā (Bühnemann 1988). On Tantric art and its modern reception, Rawson’s The Art of Tantra (Rawson 1973), Mookerjee’s Tantra Art (Mookerjee 1966) and the British Museum catalogue Tantra: Enlightenment to Revolution (Ramos 2020).

Buddhist Tantra. Snellgrove’s Indo-Tibetan Buddhism (Snellgrove 1987) and his edition of the Hevajra (Snellgrove 1959); Gray’s Cakrasaṃvara (Gray 2007); Wedemeyer’s Making Sense of Tantric Buddhism (Wedemeyer 2013); Miranda Shaw’s Buddhist Goddesses of India (Shaw 2006); English on Vajrayoginī (English 2002); Wallace on the “inner” Kālacakra (Wallace 2001); and Dalton on violence and liberation in Tibetan Buddhism (Dalton 2011).

Yoga and alchemy. Mallinson and Singleton’s Roots of Yoga (Mallinson and Singleton 2017); White’s The Alchemical Body (White 1996); Zvelebil’s The Poets of the Powers on the Tamil Siddhas (Zvelebil 1973); Ernst on the Persian and Arabic translations of yoga (Ernst 2003); and McLeod on Guru Nānak and the Nāths (McLeod 1968).

docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This is Volume 7 of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā: Itihāsa–Purāṇa: Epics and Purāṇas. After an introductory chapter on the genre, it treats the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa (Chapters 2–3), the Mahābhārata and the Harivaṃśa (Chapters 4–5), the Bhagavad Gītā (Chapter 6), and the Mahāpurāṇas, Upapurāṇas and māhātmyas (Chapters 7–8). Three thematic chapters then take up what the narrative chapters leave open: the hard cases and the limits of epic dharma (Chapter 9), the women of the epics (Chapter 10) and the philosophy of the Mokṣadharma and the Nārāyaṇīya (Chapter 11). The last chapter follows the epics’ afterlife in the regional languages, in Persian at the Mughal court and in the Sikh Dasam Granth, in Southeast Asia, in sculpture, dance, ritual theatre, film and festival, and in modern debates about their historicity.

Two perspectives run through the book. The first is that of the tradition, for which these texts are sacred history and scripture. The second is that of modern textual and historical scholarship, which dates their composition (academic dates are given first throughout, with traditional dates labelled as such), studies their growth through critical editions, and reads them alongside the Jain, Buddhist, regional and oppositional retellings — including feminist and Dalit critiques — that are part of their history. Quotations from the Sanskrit texts are given only where their wording and reference could be checked; claims that archaeology or astronomy confirm the epics are presented as the contested proposals they are. Where a heading or a sentence reports what the tradition holds, it says so. The book is a work of synthesis and introduction; a note on texts, translations and abbreviations follows, and readers are referred to the select bibliography for the standard scholarship on which it draws.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput Ramanujan College, University of Delhi Guru Pūrṇimā, 2026

docs.title: A Note on Texts, Translations and Abbreviations
docs.text:
Critical Edition and vulgate. Both epics exist in two forms that a reader will meet. The Critical Edition (CE) is the text reconstructed by modern editors from manuscripts of all regions: for the Mahābhārata, the Poona edition of the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute (BORI, 1933–1966), with the Harivaṃśa edited separately (1969–1971); for the Rāmāyaṇa, the Baroda edition (1960–1975). The vulgate is the text printed before the critical editions and still most widely read: for the Mahābhārata, the northern text of Nīlakaṇṭha (late seventeenth century), found in the Calcutta and Bombay editions, the Gita Press edition and Ganguli’s translation; for the Rāmāyaṇa, the southern text printed with the commentaries of Govindarāja and others. How the critical editions were made, and the debate over them, are described in Sections 2.3 and 4.8.

References. Mahābhārata references give book (parvan), chapter (adhyāya) and verse in the CE, so that 12.67 is chapter 67 of the twelfth book, the Śānti Parva; the eighteen books are numbered as in Table 4.1. Rāmāyaṇa references give book (kāṇḍa), canto (sarga) and verse in the CE. Where a passage exists only in the vulgate, or a vulgate number is given, this is said; chapter numbers in the two texts differ, sometimes widely. The Bhagavad Gītā is cited by chapter and verse, which are the same in all editions. Purāṇas are cited by book, chapter and verse of the usual printed editions, whose numbering varies.

Abbreviations. BORI, Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute; CE, Critical Edition; c., circa; r., reigned; trad., traditional. Within the text the epics are named in full; “Mbh.” and “Rām.” appear only in tables.

Transliteration. Sanskrit, Pali and Prakrit are given in the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (IAST), with ṃ for the anusvāra; Tamil follows the transliteration of the Tamil Lexicon of the University of Madras (so ḻ, ṟ, ṉ, as in Āḻvār). Modern places are given in their usual modern spelling (Ayodhya, Varanasi) where the modern town is meant, and with diacritics where the place of the text is meant (Ayodhyā). Persian, Hindi and Punjabi names are given in simplified form. Translations of passages are the author’s unless a translation is cited; they aim at the sense and should be checked against the editions below.

Dates. The mainstream academic date or range is given first, and traditional dates are labelled as traditional (see Table 1.5).

A short guide to translations. For the Mahābhārata, the only complete English translation of the critical text is Bibek Debroy’s, in ten volumes (Debroy 2010–2014). The Chicago translation begun by J. A. B. van Buitenen covers Books 1–5 (van Buitenen 1973–1978) and was continued by James Fitzgerald with Books 11 and the first part of 12 (Fitzgerald 2004); its introductions are the best scholarly guide to the books they cover. K. M. Ganguli’s prose translation of the vulgate (1883–1896) is complete, freely available and still useful, but it translates a different text and its English is dated (Ganguli 1883–1896). A reader who wants a single volume should begin with John D. Smith’s abridgement of the critical text, which translates the main narrative and summarises the rest (Smith 2009). For the Harivaṃśa there is Simon Brodbeck’s translation of the critical text (Brodbeck 2019). For the Bhagavad Gītā, van Buitenen prints the CE text with a facing translation and Franklin Edgerton gives a deliberately literal version (van Buitenen 1981; Edgerton 1944). For the Rāmāyaṇa, the annotated Princeton translation of the critical text by Robert Goldman and his collaborators is the standard (Goldman 1984–2017); the notes record the major vulgate passages that the CE excludes. For the Purāṇas, Dimmitt and van Buitenen’s reader gives a selection of myths in good translation (Dimmitt and Buitenen 1978); Edwin Bryant has translated the tenth book of the Bhāgavata (Bryant 2003) and Thomas Coburn the Devī Māhātmya (Coburn 1991). Translations of the Tamil, Khmer and other versions are cited where those versions are discussed.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction — What is Itihāsa?
docs.text:
ṛgvedaṃ bhagavo ’dhyemi yajurvedaṃ sāmavedam ātharvaṇaṃ caturtham itihāsapurāṇaṃ pañcamam … “Sir, I know the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Ātharvaṇa as the fourth, and Itihāsa-Purāṇa as the fifth …”

— Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.2 (Nārada to Sanatkumāra)

The word itihāsa names a genre of Sanskrit literature that presents itself as an account of what really happened, transmitted by authoritative narrators and directed towards instruction in dharma. The genre does not correspond neatly to the modern discipline of history: it combines genealogy, narrative, didactic discourse and religious teaching, and its claim to truth is a claim made by the tradition rather than one that can be tested by documentary evidence. This volume treats the two great epics — the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata — together with the related Purāṇa literature, both as the tradition understands them and as modern textual and historical scholarship has studied them (Brockington 1998; Rocher 1986).

docs.title: 1.1 The Word and Its Claim
docs.text:
The word itihāsa is formed from the particles iti (“thus”) and ha (“indeed”) and the verb form āsa (“it was”, from the root as, “to be”): “thus indeed it was.” It already occurs in late Vedic texts, often in the compound itihāsa-purāṇa, as the name of a body of narrative lore recited alongside the Vedas. The lexicon Amarakośa (c. 5th–7th century CE) glosses it briefly as itihāsaḥ purāvṛttam, “itihāsa is an account of past events.”

The gloss expresses the conviction that the events narrated in the epics actually took place, even though they are told in poetry (kāvya) and directed towards instruction in dharma. Modern historians have asked a different question: not whether the events happened, but what kind of historical consciousness the genre expresses. The colonial claim that India “had no history” before the Muslim chroniclers has been rejected. Romila Thapar has argued that early India possessed “embedded” historical traditions — genealogies (vaṃśānucarita), heroic narratives and dynastic lists preserved in the epics and Purāṇas — which later became “externalised” in chronicles, inscriptions and royal biographies, and that later dynasties legitimised their rule by attaching themselves to the Solar and Lunar lineages of these genealogies (Thapar 2013). On this view the epics are evidence for how communities remembered and used their past, and for the periods in which they were composed and transmitted, rather than records that can be read off as political history. Earlier attempts, notably Pargiter’s, to reconstruct a dynastic chronology from the Purāṇic genealogies are now generally regarded as over-confident (Pargiter 1922; Rocher 1986). Table 1.1 sets itihāsa beside the neighbouring categories of narrative.

Table 1.1. Itihāsa and Neighbouring Narrative Categories Category Basis as understood in the tradition Purpose Itihāsa Events held to have occurred (purāvṛtta) Instruction in dharma through exemplary lives Purāṇa “Ancient” lore: cosmogony, genealogy, theology, ritual Comprehensive religious instruction Kāvya Poetic composition, often on an epic theme Aesthetic experience (rasa) Kathā / Ākhyāyikā Prose narrative (invented or based on tradition) Entertainment and instruction Arthavāda Explanatory or laudatory passages in the Veda (in Mīmāṃsā usage) Supporting Vedic injunctions

docs.title: 1.2 The “Fifth Veda” and the Authority of Itihāsa
docs.text:
The tradition gives the itihāsa-purāṇa literature the title of Pañcama Veda, the “fifth Veda,” as in the epigraph above, and the Mahābhārata states its relation to the Veda in a frequently quoted line:

Mahābhārata 1.1.204 (Critical Edition)

itihāsapurāṇābhyāṃ vedaṃ samupabṛṃhayet Translation: “One should amplify (upabṛṃh-) the Veda by means of Itihāsa and Purāṇa.”

On this view what the Vedas state in compressed form, the epics and Purāṇas unfold through narrative, dialogue and exemplary lives. The claim had a social side. Vedic learning was restricted to the initiated men of the three dvija (“twice-born”) varṇas; the epics and Purāṇas were recited to everyone. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa (1.4.25) explains that Vyāsa composed the Bhārata out of compassion because “the triple Veda is not within the hearing of women, Śūdras and degenerate members of the twice-born classes.” The epics thus became the main vehicle of religious education for the majority of the population — but within a framework that took the hierarchy of varṇa and gender for granted, as the same verse shows. Table 1.2 gives examples of the kinds of knowledge the epics carried.

Table 1.2. Itihāsa as Educator: Knowledge Domains Accessible Through the Epics Domain Epic Source Specific Teaching Governance Mahābhārata, Śānti Parva Rājadharma: duties of kings, taxation, justice Medicine Rāmāyaṇa, Yuddha Kāṇḍa Suṣeṇa’s treatment of the wounded; Hanumān’s mountain of herbs Military science Mahābhārata, Bhīṣma and Droṇa Parvas Battle arrays (vyūha), weapons, codes of combat Geography Rāmāyaṇa, Kiṣkindhā Kāṇḍa Sugrīva’s description of the four quarters of the earth Law Mahābhārata, Śānti Parva Āpaddharma: conduct in times of emergency Philosophy Bhagavad Gītā; Mokṣadharma Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Vedānta and the theory of action (karman)

In the formal classification of learning the epics held a more modest place. A verse of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa lists the fourteen branches of knowledge (caturdaśa vidyās):

Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.6.27

aṅgāni vedāś catvāro mīmāṃsā nyāyavistaraḥ purāṇaṃ dharmaśāstraṃ ca vidyā hy etāś caturdaśa Translation: “The (six) auxiliaries, the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, the extensive Nyāya, Purāṇa and Dharmaśāstra — these are the fourteen branches of knowledge.”

Here itihāsa is not listed separately but is subsumed under purāṇa. In the classification of authoritative texts, too, the epics and Purāṇas are smṛti (“remembered” tradition) rather than śruti (the Veda, held to be revealed). The Mīmāṃsā school, which developed the most explicit theory of textual authority, held that smṛti is authoritative because it is presumed to rest on Vedic texts, perhaps now lost, and that where it contradicts an extant Vedic text it is to be disregarded (Mīmāṃsāsūtra 1.3.1–3 with Śabara’s commentary); narrative passages within the Veda itself were classed as arthavāda, authoritative only in so far as they support an injunction. In practice the epics — especially the Bhagavad Gītā — came to rival the Veda in religious influence, and the Vedāntic schools counted the Gītā among their three foundational texts (prasthānatraya). Figure 1.1 shows the mediating role that the tradition assigns to itihāsa-purāṇa.

Figure 1.1. The mediating role of Itihāsa-Purāṇa as the tradition conceives it

docs.title: 1.3 Itihāsa and Purāṇa Distinguished
docs.text:
Although itihāsa and purāṇa are often named together, the tradition distinguishes them (Table 1.3).

Table 1.3. Key Distinctions: Itihāsa vs. Purāṇa Criterion Itihāsa Purāṇa Meaning “Thus it was” — historical narrative “Ancient” — ancient lore Number Two: Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata Eighteen Mahāpurāṇas + Upapurāṇas Central Focus Life of a single hero or royal lineage Cosmology, genealogy, Dharma teachings Narrative Style One main story, framed and interrupted by many embedded episodes Encyclopaedic, dialogical, nested narratives Defining Feature Purāvṛtta (ancient happening) Pañca Lakṣaṇa (five characteristics) Authorship (traditional) Vālmīki (Rāmāyaṇa), Vyāsa (Mahābhārata) Attributed to Vyāsa

docs.title: 1.3.1 The Pañca Lakṣaṇa of Purāṇas
docs.text:
A verse found in several Purāṇas defines the genre by five characteristics (pañca lakṣaṇa):

Kūrma Purāṇa 1.1.12; the verse recurs in several other Purāṇas

sargaś ca pratisargaś ca vaṃśo manvantarāṇi ca vaṃśānucaritaṃ caiva purāṇaṃ pañcalakṣaṇam Translation: “Creation, secondary creation, genealogy (of gods and sages), the Manvantara periods, and the deeds of the royal lineages — (this is) a Purāṇa, possessing five characteristics.”

As Rocher and others have pointed out, the extant Purāṇas fit this definition poorly: some of the five topics occupy only a small part of most Purāṇas, while much of their bulk is devoted to ritual, pilgrimage, sectarian theology and dharma (Rocher 1986). The Bhāgavata Purāṇa (12.7) gives an expanded list of ten characteristics. Figure 1.2 sets out the classical five.

Figure 1.2. The Pañca Lakṣaṇa — Five Defining Characteristics of a Purāṇa

docs.title: 1.4 Scale and Literary Form
docs.text:
Tradition assigns the Rāmāyaṇa 24,000 ślokas in seven kāṇḍas, and the Mahābhārata 100,000 ślokas (it calls itself the śatasāhasrī saṃhitā) in eighteen parvans. The critical editions are shorter: the Poona Critical Edition of the Mahābhārata contains roughly 75,000 verses, and the Baroda Critical Edition of the Rāmāyaṇa is likewise appreciably shorter than the vulgate. A śloka is a couplet of two sixteen-syllable lines, each roughly comparable in length to a Greek hexameter; counted in this way, the critical text of the Mahābhārata is about five times the combined length of the Iliad and Odyssey (c. 28,000 lines), and the vulgate’s traditional 100,000 ślokas would be about seven times. The Purāṇic tradition assigns the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas a total of 400,000 ślokas (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 12.13); actual printed texts vary considerably (Table 1.4).

Table 1.4. Scale of Itihāsa-Purāṇa Literature Text Traditional count of ślokas Divisions Rāmāyaṇa 24,000 7 Kāṇḍas Mahābhārata 100,000 (CE c. 75,000) 18 Parvas, 100 Upaparvans Harivaṃśa (appendix) 12,000 (CE c. 6,000) 2–3 Parvas Bhagavad Gītā 700 18 Adhyāyas 18 Mahāpurāṇas 400,000 (traditional total) Varying

The forms through which this mass of material is organised recur throughout the volume. The frame narrative sets stories within stories: in the Mahābhārata the bard Ugraśravas Sauti recites to Śaunaka and the sages of the Naimiṣa forest the epic he heard Vaiśaṃpāyana recite to King Janamejaya, the great-grandson of its heroes (Section 4.18). Teaching is given in dialogue (saṃvāda) — Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, Bhīṣma and Yudhiṣṭhira, Vidura and Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Self-contained embedded stories (upākhyāna) such as Nala, Sāvitrī and the Rāmopākhyāna comment on the main story. Genealogical lists, set descriptions (varṇana) of seasons, cities and battles, and extended philosophical discourse complete the repertoire. Because the corpus gathers law, statecraft, cosmology, philosophy, geography and the arts as well as narrative, the tradition has treated it as a knowledge system in its own right; Rocher’s survey shows, however, that much Purāṇic and māhātmya material is ritual, sectarian or local in purpose, so that any single unifying aim is better described as the tradition’s ideal than as a description of the texts.

docs.title: 1.4.1 Dharma as the Tradition’s Axis
docs.text:
For the tradition, the unifying principle of the corpus is dharma: on this reading every narrative, discourse and genealogy serves to show the nature, practice and fruits of dharma and the consequences of adharma. One of the closing verses of the Mahābhārata, put in Vyāsa’s mouth, voices the tradition’s complaint that this teaching goes unheeded:

Mahābhārata, Svargārohaṇa Parva 18.5.49 (Critical Edition)

Sanskrit: ūrdhvabāhur viraumy eṣa na ca kaścic chṛṇoti me dharmād arthaś ca kāmaś ca sa kimarthaṃ na sevyate Translation: “With upraised arms I cry out, but none heeds my call: from Dharma flow Artha (prosperity) and Kāma (fulfilment); why then is Dharma not pursued?”

docs.title: 1.5 Dating: Two Chronologies
docs.text:
The chronology of the itihāsa-purāṇa texts must be approached on two levels. The tradition places the events of the Rāmāyaṇa in the Tretā Yuga and the Bhārata war at the junction of the Dvāpara and Kali Yugas; the Kali Yuga is conventionally reckoned from 3102 BCE, an epoch used by Āryabhaṭa (499 CE), and the Aihole inscription of Pulakeśin II (634 CE) dates itself 3,735 years after the Bhārata war. Modern scholarship, working from language, metre, internal cross-references, the material culture the texts describe and their relation to datable literature, dates the composition of the texts as we have them much later, and treats each as the product of centuries of growth. Table 1.5 sets out both views; academic ranges are given first throughout this volume. Attempts to confirm the traditional dates by archaeology or by the planetary positions mentioned in the epics are examined in Section 12.11.

Table 1.5. Chronological Perspectives on the Itihāsa-Purāṇa Literature Text Academic dating of composition Traditional dating Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa Core (Books 2–6) c. 5th–3rd century BCE; Books 1 and 7 added later; substantially complete by c. 2nd–3rd century CE (Brockington). Goldman places the earliest stratum somewhat earlier, c. 750–500 BCE. Composed by Vālmīki, a contemporary of Rāma, in the Tretā Yuga Mahābhārata Composite text growing c. 400 BCE–400 CE (Brockington); Hiltebeitel argues for a written composition between the mid-2nd century BCE and the turn of the era Composed by Vyāsa, a participant in the events, at the end of the Dvāpara Yuga (war conventionally c. 3102 BCE) Bhagavad Gītā Usually c. 2nd century BCE–1st century CE; estimates range from the 5th century BCE, and some scholars see layers Spoken by Kṛṣṇa on the battlefield of Kurukṣetra Harivaṃśa c. 1st–3rd century CE Appendix (khila) by Vyāsa Mahāpurāṇas Earliest layers of the oldest Purāṇas c. 3rd–5th century CE (Hazra); Bhāgavata c. 9th–10th century CE in most current estimates; all were revised and expanded until the early modern period (Rocher) Composed by Vyāsa at the beginning of the Kali Yuga

Within the tradition the ṛṣis are regarded as seers (draṣṭā) of truths that are sanātana (eternal), so the date of a text’s composition is not thought to determine the validity of its teaching. The academic dates concern the texts as literary artefacts; they neither confirm nor refute the religious claims made for them (Hazra 1940; Rocher 1986; Brockington 1998; Hiltebeitel 2001).

docs.title: 1.6 Transmission and Recitation
docs.text:
The Mahābhārata describes its own transmission as a chain of narrators: Vyāsa taught the epic to his five disciples, among them Vaiśaṃpāyana; Vaiśaṃpāyana narrated it to King Janamejaya during the snake sacrifice (sarpasattra); and Ugraśravas Sauti, who heard it there, re-narrated it to the sages assembled under Śaunaka in the Naimiṣa forest (Figure 1.3). This layered frame is a literary device, but it also mirrors the real social setting of epic recitation: the sūtas (bards attached to royal courts) and, later, brahmin reciters (paurāṇikas, kathāvācakas) who performed the epics, often at rituals and festivals. The connection of the frame with Janamejaya’s sacrifice has been analysed as a deliberate ritual structure (Minkowski 1989).

Figure 1.3. Transmission Chain of the Mahābhārata as the Epic Describes It

The epic and Purāṇic corpus was preserved by a combination of oral performance and manuscript copying. Unlike the Vedas, which were preserved word for word through techniques such as the jaṭā and ghana recitations, the epics were transmitted through a more flexible tradition of narrative recitation that allowed both the preservation of core content and adaptation to local audiences. The result, visible in the manuscripts, is a large number of regional versions and recensions — the reason critical editions were needed (Sections 2.3 and 4.8). The best-known story of the writing of the Mahābhārata, in which Gaṇeśa serves as Vyāsa’s scribe, is absent from most manuscripts and from the Critical Edition (Section 4.1).

Recitation was also a religious act. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad (1.11.1) instructs the departing student, svādhyāyān mā prama­daḥ, “Do not neglect your recitation”; in the tradition, hearing and reciting the epics and Purāṇas came to be regarded as a form of this svādhyāya, promising merit (puṇya) to reciter and listener alike, and the phalaśruti passages at the end of the epics and of individual Purāṇas spell out the rewards. Table 1.6 lists the main forms that this engagement has taken; four of them are studied in Section 12.5.

Table 1.6. Traditional Forms of Itihāsa-Purāṇa Engagement Form Sanskrit Term Description Complete recitation Pārāyaṇa Full text recited over 7–30 days; considered a sacred act Scholarly discourse Pravācana A learned speaker expounds episodes with commentary Dramatic performance Nāṭya / Līlā Rāmlīlā, Kṛṣṇa Līlā, Yakṣagāna Devotional singing Bhajana / Kīrtana Epic episodes rendered in song Temple sculpture Śilpa / Mūrti Narrative panels on temple walls Manuscript painting Citra / Paṭa Illustrated manuscripts (Mughal, Rajput, Pahari, Odia and other schools) Shadow puppetry Chāyā Nāṭaka Tolu Bommalata (Andhra), Tolpāvakkūttu (Kerala), Togalu Gombeyata (Karnataka)

docs.title: 1.7 Commentators and Levels of Meaning
docs.text:
The interpretation of the epics and Purāṇas has been shaped by a commentarial tradition that is, for the most part, medieval and early modern. The Bhagavad Gītā attracted the largest number of commentaries, from Śaṅkara’s (c. 8th century), the earliest to survive, through Rāmānuja and Madhva to Madhusūdana Sarasvatī (Table 6.3); the Bhāgavata Purāṇa was expounded by Śrīdhara Svāmin and by the theologians of the Kṛṣṇa schools (Table 7.5); and the Rāmāyaṇa found its principal commentators in the south from the sixteenth century, above all the Śrīvaiṣṇava Govindarāja (Section 2.10). The whole Mahābhārata had fewer interpreters. Madhva’s Mahābhārata­tātparya­nirṇaya is a verse digest reading the whole epic theologically, and the only complete commentary in common use is the Bhārata­bhāva­dīpa (“Lamp on the Meaning of the Bhārata”) of Nīlakaṇṭha Caturdhara, a Mahārāṣṭrian scholar working in Benares in the late seventeenth century. Nīlakaṇṭha collated many manuscripts to establish his text, which became the basis of the widely printed “vulgate” (the northern recension as he constituted it); he often offers alternative explanations of disputed passages, and his Advaitic reading of the epic remains the main traditional point of reference.

Traditional readers have long recognised that an epic narrative can be read on more than one level at once: as an account of events, as moral instruction, as philosophical allegory and as the play (līlā) of God. The Mahābhārata itself remarks that some learned brahmins begin the Bhārata with Manu, others with Āstīka and others with Uparicara (1.1.50 in the Critical Edition), and Madhva is commonly understood to have taken this as a hint that the epic carries historical, moral and spiritual senses simultaneously, while insisting that the historical sense is not cancelled by the others. Later devotional readers, especially in the Rāma and Kṛṣṇa traditions, read the narratives above all as divine līlā. A modern version of the same idea is V. S. Sukthankar’s: in lectures given shortly before his death, the editor of the Critical Edition read the epic on a mundane, an ethical and a metaphysical plane at once (Sukthankar 1957).

Classical critics were equally aware that the epics are literature. The ninth-century theorist Ānandavardhana, in the fourth chapter of his Dhvanyāloka, treats the Mahābhārata as at once a śāstra (a teaching) and a kāvya (a poem), whose dominant sentiment is the tranquillity (śānta rasa) born of disillusion with worldly ends, shown in the ruin of the Yādavas and the Pāṇḍavas’ bleak victory; and he regards the Rāmāyaṇa as founded on pathos (karuṇa), the grief of separation that begins with the poem’s own origin story (Section 2.1). These two judgements have shaped the reading of both epics ever since, and later chapters refer back to them here.

docs.title: 1.8 The Epics in Comparative Perspective
docs.text:
Comparison with other epic traditions brings out both the distinctive features of the Sanskrit epics and how much they share with heroic poetry elsewhere — bardic origins, formulaic diction, heroic codes and a long period of oral and written growth (Smith 1977; Brockington 1998). Table 1.7 sets them beside the Homeric poems and the Epic of Gilgamesh. A different kind of comparison asks whether the Mahābhārata preserves, in transposed form, myths that the Indo-European peoples inherited in common; that question is taken up in Section 4.4.

Table 1.7. The Sanskrit Epics in Comparative Perspective Feature Sanskrit epics Homeric epics Epic of Gilgamesh Length c. 75,000 ślokas (CE MBh; 100,000 trad.) and 24,000 (Rām., trad.) c. 28,000 lines c. 3,000 lines (Standard Babylonian version) Central ethical frame Dharma, often contested within the text Honour (timē) and glory (kleos) Mortality and the limits of kingship Didactic content Extensive (Gītā, Śānti and Anuśāsana Parvas) Limited Limited Later life Continuously recited, retold, performed and worshipped Central to classical education and literature Lost; recovered through archaeology in the 19th century

Three features stand out. The Sanskrit epics have been recited, performed and retold without a break for some two millennia, and remain central to religious life. They carry extended teaching on dharma, statecraft, philosophy and devotion inside the narrative. And they exist in many versions, for every region and community produced its own, including Jain, Buddhist, folk and oppositional retellings (Sections 2.8 and 4.10).

docs.title: 1.9 Approach and Scope of This Volume
docs.text:
This volume keeps two perspectives in view. It presents the texts as the tradition has understood them, respecting their status as sacred literature for many readers, and it reports the findings of modern textual criticism, comparative study and archaeology where they bear on the texts. It sets the major interpretive traditions — Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita, Dvaita, devotional, Jain, Buddhist and regional — beside modern critical readings, including feminist and Dalit critiques, without making any one of them the measure of the others; where a heading or a judgement belongs to the tradition rather than to the author, it says so. Key ślokas are given in transliteration with translation, only where their wording and reference could be checked. The sociologist Maurice Halbwachs’s idea of “collective memory” — the shared stock of narratives that gives a group its identity — offers a useful modern analogy to the Indian idea of smṛti, “that which is remembered,” and helps to explain why the epics are not only studied but recited, performed, celebrated and contested.

The volume has twelve chapters. After this introduction, Chapters 2 and 3 treat Vālmīki’s Rāmāyaṇa, first as a whole — its structure, recensions, versions and reception — and then book by book; the contested episodes of Vālin, Sītā’s ordeal and Śambūka are discussed in full in Chapter 3. Chapters 4 and 5 do the same for the Mahābhārata: Chapter 4 covers its growth, the Critical Edition and its critics, the Indo-European comparative reading and the Harivaṃśa’s life of Kṛṣṇa, and Chapter 5 surveys the eighteen books. Chapter 6 is devoted to the Bhagavad Gītā, Chapter 7 to the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas with a fuller study of the Bhāgavata, and Chapter 8 to the Upapurāṇas, the māhātmyas of sacred places and the Tamil talapurāṇams. Three thematic chapters follow: Chapter 9 on the hard cases and the limits of epic dharma, Chapter 10 on the women of the epics, and Chapter 11 on the philosophy of the Mokṣadharma and the Nārāyaṇīya. The last chapter, Chapter 12, follows the epics’ afterlife: regional retellings, the Persian translations of the Mughal court and the Sikh Dasam Granth, Southeast Asia, sculpture, dance and ritual theatre, film and festival, and the modern debate over archaeology, astronomy and the historicity of the epics.

docs.title: Chapter 2: The Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa: The Ādikāvya
docs.text:
Few works of world literature have had the cultural reach of the Rāmāyaṇa attributed to Vālmīki, the ādikavi or “first poet.” Composed in the anuṣṭubh śloka that became the standard measure of later Sanskrit narrative verse, it tells the story of Rāma — for the tradition the ideal man, the ideal king and the embodiment of dharma — and has been retold, performed, worshipped and argued over across South and Southeast Asia for more than two millennia (Brockington 1998; Goldman 1984–2017).

The tradition calls the Rāmāyaṇa the ādikāvya, the first poem. According to the opening cantos of the text itself, the śloka form was born from Vālmīki’s cry of anguish on witnessing the killing of a bird: grief (śoka) became verse (śloka). The metre itself is older — the anuṣṭubh occurs throughout the Veda — but the story makes Vālmīki the founder of secular poetry (kāvya), and later poeticians accepted that role for him.

docs.title: 2.1.1 The Life and Transformation of Vālmīki
docs.text:
The epic itself says little about its author. In the Uttarakāṇḍa Vālmīki appears as a sage who shelters the banished Sītā in his hermitage, raises her twin sons Kuśa and Lava, and teaches them to sing the poem; there he calls himself a son of Pracetas (hence the patronymic Prācetasa). The famous story that he had been a robber named Ratnākara, who was reformed by the seven sages and meditated so long that an ant-hill (valmīka) grew over him, is not found in the critical text. It belongs to later tradition — it is told, for instance, in the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, in Purāṇic māhātmyas and in regional Rāmāyaṇas — and the name is derived from valmīka by folk etymology.

The tradition knows him by several titles: ādikavi, the first poet and author of the first kāvya; Prācetasa, the son of Pracetas; and, in later devotional sources, a brahmarṣi who reached that rank through his austerities.

docs.title: 2.1.2 The Birth of the Śloka: Grief into Poetry
docs.text:
The second sarga of the Bālakāṇḍa tells how poetry itself began. Vālmīki, walking by the river Tamasā with his disciple Bharadvāja, saw a pair of krauñca birds (usually identified as cranes or curlews) mating, when a hunter’s arrow killed the male. Moved by the cry of the female, Vālmīki cursed the hunter:

Rāmāyaṇa 1.2.14 (Critical Edition)

mā niṣāda pratiṣṭhāṃ tvam agamaḥ śāśvatīḥ samāḥ / yat krauñcamithunād ekam avadhīḥ kāmamohitam // Translation: “Hunter (niṣāda), may you find no rest for endless years, since you killed one of this pair of krauñcas while it was lost in love.”

Vālmīki was astonished at what he had uttered, a verse with four equal quarters fit to be sung to the lute:

Rāmāyaṇa 1.2.17 (Critical Edition)

pādabaddho ’kṣarasamas tantrīlayasamanvitaḥ / śokārtasya pravṛtto me śloko bhavatu nānyathā // Translation: “Bound in metrical feet, with an equal number of syllables, fit for the rhythm of the lute — this utterance that came from me in my grief shall be called a śloka, and nothing else.”

The god Brahmā then appears, tells Vālmīki that this speech came forth by his will, and commissions him to compose the whole story of Rāma in the same form. Many centuries later the critic Ānandavardhana made the episode the emblem of his theory of poetry: “the very soul of poetry is that (suggested) meaning, as, long ago, the grief of the first poet, arising from the separation of the pair of krauñcas, became verse (śokaḥ ślokatvam āgataḥ)” (Dhvanyāloka 1.5).

docs.title: 2.2 Structure: Seven Kāṇḍas
docs.text:
The Rāmāyaṇa describes itself (Bālakāṇḍa, sarga 4 of the vulgate) as a poem of 24,000 ślokas in 500 sargas, arranged in six books “and the Uttara” — a formulation that itself hints that the seventh book was felt to be an addition. The printed vulgate texts come close to the traditional figure; the Baroda Critical Edition is shorter. A later tradition, the “Gāyatrī Rāmāyaṇa,” holds that each thousand ślokas begins with one of the twenty-four syllables of the Gāyatrī mantra; this is a devotional reading, not a feature of the text as transmitted (Table 2.1).

Table 2.1. Structure of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa Kāṇḍa Name Sargas (vulgate) Sargas (CE) Primary Content 1 Bāla Kāṇḍa 77 76 Birth of Rāma; breaking of Śiva’s bow; marriage 2 Ayodhyā Kāṇḍa 119 111 Exile; death of Daśaratha; Bharata’s refusal 3 Araṇya Kāṇḍa 75 71 Forest life; Śūrpaṇakhā; abduction of Sītā 4 Kiṣkindhā Kāṇḍa 67 66 Alliance with Sugrīva; killing of Vālin; search 5 Sundara Kāṇḍa 68 66 Hanumān in Laṅkā 6 Yuddha Kāṇḍa 128 116 War; death of Rāvaṇa; Sītā’s ordeal; coronation 7 Uttara Kāṇḍa 111 100 Origins of Rāvaṇa; banishment of Sītā; Śambūka; end of Rāma’s reign Total 645 606

Scholarly Note: The growth of the text

Since Hermann Jacobi’s study of 1893, most scholars have regarded Books 2–6 as the oldest part of the poem, and Books 1 and 7 as later additions: they differ in style, they contain most of the passages that present Rāma as an incarnation of Viṣṇu, and the table of contents at the opening of Book 1 originally appears to have ended with the return to Ayodhyā. Brockington distinguishes several stages of growth extending over many centuries; Goldman dates the earliest stratum c. 750–500 BCE, while others prefer the 5th–3rd centuries BCE (see Table 1.5) (Jacobi 1893; Brockington 1984; Goldman 1984–2017).

docs.title: 2.3 The Recensions: Northern and Southern Traditions
docs.text:
The manuscripts of the Rāmāyaṇa fall into distinct regional recensions. The editors of the Critical Edition prepared at the Oriental Institute, Baroda (1960–1975) grouped the manuscripts into two major families, each with sub-recensions defined largely by script (Figure 2.1; Table 2.2):
