docs.title: Chapter 7: Classical Tamil Literature: The Caṅkam Poems and After
docs.text: yātum ūrē yāvarum kēḷir tītum naṉṟum piṟartara vārā Every town is our town, everyone our kin. Evil and good do not come from others. — Kaṇiyaṉ Pūṅkuṉṟaṉār, Puṟanāṉūṟu 192

docs.title: 7.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Tamil is the only modern Indian language with a substantial literature that is as old as the classical literatures of Sanskrit and Prakrit and independent of them. Its earliest layer is a body of some 2,400 poems, by some 470 named poets, collected in eight anthologies and ten long poems. These are commonly called “Caṅkam” (Sangam) poems, after a tradition, first recorded in a commentary of about the eighth century on the Iṟaiyaṉār Akapporuḷ, that three successive “academies” (caṅkam) of poets met under the patronage of the Pāṇṭiya kings over many thousands of years, the first two in cities later swallowed by the sea. The legend is not history, but the name has stuck.

Most scholars date the bulk of the anthology poems to roughly the first three centuries CE, with some poems perhaps earlier, and place the later layers — the Kalittokai, the Paripāṭal and the Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai — in the fifth to seventh centuries. The poems were collected and arranged, with colophons naming poets and situations, several centuries after their composition (Zvelebil 1973, 1974).

This dating has been seriously challenged. In Kāvya in South India (2001) Herman Tieken argued that the poems are not the remains of an ancient bardic culture at all, but a learned literature composed at the Pāṇḍya court around the ninth century, close in time to the commentary that first tells the story of the academies (Tieken 2001). He pointed out that no external evidence for the poems is earlier than that period; that their conventions closely resemble those of Sanskrit and Prakrit court poetry, above all Hāla’s anthology of village love (Section 5.4); and that the world of poor bards and generous chiefs they describe may be a literary fiction of the kind kāvya delighted in, rather than a record of a real society. Most Tamil specialists, George Hart among them, have rejected the redating. They point to the language of the poems, which is older than that of the devotional hymns of the sixth to ninth centuries; to the internal differences between the earlier anthologies and the later layers; and to the agreement between the poems and the evidence of Tamil-Brāhmī inscriptions, hero-stones and the archaeology of Indo-Roman trade (Section 7.8). The debate has nonetheless sharpened a point that both sides accept: the anthologies as we have them, with their arrangement, colophons and commentaries, are the product of a later scholarly act of compilation, and the poems reach us only through it. This book follows the majority dating, with this caution. They were almost forgotten in the medieval period and were recovered in the late nineteenth century from palm-leaf manuscripts by C. W. Tāmōtaram Piḷḷai and U. Vē. Cāminātaiyar, whose editions transformed the understanding of Tamil literary history.

The poems are mainly secular: they speak of love and war, of kings and bards, of the landscapes and seasons of the Tamil country. Their idiom owes little to Sanskrit, though Sanskrit words and North Indian deities and ideas appear, increasingly in the later layers. David Shulman’s Tamil: A Biography is an engaging introduction to the whole tradition (Shulman 2016).

docs.title: 7.2 The Tolkāppiyam
docs.text:
The Tolkāppiyam, ascribed to Tolkāppiyar, is the oldest surviving Tamil grammar. It has three books: Eḻuttatikāram on sounds and letters, Collatikāram on words and syntax, and Poruḷatikāram on “subject matter”, that is, poetics. Its date is disputed. Some Tamil scholars, such as S. Ilakkuvanar, have argued for a date several centuries before the Common Era (Ilakkuvanar 1963). Most historians see the work as layered: the first two books may belong to the last centuries BCE or the early centuries CE, while the Poruḷatikāram, which systematises the conventions of the anthology poems, is generally considered later, perhaps as late as the fifth century (Zvelebil 1974). Its grammar is discussed further in Volume 10, Śabda Vidyā.

The Poruḷatikāram divides poetry into akam, the “interior” world of love between man and woman, and puṟam, the “exterior” world of war, kingship, generosity, death and fame. Each is subdivided into situations (tiṇai). It also describes the conventions governing who may speak in a poem, the elements that make up a poem’s setting, and the eight emotions (meyppāṭu) discussed in Chapter 6.

docs.title: 7.3 The Tiṇai: Landscape and Love
docs.text:
The most distinctive feature of classical Tamil poetics is the association of each phase of love with a landscape. Each landscape has its “first elements” (mutal: place and time), its “native elements” (karu: gods, people, animals, plants, occupations, music) and its human situation (uri). A poem need only mention a flower, a bird or a kind of terrain for an informed listener to recognise the emotional situation. A. K. Ramanujan’s translations and essays introduced this system to a wide readership (Ramanujan 1967, 1985). Table 7.1 summarises the five landscapes.

Table 7.1. The five akam landscapes (simplified, after the Tolkāppiyam) Tiṇai (flower) Landscape Situation (uri) Season and time Deity Kuṟiñci Mountains Lovers’ union, secret meetings Cool season; midnight Murukaṉ Mullai (jasmine) Forest and pasture Patient waiting of the wife Rainy season; evening Māyōṉ (Viṣṇu) Marutam Cultivated riverine land The wife’s sulking at the husband’s infidelity All seasons; dawn Vēntaṉ (Indra) Neytal (water-lily) Seashore Anxious pining All seasons; sunset Varuṇaṉ Pālai Parched wasteland Separation; the lover’s journey; elopement Summer; midday (later Koṟṟavai)

Pālai is not a separate region but any land parched by heat, and the Tolkāppiyam adds two further “situations” outside the five: one-sided love (kaikkiḷai) and mismatched love (peruntiṇai). Figure 7.1 shows the five landscapes schematically.

Figure 7.1. The five landscapes (tiṇai) of classical Tamil love poetry, with their situations and presiding deities.

docs.title: 7.4 Akam: The Poetry of Love
docs.text:
Akam poems are dramatic monologues. They are spoken by the heroine, the hero, the heroine’s friend (tōḻi), her foster-mother, the hero’s companion, or occasionally passers-by; the commentarial tradition supplies for each poem a “situation” (tuṟai) that explains who speaks to whom and when. By convention the lovers are never named: they are types, not individuals, and the poem’s meaning depends on the reader’s recognition of the conventions. Love is divided into premarital “secret” love (kaḷavu) and married love (kaṟpu).

The most famous akam poem, from the Kuṟuntokai, is known by the name of its poet only through its central image: Cempulappeyanīrār, “the poet of the rain on red earth”.

Kuṟuntokai 40

yāyum ñāyum yārā kiyarō entaiyum nuntaiyum emmuṟaik kēḷir yāṉum nīyum evvaḻi yaṟitum cempulap peyanīr pōla aṉpuṭai neñcam tāṅkalan taṉavē What was my mother to yours? How was my father kin to yours? How did you and I ever meet? Like rain falling on red earth, our loving hearts have mingled.

The poem is spoken by the hero, according to the commentary, to reassure the heroine after their first union. Its effect depends on the closing simile: as rain and red soil mix and cannot be separated, so their hearts, unrelated by kinship, have become one.

docs.title: 7.5 Puṟam: The Poetry of the Public World
docs.text: Puṟam poetry celebrates and laments the public world: the valour and generosity of kings, the hunger of bards seeking patrons, battles, cattle raids, hero-stones raised for fallen warriors, and the transience of fortune. The Puṟanāṉūṟu (“Four Hundred Poems of the Exterior”), translated by George Hart and Hank Heifetz, is the great collection (Hart and Heifetz 1999). Its poems range from praise of patrons to meditations on death. In poem 278 an old mother, told that her son fled from battle, swears to cut off the breasts that fed him if it is true; she searches the battlefield, sword in hand, turning over the bodies, and when she finds him lying cut to pieces her joy is greater than on the day she bore him. The poem embodies the harsh martial ethic of the society. Others, like poem 192 quoted at the head of this chapter, express a broad and humane wisdom.

docs.title: 7.5.1 The Situations of Puṟam
docs.text:
Just as akam poetry has its landscapes, the Tolkāppiyam divides puṟam poetry into situations (tiṇai), each named after a flower worn by warriors and each paired with one of the akam landscapes. The principal ones are listed in Table 7.2.

Table 7.2. The puṟam situations of the Tolkāppiyam Tiṇai Situation Veṭci Cattle raid, the opening act of hostilities Vañci Invasion of enemy territory Uḻiñai Siege of a fort Tumpai Pitched battle Vākai Victory, and excellence in one’s calling Kāñci The transience of life and fortune Pāṭāṇ Praise of a king or patron, and the bard’s request for gifts

The kāñci theme, meditation on impermanence, gives some of the most memorable puṟam poems, and the Maturaikkāñci takes its name from it: its long description of the splendour of Madurai is framed as a warning to the king that all this will pass.

docs.title: 7.5.2 Hero-Stones
docs.text: Several puṟam poems refer to the custom of erecting a memorial stone (naṭukal) for a warrior who fell in battle, especially in defending cattle against raiders. The stone was inscribed with his name and deeds, decorated with peacock feathers and worshipped with offerings. The Tolkāppiyam lists the stages of the rite, from finding a suitable stone to its consecration. Hundreds of hero-stones, some inscribed in Tamil-Brāhmī and early Vaṭṭeḻuttu script, have been found in Tamil Nadu and neighbouring regions, confirming the poems’ picture of a society in which cattle raids and the cult of the heroic dead were important, and showing how closely the poetic conventions were tied to actual practice.

docs.title: 7.5.3 Suggestion in Akam Poetry
docs.text: The commentators describe two techniques by which akam poems convey meaning indirectly. In uḷḷuṟai uvamam, “implicit comparison”, a description of nature parallels the human situation without any word of comparison: a poem spoken by a wife whose husband is unfaithful may describe a buffalo trampling a pond full of lilies, leaving the listener to see the husband in the careless animal. In iṟaicci, “suggestion”, a detail of the landscape implies something about the speaker’s feelings that she cannot say directly. Such techniques make the Tamil poems remarkably dense, and they invite comparison with the Sanskrit theory of dhvani (Chapter 6), although the two developed independently (Ramanujan 1985). Modern readers have also compared the juxtaposition of scene and feeling with Imagism or with the “objective correlative”; such comparisons can help a newcomer, but the poems belong to their own system of landscapes and situations, as Ramanujan and Hart have shown.

docs.title: 7.5.4 Bards and Patrons: Kapilar and Pāri
docs.text: The Puṟanāṉūṟu preserves something like the story of a friendship. Pāri, chief of the hill country of Paṟampu, was celebrated as one of the most generous patrons of the age; legend says he once gave his chariot to a jasmine creeper that had no support to climb on. The three crowned kings besieged his hill and, unable to take it, killed him by treachery. The poet Kapilar, his friend, wrote poems on the siege, mocking the kings with the boast that they could never take Paṟampu by force, though they could have it for the asking if they came as bards; and after Pāri’s death he mourned his friend. A short poem ascribed to Pāri’s daughters themselves (Puṟanāṉūṟu 112) recalls the moonlit night of a month ago, when they had their father and their hill, and contrasts it with the present, when enemies hold both. Kapilar then took the orphaned daughters in search of husbands among the chiefs. Whatever the historical basis of the story, these poems give the bardic relationship between poet and patron a moving human face.

docs.title: 7.6 The Corpus: Eight Anthologies and Ten Long Poems
7.6.1 The Eight Anthologies (Eṭṭuttokai)
docs.text:
The eight anthologies, their size and their character are summarised in Table 7.3.

Table 7.3. The Eight Anthologies (Eṭṭuttokai) Anthology Poems Type Remarks Naṟṟiṇai 400 akam Poems of 9–12 lines Kuṟuntokai 401 akam Short poems of 4–8 lines Aiṅkuṟunūṟu 500 akam 100 very short poems for each landscape, each set by a different poet Akanāṉūṟu 400 akam Longer poems of 13–31 lines, ordered by landscape Kalittokai 150 akam Later; dramatic poems in kali metre, including unconventional loves Puṟanāṉūṟu 400 puṟam War, kingship, patronage, death (a few poems lost) Patiṟṟuppattu 100 puṟam Ten decads on Cēra kings; the first and last decads are lost Paripāṭal 70 mixed Later; hymns to Murukaṉ and Tirumāl, and poems on the river Vaiyai; about 24 survive

docs.title: 7.6.2 The Ten Long Poems (Pattuppāṭṭu)
docs.text:
The ten long poems, with the poets named in the colophons, are listed in Table 7.4.

Table 7.4. The Ten Long Poems (Pattuppāṭṭu) Poem Poet Subject Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai Nakkīrar A later devotional “guide” poem to the shrines of Murukaṉ Porunarāṟṟuppaṭai Muṭattāmakkaṇṇiyār A war-bard guides another to the Cōḻa Karikāl Ciṟupāṇāṟṟuppaṭai Nattattaṉār A bard guides another to a generous chief Perumpāṇāṟṟuppaṭai Kaṭiyalūr Uruttiraṅkaṇṇaṉār Guide to the chief Toṇṭaimāṉ Iḷantiraiyaṉ of Kāñci Mullaippāṭṭu Nappūtaṉār A queen awaits her husband’s return from war in the rains Maturaikkāñci Māṅkuṭi Marutaṉār 782 lines on the Pāṇṭiya capital Madurai and the transience of power Neṭunalvāṭai Nakkīrar The long cold north wind; a queen’s loneliness while the king is at war Kuṟiñcippāṭṭu Kapilar A love poem of the mountain landscape Paṭṭiṉappālai Uruttiraṅkaṇṇaṉār The port city of Kāvirippūmpaṭṭiṉam, in a frame of separation Malaipaṭukaṭām Peruṅkuṉṟūr Peruṅkaucikaṉār A guide poem for musicians to the chief Naṉṉaṉ

The āṟṟuppaṭai (“guide”) poems are a distinctive genre: a bard returning laden with gifts meets a poor bard and directs him to the generous patron, describing the route and the landscapes along it.

docs.title: 7.6.3 The Later Layer: Toward Devotion
docs.text: The later poems of the corpus show a changing religious world. The Paripāṭal contains hymns to Tirumāl (Viṣṇu) and Murukaṉ in which Purāṇic myths — Viṣṇu’s incarnations, the birth of Murukaṉ from Śiva’s seed — are told in Tamil, alongside lively descriptions of festivals on the river Vaiyai at Madurai, where townspeople bathe and make love. The Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai adapts the secular “guide” genre to religion: instead of directing a bard to a generous patron, the poet directs a devotee to the six shrines of Murukaṉ, describing the god’s forms and the worship at each. These works stand at the threshold of the devotional poetry of the Āḻvārs and Nāyaṉmārs (Chapter 9), and show how classical Tamil forms could be turned to new purposes.

docs.title: 7.7 The Poets
docs.text: The colophons name some 470 poets. They include brahmins, kings, merchants, artisans and bards, and about thirty women. Among the most celebrated are Kapilar, the most prolific poet of the corpus and a master of the kuṟiñci landscape; Paraṇar, known for his historical allusions; Nakkīrar; Māmūlaṉār; and Avvaiyār, a woman poet of both akam and puṟam who appears in the poems as a confidante of the chief Atiyamāṉ. The name Avvaiyār was also borne, or given by tradition, to later poets, including the medieval author of the didactic verses Ātticcūṭi and Koṉṟaivēntaṉ that are still taught to Tamil children.

docs.title: 7.7.1 Women Poets of the Anthologies
docs.text: The women poets of the anthologies write in both akam and puṟam modes. Veḷḷivītiyār is remembered for poems of a woman’s longing and of her defiance of convention in following her lover; Okkūr Mācāttiyār and Kākkaipāṭiṉiyār Nacceḷḷaiyār, to whom the Puṟanāṉūṟu poem on the heroic mother (no. 278) is ascribed, wrote of women’s pride and grief in a warrior society; and Avvaiyār’s poems range from tender love lyrics to sharp exchanges with chiefs. George Hart has argued that the presence of women poets and the prominence of women’s voices reflect a society in which women’s sexuality and power were viewed with both reverence and fear (Hart 1975). Whatever the explanation, the Tamil anthologies and the Pali Therīgāthā together preserve the largest body of early Indian poetry ascribed to named women.

docs.title: 7.8 The Poems as Historical Evidence
docs.text: The poems refer to the three crowned dynasties, the Cēra, Cōḻa and Pāṇṭiya, and to many lesser chiefs; to trade with the Yavanas (Greeks and Romans) who brought wine and gold for pepper; to ports such as Muciṟi and Kāvirippūmpaṭṭiṉam; and to a society of farmers, herders, fishers, hunters, bards and warriors. Much of this is consistent with external evidence: the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (first century CE) and Pliny describe the pepper trade of the Malabar coast; Roman coins and amphorae have been found in South India; excavations at Arikamedu near Puducherry and at Pattanam in Kerala have revealed Indo-Roman trading sites; and Tamil-Brāhmī inscriptions from the second century BCE onwards document the early written language. Recent excavations at Kīḻaṭi near Madurai have uncovered an urban settlement of the early historic period whose dating and interpretation continue to be discussed. The poems are, however, poetry, written within strict conventions; they should be used as historical evidence with care.

docs.title: 7.9 After the Anthologies: The Eighteen Minor Works and the Tirukkuṟaḷ
docs.text: The period after the anthologies, roughly the fourth to sixth centuries, produced a collection known as the “Eighteen Minor Works” (Patiṉeṇkīḻkkaṇakku), mostly short didactic texts in the veṇpā metre, together with a few works on love and war. Several show Jain influence. The most famous is the Tirukkuṟaḷ, and among the others the Nālaṭiyār, a Jain anthology of 400 quatrains on ethics, is the best known. Neither belongs to the Caṅkam anthologies proper, although popular accounts often treat them so.

docs.title: 7.9.1 The Tirukkuṟaḷ
docs.text:
The Tirukkuṟaḷ is ascribed to Tiruvaḷḷuvar, about whom nothing reliable is known; the traditional biographies are late legends. Most scholars date the work to about the fifth century CE, though earlier and later dates have been proposed. It consists of 1,330 couplets (kuṟaḷ veṇpā) in 133 chapters of ten, arranged in three books that correspond to three of the classical aims of life: virtue (aṟam, 38 chapters), wealth and polity (poruḷ, 70 chapters) and love (iṉpam or kāmam, 25 chapters). It speaks of God in general terms, and has been claimed by Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, Jains and Buddhists; its ethic of non-violence and vegetarianism has led many scholars to see Jain influence, though this remains debated. The first couplet opens the work:

Tirukkuṟaḷ 1

akara mutala eḻuttellām āti pakavaṉ mutaṟṟē ulaku As all letters have the letter a as their first, so the world has the Primal Lord as its first.

The chapter on learning (kalvi) begins:

Tirukkuṟaḷ 391

kaṟka kacaṭaṟak kaṟpavai kaṟṟapiṉ niṟka ataṟkut taka Learn thoroughly, without fault, what should be learned; and having learned it, live in accordance with it.

The first book, on virtue, begins with praise of God, rain, ascetics and virtue itself, and then treats the life of the householder — the good wife, children, love, hospitality, gratitude, impartiality, self-control, patience, non-violence — and the life of renunciation. The book on polity contains a realistic treatment of kingship, ministers, alliances and war; one of its couplets states that all living beings are alike by birth and that distinctions arise only from the differing quality of their actions (972), a statement often cited against caste. The book on love, in the voices of the lovers, draws on the conventions of the akam poems. The Tirukkuṟaḷ has been translated into English many times, and into many other languages, since the nineteenth century. A statue of Tiruvaḷḷuvar 133 feet (about 40 metres) high, one foot for each chapter, was erected in 2000 on a rock off Kanyakumari (Figure 7.2).

Figure 7.2. The statue of Tiruvaḷḷuvar off Kanyakumari (completed 2000), with the Vivekananda Rock Memorial on the left. Photo: N. Vivekananthamoorthy, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 7.10 The Tamil Epics
docs.text:
Tradition speaks of “five great epics” (aimperuṅkāppiyam): the Cilappatikāram, the Maṇimēkalai, the Cīvakacintāmaṇi, and two works that survive only in fragments, the Vaḷaiyāpati and the Kuṇṭalakēci.

The Cilappatikāram (“The Tale of the Anklet”), ascribed to Iḷaṅkō Aṭikaḷ, a prince-turned-ascetic of the Cēra line, is usually dated to the fifth or sixth century. Its three books are set in the three Tamil kingdoms. The merchant Kōvalaṉ leaves his wife Kaṇṇaki for the courtesan-dancer Mātavi, loses his wealth, and returns to Kaṇṇaki; they go to Madurai to rebuild their fortune by selling one of her anklets, but Kōvalaṉ is falsely accused of stealing the queen’s anklet and executed on the king’s order. Kaṇṇaki proves his innocence before the king, who dies of remorse, and in her fury tears off her breast and burns the city. She becomes a goddess, Pattiṉi, whose cult the poem’s last book describes. The work is a rich source for music, dance and urban life, and blends Jain, Hindu and local religious elements.

The Cilappatikāram is unusual among Indian epics in its heroes: not kings or gods but a merchant couple and a courtesan. Its second canto-group, set in Madurai, includes the songs of cowherd women dancing in a circle to Kṛṣṇa (the āycciyar kuravai) and of hunters worshipping the goddess Koṟṟavai, and its account of Mātavi’s dance performance and training is a primary source for the history of South Indian music and dance. Its framing — a prince-poet who renounces the throne, and a prologue that states the work’s three morals (that dharma destroys an erring king, that the world honours a chaste wife, and that karma bears its fruit) — gives it a moral structure that later Tamil readers took to heart; Kaṇṇaki became a symbol of Tamil womanhood, a figure revered and, in modern feminist criticism, questioned.

Its sequel, the Maṇimēkalai of Cīttalaic Cāttaṉār, follows Kōvalaṉ and Mātavi’s daughter Maṇimēkalai, who renounces the world and becomes a Buddhist nun; it includes expositions of Buddhist and other philosophies. The Cīvakacintāmaṇi of Tiruttakkatēvar (ninth–tenth century), a Jain epic in the manner of the Sanskrit mahākāvya, tells of a prince who wins eight wives and a kingdom before renouncing all. The devotional poetry that arose between the sixth and ninth centuries is the subject of Chapter 9.

docs.title: 7.11.1 Kampaṉ and the Cōḻa Age
docs.text:
Under the Cōḻa kings (ninth to thirteenth centuries) Tamil literature combined the devotional heritage of the Āḻvārs and Nāyaṉmārs with the conventions of the Sanskrit court epic. Kampaṉ’s Irāmāvatāram, usually dated to the twelfth century, retells the story of Rāma in some ten thousand stanzas in six books, ending with Rāma’s coronation. It is not a translation of Vālmīki: Kampaṉ reshapes episodes, gives Rāvaṇa a tragic grandeur, and fills the poem with Tamil landscapes and a devotional vision of Rāma as the supreme God. Its passages on the death of Vāli and on Rāvaṇa’s last battle are among the summits of Tamil poetry.

Other works of the period include Jayaṅkoṇṭār’s Kaliṅkattupparaṇi (early twelfth century), a war poem of the paraṇi genre on the Kaliṅga campaign of Kulōttuṅka I, which describes the battlefield as a feast for ghouls; the court poems of Oṭṭakkūttar; and Cēkkiḻār’s Periya Purāṇam, the lives of the sixty-three Śaiva saints, written for Kulōttuṅka II and later added to the Śaiva canon. Villiputtūrār’s Tamil Mahābhārata (fourteenth century) and Aruṇakirinātar’s Tiruppukaḻ (fifteenth century), rhythmically intricate hymns to Murukaṉ, continued the narrative and devotional traditions.

docs.title: 7.11.2 Islamic and Christian Tamil Literature
docs.text: Tamil literature was never confined to one religion. Jains and Buddhists wrote some of its classics, as we have seen; later, Muslims and Christians adopted its forms. Umaṟuppulavar’s Cīṟāppurāṇam (c. 1700), a life of the Prophet Muḥammad in the form of a Tamil epic, with descriptions of Arabian landscapes rendered in the conventions of the tiṇai, is the classic of Tamil Muslim literature. The Italian Jesuit Costanzo Beschi, known in Tamil as Vīramāmunivar, wrote the Tēmpāvaṇi (1726), an epic on the life of Saint Joseph, as well as Tamil grammars and a dictionary; and H. A. Kiruṣṇapiḷḷai’s Iraṭcaṇiya Yāttirikam (1894) adapted Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress as a Tamil epic.

docs.title: 7.11.3 Towards the Modern
docs.text:
Modern Tamil literature begins in the late nineteenth century with Vētanāyakam Piḷḷai’s Piratāpa Mutaliyār Carittiram (1879), generally regarded as the first Tamil novel, and with the rediscovery of the classical anthologies. Subramania Bharati (1882–1921) created a modern Tamil poetry. A journalist and nationalist in Madras and later an exile in French Pondicherry, he wrote patriotic songs, devotional poems to Kṛṣṇa, Kāḷī and Murukaṉ, a long poem retelling the humiliation of Draupadī as an allegory of India in bondage (Pāñcāli Capatam, 1912), prose poems influenced by Whitman, and essays calling for the education and freedom of women and the abolition of caste; his language, close to everyday speech yet rich in classical echoes, became the starting point of modern Tamil verse. The short stories of Putumaippittaṉ in the 1930s and 1940s inaugurated Tamil modernism. The little magazine Maṇikkoṭi (from 1933) gathered the first generation of modern short-story writers, among them Putumaippittaṉ, Ku. Pa. Rājagōpālaṉ and the elliptical Mauṉi, and later magazines such as Eḻuttu (from 1959) fostered a Tamil putukkavitai (“new poetry”) in free verse.

The rediscovered Caṅkam poetry became central to Tamil cultural identity and to the politics of the Dravidian movement. Bhāratidāsaṉ (1891–1964), a disciple of Bharati, became the poet of the Self-Respect movement, celebrating the Tamil language and attacking caste and religious orthodoxy, and the Dravidian leaders C. N. Aṇṇāturai and M. Karuṇānidhi wrote plays and film scripts — Karuṇānidhi’s dialogue for the film Parāśakti (1952) is the best-known example — that carried the movement’s ideas to mass audiences. Novelists such as Akilaṉ and Jeyakāntaṉ, both recipients of the Jnanpith Award, wrote of urban and working-class life; Sundara Rāmacāmi, Ambai and others developed a modernist and feminist fiction; and from the 1990s Dalit writers such as Bama and Imaiyam (Chapter 13) gave a voice to communities the older literature had excluded. In 2004 Tamil became the first language to be officially declared a “classical language” by the Government of India.

docs.title: 7.12 Tamil and Sanskrit
docs.text: The relation between Tamil and Sanskrit has been debated, often passionately, since the nineteenth century. The classical anthologies show a literature with its own conventions, owing little to Sanskrit; yet Sanskrit loanwords, North Indian gods and Brahmanical institutions appear in them, increasingly in the later layers, and the Tamil grammarians knew Sanskrit grammar. In the following centuries the two languages lived side by side in the Tamil country: the Pallava and Cōḻa courts patronised Sanskrit as well as Tamil, the devotional poets drew on Purāṇic myth while asserting the equality of Tamil hymns with the Veda, and the maṇipravāḷam commentaries of the Śrīvaiṣṇavas mixed the two languages freely. In the twentieth century the Dravidian movement emphasised Tamil’s independence from Sanskrit and its antiquity, while others stressed the long interaction between them. Modern scholarship, represented by George Hart and David Shulman, tends to see both continuity and independence: Tamil developed a distinct classical literature of its own, which entered into a long and creative dialogue with Sanskrit (Hart 1975; Shulman 2016).

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Ramanujan (1967) and Ramanujan (1985): translations of akam and puṟam poetry with essays on the conventions.

  • Hart and Heifetz (1999): the complete Puṟanāṉūṟu.

  • Hart (1975): the cultural world of the poems and their relation to Sanskrit.

  • Zvelebil (1973) and Zvelebil (1974): histories of Tamil literature.

  • Tieken (2001): the case for a late date of the anthologies, to be read with the replies it provoked.

  • Shulman (2016): an introduction to the whole Tamil tradition.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Nīti Literature: Fable, Maxim and Anthology
8.1 Introduction: Worldly Wisdom
docs.text:
Nīti (from the root nī, “to lead”) means “guidance”: prudent conduct, policy, the art of getting on in the world and, for a king, statecraft. A large literature in Sanskrit and the regional languages is devoted to it. It takes three main forms: the fable collection, in which stories, often of animals, illustrate maxims of policy; the gnomic verse (subhāṣita, “well said”), a single stanza expressing a general truth; and the didactic sections of the epics.

Nīti literature is closely related to the science of political economy (arthaśāstra), whose classic text, the Arthaśāstra ascribed by tradition to Kauṭilya (Cāṇakya), is a composite work dated by its most recent translator to c. 50 BCE–300 CE (Olivelle 2013); the text and its political theory are treated in Volume 18, Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra. Kāmandaka’s Nītisāra (perhaps sixth to eighth century) restates its doctrines in verse. The fables and maxims, however, address a wider audience than kings, and their outlook is practical rather than moralising: they teach how to secure friends, defeat enemies, avoid being deceived and survive misfortune.

docs.title: 8.1.1 The Arthaśāstra and the Literature of Policy
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra itself is a technical treatise, not a work of literature, but its influence on literature was profound. It analyses the state into seven “limbs” — the king, ministers, territory, fort, treasury, army and ally — and treats foreign relations through the “circle of kings” (maṇḍala), in which a king’s neighbour is his natural enemy and his neighbour’s neighbour his natural friend. It discusses the training of princes, the employment of spies, the testing of ministers’ loyalty and the means of dealing with enemies: conciliation, gifts, dissension and force. These categories reappear in the Pañcatantra, in Viśākhadatta’s Mudrārākṣasa (Chapter 3), in the debates of the Kirātārjunīya (Chapter 2), and in the court episodes of countless poems. Kāmandaka’s Nītisāra put this political science into easy verse, and it was studied as far afield as Java and Bali.

docs.title: 8.2 The Pañcatantra
docs.text: The Pañcatantra (“Five Books”) is the most widely travelled work of Indian literature. Its original text is lost; it survives in many recensions, of which the Kashmiri Tantrākhyāyika is considered the oldest, and the work as a whole is usually dated to around the third to fifth century CE. Arthur Ryder’s lively translation of a later recension and Patrick Olivelle’s translation of a reconstructed text are both widely read (Ryder 1925; Olivelle 1997).

docs.title: 8.2.1 Frame Story and Structure
docs.text:
A king, Amaraśakti of Mahilāropya, despairs of his three dull-witted sons. The aged brahmin Viṣṇuśarman undertakes to make them expert in policy within six months, and composes the five books for the purpose. Each book has a frame story into which further stories are inserted, often several levels deep, and the prose narrative is punctuated by verse maxims that characters quote to one another as arguments (Table 8.1).

Table 8.1. The five books of the Pañcatantra Book Title Frame story and theme I Mitrabheda (“Breaking of Friends”) The jackal Damanaka, against the advice of his brother Karaṭaka, sets the lion-king Piṅgalaka against his friend the bull Sañjīvaka, who is killed. How enmity is sown between allies II Mitrasamprāpti (“Winning of Friends”) A crow, a mouse, a tortoise and a deer become friends and rescue one another from hunters. The value of alliance among the weak III Kākolūkīya (“Crows and Owls”) A crow minister pretends to defect to the owls, learns their weaknesses and destroys them. War, peace and stratagem IV Labdhapraṇāśa (“Loss of What Was Gained”) A crocodile, urged by his wife, tries to get the heart of his friend the monkey, who escapes by his wits. How gains are lost through folly V Aparīkṣitakāraka (“Ill-Considered Action”) Stories of rash acts, including the brahmin’s wife who kills the faithful mongoose that has saved her child from a snake

Well-known stories include the lion and the hare (who tricks the lion into leaping at his reflection in a well), the talkative tortoise carried through the air by two geese, and the blue jackal who passes himself off as king of the beasts until he betrays himself by howling — all from the first book.

The third book applies the six measures of foreign policy (ṣāḍguṇya) of the arthaśāstra tradition: peace (sandhi), war (vigraha), marching (yāna), waiting (āsana), alliance (saṃśraya) and the double policy of peace with one and war with another (dvaidhībhāva).

docs.title: 8.2.2 The Travels of the Pañcatantra
docs.text:
The westward journey of the Pañcatantra can be traced through a chain of translations (Table 8.2).

Table 8.2. Some stages in the transmission of the Pañcatantra Date Language Version 6th c. Middle Persian (Pahlavi) Translation by the physician Burzōy for the Sasanian king Khusraw I (r. 531–579); lost c. 570 Syriac Kalīlag wa-Damnag, from the Pahlavi c. 750 Arabic Kalīla wa-Dimna of Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, a classic of Arabic prose and the source of most later versions c. 1080 Greek Stephanitēs kai Ichnēlatēs of Symeon Seth 12th c. Hebrew Version attributed to Rabbi Joel 1251 Castilian Calila e Dimna c. 1270 Latin Directorium vitae humanae of John of Capua, from the Hebrew c. 1480 German Das Buch der Beispiele der alten Weisen, one of the early printed German books 1570 English Sir Thomas North’s The Morall Philosophie of Doni, from an Italian adaptation

Persian versions such as the Anvār-i Suhaylī (fifteenth century) carried the stories into Turkish and back into India, and the French fabulist La Fontaine acknowledged a debt to “Pilpay”, a name derived from the Arabic versions, in his later fables. The stories also travelled east, into Southeast Asian, Tibetan and Mongolian literatures.

docs.title: 8.2.3 The Ethics of the Pañcatantra
docs.text: Readers since the nineteenth century have been struck by how little the Pañcatantra moralises. Its heroes are often the clever rather than the good: the jackal Damanaka wins by slander, the crow minister of the third book wins by treachery, and the hare kills the lion by deceit. Its verses frequently advise distrust — of kings, of enemies who seem friendly, of women, of servants. This is because the book belongs to the tradition of nīti and arthaśāstra, whose subject is how to succeed and survive in a world of competing interests, not how to attain moral perfection. As Patrick Olivelle’s introduction emphasises, the work is a textbook of nīti: its aim is practical intelligence — the ability to read situations, weigh advice and act at the right moment — and its characters use stories and maxims as arguments rather than as simple moral lessons (Olivelle 1997). Its teachings are not without ethical limits: the second book praises steadfast friendship, and many verses condemn greed, cruelty and ingratitude. But its ethics are those of a courtly and commercial world in which survival depends on prudence.

docs.title: 8.3 The Hitopadeśa
docs.text:
The Hitopadeśa (“Beneficial Instruction”), by Nārāyaṇa, a poet patronised by a king Dhavalacandra, probably of eastern India, reworks Pañcatantra material into four books: Mitralābha (“Winning of Friends”), Suhṛdbheda (“Separation of Friends”), Vigraha (“War”) and Sandhi (“Peace”). Its date is uncertain; the oldest manuscript is of 1373, and the work is usually placed between the ninth and fourteenth centuries. With its simple prose and abundant verse maxims it became a standard first reader for students of Sanskrit, in India and later in Europe. Among its introductory verses is a famous chain of causes:

Hitopadeśa, introductory verses

vidyā dadāti vinayaṃ vinayād yāti pātratām | pātratvād dhanam āpnoti dhanād dharmaṃ tataḥ sukham || Learning gives modesty; from modesty one becomes worthy; from worthiness one gains wealth; from wealth, righteousness; and from that, happiness.

docs.title: 8.4 Subhāṣita: The Single Stanza and the Anthologies
docs.text:
The single, self-contained stanza was a favourite form of Sanskrit poetry. Such verses, whether on love, nature, the seasons, kingship, poverty or the follies of mankind, were quoted in conversation and in learned discussion, and collected in anthologies arranged by topic. The anthologies preserve the work of hundreds of poets, many otherwise unknown, and include women poets such as Vijjakā (Vijjā) and Śīlābhaṭṭārikā. The major anthologies are listed in Table 8.3.

Table 8.3. Major Sanskrit anthologies Anthology Compiler Date Remarks Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa Vidyākara c. 1100 About 1,730 verses; compiled in a Buddhist monastery in Bengal Saduktikarṇāmṛta Śrīdharadāsa 1205 About 2,370 verses; Bengal, court of Lakṣmaṇasena Sūktimuktāvalī Jalhaṇa 1258 Yādava court of Devagiri Śārṅgadhara­paddhati Śārṅgadhara 1363 Over 4,000 verses on a wide range of subjects Subhāṣitāvali Vallabhadeva 15th c. (?) Over 3,500 verses; Kashmir Subhāṣita­ratna­bhāṇḍāgāra K. P. Parab (ed.) 1886 A modern printed compilation, often reprinted

Many subhāṣitas circulated anonymously and are still widely quoted. Two examples:

Anonymous; also in the Cāṇakyanīti (vulgate 14.1)

pṛthivyāṃ trīṇi ratnāni jalam annaṃ subhāṣitam | mūḍhaiḥ pāṣāṇakhaṇḍeṣu ratnasaṃjñā vidhīyate || There are three jewels on earth: water, food and a well-turned saying. Only fools give the name “jewel” to bits of stone.

Anonymous

paropakārāya phalanti vṛkṣāḥ paropakārāya vahanti nadyaḥ | paropakārāya duhanti gāvaḥ paropakārārtham idaṃ śarīram || Trees bear fruit for the good of others; rivers flow for others; cows give milk for others: this body too exists for the good of others.

docs.title: 8.4.1 Vidyākara’s Treasury
docs.text:
The Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa (“Treasury of Well-Turned Verse”) shows what an anthology was and how one was made. Its compiler, Vidyākara, was a Buddhist scholar of the Jagaddala monastery in northern Bengal, a late Pāla foundation (see Volume 4, Buddha–Jina Prabhā), and he made it around 1100, apparently revising and enlarging it later. An earlier and shorter form was published in 1912 from a Nepalese manuscript under the title Kavīndravacanasamuccaya; the full work was edited by D. D. Kosambi and V. V. Gokhale from a palm-leaf manuscript preserved in Tibet (Kosambi and Gokhale 1957), and translated by Daniel Ingalls (Ingalls 1965).

Its some 1,730 stanzas are arranged in fifty sections (vrajyā). It opens, as a Buddhist compiler’s work would, with verses to the Buddha and the bodhisattvas, but passes at once to Śiva, Pārvatī and Viṣṇu, and then through the seasons, the many phases of love, the beauties of women, sunset and moonrise, the court, the village, the virtuous and the wicked, and the poets themselves. That a Buddhist monk should collect erotic and Śaiva verses in this way shows how far kāvya was a shared culture that crossed religious boundaries. The anthology preserves the work of more than two hundred poets, among them Kālidāsa, Bhavabhūti and Rājaśekhara, but many are known only from such collections. Ingalls drew particular attention to a group of poets of Pāla Bengal, such as Yogeśvara, who described the countryside with unusual realism: the village in the rains, the farmer’s fields, the poor man’s household with its leaking roof and hungry children, subjects that the court epic seldom admitted.

The anthologies were also a working tool. Compilers chose and arranged stanzas by topic so that a reader could find a verse for an occasion or a figure; they recorded authors’ names, though the same stanza is often ascribed to different poets in different collections; and theorists and commentators quoted from them. Many poets, including most of the women poets of Sanskrit (Section 2.11), survive only because an anthologist chose one or two of their verses.

docs.title: 8.5 Bhartṛhari’s Three Centuries
docs.text:
The best-known collection of single stanzas is the Śatakatraya (“Three Centuries”) attributed to Bhartṛhari: the Nītiśataka on worldly wisdom, the Śṛṅgāraśataka on love and the Vairāgyaśataka on renunciation. Tradition identifies the poet with a king who renounced his throne, and sometimes with the grammarian-philosopher Bhartṛhari (fifth century), author of the Vākyapadīya; neither identification can be confirmed. The collections exist in many recensions with widely varying contents. D. D. Kosambi’s critical edition (1948) showed that only a core of about two hundred verses is common to the manuscript traditions, and that the rest was added over time (Kosambi 1948). The verses move between ironic observation of human folly, celebration of women’s beauty and desire, and a weary longing for release, and the arrangement in three centuries invites readers to see these as stages of a life.

The Nītiśataka mocks the fool who cannot be taught, the arrogance of the rich, the servility of courtiers and the injustice of fate, and praises learning, courage, friendship and the steadfastness of the good, who do not abandon a task once begun however great the obstacles. The Śṛṅgāraśataka alternates celebration of women’s beauty with warnings against desire as a snare. The Vairāgyaśataka speaks of the humiliations of seeking patronage, the decay of the body, the passing of time that devours all, and the peace of the ascetic who lives in the forest with the earth for his bed and the sky for his garment. Many verses are among the most quoted in Sanskrit, and they were among the first Sanskrit poems translated into European languages, appearing in Dutch as early as 1651.

docs.title: 8.6 Satire: Kṣemendra and Others
docs.text: Worldly wisdom shades into satire, and Sanskrit has a lively satirical literature. The Kashmiri polymath Kṣemendra (eleventh century), already met as a theorist of propriety (Chapter 6), wrote a series of satirical poems on the society of his time: the Narmamālā (“Garland of Jests”) on corrupt scribes and officials, the Deśopadeśa (“Advice to the Country”) on rogues, misers, quack doctors, false ascetics and procuresses, and the Kalāvilāsa (“Sport of the Arts”) on the many arts of deception practised by merchants, goldsmiths, astrologers and others. His Samayamātṛkā follows the career of a courtesan guided by a scheming old bawd. These works, with their unsparing portraits of the Kashmiri bureaucracy and of hypocrisy in every class, complement Kalhaṇa’s history and show that Sanskrit literature was not confined to idealised kings and lovers. Later satirists include Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita in the seventeenth century (Chapter 2), and the farces of the theatre (Chapter 3) belong to the same tradition.

docs.title: 8.7 The Cāṇakya Collections
docs.text:
Collections of maxims under the name of Cāṇakya, the minister of Candragupta Maurya to whom tradition ascribes the Arthaśāstra, circulated widely in many versions (Cāṇakyanīti, Vṛddhacāṇakya and others). They are medieval compilations, not works of the historical Cāṇakya, and their contents vary greatly. They deal with friendship, family, wealth, learning, women and the conduct of the wise, often in blunt and sometimes misogynistic terms. A typical verse:

Cāṇakyanīti 3.15 (vulgate)

ekena śuṣkavṛkṣeṇa dahyamānena vahninā | dahyate tad vanaṃ sarvaṃ kuputreṇa kulaṃ yathā || As a whole forest is burned by a single dry tree set on fire, so is a family by a single bad son.

docs.title: 8.8 Nīti in the Mahābhārata
docs.text:
The Mahābhārata contains two great bodies of nīti. The Viduranīti (Udyogaparvan, chapters 33–40) is the counsel given by the wise Vidura to the sleepless king Dhṛtarāṣṭra on the eve of the war: a series of maxims on the marks of the wise and the foolish, the duties of kings, and the dangers of greed and anger, framed by Vidura’s vain attempt to persuade the king to restrain his son.

Far longer are the teachings of the dying Bhīṣma to Yudhiṣṭhira in the Śāntiparvan and Anuśāsanaparvan: on the duties of kings (rājadharma), conduct in times of distress (āpaddharma) and liberation (mokṣadharma), and, in the Anuśāsanaparvan, on gifts, the duties of women and much else. These books are an encyclopaedia of the political and ethical thought of their time, including some of its harshest teachings on caste and gender, and the commentarial and scholarly literature on them is large.

docs.title: 8.9 Wisdom Literature in the Regional Languages
docs.text:
Every Indian literature has its own wisdom verse, often among its most popular and most quoted works (Table 8.4).

Table 8.4. Some wisdom literature in the regional languages Language Works and poets Remarks Tamil Tirukkuṟaḷ; Nālaṭiyār; Avvaiyār’s Ātticcūṭi See Chapter 7 Telugu Sumati Śatakamu; Vēmana (c. 17th c.?) Śataka verse (Section 10.3) Kannada Sarvajña (16th–17th c.?) Pithy three-line tripadi verses on everyday life Hindi Kabīr’s sākhīs; Rahīm’s dohās; Vṛnd’s Satsaī Couplets quoted as proverbs Marathi Rāmdās’s Manāce Ślok Verses of instruction “to the mind” Persian and Urdu Saʿdī’s Gulistān (widely read in India); Urdu ghazal couplets Couplets as proverbs (Chapter 12)

docs.title: 8.10 Oral Wisdom: Proverbs, Riddles and Sayings
docs.text: Beside the written collections there has always been a vast oral literature of proverbs, riddles and sayings in every Indian language, much of it never recorded until modern times. Sanskrit theorists recognised the riddle (prahelikā) as a minor poetic form, and riddling verses appear in the epics and the anthologies. In Bengal, sayings ascribed to Khanā, a legendary woman astrologer, give practical advice on agriculture, weather and household life (“Khanār bacan”); in the Hindi region similar agricultural and weather sayings are attributed to Ghāgh and Bhaḍḍarī. Proverbs about castes, women and neighbouring peoples record social attitudes, sometimes harsh, that rarely appear so openly in written literature. Folklorists since the nineteenth century, Indian and European, have collected such material, and it forms an important link between written literature and the oral traditions discussed in Volume 23 of this series.

docs.title: 8.11 Women, Caste and the Limits of Proverbial Wisdom
docs.text:
Wisdom literature records the assumptions of the people who composed and transmitted it, and these were overwhelmingly men of the upper castes. Many nīti verses in Sanskrit and in the regional languages describe women as fickle, deceitful and in need of constant guardianship, echoing the prescriptions of the Dharmaśāstras; others treat low-caste people as naturally base, or wealth and birth as the measure of worth. Modern editions and popular anthologies often omit such verses, so that the tradition appears more humane than its manuscripts show. The same collections that teach shrewd advice on friendship and enmity also teach contempt for women and the low-born, often in the same metre and with the same wit.

The tradition also contained its own counter-voices. Bhartṛhari’s Vairāgyaśataka mocks the pride of wealth and birth; the Telugu verses of Vēmana and the Hindi couplets of Kabīr ridicule caste distinctions and ritual purity; and the Tirukkuṟaḷ declares that all living beings are alike by birth and differ only in their deeds. Proverbial wisdom, in India as elsewhere, was never a single consistent body of teaching but a store of contradictory sayings, each available to be quoted when it suited.

docs.title: 8.12 Shared Stories: Jātaka and Pañcatantra
docs.text: Many stories occur in both the Buddhist Jātaka and the Pañcatantra family, as well as in Jain collections and in the epics, which shows that all of them drew on a common stock of Indian folk narrative. The tale of the talkative tortoise carried by geese, for example, appears in the Pañcatantra as a warning against ignoring the advice of friends and in the Jātaka as a lesson told to a king who talked too much; the tale of the ass in the lion’s skin, betrayed by its braying, appears in the Jātaka and has close parallels in the Aesopic collections. Each tradition framed the shared stories for its own ends: the Buddhist collection made them illustrations of the virtues of the future Buddha, the Pañcatantra made them arguments in a debate on policy, and the Jain collections made them demonstrations of the workings of karma. The same story could thus carry very different morals in different hands — a fact that warns against reading any one moral as the “meaning” of an Indian tale.

docs.title: 8.13 Indian and Aesopic Fable
docs.text: The Indian fable is often compared with the Greek fables ascribed to Aesop. The two traditions share some stories, and scholars have long debated the direction of borrowing; in most cases it cannot be determined. The most obvious difference is structural: Aesop’s fables are short, self-contained stories with an appended moral, whereas the Pañcatantra embeds its stories in frames and has characters argue with stories and verses, so that each story serves as a move in a debate. Its “morals” are also more pragmatic: cleverness is rewarded even when it is ruthless, and the clever jackal Damanaka is, for much of the first book, its hero. On the Jātaka versions of the shared stories see the previous section and Chapter 5.

docs.text:
