His most lasting creation was a school of chemists. Among his students at Presidency College and, after 1916, at the new University College of Science in Calcutta, where he became the first Palit Professor of Chemistry, were Nil Ratan Dhar, Jnan Chandra Ghosh, Jnanendra Nath Mukherjee and Priyadaranjan Ray, who between them founded research traditions in physical, colloid and inorganic chemistry at Calcutta, Dacca, Allahabad and Bangalore; the physicist Meghnad Saha also attended his lectures. In 1924 Ray became the first president of the Indian Chemical Society, whose journal gave Indian chemists a forum of their own. The History of Hindu Chemistry belongs to the same project. It was written, in part, to give Indian students of a European science a history of their own, and it presented the Sanskrit tradition both as evidence of past achievement and, through its account of caste and the contempt for manual work, as an explanation of later decline (Ray 1902–1909; Prakash 1999).

The Calcutta school shaped the teaching of chemistry in India for half a century. Its graduates staffed the chemistry departments of the new universities, and the institutions in which they worked—the University College of Science, the Indian Institute of Science, the national laboratories of the CSIR—trained the chemists and metallurgists who, after 1947, carried out much of the analytical work on Indian iron, steel, zinc, glass and medicines on which this volume relies (Kumar 1995; Arnold 2000).

This modern history is linked to the older one in two ways. Some of the earliest work in the history of Indian chemistry was done by modern Indian chemists, notably Ray, who saw it as part of a national scientific revival. And it was modern laboratory science, including Indian laboratories, that made possible the archaeometallurgical research on which much of this volume depends.

docs.title: 15.4 From Salts to Soda Ash: The Modern Chemical Industry
docs.text:
The substances discussed in Chapter 13—saltpetre, borax, alum, alkalis, salt—were, in the 19th century, among India’s exports of raw materials, along with indigo, lac and the myrobalans used in European tanning. Manufactured chemicals, by contrast, were largely imported: soda ash, caustic soda, acids, synthetic dyes, drugs and fine chemicals came from Britain and, increasingly, Germany. Indian chemical manufacture in the modern sense began on a small scale at the end of the century, with ventures such as Ray’s Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works, and with government laboratories that made vaccines and sera, such as the Plague Research Laboratory set up in Bombay in 1899 under Waldemar Haffkine (Arnold 2000).

The modern successors of the old salt economy grew out of this dependence. The First World War, which cut off German dyes and drugs, led the Indian Industrial Commission (1916–1918) to recommend government support for industrial research (Arnold 2000; Kumar 1995), and the inter-war decades saw the first Indian firms in several branches of the industry: factory soap made from vegetable oils and caustic soda gradually replaced the washermen’s sajjī, reh and soapnut (Chapter 13). From 1939 Tata Chemicals built a works at Mithapur in Gujarat to make soda ash by the ammonia–soda (Solvay) process from the two cheapest raw materials of the old salt economy, brine and limestone. The successor of Bihar saltpetre was synthetic nitrogen: the public-sector fertiliser factory at Sindri, producing from 1951, was a showpiece of the first Five-Year Plans, and synthetic ammonia later underpinned the Green Revolution (Volume 15). The pharmaceutical industry that grew after Independence, and the generic manufacturing made possible by the Patents Act of 1970, belong to the economic history of modern India rather than to this volume.

The modern industry also inherited, on a far larger scale, the dangers that run through this volume. The release of methyl isocyanate from the Union Carbide pesticide plant at Bhopal on the night of 2–3 December 1984, which killed thousands within days, remains the worst disaster in the history of the chemical industry; less dramatic, but widespread, are chromium from tannery effluents, mercury from older chlor-alkali plants and pesticide residues. From the mercury of the rasa laboratory and the lead of the cupelling hearth to Bhopal, the history of Indian chemistry is also a history of the people who bore its costs.

docs.title: 15.5 The Evidence and How It Is Weighed
docs.text:
The kinds of evidence used in this volume, and what each can show, are summarised in Table 15.1.

Table 15.1. Kinds of Evidence for the History of Indian Chemistry and Metallurgy Kind Examples What it can show Artefacts Iron pillars, steel ingots, bronzes, beads, textiles What could be made; composition and structure Production debris Slag, crucibles, retorts, kiln remains How and on what scale things were made; dates Mining remains Workings at Zawar, Rajpura–Dariba, Khetri, Hutti Sources of raw materials; dates Texts Arthaśāstra, gem treatises, rasa texts Classifications, terminology, some processes, ideas Observers’ accounts Xuanzang, al-Bīrūnī, Tavernier, Buchanan, Voysey Practices at particular times and places Ethnography Elwin on the Agaria; studies of living crafts Practices surviving into modern times Laboratory analysis Metallography, chemical and isotopic analysis Composition, microstructure, provenance, date

The methods by which production debris, mine workings and objects are analysed are explained in Section 4.5. The strongest conclusions come where several kinds of evidence agree—for example, where travellers’ descriptions of crucible steel making, excavated crucibles and the analysis of steel ingots tell the same story. Texts alone are a weak guide to practice, and analysis alone cannot recover the meanings that materials had for their makers.

docs.title: 15.6 Connections to Modern Chemistry
docs.text:
Did Indian chemical knowledge contribute to modern chemistry? The honest answer is: in specific ways, and mostly indirectly.

  • European study of wootz in the early 19th century contributed to the understanding of carbon in steel (Chapter 6).

  • European attempts to reproduce Indian mordant-dyed cottons stimulated the growth of textile printing and dye chemistry in the 18th century (Chapter 11).

  • Indian indigo was the most important natural dye of the 19th century, and the research that led to its synthesis was central to the German dye industry.

  • Indian zinc, steel, saltpetre, borax and other materials were traded internationally and studied by European chemists; Bihar saltpetre in particular was a principal source of nitre for Britain in the period when European chemists made nitre central to their study of combustion (Chapter 13).

Modern chemistry, however, developed in 17th–19th-century Europe from its own sources, including European alchemy and pharmacy. There is no evidence that Sanskrit alchemical texts influenced it. Claims that the rasa texts anticipated the conservation of mass, stoichiometry, catalysis or coordination chemistry rest on reading modern concepts into texts that do not contain them.

docs.title: 15.7 Against Presentism
docs.text:
Several modern ways of describing the Indian tradition deserve particular caution.

“Ancient nanotechnology” Bhasmas and Damascus blades contain very small particles or structures, but their makers did not and could not aim at nanostructures. Calling them nanotechnology misdescribes both the past and the present (Chapters 6 and 9). “Green chemistry” Traditional processes used renewable fuels and plant materials because those were what was available, and some were highly polluting or dangerous to workers (mercury vapour, lead fumes, charcoal-driven deforestation). They are not models of sustainable industry merely because they are old. “Validated by science” When modern analysis confirms that the Delhi pillar resists corrosion, it validates a material, not a theory. When analysis shows that a bhasma contains fine particles, it does not validate the claims made for it as a medicine. “First in the world” Priority claims are often wrong, and always provisional. They also distract attention from what is genuinely interesting: how particular communities solved particular problems with the means available to them.

docs.title: 15.8 Rasaśāstra Today
docs.text:
The present status of rasaśāstra—as a college subject, an industry and a regulated class of medicines—and the toxicological evidence about its products were set out in Chapter 9. Research in Indian institutions has focused on the characterisation and standardisation of these products and on their safety in animals (Kumar et al. 2006; Chaudhari et al. 2016), and some of it has been critical of quality.

Health and Safety Note

Metal-containing traditional medicines remain a recognised cause of lead, mercury and arsenic poisoning in India and abroad (Kales and Saper 2009). Nothing in this book is a recommendation to use them; see the full note in Section 1.1.

The contemporary debate is often framed as a conflict between “tradition” and “Western science”. It need not be. The authors of the rasa texts were themselves concerned with the dangers of metals and devised tests to guard against them; modern toxicology offers better tests. Practitioners and regulators in India have increasingly accepted that metal-containing products must meet modern safety standards, and that claims of efficacy require properly designed clinical trials. Respect for the tradition is compatible with—indeed requires—subjecting it to the best available evidence.

docs.title: 15.9 Caste, Gender and the Ownership of Knowledge
docs.text:
The history of Indian chemistry and metallurgy is also a history of who was allowed to know, to write and to profit. The Sanskrit texts were composed by and for literate men of high status: physicians, ascetics, officials, connoisseurs. The smelters, smiths, miners, dyers, potters and bead-makers who carried out most of the processes described in this volume belonged to hereditary occupational groups whose status in the Brahmanical order ranged from respectable to untouchable. Some iron-smelting and leather-working communities were treated as polluting; forest communities such as the Agaria and Asur were marginal to the agrarian order altogether. As P. C. Ray observed, the separation of learning from manual work was one reason why practical knowledge so rarely entered the learned literature (Ray 1902–1909).

Women’s work is especially poorly recorded. Women took part in many crafts—in mining and ore-dressing (Tavernier saw women and children in the diamond diggings), in bead-making and pottery decoration, in spinning and dyeing, in bangle-making—usually as unpaid family labour or as low-paid workers (Tavernier 1889). In the rasa texts women appear chiefly in ritual roles, and the texts’ theory of sulphur as the Goddess’s generative fluid reflects a male-authored symbolism rather than women’s own knowledge. The modern glass bangle industry of Firozabad, with its home-based women and child workers, shows that these patterns are not only historical.

Recognising this does not diminish the achievements described in this book; it attributes them to the people who made them. A history of Indian chemistry that celebrated the Delhi pillar while ignoring the smelters who made the iron, or the kalamkari while ignoring the dyers, would repeat the very separation of knowledge from labour that Ray regretted.

docs.title: 15.10 Craft Knowledge, Colonial Rule and Decline
docs.text:
Many of the industries discussed in this volume declined in the 19th century: iron smelting, crucible steel, zinc distillation, natural indigo, hand-printed cottons. Colonial rule played a large part—through tariffs and market policies favouring British manufactures, forest laws restricting charcoal, the coercive organisation of indigo cultivation, and the general subordination of the Indian economy. Other causes were global: the industrial production of iron, steel and zinc, the synthesis of dyes, and changes in warfare and fashion affected traditional producers everywhere (Riello 2013; Balfour-Paul 1998; Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004).

Colonial officials and scientists also produced much of our documentation of these industries: Buchanan, Voysey and Heath on steel; the gazetteers and economic surveys; the first chemical analyses. Earlier still, the Mughal administration had recorded the work of its mints and workshops in the Āʾīn-i Akbarī (Chapter 8), a reminder that the documentation of Indian crafts did not begin with colonial rule. Their records are indispensable, even when written from the perspective of a ruling power interested in Indian resources.

docs.title: 15.11 Traditional Knowledge and Intellectual Property
docs.text: Since the 1990s, Indian institutions have sought to protect traditional knowledge from inappropriate patenting. Two cases became famous: a United States patent on the use of turmeric for wound healing, revoked in 1997 after the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) showed that the use was documented in old Indian texts; and a European patent on a neem-based fungicide, revoked after opposition proceedings. In response the Government of India created the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL), which records formulations from classical Āyurvedic, Unani, Siddha and Yoga texts in a form that patent examiners can consult as prior art. Documenting a formulation as traditional knowledge, it should be noted, does not imply that it is safe or effective.

docs.title: 15.12 Teaching the History of Indian Chemistry
docs.text:
The National Education Policy of 2020 encourages the inclusion of Indian knowledge traditions in education. The history of chemistry and metallurgy is a natural subject for this: it connects the laboratory with the museum and the archaeological site, and it shows students how scientific methods can be used to investigate the past. Good teaching in this field would:

  • use case studies with strong evidence—the Delhi pillar, Zawar, crucible steel, Indo-Pacific beads, indigo and kalamkari;

  • distinguish clearly between what texts claim and what evidence shows;

  • place Indian developments in a comparative frame, alongside Chinese, Islamic and European ones;

  • include the craftspeople, and the social hierarchies that shaped who was allowed to know and to write;

  • treat the medical uses of metals with the safety warnings they require.

docs.title: 15.13 Where to See the Evidence
docs.text:
Much of the material discussed in this volume can be seen in museums and at sites in India and abroad.

Sites The iron pillar stands in the Qutb complex at Mehrauli, Delhi. The Dhar pillar fragments are at Dhar in Madhya Pradesh. Ancient mine workings and retort heaps survive at Zawar near Udaipur. Harappan sites with museums include Lothal and Dholavira in Gujarat; Kodumanal and Keezhadi in Tamil Nadu have been the subject of recent excavations by the Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology, whose reports have dated the urban levels of Keezhadi to the 6th century BCE and later (Sivanantham and Seran 2019). Indian museums The National Museum, New Delhi, holds Harappan material, including the bronze “dancing girl” from Mohenjo-daro, and a major collection of bronzes and arms. The Government Museum, Chennai, has one of the finest collections of South Indian bronzes. The Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya in Mumbai, the Indian Museum in Kolkata and the Salar Jung Museum in Hyderabad hold metalwork, arms, Bidri, jade and textiles. The Calico Museum of Textiles in Ahmedabad has outstanding painted and printed cottons. Museums abroad The British Museum, the Victoria and Albert Museum (which holds the jade wine cup of Shāh Jahān and large textile and metalwork collections) and Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery (the Sultanganj Buddha) in Britain, and many museums in Europe, North America and Southeast Asia, hold Indian metalwork, arms and textiles, many of them acquired in the colonial period.

The presence of so many objects abroad raises questions of history and ownership that are now widely discussed. For the historian of technology, wherever they are, the objects themselves—examined with the methods described in this volume—remain the primary evidence.

docs.title: 15.14 Open Questions
docs.text:
1. The beginnings of iron. How early, and where, did regular iron smelting begin in South Asia? The claims of very early dates from Tamil Nadu (Chapter 5) need full publication and independent testing.

  2. Crucible steel. When did crucible steel first appear in South Asia, and how were the South Asian and Central Asian traditions related?

  3. The rasa texts. Few rasa texts have critical editions or reliable translations, and their chronology remains uncertain. Philological work is needed before their history can be written with confidence.

  4. Transmission. Were the Indian, Chinese and Islamic alchemical traditions historically connected, and if so how? Did Indian zinc technology influence China or Europe?

  5. Indo-Persian sources. The Persian literature on alchemy, pharmacy and materials written or copied in India is largely unstudied. Its relationship to the rasa texts, and the history of Unani kushtas, could change our picture of how the two traditions met (Chapter 14).

  6. Salts and acids. When and where were mineral acids first prepared in India, and what were the drāvakas of the late texts? The 19th-century descriptions of saltpetre, alum, sal ammoniac and borax production deserve to be compared with surviving practice and with archaeological evidence (Chapter 13).

  7. Craft documentation. Many traditional metallurgical, ceramic and dyeing practices survive only among elderly practitioners and should be recorded before they disappear.

  8. Safety. The heavy-metal content of traditional medicines and cosmetics, and its health effects, need continued monitoring; any therapeutic claims require properly designed trials.

docs.title: 15.15 Concluding Reflections
docs.text:
The history surveyed in this volume is one of skill, ingenuity and persistence: of smelters who forged a six-tonne pillar that has stood for sixteen centuries, of zinc distillers at Zawar who produced the metal on an industrial scale some centuries before the earliest dated Chinese production and long before European, of dyers whose cottons clothed much of the world, and of alchemists who handled mercury and sulphur with remarkable practical command. It is also a history of hierarchy, in which those who did the work were seldom those who wrote the books, and of danger, in which toxic metals were taken as medicines and continue to be taken today.

To study this history well is to hold both sides in view. The achievements need no exaggeration, and the dangers need no concealment. The materials themselves—the slag heaps of Zawar, the crucibles of the Deccan, the iron of the Delhi pillar, the faded kalamkari in museum stores—remain the most reliable witnesses, and modern science, used carefully, allows them to tell their story.

What Is Secure and What Is Debated

Secure: the practical achievements listed at the start of this chapter, each attested by archaeology and analysis; P. C. Ray’s foundation of the subject; and the specific, mostly indirect routes by which Indian materials entered the history of modern chemistry. Debated: the causes of the 19th-century decline of the crafts, and the weight of colonial policy among them; the safety of metal medicines; and how the knowledge of craftspeople—often of low caste status, and often women—can be recovered from a record written by others.

docs.title: Guide to Further Reading
docs.text: This guide points to the works that are most useful as starting points. Full details are given in the Select Bibliography.

docs.title: General surveys
docs.text: The classic survey of Indian chemistry is P. C. Ray’s History of Hindu Chemistry (Ray 1902–1909), best used in the revised edition by Priyadaranjan Ray (Ray 1956); its datings and some attributions need correction from later work. A Concise History of Science in India (Bose et al. 1971) contains chapters on chemistry and metallurgy. Arun Kumar Biswas and Sulekha Biswas’s Minerals and Metals in Ancient India (Biswas and Biswas 1996) gathers textual and archaeological evidence. D. P. Agrawal’s Ancient Metal Technology and Archaeology of South Asia (Agrawal 2000) is a convenient archaeological overview, and Paul Craddock’s Early Metal Mining and Production (Craddock 1995) places Indian mining and smelting in world perspective. The chemistry volume of the History of Science, Philosophy and Culture in Indian Civilization, edited by B. V. Subbarayappa (Subbarayappa 1999), is the fullest modern collaborative survey.

docs.title: Rasaśāstra and alchemy
docs.text: David Gordon White’s The Alchemical Body (White 1996) is the essential study of rasaśāstra in its Tantric and Siddha context, with a careful discussion of the chronology of the texts. G. J. Meulenbeld’s History of Indian Medical Literature (Meulenbeld 1999–2002) is the indispensable bibliographical guide to individual texts, authors and dates. Dominik Wujastyk’s article on the “ghost” Rasaratnākara (Wujastyk 1984) is a model of how attributions can be tested, and his Roots of Āyurveda (Wujastyk 2003) offers translated selections from the classical medical texts. Bhagwan Dash’s Alchemy and Metallic Medicines in Ayurveda (Dash 1986) presents the subject from a practitioner’s standpoint. For comparison with European and Arabic alchemy, Lawrence Principe’s The Secrets of Alchemy (Principe 2013) is an excellent introduction. Barbara Gerke’s study of Tibetan mercury processing (Gerke 2013) and Richard Weiss’s book on Siddha medicine (Weiss 2009) cover two related traditions. For the texts themselves, the Rasārṇava was edited by P. C. Ray and Hariśchandra Kaviratna (Ray and Kaviratna 1908–1910), and the Rasārṇava, the Rasahṛdayatantra and the Rasaratnasamuccaya can be read in the GRETIL electronic texts cited in Chapters 2 and 3 (GRETIL 2020a, 2020b). Kamil Zvelebil’s The Siddha Quest for Immortality (Zvelebil 1996) and Richard Weiss’s Recipes for Immortality (Weiss 2009) introduce the Tamil Siddha tradition, and Barbara Gerke’s Taming the Poisonous (Gerke 2021) is the fullest study of mercury in Tibetan medicine.

docs.title: Safety of metal-containing medicines
docs.text: The studies by Saper and colleagues in JAMA (Saper et al. 2004, 2008) are the most widely cited surveys of heavy metals in Ayurvedic products. Ernst’s review (Ernst 2002), the report of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2004) and the editorial by Kales and Saper (Kales and Saper 2009) document poisoning cases. On the toxicology of cinnabar, see Liu and colleagues (Liu et al. 2008). For the Indian laboratory and animal studies that defend the products, see for example Kumar and colleagues on the composition of bhasmas (Kumar et al. 2006), Chaudhari and colleagues on the toxicity of copper bhasma in rats (Chaudhari et al. 2016) and the review by Kamath and colleagues (Kamath et al. 2012).

docs.title: Mining and archaeometallurgy
docs.text: Paul Craddock’s Early Metal Mining and Production (Craddock 1995) is a general account of pre-industrial mining with much Indian material, and the survey of the Rajasthan mines by Willies and colleagues (Willies et al. 1984) describes the best-dated ancient workings in South Asia. V. Ball’s Economic Geology (Ball 1881) records the old workings and slag heaps known to 19th-century geologists. For the methods of archaeometallurgy, Killick and Fenn’s review (Killick and Fenn 2012) is a concise introduction, Pollard and Heron’s Archaeological Chemistry (Pollard and Heron 2008) explains the analytical techniques, including lead isotopes, and Bachmann’s handbook (Bachmann 1982) remains the standard guide to the identification of slags; Rehren and Pernicka (Rehren and Pernicka 2008) review the development of the field, including lead isotope provenancing. Srinivasan’s study of South Indian images (Srinivasan 1999) applies these methods to Indian bronzes. On the discoloration of the Taj Mahal see Bergin and colleagues (Bergin et al. 2015).

docs.title: Iron and steel
docs.text: On the beginnings of iron, see Chakrabarti’s Early Use of Iron in India (Chakrabarti 1992) and Tewari’s report of early dates from the Ganga plain (Tewari 2003). R. Balasubramaniam’s Delhi Iron Pillar: New Insights (Balasubramaniam 2002) and his paper in Corrosion Science (Balasubramaniam 2000) are the standard accounts of the pillar; T. R. Anantharaman’s The Rustless Wonder (Anantharaman 1996) is a readable earlier study. Verrier Elwin’s The Agaria (Elwin 1942) remains the classic ethnography of iron-smelters. For Sri Lanka, see Juleff’s work (Juleff 1996, 1998). On the Khasi Hills, see Yule’s early description (Yule 1842) and the radiocarbon study by Prokop and Suliga (Prokop and Suliga 2013); the Tamil Nadu dates of 2025 are published in Rajan and Sivanantham’s report (Rajan and Sivanantham 2025).

docs.title: Crucible steel
docs.text: Sharada Srinivasan and Srinivasa Ranganathan’s India’s Legendary Wootz Steel (Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004) is the best general account; Bennet Bronson’s article (Bronson 1986) surveys the historical sources. On the metallurgy of the watered pattern, see Verhoeven, Pendray and Dauksch (Verhoeven et al. 1998), Wadsworth and Sherby (Wadsworth and Sherby 1980) and Cyril Stanley Smith’s History of Metallography (Smith 1960). Rehren and Papachristou compare South Asian and Central Asian crucibles (Rehren and Papachristou 2003).

docs.title: Zinc, lead and silver
docs.text: The Zawar work is published in Craddock, Gurjar and Hegde’s article (Craddock et al. 1983), in the British Museum volume 2000 Years of Zinc and Brass (Craddock 1998) and, most fully, in Craddock’s Early Indian Metallurgy (Craddock 2017).

docs.title: Bronze, images and the precious metals
docs.text: On Harappan metallurgy see Kenoyer and Miller (Kenoyer and Miller 1999) and Kenoyer’s Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization (Kenoyer 1998). Srinivasan and Glover describe the high-tin bronzes of Kerala (Srinivasan and Glover 1995), and Vidya Dehejia’s exhibition catalogue introduces the Chola bronzes (Dehejia 2002). Meera Mukherjee’s Metalcraftsmen of India (Mukherjee 1978) describes the living crafts.

docs.title: Gems
docs.text: Louis Finot’s Les lapidaires indiens (Finot 1896) edits and translates the Sanskrit gem treatises; M. Ramakrishna Bhat’s translation of the Bṛhatsaṃhitā (Bhat 1981–1982) includes Varāhamihira’s gem chapters. Tavernier’s Travels (Tavernier 1889) describes the diamond mines, and Dalrymple and Anand’s book on the Koh-i-Noor (Dalrymple and Anand 2017) separates its history from its legends.

docs.title: Glass, beads, dyes and textiles
docs.text: Julian Henderson’s Ancient Glass (Henderson 2013) and the article by Dussubieux and colleagues (Dussubieux et al. 2010) cover glass composition; Peter Francis’s Asia’s Maritime Bead Trade (Francis 2002) and the Arikamedu report (Begley et al. 1996) deal with beads. On indigo, see Jenny Balfour-Paul’s Indigo (Balfour-Paul 1998) and, for the Bengal indigo disturbances, Blair Kling’s The Blue Mutiny (Kling 1966). Giorgio Riello’s Cotton (Riello 2013) sets Indian dyed textiles in the history of global trade.

docs.title: Other chemical crafts
docs.text: For the Harappan vitreous crafts, Kenoyer’s Ancient Cities (Kenoyer 1998) and Massimo Vidale’s Archaeology of Indus Crafts (Vidale 2000) are the best introductions. George Watt’s Dictionary of the Economic Products of India (Watt 1889) and his later Commercial Products of India (Watt 1908) remain the fullest sources for the 19th-century production of salts, alkalis, alum, sal ammoniac, borax and saltpetre. On the saltpetre trade see Om Prakash’s study of the Dutch company in Bengal (Prakash 1985) and James Frey’s article (Frey 2009); Irfan Habib’s Technology in Medieval India (Habib 2008) surveys the technologies of the Sultanate and Mughal periods. On distillation see Allchin’s article (Allchin 1979), R. J. Forbes’s Short History of the Art of Distillation (Forbes 1948) and the volume of Science and Civilisation in China on chemical apparatus (Needham et al. 1980); on gunpowder and saltpetre, Iqtidar Alam Khan’s Gunpowder and Firearms (Khan 2004); on sugar, Christian Daniels’s volume in Science and Civilisation in China (Daniels 1996). On perfumery and its literature, see James McHugh’s Sandalwood and Carrion (McHugh 2012). The first book of the Āʾīn-i Akbarī (Abuʾl-Faẓl ʿAllāmī 1873), with its chapters on the mint, the origin and specific gravity of metals, saltpetre, spirits and perfumes, and al-Bīrūnī’s India (Sachau 1888) are rich primary sources for the medieval and early modern periods.

docs.title: Islamic alchemy and Indo-Persian sources
docs.text: Principe’s Secrets of Alchemy (Principe 2013) introduces Arabic alchemy and its transmission to Europe, and Pormann and Savage-Smith’s Medieval Islamic Medicine (Pormann and Savage-Smith 2007) the medical and pharmaceutical context, including the translation of Indian works. Ibn al-Nadīm’s Fihrist, in Bayard Dodge’s translation (Ibn al-Nadīm 1970), records the Indian books known in Abbasid Baghdad. Al-Hassan and Hill’s Islamic Technology (al-Hassan and Hill 1986) describes distillation and chemical industry in the Islamic world, and Berthold Laufer’s Sino-Iranica (Laufer 1919) remains useful on the names and trade of sal ammoniac, borax and other substances. Seema Alavi’s Islam and Healing (Alavi 2008) treats the Indo-Muslim medical tradition. Jahāngīr’s memoirs are available in Thackston’s translation (Thackston 1999). Al-Bīrūnī’s books on precious stones and on pharmacy are available in the English translations edited by Hakim Mohammad Said (al-Bīrūnī, Abū Rayḥān 1989, 1973).

docs.title: Modern chemistry in India
docs.text: P. C. Ray’s autobiography (Ray 1932) is the best source for his life and for the beginnings of the chemical industry in Bengal. David Arnold’s Science, Technology and Medicine in Colonial India (Arnold 2000) and Deepak Kumar’s Science and the Raj (Kumar 1995) place Indian science in its colonial setting, and Gyan Prakash’s Another Reason (Prakash 1999) discusses the nationalist uses of the history of Indian science, including Ray’s.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Terms are Sanskrit unless marked (Ta. = Tamil, Ka. = Kannada, Te. = Telugu, Pe. = Persian, Ar. = Arabic, Hi. = Hindi). Glosses give the meaning in the texts discussed; identifications of minerals with modern species are often uncertain and are marked “usually identified as”.

Term Meaning abhraka Mica; one of the mahārasas of the rasa texts adhaḥpātana “Downward fall”: distillation in which the vapour is led downwards to a cooler receiver āgama Traditional scripture; in rasa texts, the authority of the teaching lineage ajrakh (Hi.) Block-printed cotton of Sindh and Kutch, resist-printed and mordant-dyed on both sides, usually with indigo and madder ākara A mine; also khani ākarādhyakṣa Superintendent of mines in the Arthaśāstra amlavarga “Sour class”: sour fruits, plant juices and fermented liquids used as reagents in the rasa texts anbīq (Ar.) The head of a still, which condenses the vapour and leads it to a receiver; English “alembic” añjana Collyrium; also a mineral (usually identified as stibnite or galena) used for eye-cosmetics anupāna Vehicle or after-drink with which a medicine is taken apunarbhava “Not becoming again”: the rasa texts’ test that a calcined metal should not revert to metal ʿaraq (Ar.–Pe.) “Sweat”: a distillate; distilled water (Unani ʿaraqiyāt) or spirit (English “arrack”) arka In later texts, a distillate of plant material (after Arabic ʿaraq) aṣṭādaśa saṃskāra The eighteen “processings” of mercury in the rasa texts aṣṭadhātu “Eight metals”: an alloy named in later texts and craft usage for images audbhida “Sprung from the ground”: salt obtained from saline earth ayas In the Ṛgveda, metal (probably copper or bronze); later, iron bandha “Binding”: the fixation of mercury, making it non-volatile or solid bandhani (Hi.) Tie-dyeing: cloth bound tightly with thread at many points so that the bound areas resist the dye bhapkā (Hi.) The receiving vessel of the Kannauj attar still, containing sandalwood oil bhasma “Ash”: a calcined preparation of a metal or mineral bhāvanā Wet grinding of a substance with a plant juice or decoction Bidri (Hi.) Inlaid ware of a blackened zinc alloy, named after Bidar cāraṇa “Feeding”: in the mercury saṃskāras, making mercury absorb other substances centūram (Ta.) A red calcined or sublimed preparation in Siddha medicine cūlikālavaṇa “Hearth salt”: a synonym of navasāra, sal ammoniac dabu (Hi.) A resist paste of mud, gum and lime used in the block printing of Bagru and other Rajasthan centres deg (Hi.) The copper boiling vessel of the Kannauj attar still dehavāda “Doctrine of the body”: the alchemical aim of transforming the body dhātu Metal; in medicine, a bodily tissue dhātuvāda “Doctrine of metals”: alchemy aimed at transmuting metals ḍolāyantra “Swing apparatus”: a bundle suspended in a heated liquid drāvaka “Solvent”: in late texts, distilled liquids said to dissolve shells and metals, possibly mineral acids gandhaka Sulphur garbhadruti “Internal liquefaction”: a mercury saṃskāra haritāla Orpiment (arsenic trisulphide) hiṅgula Cinnabar (mercuric sulphide) iksīr (Ar.) Elixir; the transmuting or life-giving agent of Arabic alchemy jāraṇa “Digestion”: making mercury absorb other substances, especially metals jīvanmukti “Liberation in life”; in the rasa texts, liberation attained in a body made imperishable by mercury kāca Glass kajjalī “Lamp-black”: the black product of grinding mercury with sulphur (black mercuric sulphide) kalamkari (Pe.) “Pen-work” (from Persian qalam, pen): mordant-painted and printed cotton kalmī shorā (Hi.) Refined, recrystallised saltpetre, in long prismatic crystals kāṃsya Bronze; bell-metal kāñjika Sour fermented rice gruel, used as an acid reagent kāṅkṣī Alum (also sphaṭikā; Hindi phiṭkarī) kāsīsa Green vitriol (iron sulphate) khalva Mortar for grinding khani A mine (also ākara) kīmiyā (Ar.–Pe.) Alchemy; in modern Urdu and Arabic, chemistry koṣṭhī Furnace kṣāra Caustic or alkaline substance, especially the alkali made from plant ash kṣāratraya The “three alkalis” of the later rasa texts: yavakṣāra, sarjikākṣāra and borax kushta (Pe.) “Killed”: a calcined metallic or mineral preparation of Indian Unani pharmacy lākṣā Lac, the resinous secretion of the lac insect, source of a red dye lakṣaṇādhyakṣa Superintendent of the mint in the Arthaśāstra lavaṇa Salt, especially common salt loha Metal in general; specifically iron lohādhyakṣa Superintendent of metals in the Arthaśāstra madhūcchiṣṭa Beeswax; madhūcchiṣṭa-vidhāna, the lost-wax method of casting images mahārasa “Great rasa”: a class of minerals in the rasa texts manaḥśilā Realgar (arsenic sulphide) mañjiṣṭhā Indian madder (Rubia cordifolia), a red dye māraṇa “Killing”: calcination of a metal or mineral multānī miṭṭī (Hi.) Fuller’s earth, an absorbent clay used for cleaning, including the cleaning of marble mūrchana “Swooning”: a mercury saṃskāra in which mercury loses its fluidity mūṣā Crucible nāga Lead navaratna The “nine gems” of medieval astrological and ornamental usage navasāra Sal ammoniac (ammonium chloride; also navasādara; Hindi nausādar) nīla Indigo; also blue sapphire (indranīla) pañcaloha “Five metals”: a name for alloys used for images pārada Mercury parpam (Ta.) A calcined powder of Siddha pharmacy pātana Distillation or sublimation (upward, downward or lateral) peori (Hi.) “Indian yellow”, a pigment made, according to an account of 1883, from the urine of cows fed on mango leaves piṇḍadhāraṇa “Preserving the body”: in the Rasārṇava, the aim attained by mercury and breath-control piṣṭi A finely ground (not calcined) preparation, e.g. of pearl or coral puṭa Heating in a closed vessel set in a pit of burning fuel; the size of the pit and fuel defines named grades qalaʿī (Ar.–Pe.) Tinning of copper and brass vessels qarʿ (Ar.) The boiling vessel (cucurbit) of a still rasa Juice, essence, taste; in the rasa texts, mercury rasaka A mineral of the rasa texts, usually identified as calamine (zinc ore) rasakarpūra “Mercury-camphor”: a white mercurial sublimate, usually identified as a mercury chloride rasaśālā Alchemical laboratory rasaśāstra The science of mercury: Indian alchemy and iatrochemistry rasasindūra A red sublimed mercuric sulphide preparation rasāyana Rejuvenation therapy, one of the eight branches of Āyurveda; also, by extension, alchemy ratnaparīkṣā The examination of gems; title of several gem treatises reh (Hi.) White saline efflorescence of north Indian soils, a natural source of soda rīti Brass sajjī (Hi.) Crude soda made from the ash of plants of saline ground saṃskāra Processing, refinement śarāvasampuṭa Two shallow earthen dishes sealed rim to rim, in which a substance is heated in a puṭa sarjikākṣāra Crude soda from plant ash (Hindi sajjī) sattva “Essence”: a metal extracted from a mineral by heating sauvarcala A salt of the medical texts, of uncertain identity, often taken to be a black salt ṣayrafī (Ar.–Pe.) Assayer, especially of the Mughal mint shorā (Hi.) Saltpetre (potassium nitrate) siddha A perfected being; in Tamil, cittar, the authors of Siddha medical and yogic poetry śilājatu A dark exudate from Himalayan rocks (shilajit) śodhana “Purification”: the preliminary processing of a metal, mineral or poison sphaṭikā Alum; to be distinguished from sphaṭika, rock crystal sthapati Architect or master image-maker; the hereditary bronze-casters of Swamimalai sudhā Lime; lime plaster or stucco (the word also means “nectar”) surkhī (Hi.–Pe.) Crushed burnt brick added to lime to make a partly hydraulic mortar sūryakṣāra In late texts, saltpetre (Hindi shorā) sūta Mercury (“that which brings forth”, in the etymology of the rasa texts) suvarṇa Gold svedana “Sweating”: steaming, the first mercury saṃskāra tāmra Copper ṭaṅkaṇa Borax, a flux for metals (English “tincal”) tezāb (Hi.–Pe.) “Sharp water”: acid, especially nitric acid tīkṣṇa loha “Sharp iron”: steel tuttha Blue vitriol (copper sulphate) ukku (Ka., Te.) Steel; source of the English “wootz” uparasa “Secondary rasa”: a class of minerals in the rasa texts ūrdhvapātana Upward sublimation or distillation urukku (Ta.) Steel (literally “melted”), cognate with Kannada and Telugu ukku ūsar (Hi.) docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This is Volume 15 of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā: Kṛṣi and Jīva Vijñāna: Agriculture, Plants and Animals. It is about the knowledge with which the people of the subcontinent fed themselves and lived alongside plants and animals: how fields were prepared, watered and manured, how rain was forecast, which crops were grown and where they came from, how trees and gardens were tended, how plants were named and classified, how cattle, buffaloes, sheep, goats, camels, elephants and horses were bred, kept and treated, and how birds, insects and fishes were observed and used.

Two kinds of evidence run through the book. The first is textual: Vedic hymns, the Arthaśāstra, the Bṛhatsaṃhitā of Varāhamihira, the medical saṃhitās, and a small group of specialised treatises — the Kṛṣi-Parāśara, Surapāla’s Vṛkṣāyurveda, the Upavanavinoda, the Kāśyapīya Kṛṣisūkti, Pālakāpya’s Hastyāyurveda, the horse books ascribed to Śālihotra, Someśvara’s Mānasollāsa — together with Tamil poetry, Persian chronicles and inscriptions. The second is the evidence of practice: archaeobotany and zooarchaeology, surviving irrigation works, farmers’ and herders’ vocabularies, and the observations of travellers and colonial officials. The texts are precious but partial. Most were written by and for elites, many are late, and none of them records the full knowledge of the cultivators, labourers, pastoralists and fisherfolk who did the work; the book tries to keep both in view, and to be honest about caste, labour and gender in Indian agriculture.

This volume combines and corrects two earlier drafts, one centred on the Kṛṣi-Parāśara and agriculture, the other on plant and animal science. In the course of revision the editors removed a great deal: verses that could not be found in the texts they were ascribed to, invented tables and “modern validations”, statistics without a source, and claims that ancient texts anticipated modern science. Where a quotation is given, it is one the editors believe to be genuine; where a traditional claim is reported, it is reported as a claim. Dates are given as the range accepted in current scholarship, with traditional dates labelled as such. Several texts discussed here — among them the Kṛṣi-Parāśara, which is not the work of the Vedic sage, and the Mṛgapakṣiśāstra — are later or less secure than popular accounts suggest, and the book says so.

Nothing in this volume is advice on the treatment of people or animals. Medicinal plants are treated here as plants; their use in medicine is the subject of Volume 13 (Āyurveda), and readers are referred there and to qualified practitioners. References to editions, translations and studies are given in the text and collected in the select bibliography; a glossary and a chronology of the principal texts are provided at the end.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput Ramanujan College, University of Delhi Guru Pūrṇimā, 2026

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction: Knowledge of Fields, Plants and Animals
1.1 Scope of the Volume
docs.text:
This volume is about how people in the Indian subcontinent grew crops, tended trees and gardens, kept and treated animals, and thought and wrote about living things. Its title, Kṛṣi and Jīva Vijñāna, joins three Sanskrit words. Kṛṣi, from the root kṛṣ, “to draw (a furrow), to plough”, is the ordinary word for agriculture. Jīva, “living being”, is the widest of the three: in Jain, Buddhist and Brahmanical thought alike it covers animals and, with qualifications discussed below, plants. Vijñāna means knowledge, especially knowledge of a discriminating, systematic kind, and is used here in the broad sense of “science”. Two further words recur throughout the book. Vṛkṣāyurveda, “the science of the life of trees”, is the name of a small group of texts on arboriculture and horticulture; and paśu, “domestic animal”, names the cattle, buffaloes, sheep, goats and other animals on which farming depended.

The Arthaśāstra groups agriculture, animal husbandry and trade together under the name vārttā, “livelihood” or economics, one of the four fields of knowledge a king must master (Arthaśāstra 1.4.1; (Kangle 1965)). That grouping is a useful reminder that in South Asia, as elsewhere before the modern period, agriculture, gardening and animal-keeping were not separate sciences but parts of a single economy of field, pasture, forest and household. For that reason this volume treats them together. It brings into one book material that the series had previously divided between a volume on agriculture and a volume on plant and animal knowledge.

Two kinds of knowledge run through the book. The first is practical knowledge: the skills of cultivators, herders, gardeners, fishers, mahouts, horse-keepers, cattle-healers and many others, learned by doing and passed on by example and word of mouth. Most of it was never written down by the people who held it. The second is textual knowledge: what Sanskrit, Tamil, Kannada, Persian and other authors chose to record about fields, plants and animals, usually for patrons and readers far removed from the plough. The two overlap, but they are not the same, and much of this book is concerned with the relation between them.

The volume does not claim that this knowledge was uniquely profound, that it anticipated modern science, or that it offers ready-made solutions to present-day agricultural problems; the reasons are set out once, in Section 1.5. The Indian record is rich enough to be studied on its own terms: as the experience of farmers and herders in a monsoon environment over nine thousand years, and as a literate tradition that tried, in its own categories, to describe and regulate that experience.

Cross-Reference: Related volumes

Medicinal plants and therapeutics are treated in Volume 13 (Āyurveda); the nakṣatra calendar and astronomy in Volume 12 (Khagola Jyotiṣa); minerals in Volume 14 (Rasāyana); textiles in Volume 17 (Śilpa–Kāru); law, kingship and the Arthaśāstra in Volume 18 (Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra); trade and the monsoon in Volume 19 (Vāṇijya and Samudra); war elephants and cavalry in Volume 20 (Yuddha); and tribal knowledge, sacred groves and water harvesting in Volume 23 (Jana–Jāti).

docs.title: 1.2 The Sources
docs.text: No single source, and no single kind of source, gives an adequate picture. The chapters that follow draw on the following groups.

docs.title: 1.2.1 Vedic literature
docs.text:
The Ṛgveda and Atharvaveda contain hymns addressed to the field, the furrow, the plough, the rain and the plants, as well as charms for the growth of crops and the protection of cattle. The later Vedic prose texts (Brāhmaṇas and Śrautasūtras) describe ritual ploughing and sowing, and the early Upaniṣads use agricultural and food imagery to make philosophical points. These texts were composed by and for a priestly elite and are primarily religious, but they are our earliest written evidence for the crops, implements and animals of northern India (Chapter 2).

The Ṛgveda’s hymn to the plants (10.97), often quoted for its “hundred and seven domains” of the plants, is a healer’s praise of medicinal herbs, not a botanical survey; its opening verse is given and discussed in Chapter 6, and its medical setting in Volume 13.

docs.title: 1.2.2 Dharmaśāstra and Arthaśāstra
docs.text: The legal literature (Dharmaśāstra), above all the Mānava-Dharmaśāstra or Manusmṛti (Olivelle 2005), sets out who may farm, who may own land and cattle, the liabilities of herdsmen for lost animals, the penalties for damage to crops and trees, and rules on food. The Arthaśāstra (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013) is a treatise on statecraft with chapters on crown farms, pastures, cattle, horses, elephants, forests, slaughterhouses and irrigation dues. Both are normative texts: they tell us what their authors thought ought to happen, which is not necessarily what did happen.

docs.title: 1.2.3 Saṃhitās and Purāṇas
docs.text: The Bṛhatsaṃhitā of Varāhamihira (6th century CE) is an encyclopaedia of omens and natural knowledge. Its chapters on forecasting rain (21–28), on finding groundwater (54, dakārgala) and on the care of trees (55, vṛkṣāyurveda) are among the most important early sources for this volume (Bhat 1981). Several Purāṇas, notably the Agni Purāṇa, contain chapters on tree-planting and on the treatment of cattle, horses and elephants. These compilations borrowed freely from one another and from the specialised treatises, and the numbering of their chapters varies between editions.

docs.title: 1.2.4 Āyurveda
docs.text: The medical compendia of Caraka and Suśruta (Sharma 1981; Bhishagratna 1907) classify plants and animals for the purposes of diet and therapy, describe the qualities of grains, pulses, vegetables, fruits, milk and meat, and distinguish types of land and the animals that live on them. They are therefore indispensable for the history of food and of natural history, even though their concern is the human patient (Wujastyk 2003; Meulenbeld 1999).

docs.title: 1.2.5 The specialised treatises
docs.text: A small number of Sanskrit and regional-language works are devoted wholly or largely to agriculture, horticulture or the care of particular animals: the Kṛṣi-Parāśara and the Kāśyapīya Kṛṣisūkti on field agriculture; Surapāla’s Vṛkṣāyurveda, the Upavanavinoda and the relevant parts of the Lokopakāra and Viśvavallabha on trees and gardens; the Mānasollāsa, a royal encyclopaedia with sections on gardens, animals, hunting and fishing; the Hastyāyurveda and Mātaṅgalīlā on elephants; and the Śālihotra and related texts on horses. They are later than often supposed, mostly dating from the late first and the second millennium CE, and their dates and authorship are frequently uncertain. Table 1.2 summarises current scholarly opinion.

docs.title: 1.2.6 Tamil and other regional literatures
docs.text: Classical Tamil poetry organises its themes by landscape (tiṇai), each with its own plants, animals, occupations and seasons, and so preserves a picture of farming, herding, hunting and fishing in early south India. The Tirukkuṟaḷ devotes a chapter to ploughing (Pope 1886). Kannada, Telugu, Marathi, Bengali, Hindi and other literatures contain agricultural lore, and the Kannada Lokopakāra is itself a regional-language treatise. Chapter 2 discusses the Tamil material.

docs.title: 1.2.7 Persian sources
docs.text: From the thirteenth century, Persian chronicles, memoirs and administrative manuals add a new kind of evidence. Bābur’s memoirs describe the plants and animals of Hindustan as a newcomer saw them (Thackston 1996); Jahāngīr’s memoirs record close observations of birds and animals (Thackston 1999); and Abū’l-Faẓl’s Āʾīn-i Akbarī gives crop lists, revenue rates, prices, fruits, and the management of the imperial elephants, horses and cattle (Abū’l-Faẓl 1873). Persian translations and adaptations of Sanskrit veterinary works also circulated. These sources, and the revenue records of the Mughal state analysed by Habib (1999), are treated in Chapters 15 and 18; the Persian agricultural record as a whole is surveyed in Section 18.7.

docs.title: 1.2.8 Inscriptions
docs.text: Stone and copper-plate inscriptions are the best evidence we have for actual, datable arrangements on the ground. Aśoka’s edicts record the planting of trees and medicinal herbs and the digging of wells; Rudradāman’s inscription at Junagadh (150 CE) records the history of the Sudarśana reservoir; thousands of later land grants name fields, crops, trees, tanks, pastures and the rights and dues attached to them. South Indian temple and village inscriptions document the management of tanks and the gifts of cattle and land that supported temples. See Chapters 2, 8 and 18.

docs.title: 1.2.9 Archaeology
docs.text: Archaeobotany (the study of charred seeds, plant impressions and microscopic plant remains) and zooarchaeology (the study of animal bones) have transformed the early history of farming in South Asia since the 1970s. They show farming at Mehrgarh from about 7000 BCE, the local domestication of zebu cattle, several independent centres of plant domestication within the subcontinent, and the arrival of crops from south-west Asia, Africa and East Asia (Fuller 2006, 2011). Archaeology is the only source for the first five millennia of farming, and it remains an essential check on the texts thereafter.

docs.title: 1.2.10 Folk sayings and practice
docs.text: Much agricultural knowledge survives in proverbs and weather sayings attributed to legendary figures — Khanā in Bengal, Ghāgh and Bhaḍḍarī in the Hindi-speaking north — and in the practice of farmers, herders and craftspeople recorded by ethnographers, colonial officials and modern researchers. Two colonial scientists in particular, the agricultural chemist J. A. Voelcker and the economic botanist Albert Howard, recorded Indian practice with respect (Sections 7.5.2 and 10.7). Such sources are invaluable, but the dates of oral sayings are almost always unknown, and observers’ reports reflect their own purposes.

docs.title: 1.3 Dating the Texts
docs.text:
Few Indian texts are dated by their authors, and many survive only in late manuscripts. Popular literature often assigns very early dates to agricultural and veterinary works on the strength of their attribution to ancient sages. This volume follows current academic opinion and hedges where the evidence is weak. Tables 1.1 and 1.2 give the dates used throughout.

The pattern that emerges is clear. The Vedic and early historic sources speak of agriculture and animals in passing, within religious, legal or political works. The specialised agricultural and veterinary treatises belong overwhelmingly to the period after about 900 CE. This matters, because a practice described in a twelfth-century text cannot be assumed to have existed a thousand years earlier simply because the text is ascribed to an ancient sage.

docs.title: 1.4 Reading Śāstra and Practice
docs.text:
The Sanskrit word śāstra means both a body of systematic knowledge and an authoritative text that prescribes. Śāstric writing on agriculture and animals has several features that the reader should keep in mind.

First, it is prescriptive. A text that tells the farmer to plough when the moon is in a particular nakṣatra, or a king to establish a superintendent of crown lands, records an ideal. Whether farmers or kings followed the prescription must be established from other evidence, and often cannot be.

Second, it is written from above. With few exceptions, the authors were literate men from priestly, scribal or courtly backgrounds, writing for patrons who owned land and animals rather than for those who worked them. Some authors clearly had first-hand experience; others compiled from earlier works. Verses on rain forecasting, for example, circulate between the Bṛhatsaṃhitā, the Kṛṣi-Parāśara, the Purāṇas and later almanacs, so that agreement between texts may mean borrowing rather than independent observation.

Third, it is selective. The texts say much about rice, barley and wheat, and about cattle, horses and elephants, which mattered to their patrons; they say little about the millets and pulses that fed most of the rural population in dry regions, about shifting cultivation, or about the knowledge of pastoral and forest communities. Archaeology, inscriptions, travellers’ accounts and ethnography are needed to fill these gaps.

Fourth, it mixes what we would call empirical, ritual and astrological knowledge. Instructions on manuring, seed storage or the treatment of a lame horse stand beside rules on auspicious days and omens. It is anachronistic to separate the “scientific” parts and discard the rest; it is equally misleading to present the whole as an early form of modern science. This volume therefore describes what the texts say, in their own terms, and does not claim that they “anticipated” modern discoveries. Where a practice described in a text has been tested by modern research, the research is cited by name; where it has not, nothing is claimed.

Finally, modern editions and translations differ greatly in reliability, a point taken up in the next section.

docs.title: 1.5 Popular Claims and This Volume
docs.text:
Much that is written about Indian agriculture and biology in popular books, websites and some textbooks cannot be traced to the sources it cites. Because the same claims recur from topic to topic, they are described here once, and the later chapters do not argue with them again. They fall into four kinds.

The first is the invented or misattributed text: verses with chapter-and-verse numbers that are not in any edition of the work named, and tables built from them. Examples include classifications of twelve soils, earthworm tests and pesticide recipes credited to the Kṛṣi-Parāśara; tables of grafting methods, companion plantings, water requirements and special prescriptions for medicinal trees credited to Surapāla and the other vṛkṣāyurveda texts; and tables of well depths in modern units credited to Varāhamihira. The second is the late or doubtful text presented as ancient, such as the Vṛkṣāyurveda ascribed to Parāśara (Section 4.1) or the Mṛgapakṣiśāstra (Section 17.3). The third is the “modern validation”: yield increases, efficiency percentages and trials reported without a source that can be checked. The fourth is the claim of priority or descent, that a text anticipated a modern discovery, or that a modern preparation such as jīvāmṛta or a “homa” ritual descends from a classical one (Chapter 20).

This volume does not repeat these claims or rebut them case by case. The later chapters say plainly what each text contains, on the authority of the editions named, and add a correction only where a specific misreading would otherwise mislead. A reader who meets a striking claim elsewhere should ask for the edition and verse number and check them. The practice of the present volume is to cite only verses that can be checked against an edition, and otherwise to paraphrase with the locus.

docs.title: 1.6 Conceptual Frameworks
docs.text: Several ideas recur across the sources and are worth introducing here.

docs.title: 1.6.1 The five elements
docs.text: Brahmanical, Buddhist and Jain thought all analysed the material world into elements (bhūta). The classical Sanskrit scheme has five: earth (pṛthivī), water (āp, jala), fire (tejas, agni), wind (vāyu) and space (ākāśa). The Taittirīya Upaniṣad (2.1) gives a famous cosmogony in which space, wind, fire, water and earth arise in turn, then plants from earth, food from plants, and the person from food (Olivelle 1998). Āyurveda uses the elements, and the three doṣas derived from them, to explain the qualities of foods and drugs; the vṛkṣāyurveda texts extend the same vocabulary to trees, describing some of their disorders as disturbances of vāta, pitta and kapha (Chapter 4). These frameworks organised observation; they were not measurements.

docs.title: 1.6.2 Plants as living beings
docs.text:
Whether plants are living, sentient beings was a long-standing question. The Manusmṛti (1.49) says that plants, enveloped by the darkness that results from past actions, are “inwardly conscious” (antaḥsaṃjña) and experience pleasure and pain (Olivelle 2005). Jain thought is the most explicit: plants are among the beings with a single sense, touch, along with earth-, water-, fire- and air-bodies, and harming them is a form of violence (hiṃsā) (Tatia 1994). Buddhist monastic rules forbid monks to destroy plant life, though Buddhist doctrine generally did not count plants as sentient in the full sense. These views had practical consequences: they shaped attitudes to ploughing, to the felling of trees and to the occupations Jains and some others considered acceptable.

J. C. Bose’s experiments on the electrical responses of plants, sometimes hailed as a vindication of these ideas, belong to plant physiology and neither confirm nor refute a doctrine about consciousness (Section 4.2.3).

docs.title: 1.6.3 Dry land and wet land
docs.text: Āyurvedic texts classify country (deśa) into three kinds: jāṅgala, dry, open land with sparse trees and thorny scrub; ānūpa, wet, marshy land with abundant water and vegetation; and sādhāraṇa, land of a middle character. Each has its characteristic animals, plants and diseases, and the meat of dry-land animals is generally preferred in diet. Francis Zimmermann (1987) showed how this scheme structures Āyurvedic thinking about food and health, and pointed out that the English “jungle”, borrowed from jāṅgala, has come to mean almost the opposite of the original. The Sanskrit word names dry, open savanna; the English word names dense, wet forest. The same distinction between dry and wet land appears in the Arthaśāstra’s rainfall norms (Chapter 2) and in later soil classifications (Chapter 7).

docs.title: 1.6.4 Seasons and the calendar
docs.text: The texts divide the year into six seasons (ṛtu) of two months each and time agricultural operations by the lunar months and the nakṣatras, the twenty-seven or twenty-eight lunar mansions. Farmers in practice relied as much on the onset and behaviour of the monsoon as on the almanac. The familiar terms kharīf (monsoon crop), rabī (winter crop) and zāid (the minor summer crop) are Arabic in origin and entered Indian usage through the revenue administration of the Sultanate and Mughal periods; they are not classical Sanskrit categories. The crop calendar is set out in Section 9.12 (Figure 9.1), the lunar calendar of the texts in Chapter 3, and its astronomy in Volume 12.

docs.title: 1.7 Transmission and Modern Editing
docs.text:
Agricultural and veterinary skills were transmitted mainly within households, castes and occupational communities, by apprenticeship and oral instruction. Texts were transmitted in manuscripts on palm leaf, birch bark and paper. Many of the treatises discussed in this volume survive in only a handful of manuscripts, sometimes in a single one, and copyists added, omitted and altered material. Critical editions are few.

Modern study of the agricultural texts began largely in Bengal. Girija Prasanna Majumdar published a translation of the Upavanavinoda in 1935 (Majumdar 1935) and, with Sures Chandra Banerji, an edition and translation of the Kṛṣi-Parāśara in the Bibliotheca Indica in 1960 (Majumdar and Banerji 1960). From the 1990s the Asian Agri-History Foundation in Secunderabad, associated above all with the plant pathologist Y. L. Nene, published a series of translations in its Agri-History Bulletin series, including Nalini Sadhale’s versions of Surapāla’s Vṛkṣāyurveda (Sadhale 1996) and the Kṛṣi-Parāśara (Sadhale 1999) and S. M. Ayachit’s Kāśyapīya Kṛṣisūkti (Ayachit 2002). M. S. Randhawa’s four-volume History of Agriculture in India (Randhawa 1980) remains a useful survey, though it should be used with caution on dates; the multi-author History of Agriculture in India (up to c. 1200 AD) edited by Lallanji Gopal and V. C. Srivastava (Gopal and Srivastava 2008) goes deeper into the Sanskrit and epigraphic sources. These works made the texts accessible; they should be read alongside the original Sanskrit wherever possible, since translators sometimes interpret technical terms in the light of modern agronomy.

European study of Indian plants began with the trading companies. The Hortus Malabaricus (Amsterdam, 1678–1693), compiled for the Dutch governor of Malabar, Hendrik van Rheede, rested on the knowledge of the Ezhava physician Itty Achuden and Konkani brahmin scholars and was later used by Linnaeus (Section 6.9; (Manilal 1980)). Colonial botanical gardens, surveys and gazetteers followed. George Watt’s Dictionary of the Economic Products of India (Watt 1889) and Kirtikar and Basu’s Indian Medicinal Plants (Kirtikar and Basu 1935) compiled vernacular names and uses on a vast scale. This colonial science depended heavily on Indian informants whose contributions were often unacknowledged, and it served the revenue and commercial purposes of the state (Arnold 2000). It is nevertheless the foundation of much later ethnobotany, and it is discussed in Chapters 6, 12 and 18.

docs.title: 1.8 Who Did the Work
docs.text:
Any honest account of Indian agriculture must ask who ploughed, sowed, weeded, harvested, herded and skinned, and who owned the land and the animals. The answers are uncomfortable. The Brahmanical texts assign agriculture, cattle-keeping and trade to the vaiśya and service to the śūdra, but they also discourage the higher varṇas from ploughing themselves (Manusmṛti 10.83–84; Chapter 2). In practice, from at least the first millennium CE, the actual cultivators were very often śūdra peasants, dependent tenants and labourers, while ownership and the rights to the produce lay with landholding lineages, temples, brahmin grantees and the state (Sharma 1980).

Below the cultivating castes stood communities later called untouchable and today Dalit, who in many regions supplied the agricultural labour force, often in hereditary bondage, and who also did the work of removing dead cattle, flaying and tanning on which the leather buckets of irrigation wells and the harnesses of ploughing depended (Ambedkar 1948; Prakash 1990). Pastoral communities — Ahīr, Gujar, Rabārī, Kuruba, Dhangar, Gaddi, Toda and many others — managed the herds and much of the knowledge of breeding and animal health. Fishing, the catching and training of elephants, the keeping of horses and the gathering of forest produce were each the work of particular communities. Women did much of the transplanting, weeding, harvesting, processing of grain, dairying and seed selection, while being largely excluded from ownership of land (Agarwal 1994).

The knowledge of these people is mostly absent from the texts discussed in this volume, which were written by and for those who did not do the work. The volume tries to keep them in view, and Chapter 18 discusses the history of land, caste and labour from the early centuries CE to 1950 in detail; the place of hides, leather and cattle in the caste order is discussed in Chapter 13.

docs.title: 1.9 Conventions
docs.text:
Sanskrit, Pali and Prakrit words are given in the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (IAST). A short guide to pronunciation: a line over a vowel (ā, ī, ū) marks a long vowel, and e and o are always long; c is pronounced as in English “church”; ś and ṣ are both close to English “sh”; consonants with a dot below (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ) are retroflex, made with the tongue curled back; h after a consonant is aspirated, so that th is as in “hothouse”, not “thin”; ṛ is a vowel, now usually pronounced ri; ṃ nasalises the preceding vowel; and ḥ is a light breath after a vowel. Tamil follows the transliteration of the Tamil Lexicon of the University of Madras, which adds ḻ (a retroflex approximant, as in Uḻavu), ṟ (a trilled r) and ṉ (an alveolar n) and distinguishes short e and o from long ē and ō. Persian and Arabic words are transliterated in a simplified form of the system used by the historians cited (for example Āʾīn-i Akbarī, zamīndār), with ʿ for the Arabic letter ʿayn and ʾ for the glottal stop. Words from Hindi and the other modern languages are given in their modern form, with long vowels marked where this helps (khejrī, bājrā), and without the final a that Hindi does not pronounce. Personal names of modern people, place names and the names of communities are given in their usual English spelling (Bishnoi, Raika, Kannauj) unless a transliterated form is needed to show a Sanskrit or Tamil word. Dates follow the tables above.

Primary texts are cited by the divisions of the edition named: the Ṛgveda and Atharvaveda by book, hymn and verse; the Mahābhārata by the book, chapter and verse of the Poona critical edition; the Arthaśāstra by the book, chapter and sentence of Kangle’s edition; the Bṛhatsaṃhitā by the chapter numbers of Bhat’s translation; and the Sutta Nipāta by sutta number with the verse number of the Pali Text Society edition (so “Sn 1.4, v. 77”). Quotations from primary texts are given in the original only when both the wording and the reference can be verified; otherwise the content is paraphrased and attributed. Where chapters discuss poisons, remedies for humans or animals, or the consumption of cattle products, they include a safety note: classical prescriptions are described as historical evidence, not as advice, and no doses or usable recipes are given.

docs.title: 1.10 Plan of the Volume
docs.text:
The volume has twenty chapters. The first two are introductory and historical; Chapters 3 to 12 deal with agriculture and plants; Chapters 13 to 17 with animals; and the last three with agrarian history, the rise of agricultural science, and the present. Readers who want the social frame before the treatises may read Sections 18.2 and 18.3 of Chapter 18 after Chapter 2.

  1. Introduction (Chapter 1): scope, sources, dating and frameworks.

  2. From Mehrgarh to the early historic period (Chapter 2): archaeobotany and the domestication of plants and animals; Harappan and Neolithic farming; agriculture in Vedic, Buddhist, Jain, Mauryan and early Tamil sources.

  3. The Kṛṣi-Parāśara and rain forecasting (Chapter 3): the Kṛṣi-Parāśara, the Bṛhatsaṃhitā’s rain chapters, folk forecasting, and the other agricultural treatises.

  4. The vṛkṣāyurveda tradition (Chapter 4): the texts on arboriculture and horticulture, from the Bṛhatsaṃhitā to the Upavanavinoda and the Viśvavallabha.

  5. Gardens, flowers and aromatics (Chapter 5): the flowers of worship and poetry, garland-makers and temple gardens, perfumery and the attar distillers, and betel.

  6. Classifying plants (Chapter 6): Vedic, legal, medical, lexical, Jain and Buddhist schemes; folk taxonomies; comparison with Linnaean botany.

  7. Soil, tillage and implements (Chapter 7): concepts and classifications of soil, manuring and conservation, and the plough and other tools of field work.

  8. Water and irrigation (Chapter 8): tanks, anicuts, canals, wells and stepwells, lifting devices, and the social management of water.

  9. Crops and seeds (Chapter 9): the major crops, introduced crops, seasons, rotation and mixed cropping, seed saving and landraces.

  10. Agroecology (Chapter 10): pest management, crop–livestock integration, agroforestry, home gardens, shifting cultivation and the farming systems of the Himalaya and the North-East, and the limits of “sustainability” claims.

  11. Forests and sacred groves (Chapter 11): forests in texts and inscriptions, sacred groves and trees, the Bishnoi and Chipko, and colonial forestry.

  12. Medicinal and useful plants (Chapter 12): identification, cultivation, trade and conservation of plants used in medicine.

  13. Livestock and veterinary knowledge (Chapter 13): domestication, cattle and other livestock, pastoralists, breeds, ethnoveterinary knowledge, the history of cow veneration, and hides and caste.

  14. Dairy and food processing (Chapter 14): milk products, fermentation, grain processing, oil pressing, sugar and preservation.

  15. Elephants and horses (Chapter 15): the Hastyāyurveda, the Mātaṅgalīlā, the capture and keeping of elephants, the Śālihotra tradition and the horse trade.

  16. Wild animals (Chapter 16): wild mammals in texts and art, hunting and its critics, royal and colonial hunting, the history of wildlife protection, and conflict between wildlife and farming.

  17. Birds, insects and aquatic life (Chapter 17): birds in literature and practice, silk, lac and bees, fish and fisheries, pearls and fishing communities.

  18. Agrarian society and change, from the early centuries CE to 1950 (Chapter 18): land grants, Indo-Islamic agriculture and gardens, the Mughal agrarian system and the Persian agricultural record, caste and labour, and colonial agrarian change.

  19. Agricultural science and the state, 1870–1970 (Chapter 19): famine commissions and agricultural departments, Pusa and the research institutes, crop breeding, crop surveys, the Royal Commission on Agriculture, and the coming of the high-yielding varieties.

  20. The modern period (Chapter 20): the Green Revolution and its critics, natural-farming movements, genetically modified crops, the documentation and protection of traditional knowledge, biodiversity law and conservation.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This volume treats agriculture, plants and animals together because they formed a single economy in which field, pasture, forest and household depended on one another. Its sources are diverse: Vedic hymns, legal and political treatises, medical compendia, the Bṛhatsaṃhitā, a small number of specialised agricultural, horticultural and veterinary treatises that mostly date from after 900 CE, Tamil poetry, Persian memoirs and records, inscriptions, archaeology, and the sayings and practices of farmers and herders. The texts are prescriptive, written from above and selective, and they should be read as evidence of what their authors thought and recommended, not as proof of early modern science. The people who did most of the work — śūdra and Dalit cultivators and labourers, pastoralists, fishers and women — are largely absent from them, and the chapters that follow try to keep both the texts and the workers in view.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Fuller (2006) is the best synthesis of the archaeological evidence for early agriculture. Gopal and Srivastava (2008) is the fullest critical survey of the Sanskrit, Pali and epigraphic evidence for agriculture up to about 1200 CE, and Randhawa (1980) offers a broad, well-illustrated survey of agricultural history. Zimmermann (1987) is a classic study of ecological ideas in Āyurveda. Sadhale (1996) gives an accessible translation of a major horticultural text. Trautmann (2015) shows how a single animal can illuminate Indian political and environmental history, and Ludden (1999) provides the long-term agrarian context.

docs.title: Chapter 2: From Mehrgarh to the Early Historic Period: Agriculture in Early India
docs.text: Farming in South Asia is some nine thousand years old. For more than five thousand of those years our only evidence is archaeological: seeds, bones, buildings and tools. Texts begin with the Ṛgveda in the second millennium BCE, and for many centuries afterwards they speak of agriculture only in passing, in hymns, ritual manuals, philosophical dialogues, legal rules and poetry. This chapter follows both kinds of evidence from the first farming villages to the early centuries CE, when land grants, the Arthaśāstra and the Tamil anthologies give a fuller picture. The later agrarian history of the subcontinent is taken up in Chapter 18.

docs.title: 2.1 The Evidence of Archaeology
docs.text:
Two specialised fields supply most of what we know about early farming. Archaeobotany studies plant remains recovered from excavations: seeds and grains preserved by charring, impressions of grain and chaff in pottery and mud-brick, and microscopic remains such as phytoliths and starch grains. Since the 1970s the systematic recovery of charred remains by flotation (washing soil samples in water so that light plant material floats free) has greatly increased the quantity and reliability of the data. Zooarchaeology studies animal bones, identifying species, estimating the age and sex of slaughtered animals, and measuring changes in size and shape that may indicate domestication.

Both fields depend on careful identification and on secure dating, usually by radiocarbon. Many older reports, including some still widely quoted, rest on identifications that have since been questioned or on dates obtained from material not directly associated with the plants concerned. The syntheses by Dorian Fuller (Fuller 2006, 2011) sift this evidence critically, and this chapter relies on them for the overall picture. For the Indus civilisation the standard accounts are those of Allchin and Allchin (1982), Kenoyer (1998) and Possehl (2002).

docs.title: 2.2 Mehrgarh and the First Farmers of the North-West
docs.text:
Mehrgarh lies on the Kachi plain at the foot of the Bolan Pass in Balochistan, Pakistan, where the hills of the Iranian plateau meet the Indus plain. Excavated by a French mission under Jean-François Jarrige from 1974, it is the best-documented early farming site in South Asia. Its earliest levels, without pottery, begin around 7000 BCE (Allchin and Allchin 1982; Possehl 2002).

The people of early Mehrgarh lived in houses of mud brick, some of them divided into small compartments that the excavators interpreted as storerooms. Their plant remains are dominated by barley, with smaller amounts of wheat. Whether these crops were brought from south-west Asia, where wheat and barley were first domesticated, or whether barley at least was domesticated locally from the wild barley that grows in the region, is still debated; current opinion favours the introduction of most of the cereal crops from the west, adapted to local conditions (Fuller 2006).

The animal bones tell a clearer story. Richard Meadow’s analysis showed that in the earliest levels hunted animals — gazelle, deer, wild cattle, wild sheep and goats, wild pig, the onager — are well represented alongside goats, which may already have been domestic. Over the following millennia the proportion of cattle, sheep and goats rises until they dominate the assemblage, and the cattle, sheep and goats all become smaller in size, a change Meadow interpreted as evidence for local domestication (Meadow 1996). In the case of cattle, the animals concerned are the humped zebu (Bos indicus), which was domesticated in this region independently of the humpless taurine cattle of south-west Asia. Zebu cattle were to become the foundation of South Asian agriculture, as draught animals, as sources of milk and dung, and as a measure of wealth (Chapter 13).

Mehrgarh has also yielded some of the earliest evidence for cotton anywhere. Moulherat et al. (2002) identified mineralised cotton fibres preserved inside a copper bead from a burial dated to around the sixth to fifth millennium BCE. Whether the plant was cultivated or gathered from the wild cannot be determined from fibres alone, but the find shows that cotton was being processed into thread at a very early date. The later history of cotton textiles is treated in Volume 17.

docs.title: 2.3 Many Centres of Domestication
docs.text:
Older accounts, following the botanist N. I. Vavilov, treated India as one of a small number of “centres of origin” of cultivated plants (Vavilov 1951). Archaeobotany has replaced this with a more complex picture. Fuller has argued that the subcontinent contained several distinct regions in which local wild plants were independently taken into cultivation, in addition to receiving crops from south-west Asia, Africa and East Asia (Fuller 2006, 2011). Among the regions he identifies are:

  • the southern Deccan, where mung bean (Vigna radiata), horse gram (Macrotyloma uniflorum) and small millets such as browntop millet (Urochloa ramosa, syn. Brachiaria ramosa) and bristly foxtail (Setaria verticillata) were cultivated by Neolithic communities;

  • Gujarat and Saurashtra, where native small millets, probably including little millet (Panicum sumatrense), formed the basis of early farming;

  • the Ganga plain, where a form of rice was cultivated and eventually domesticated (Section 2.5);

  • the greater Indus region, which contributed sesame (Sesamum indicum), domesticated from a wild relative native to India, and probably the tree cotton Gossypium arboreum, as well as zebu cattle and, probably, the water buffalo.

The evidence is uneven and some identifications and dates remain disputed, but the general conclusion — that South Asian agriculture was built from several local beginnings combined with crops that arrived from outside — is now widely accepted. Table 2.1 summarises the main groups of early crops, and Figure 2.1 shows the sites named in this chapter.

Figure 2.1. Some early farming sites named in this chapter: Mehrgarh; the Harappan sites of Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Kalibangan, Banawali, Rakhigarhi, Dholavira and Rojdi; the Ganga-plain rice sites of Lahuradewa, Senuwar and Chirand; the Deccan villages of Inamgaon and Daimabad; and the ash-mound site of Kupgal in the southern Deccan. Positions are plotted by latitude and longitude, and open circles mark approximate positions; the coastline is simplified, islands other than Sri Lanka are omitted, and no rivers or political boundaries are shown. The regions of domestication discussed in the text are not drawn, because their limits are not precisely known. Table 2.1. Main groups of early crops in South Asia and their origins, after Fuller (2006, 2011). Dates are approximate and several are debated.
