Crop group Examples Origin and earliest evidence Winter cereals Barley, wheat South-west Asia (local barley debated); Mehrgarh, from c. 7000 BCE Winter pulses and oilseeds Lentil, pea, chickpea, grass pea, linseed South-west Asia; widespread in Harappan sites Native millets Little millet, browntop millet, bristly foxtail Gujarat and the southern Deccan; 3rd millennium BCE Native pulses Mung bean, black gram (urd), horse gram Several Indian regions; 3rd–2nd millennium BCE Oil and fibre crops Sesame, tree cotton Indus region; Harappan (cotton fibres earlier at Mehrgarh) Rice Oryza sativa Ganga plain and East Asia; origins debated (Section 2.5) African crops Sorghum, pearl millet, finger millet, hyacinth bean, cowpea Africa, via Arabia; from c. 2000 BCE

docs.title: 2.4 Harappan Agriculture
docs.text: The Indus or Harappan civilisation developed out of the farming cultures of the north-west. Its Early Harappan phase begins around 3300 BCE and its Mature, urban phase lasts from about 2600 to 1900 BCE. At its height it extended from Balochistan and the Indus valley to Gujarat, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, with cities such as Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Ganweriwala, Rakhigarhi and Dholavira and hundreds of smaller settlements (Kenoyer 1998; Possehl 2002). The cities depended on the surplus of a large farming and herding population.

docs.title: 2.4.1 Crops and seasons
docs.text:
The Harappan crop repertoire combined winter crops of south-west Asian origin — wheat, barley, lentil, pea, chickpea, grass pea and linseed — with summer crops sown with the monsoon: small millets, native pulses such as mung and urd, sesame, cotton and, in some areas, rice. Fruits such as the jujube (ber) were collected or grown. The combination of a winter and a summer crop season, which remains characteristic of much of South Asian agriculture, is thus visible in the Harappan period, though its importance varied from region to region.

Steven Weber’s study of the plant remains from Rojdi in Saurashtra showed an agriculture based mainly on summer-grown small millets rather than on wheat and barley, and a crop mix that changed over the life of the settlement (Weber 1991). In a later synthesis he argued that Harappan farming was regionally diverse: winter cereals predominated in the Punjab and the Indus valley, summer millets in Gujarat, and the combination of the two seasons allowed some communities to spread risk and to increase production (Weber 1999). There was no single “Harappan agriculture”, but a set of regional systems adapted to differences in rainfall, river regime and soil.

docs.title: 2.4.2 Fields, ploughs and water
docs.text:
At Kalibangan in northern Rajasthan, excavators found beneath later deposits a field surface of the Early Harappan period (first half of the third millennium BCE) bearing criss-cross plough furrows. The furrows ran in two directions, closely spaced one way and widely spaced the other, and the excavator B. B. Lal compared this pattern with the local practice, still observed in the twentieth century, of sowing two different crops in the same field in rows at right angles (Allchin and Allchin 1982). It remains one of the earliest excavated ploughed fields anywhere. A terracotta model of a plough from Banawali in Haryana confirms the use of the ard, a simple plough that scratches rather than turns the soil. Bullock carts are known from numerous terracotta models, and zebu oxen were evidently the draught animals.

There is no clear evidence for large-scale canal irrigation in the Mature Harappan heartland. Agriculture seems to have relied on rainfall, on the annual floods of the Indus and its tributaries, which deposited moisture and silt on the fields for winter sowing, and on wells: Mohenjo-daro alone had a very large number of brick-lined wells. At Dholavira, in the arid Rann of Kachchh, large rock-cut reservoirs stored water for the city. The history of water management is followed in Chapter 8.

docs.title: 2.4.3 Storage
docs.text: Large buildings at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa were identified by Mortimer Wheeler as state “granaries”. Later excavators have questioned this: no grain was found in them, and they may have been halls or warehouses of other kinds (Kenoyer 1998). Storage jars, bins and sealings show that goods, including grain, were stored and controlled, but the scale and organisation of grain storage remain uncertain.

docs.title: 2.4.4 Animals
docs.text:
Animal bones from Harappan sites are dominated by cattle, most of them zebu, followed by sheep and goats; water buffalo and pigs are also present, together with wild animals and large quantities of fish (Meadow 1996; Possehl 2002). The elephant, rhinoceros, tiger and buffalo appear on seals; their depiction does not imply domestication. No securely identified domestic horse has been found in a Mature Harappan context; horses and spoked-wheel chariots become prominent only with the Ṛgveda (Chapter 15).

Harappan craftspeople also used animal products in sophisticated ways. Analysis of fibres from Harappa and Chanhu-daro has shown that silk from wild silk moths was being used in the third millennium BCE (Good et al. 2009); silk and other insect products are discussed in Chapter 17.

docs.title: 2.4.5 African millets and the late Harappan period
docs.text: From about 2000 BCE, crops of African origin — sorghum, pearl millet and finger millet among the cereals, hyacinth bean and cowpea among the pulses — appear in Gujarat, the Indus region and peninsular India, probably having crossed the Arabian Sea through contacts with Arabia and East Africa (Fuller 2006). Some early identifications, especially of finger millet, have been questioned, and the routes and dates are still being refined. These drought-tolerant summer crops became important in the late and post-urban phases of the Harappan tradition, when settlement shifted eastwards and southwards and, in several regions, summer cropping increased. Sorghum (jowar), pearl millet (bajra) and finger millet (ragi) were to become staples of the drier parts of India (Chapter 9).

docs.title: 2.5 Rice and the Ganga Plain
docs.text:
Rice has a complicated history in South Asia. Wild rices grow widely in the subcontinent, and their grains were gathered long before domestication. Rice remains reported from the middle Ganga plain, at sites such as Lahuradewa in Uttar Pradesh, have been dated by their excavators as early as the seventh millennium BCE. These claims are debated: the rice may have been wild or gathered from wild stands, and the association between the dated material and the rice is not always secure. More generally accepted evidence for domesticated rice in the Ganga plain, at sites such as Senuwar and Chirand in Bihar, belongs to the third and second millennia BCE (Fuller 2006, 2011).

One influential model, developed by Fuller, holds that people in the Ganga plain cultivated a local wild rice for a long period without its becoming fully domesticated, and that domesticated japonica rice, arriving from East Asia in the late third or early second millennium BCE, hybridised with it to produce the domesticated indica rices of South Asia (Fuller 2011). Other scholars favour a more independent domestication in India. Rice also appears at a number of Harappan sites, particularly in the eastern Harappan region, but how much of it was cultivated or domesticated is debated. Whatever the details, by the first millennium BCE rice was the principal crop of the middle and lower Ganga plain and of the eastern and southern river deltas, and it is the crop around which the Kṛṣi-Parāśara and the Kāśyapīya Kṛṣisūkti were later written (Chapter 3).

docs.title: 2.6 Neolithic South India and the Deccan
docs.text:
In the southern Deccan — northern Karnataka and western Andhra Pradesh — a Neolithic culture flourished from about 3000 BCE. Its most striking monuments are the ash-mounds found at sites such as Utnur, Kupgal and Budihal: great accumulations of burnt cattle dung, sometimes vitrified, which mark places where cattle were penned and the dung periodically burnt. F. R. Allchin interpreted them as the cattle stations of a pastoral society, and the large proportion of cattle bones at southern Neolithic sites confirms the central place of herding (Allchin and Allchin 1982). The burning of dung heaps may have had ritual as well as practical purposes; their exact function is still discussed.

These cattle-keepers were also cultivators. Archaeobotanical work at southern Neolithic sites has shown that their staples were native crops: the pulses mung bean and horse gram, and small millets such as browntop millet and bristly foxtail. Wheat and barley from the north and, later, African millets and pulses were added to this base (Fuller 2006). The pairing of millets and pulses on rain-fed land, with cattle supplying traction and dung, is a pattern that persisted in the peninsula for millennia.

Further north in the Deccan, Chalcolithic farming villages of the second millennium BCE, such as Inamgaon and Daimabad in Maharashtra, grew barley, wheat, lentils, other pulses and millets, and kept cattle, sheep, goats and pigs. At Inamgaon the excavators reported an embankment and channel that they interpreted as a work for diverting flood water to fields. Such villages show that farming had spread across most of the subcontinent long before the earliest written references to it.

docs.title: 2.7.1 The Ṛgveda
docs.text:
The Ṛgveda (core c. 1500–1200 BCE) was composed in the north-west, in the land of the Indus and its tributaries, by communities for whom cattle were the chief form of wealth. Cows are prayed for, fought over and praised; a word for battle, gaviṣṭi, means literally “desire for cows”. But the hymns also know agriculture. They speak of the field (kṣetra) and the fertile field (urvarā), of grain (yava, usually understood as barley but sometimes grain in general), of the plough (lāṅgala, sīra), the ploughshare (phāla), the furrow (sītā), the ploughman (kīnāśa) and the sickle (sṛṇi), and of oxen yoked to the plough (Jamison and Brereton 2014).

The fullest agricultural hymn is Ṛgveda 4.57, addressed to the Lord of the Field (kṣetrasya pati), to the pair Śuna and Sīra, and to the Furrow (Sītā). It asks for the success of ploughing: that the ploughshares cut the earth auspiciously (śunam), that the ploughmen go with their draught animals, that the furrow be turned towards the worshippers and give them good fortune, and that Parjanya, the rain god, water it. The furrow personified as a goddess is the background to the later story, told in the Rāmāyaṇa, that Sītā was found by King Janaka in a furrow as he ploughed ground for a sacrifice. A late hymn (Ṛgveda 10.101) uses the images of yoking the ploughs, sowing seed in the prepared furrow and drawing water from a well to describe the work of the priests.

A well-known verse comes from an unexpected source, the lament of a ruined gambler:

Ṛgveda 10.34.13

akṣair mā dīvyaḥ kṛṣim it kṛṣasva Do not play with dice: plough your field.

The verse goes on to bid the gambler take pleasure in the wealth that farming brings, for there are his cows and there his wife (Jamison and Brereton 2014). Agriculture here stands for a settled, respectable livelihood.

docs.title: 2.7.2 The Atharvaveda
docs.text:
The Atharvaveda contains many charms concerned with everyday life, including the success of ploughing (3.17 is a ploughing hymn), the growth of grain, protection against pests that damage crops, rain, and the health and increase of cattle (Whitney 1905). Its twelfth book opens with the long hymn to the Earth (Pṛthivīsūkta, 12.1), which praises the earth as the ground on which food and the ploughed fields came into being, on which plants and trees grow, and which supports all creatures. One verse asks that whatever is dug from her may quickly grow again, and that the digger may not wound her vital parts. The best-known line declares:

Atharvaveda 12.1.12

mātā bhūmiḥ putro ahaṃ pṛthivyāḥ The Earth is my mother; I am the son of the Earth.

The same verse names Parjanya, the rain-cloud, as father. The hymn is a religious and poetic text, not an agricultural manual; but it shows that the dependence of human life on soil and rain was a theme of reflection at an early date. Modern readings of it as an environmental ethic are a later interpretation, and should be presented as such.

docs.title: 2.7.3 The later Vedic period
docs.text:
Between about 1200 and 500 BCE the centre of Vedic culture moved east into the Ganga–Yamuna doab and the middle Ganga plain, and agriculture became much more prominent in the texts. Rice (vrīhi) now appears alongside barley, together with wheat (godhūma), pulses, sesame, millets and sugarcane (ikṣu), while wild grains such as nīvāra (wild rice) retained a place in ritual. A passage of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (5.1.7) observes that the crop ripens twice a year (Macdonell and Keith 1912), reflecting the two cropping seasons already seen in the archaeological record. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (6.3.13) lists ten “village” (grāmya) grains used in a ritual preparation — rice, barley, sesame, beans, two small millets, wheat, lentils and two pulses of uncertain identity — in contrast to the wild (āraṇya) plants, a distinction that runs through Vedic ritual classifications of both plants and animals; the verse is quoted in Chapter 9 (Olivelle 1998).

The Brāhmaṇas describe ritual ploughing as part of the construction of the great fire altar: the site is ploughed with a team of oxen and sown with seeds of many kinds. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa summarises agricultural work as ploughing, sowing, reaping and threshing. Some texts speak of ritual plough teams of six, eight, twelve or even twenty-four oxen; whether such large teams were ever used in ordinary farming is doubtful.

The spread of agriculture in the Ganga plain coincided with the spread of iron, which appears in northern India from around the end of the second millennium BCE. D. D. Kosambi argued that iron axes and ploughshares made possible the clearing of the plain’s forests and the expansion of plough agriculture that underlay the growth of states and cities in the mid-first millennium BCE (Kosambi 1956). Later scholars have qualified this view: iron tools are scarce in early levels, forests could be cleared with fire, and iron ploughshares become common only later. The relation between iron, agriculture and social change remains a subject of debate (Singh 2008).

docs.title: 2.8 Food in the Upaniṣads
docs.text:
The early Upaniṣads (c. 7th–5th century BCE) often use food (anna) as a philosophical theme. In the third section of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, Bhṛgu, son of Varuṇa, asks his father to teach him brahman. Told to practise austerity and discover it himself, he first concludes:

Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.2

annaṃ brahmeti vyajānāt He perceived that brahman is food.

The text continues that from food beings are born, by food they live, and into food they pass at death. It is important to read this in context. Food is the first and lowest stage of Bhṛgu’s inquiry: he returns to his father and is sent back to practise austerity again, and successively identifies brahman with breath, mind, perception and finally bliss (ānanda) (Olivelle 1998). The passage is a teaching about levels of reality, not a doctrine about agriculture. Later in the same section, however, the text lays down as vows that one should not despise food, should not reject it, and should make food plentiful — injunctions that connect the philosophy of food with the duty of hospitality and the reality of scarcity.

That reality appears elsewhere. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (1.10) opens a story with the country of the Kurus devastated — by hail or, as some translate, by locusts — and the learned Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa reduced to begging leftover beans from an elephant-keeper. Crop failure and famine were familiar experiences.

docs.title: 2.9 Varṇa, Vārttā and Labour
docs.text:
The Brahmanical texts assign occupations to the four varṇas. Agriculture, cattle-keeping and trade together form vārttā, the livelihood proper to the vaiśya. The Bhagavad Gītā states the scheme concisely:

Bhagavad Gītā 18.44

kṛṣigorakṣyavāṇijyaṃ vaiśyakarma svabhāvajam | paricaryātmakaṃ karma śūdrasyāpi svabhāvajam || Agriculture, cattle-herding and trade are the vaiśya’s work, born of his nature; work consisting of service is likewise the śūdra’s, born of his nature.

The Manusmṛti (1.90) likewise lists protecting animals, agriculture and trade among the vaiśya’s duties (Olivelle 2005). Yet the same text is ambivalent about ploughing. It advises a brahmin or kṣatriya forced to live by a vaiśya’s occupation to avoid agriculture, which involves violence and depends on others; some, it says, consider agriculture good, but it is condemned by the virtuous, because the wooden implement with its iron tip injures the earth and the creatures that live in it (Manusmṛti 10.83–84). This concern with the killing of small creatures in the soil was shared with Jain and Buddhist thought (Section 2.10), and it contributed to the low status of the actual work of ploughing.

The scheme of four varṇas was an ideal, not a description. In practice, the people who worked the land were often not vaiśyas. Pali texts speak of dāsa-kammakara, slaves and hired workers, labouring in the fields of wealthy householders (gahapati) (Chakravarti 1987). The Arthaśāstra has crown lands worked by slaves, hired labourers and people working off fines. R. S. Sharma showed how, over the first millennium CE, the śūdra came increasingly to be identified with the peasant cultivator; the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang in the seventh century described the śūdras as agriculturists (Sharma 1980). Below them, groups regarded as untouchable were increasingly confined to the most degraded forms of labour. The history of caste, land and agricultural labour is treated more fully in Chapter 18, and that of hides and leather in Chapter 13.

docs.title: 2.10 Buddhist and Jain Perspectives
docs.text:
The Buddha (c. 480–400 BCE) taught in the agrarian kingdoms of the middle Ganga plain, and Pali texts are full of agricultural images. In the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta (Sutta Nipāta 1.4, vv. 76–82), the Buddha comes for alms to a brahmin farmer at sowing time, when five hundred ploughs are being yoked. The brahmin rebukes him: he himself ploughs and sows and then eats, and the Buddha too should plough and sow before he eats. The Buddha replies that he also ploughs and sows, and explains in a sustained metaphor: faith is his seed, austerity the rain, wisdom his yoke and plough, mindfulness his ploughshare and goad, and effort his draught ox; and his ploughing yields the deathless. The dialogue shows both the dignity of the landowning farmer and the challenge that the renouncer’s life posed to it.

Buddhist tradition also connects the Buddha’s first experience of meditation with agriculture. In the Majjhima Nikāya he recalls sitting in the shade of a rose-apple tree as a boy while his father was at work; later tradition places the scene at a royal ploughing festival. Royal ploughing ceremonies to open the agricultural season are still held in Thailand and Cambodia, and ritual ploughing by kings is mentioned in several Indian texts.

Buddhist monastic rules forbid monks to dig the ground or destroy plant life, and Jain ethics go further. Because Jain doctrine holds that earth, water and plants are themselves inhabited by living beings (Tatia 1994), ploughing and digging necessarily involve violence. Jain lay codes discouraged occupations involving much harm, and some lists of forbidden trades include digging and ploughing the earth. This is often cited as one reason why many Jain lay communities came to be concentrated in trade rather than agriculture, though economic and historical factors were also at work.

docs.title: 2.11 The Mauryan State and the Arthaśāstra
docs.text: The Mauryan empire (c. 321–185 BCE) was the first state to rule most of the subcontinent. The Greek envoy Megasthenes, whose account survives only in quotations by later Greek writers, reported that India had two harvests a year, because rain fell in both summer and winter, and that farmers formed a large class who were left unmolested even when armies fought nearby. These reports are idealised and filtered through Greek expectations, but they confirm the double cropping already attested in Indian sources.

docs.title: 2.11.1 The Superintendent of Agriculture
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra, traditionally attributed to Kauṭilya, minister of Candragupta Maurya, is in its present form a composite text compiled between about 50 BCE and 300 CE (Olivelle 2013). It cannot therefore be read as a direct description of Mauryan administration, but it reflects long experience of governing agrarian kingdoms. Its chapter on the Superintendent of Agriculture (sītādhyakṣa, 2.24) concerns the management of crown land (sītā). Because this chapter is drawn on in several later chapters of this volume, its contents are summarised here once. Its opening sentence (2.24.1) requires the superintendent to be conversant with the science of agriculture (kṛṣitantra) and the science of the life of plants (vṛkṣāyurveda), or to be assisted by those who are (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013). A third term in the same compound is transmitted in two forms: gulma, “shrubs”, in the text translated by Shamasastry (1915), and śulba, literally “cord”, in the text adopted by Kangle. Since the cord was the surveyor’s measuring line, śulba may refer to the measurement of land, though it has also been taken to mean knowledge of water; its sense here is uncertain, and this volume renders the qualification simply as agriculture and the science of plant life. The superintendent is to collect in good time the seeds of all grains, flowers, fruits, vegetables, bulbous roots, creepers, flax and cotton, and have them sown, on land ploughed many times, by serfs (dāsa), hired labourers and those working off fines. Work is not to be held up for want of ploughs and other implements, bullocks, or the smiths, carpenters, rope-makers, snake-catchers and other workers who serve the farm.

The rest of the chapter covers the matters taken up later in this volume. It states the normal annual rainfall of dry (jāṅgala) and wet (ānūpa) country and of named regions, measured in droṇas with a rain gauge kept at the royal storehouse, and links the expected rain to planetary signs (Section 3.5); the jāṅgala/ānūpa distinction is the same one found in the medical texts (Section 1.6). It classes crops by sowing time (Section 9.12), prescribes the treatment of seeds and cuttings before sowing (Section 9.14), and matches particular crops to particular ground, from river banks to the ridges between beds (Section 7.1). It ranks crops by their returns, placing rice and similar grains highest and sugarcane lowest because it is exposed to many dangers and costly to grow. And it fixes a water rate (udakabhāga) for those who irrigate from the king’s water-works, graded by the method by which the water reaches the field: by hand, carried on the shoulder, by a water-lifting device, or drawn from rivers, lakes, tanks and wells (Kangle 1965). How far such rules were ever applied is unknown. They show at least that the authors treated seed, the relative risks of crops and the cost of irrigation as matters of state concern.

Other superintendents described in the Arthaśāstra were responsible for cattle (go’dhyakṣa, 2.29), pastures, horses, elephants, forest produce, and the slaughter of animals and the protection of certain species. These are discussed in Chapters 13, 15 and 11, and the text as a whole in Volume 18.

docs.title: 2.11.2 The Sudarśana reservoir
docs.text: The best documented water project of the period is the Sudarśana lake near Junagadh in Gujarat, built under Candragupta Maurya, given conduits under Aśoka, and repaired by the Western Kṣatrapa Rudradāman (inscription of 150 CE) and again under the Gupta Skandagupta in the mid-fifth century: more than seven centuries of use, traced in Section 8.2.

docs.title: 2.11.3 Aśoka’s edicts
docs.text: The edicts of Aśoka (r. c. 268–232 BCE) are the earliest datable Indian documents concerned with plants and animals. They record medical treatment for people and animals, the planting of medicinal herbs, roadside banyans and mango groves, the digging of wells, a list of animals not to be killed and a ban on burning forests without purpose (Singh 2008); their provisions are set out in Chapter 11. These measures belong within Aśoka’s policy of dhamma; they should not be read as a modern conservation programme or as “veterinary hospitals” in the modern sense, but they show a ruler taking public responsibility for the welfare of animals as well as people.

docs.title: 2.12.1 The landscapes of Saṅgam poetry
docs.text:
The earliest Tamil literature, the poems collected in the Saṅgam anthologies (roughly the early centuries CE; dates debated), classifies its subject matter by tiṇai, a term that combines the ideas of landscape, mode of life and poetic theme. Each of the five tiṇais of love poetry is associated with a type of country, its plants and animals, its people and their occupations, and a phase of love (Zvelebil 1973; Hart 1975). A. K. Ramanujan’s translations from the anthologies (Ramanujan 1985) are the most accessible way into the poems themselves. Table 2.2 gives a simplified summary.

Table 2.2. The five landscapes (tiṇai) of Saṅgam love poetry (simplified). Tiṇai Landscape Characteristic people and livelihoods kuṟiñci Mountains Hill people; millet fields guarded from parrots; honey gathering; hunting mullai Forest and pasture Herders (āyar, kōvalar); cattle; rain-fed millets marutam Riverine farmland Ploughmen (uḻavar); paddy fields, buffaloes, irrigation; towns neytal Seashore Fishers; fishing and salt-making pālai Parched land Not a fixed region but any land dried by heat; travellers and bandits

The scheme is a literary convention, not a geographical survey, and it should not be described as “agro-ecological zoning” in the modern sense. But it rests on a real observation: that the Tamil country contained distinct ecologies, each supporting a different way of life. In marutam poems the paddy fields, canals, buffaloes and wealthy farming households of the river valleys are part of the setting; in mullai poems the herders, their cattle and the rains; in kuṟiñci poems the girls who guard the millet (tiṉai) from parrots. Longer poems such as the Paṭṭiṉappālai and Maturaikkāñci describe the Kāvēri delta and the Pāṇḍya country with their fields, tanks, markets and ports. The Tamil kings’ patronage of irrigation is remembered in the tradition that the Cōḻa king Karikāla built the first dam across the Kāvēri, the Kallaṇai or Grand Anicut; the structure as it now stands was largely rebuilt in the nineteenth century (Chapter 8).

docs.title: 2.12.2 The Tirukkuṟaḷ on ploughing
docs.text:
The Tirukkuṟaḷ, a collection of 1,330 couplets on ethics, statecraft and love ascribed to Tiruvaḷḷuvar (proposed dates range from the early centuries CE to about 500 CE), devotes its chapter 104, Uḻavu (“Ploughing”), to agriculture. Its ten couplets (1031–1040) may be paraphrased as follows, after the translations of Pope (1886) and Tiruvalluvar (1990):

  • However the world may turn, it follows the plough; so, for all its toil, farming is foremost (1031).

  • Ploughmen are the linchpin of the world, for they support those who take up other work (1032).

  • Only those who live by ploughing truly live; all others follow behind them, eating by their favour (1033).

  • A land of prosperous ploughmen will see other kings bow before its own (1034).

  • Those who plough with their own hands never beg, and give to those who do (1035).

  • If the ploughman folds his hands, even ascetics who have given up desire cannot endure (1036).

  • If the ploughed soil is dried until a measure of it shrinks to a quarter of its weight, the crop will flourish without even a handful of manure (1037).

  • Manuring is better than ploughing; and after weeding, guarding the crop is better than watering it (1038).

  • If the owner does not visit his field, it will sulk like a neglected wife (1039).

  • The earth laughs to see those who sit idle, pleading that they have nothing (1040).

The chapter is a work of ethics, not a manual: its purpose is to establish the farmer’s dignity and the dependence of society on his labour. Yet couplets 1037 to 1039 reflect practical maxims about tilth, manure, weeding, watching over the crop and the owner’s personal attention to the land. The “ploughman” praised here is, in social terms, usually the landholding cultivator; the agricultural labourers of the Tamil country, many of them from communities later treated as untouchable, appear rarely in this literature (Chapter 18).

docs.title: 2.13 The Epics and the Early Land Grants
2.13.1 The epics
docs.text: The Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa, composed over many centuries and reaching their present form in the early centuries CE, treat the prosperity of agriculture as a test of good kingship. In the Sabhāparvan of the Mahābhārata (2.5 in the critical edition), the sage Nārada questions Yudhiṣṭhira about his government, asking among other things whether large, full tanks have been built at intervals across his kingdom so that agriculture does not depend on rain alone, and whether farmers in distress are given seed and food and loans at a modest rate of interest. The Rāmāyaṇa contains a comparable catechism, and its account of Sītā’s birth from the furrow links the heroine to the earth and to ploughing. Such passages describe ideals of royal duty, but they show what was expected of a king: irrigation works, relief in hard times and protection of cultivators and cattle.

docs.title: 2.13.2 Land grants
docs.text:
From the early centuries CE, inscriptions begin to record grants of land. Cave inscriptions at Nasik in Maharashtra record gifts of fields and villages by Sātavāhana kings and their contemporaries to Buddhist monks, with privileges that exempted the donated land from entry by royal officials and from royal claims such as the right to dig for salt. In Bengal, copper-plate inscriptions of the Gupta period record the purchase of land for religious gifts, giving prices and measuring land in units such as kulyavāpa and droṇavāpa, named after the quantity of seed needed to sow it (Singh 2008).

From the fourth and fifth centuries, grants of land and villages to brahmins (agrahāra, brahmadeya) multiplied across India. They brought new land under the plough, extended Brahmanical institutions into frontier and forest regions, and transferred to the grantees rights over the produce and labour of the cultivators. Grant documents name fields, wet and dry land, trees, tanks, wells, pastures and boundaries, and so become an important source for the history of cultivation. Their significance for the agrarian order of early medieval India is discussed in Chapter 18.

docs.title: 2.14 The Agricultural Year and Its Festivals
docs.text:
Throughout this period the agricultural year was shaped by the monsoon, with a main sowing at the onset of the rains and, where water allowed, a second crop in the cool season. Texts divided the year into six seasons and timed operations by the lunar months and the nakṣatras (Chapter 3; for the astronomy, Volume 12). The terms kharīf and rabī for the monsoon and winter crops are Arabic in origin and belong to the revenue usage of the Sultanate and Mughal periods.

Many of India’s festivals mark points in the agricultural year, though most are attested in their present form only from later periods. In the Tamil country Poṅkal, in the month of Tai (mid-January), celebrates the harvest and is followed by a day honouring cattle. In Assam the three Bihu festivals mark stages in the rice year; in Kerala, Onam is a harvest festival; in Punjab, Baisakhi marks the wheat harvest; in western Odisha, Nuakhai celebrates the new rice; and in coastal Odisha, during Raja Parba, the earth is held to be menstruating and ploughing is suspended for three days. These observances express the importance of the agricultural cycle in social and religious life. Claims that they encode precise agronomic knowledge should be treated with caution.

docs.title: 2.15 Towards the Treatises
docs.text: By the middle of the first millennium CE, the elements of the later agricultural literature were in place: a crop repertoire combining winter and summer crops of local, south-west Asian, African and East Asian origin; the zebu ox and plough as the basis of tillage; tanks, wells and channels for irrigation; a body of weather lore and calendrical rules; and state and religious institutions with an interest in land and its produce. Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā in the sixth century gathers much of this lore, including the rain-forecasting chapters (21–28), the chapter on finding groundwater (54) and the chapter on trees (55) (Bhat 1981). These are discussed in Chapters 3, 8 and 4, where the specialised treatises of the following centuries are also examined.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Agriculture in South Asia began at Mehrgarh around 7000 BCE with barley, wheat, goats, sheep and locally domesticated zebu cattle, and cotton was in use there by the sixth or fifth millennium BCE. Archaeobotany has shown that farming in the subcontinent drew on several independent centres of domestication — the southern Deccan, Gujarat, the Ganga plain and the Indus region — as well as on crops from south-west Asia, Africa (from about 2000 BCE) and East Asia. Harappan farmers combined winter and summer crops in regionally varied systems, ploughed with the ard, and kept zebu cattle, buffalo, sheep and goats, but no securely identified domestic horse. Neolithic cattle-keepers of the southern Deccan grew native pulses and millets. The Vedic texts record the plough, the furrow and the crops of the north, and the Upaniṣads reflect on food; Buddhist, Jain and Brahmanical texts reveal both the importance of agriculture and the low status of the labour of ploughing. The Arthaśāstra, Aśoka’s edicts, the Sudarśana reservoir, the Tamil anthologies and the Tirukkuṟaḷ, the epics and the early land grants show agriculture as a central concern of states, religious institutions and poets by the early centuries CE.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Fuller (2006) is the essential synthesis of archaeobotanical evidence, and Fuller (2011) a shorter statement of the argument for multiple centres of domestication. Meadow (1996) treats the domestication of animals in the north-west. Possehl (2002) and Kenoyer (1998) describe the Indus civilisation. Singh (2008) provides a reliable general history of the whole period, and Gopal and Srivastava (2008) a detailed survey of the textual and epigraphic evidence for agriculture; Sharma (1980) remains fundamental on labour and the śūdra. For the Tamil poems, Hart (1975) on their setting and Ramanujan (1985) for translations.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Kṛṣi-Parāśara, Rain Forecasting and the Agricultural Treatises
docs.text:
Sanskrit learning produced only a handful of works devoted to field agriculture. The best known is a short verse manual called the Kṛṣi-Parāśara, “Agriculture according to Parāśara”. It is often presented as an ancient compendium of farming science; the published text is shorter, later and more practical than that (Section 1.5). This chapter describes what the Kṛṣi-Parāśara contains, as far as the editions of Majumdar and Banerji (1960) and Sadhale (1999) allow. It then sets the text beside the older and fuller rain lore of Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā, the rain records of the Arthaśāstra, and the weather sayings of the regional languages. A section asks what such forecasting could and could not achieve. The chapter ends with the other agricultural treatises of medieval India and a brief look at farming books written elsewhere in the pre-modern world.

These treatises have to be read against the society that produced them, which is described more fully in Chapter 18. By the time the Kṛṣi-Parāśara was written, land grants to brahmins, temples and monasteries had spread settled rice farming across eastern and southern India, and the grantees held rights over the produce and labour of the cultivators (Section 18.3). The texts assign agriculture to the vaiśya and discourage the higher varṇas from ploughing, while much of the actual work was done by śūdra peasants, by dependent labourers, many of them from castes later treated as untouchable, and by women (Section 18.2). The farming manuals speak for the landholder who supervised this work, not for those who did it, and the reader should keep that in mind throughout this chapter and the next.

docs.title: 3.1 The Text, Its Attribution and Its Date
3.1.1 Editions
docs.text:
The Kṛṣi-Parāśara first became widely available to scholars in the edition and English translation of Girija Prasanna Majumdar and Sures Chandra Banerji, published by the Asiatic Society in its Bibliotheca Indica series in 1960 (Majumdar and Banerji 1960). Majumdar, a botanist with a long interest in Sanskrit plant literature, had earlier translated the Upavanavinoda (see Chapter 4). In 1999 Nalini Sadhale published a further text and translation, with notes, as the second of the Agri-History Bulletins of the Asian Agri-History Foundation (Sadhale 1999). These two editions are the basis of everything said about the text in this chapter. Where they leave a point uncertain, it is left uncertain here.

The text is short: a few hundred verses of simple, mostly unadorned Sanskrit, with no commentary. It reads as a working manual for a landholding householder rather than as a learned treatise. Its language is sometimes irregular, and some of its technical words for tools and operations are rare. Both features suggest a regional text written for practical use.

docs.title: 3.1.2 Who was “Parāśara”?
docs.text: The name Parāśara belongs, in the epics and Purāṇas, to a Vedic seer, the father of Vyāsa, to whom the Viṣṇu Purāṇa and several other works are traditionally ascribed. A Parāśara was also cited as an early authority on astral science and omens: Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā and its tenth-century commentary by Utpala refer to older works on rain and portents ascribed to sages such as Garga and Parāśara (Bhat 1981). Placing a farming manual under the name of a famous seer was a way of giving it authority. It tells us nothing about the actual author, who is unknown. The attribution to Parāśara should be treated as traditional, in the same way as the attribution of the Arthaśāstra to Kauṭilya.

docs.title: 3.1.3 Date and place
docs.text:
Some modern accounts place the text in the Gupta period or even earlier, but there is no evidence for this. Majumdar and Banerji (1960) placed its composition between about 950 and 1100 CE; other scholars have argued for a later date. The text cannot be dated precisely, and any date before the late first millennium CE should be regarded as unsupported.

Its place of origin is more securely indicated. The agriculture it describes is centred on wet rice: nurseries, transplanting, standing water in the fields and its drainage. The sequence of operations fits the monsoon regime of the lower Gangetic plain, and part of its vocabulary is eastern Indian. For these reasons the text is generally assigned to Bengal or a neighbouring region of eastern India (Majumdar and Banerji 1960; Sadhale 1999). It belongs, then, to the same broad world as the Pāla and Sena kingdoms, whose copper-plate land grants record villages, fields, ponds and rice lands in some detail (see Chapter 18).

Scholarly Note: What the Kṛṣi-Parāśara does not contain

Much that circulates under the name of the Kṛṣi-Parāśara is not in the published text. It does not contain:

  • a recipe for kuṇapajala, the fermented liquid manure made from animal remains. That preparation belongs to the Vṛkṣāyurveda of Surapāla and to the Upavanavinoda (Chapter 4);

  • a classification of twelve soils, a “soil-testing section” using earthworms, or a description of petrichor;

  • pesticide formulas using tobacco or custard apple. Both plants came from the Americas and reached India only after 1500;

  • tables of cloud names, wind directions or animal signs with numbered verses;

  • a division of the year into kharīf, rabī and zāid seasons, which are Perso-Arabic revenue terms (Section 9.12), or recommendations of particular rice varieties for deep water or uplands.

On such attributions in general, see Section 1.5.

docs.title: 3.2 The Praise of Agriculture
docs.text:
The text opens, after the customary invocation, with a praise of agriculture. One of its verses begins kṛṣir dhanyā kṛṣir medhyā jantūnāṃ jīvanaṃ kṛṣiḥ, “agriculture is blessed, agriculture is pure, agriculture is the life of creatures” (Majumdar and Banerji 1960; Sadhale 1999). These verses praise agriculture as the means of life of all creatures and set it above other ways of earning a living. Even learned men, the text suggests, depend on food, and food depends on the farmer. The theme is old: the Ṛgvedic gambler is told to give up dice and plough his field, and the Tamil Tirukkuṟaḷ gives a whole chapter to the ploughman as the linchpin of the world (Sections 2.7 and 2.12).

The Kṛṣi-Parāśara addresses a householder who owns land and cattle and is expected to watch over the work himself. Its warm praise of farming stands in contrast to the normative literature, which was more ambivalent about the plough (Section 2.9).

docs.title: 3.3 What the Text Covers
docs.text: The contents may be summarised under the headings that both editors recognise. The order below follows the logic of the farming year rather than the exact sequence of the verses.

docs.title: 3.3.1 Forecasting the year’s rain
docs.text:
Rain is the first concern of the text, and forecasting takes up a large part of it. The methods are those of the astral sciences (jyotiṣa) applied to the farmer’s needs.

The rulers of the year. Each year, in this system, has a planetary “king” and “minister”, fixed by an arithmetical rule applied to the number of the Śaka year; the minister is the fourth planet counted from the king. The character of the rains, and so of the harvest, is predicted from these rulers: some planets as king are said to bring abundant rain, others scanty rain or drought (Majumdar and Banerji 1960; Sadhale 1999). The same idea survives in the annual almanacs (pañcāṅga) of many Indian regions, which still announce the “king” and “minister” of the coming year.

The cloud of the year. The text names four kinds of cloud, āvarta, saṃvarta, puṣkara and droṇa, and gives a simple arithmetical rule, applied to the number of the year, for finding which of them governs a given year. Each cloud is associated with a different quality of rain, from patchy or scanty to abundant. These four are the classic cloud names of Sanskrit literature; they are not meteorological cloud types in the modern sense of forms such as cumulus or stratus. Kālidāsa’s Meghadūta, near its beginning, addresses the cloud-messenger as born in the famous lineage of the Puṣkaras and Āvartakas.

Observations in particular months. Beside these calendrical rules the text prescribes observations of wind, cloud, rain and sky on fixed days of particular months, from which the rain of the coming season is to be inferred. What is seen in the months before the rains is read as a sign of what will follow during the monsoon. The underlying idea, that the weather of one season is “carried” into another, is shared with the doctrine of the “pregnancy” of clouds in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā (Section 3.4).

The quantity of rain. The text also treats the amount of the year’s rain, reckoned in traditional measures, and how it is to be known. Here too it stands close to the older astral literature, in which rainfall was measured by collecting it in a vessel of standard size (Sections 3.4 and 3.5).

The rain lore of the Kṛṣi-Parāśara is less detailed than Varāhamihira’s, and much of it is clearly derived from the same tradition. Its distinctive contribution is to place these forecasts at the head of a manual of field operations. For its author, judging the year’s rain was the first thing a cultivator needed to do.

docs.title: 3.3.2 Cattle and the cattle shed
docs.text: Draught cattle were the farmer’s capital, and the text gives them close attention (Sadhale 1999). It describes the cattle shed: where it should be built, the need to keep it clean and to remove dung and urine, and the protection of animals from damp and disease. It also gives rules for the care of the animals, and prescribes auspicious times and rites connected with them. The tone is that of a householder protecting valuable property. Livestock husbandry in general, including the veterinary literature, is treated in Chapter 13.

docs.title: 3.3.3 Manure
docs.text: The text gives a seasonal routine for cow-dung manure: in Māgha the dung heap is to be dug out, then dried in the sun and broken up, laid in a pit in each field in Phālguna, and spread at sowing time (Majumdar and Banerji 1960; Sadhale 1999). The text warns that a crop grown without manure will bear no fruit. It does not offer a theory of soil fertility, and it does not describe the elaborate fermented preparations of the horticultural texts. Its manure is the ordinary farmyard manure of a mixed rice-and-cattle economy. Soil and manuring are discussed more fully in Chapter 7, and the later scientific study of Indian manuring in Section 10.7.

docs.title: 3.3.4 The plough
docs.text: One of the most frequently cited passages of the Kṛṣi-Parāśara names the parts of the plough and gives their dimensions in traditional units such as the hasta (cubit), vitasti (span) and aṅgula (finger-breadth). Among the parts named are the īṣā, the long pole or beam joining plough to yoke, and the yuga, the yoke itself. Several of the other names are rare words whose exact reference is uncertain, and the two editors do not always agree on them; they are not listed here. The plough described is the light wooden ard drawn by a pair of oxen, with an iron share, that remained the standard implement of Indian farming until the twentieth century (Randhawa 1980). The passage is valuable to historians of technology precisely because it is so plain: it records a real tool, not an idealised one. The parts of such a plough are shown in Figure 7.1, and the history of the plough in India is traced in Chapters 2 and 7.

docs.title: 3.3.5 Seed
docs.text: The text gives rules for collecting seed from the harvest, drying it and storing it so that it remains fit for sowing. Seed is to be kept dry and free from damage, and seed of poor quality will not give a good crop (Majumdar and Banerji 1960; Sadhale 1999). The text also prescribes rites and auspicious times for taking out the seed and beginning to sow. The wider history of seeds, landraces and their storage is treated in Chapter 9.

docs.title: 3.3.6 Sowing, transplanting, weeding and drainage
docs.text:
The heart of the practical section concerns rice. The text describes sowing, raising seedlings, and transplanting them into flooded fields during the rains. It insists on timely weeding, and it gives instructions for the management of water in the field: water is to be kept in the field while the crop needs it and drained out at the proper stage so that the grain can ripen (Majumdar and Banerji 1960; Sadhale 1999). This attention to letting water out of the field, as well as holding it in, is characteristic of a deltaic region where too much water was as great a danger as too little.

No yields, seed rates or spacings are given that could be converted into modern figures, and the text times its operations by lunar months and nakṣatras rather than by named crop seasons.

docs.title: 3.3.7 Harvest, threshing and storage
docs.text: The text closes the agricultural cycle with the harvest, the preparation of the threshing floor, threshing, and the storage of grain. These operations, too, are linked to auspicious times and to rites performed on the threshing floor. The details are practical rather than technical, and the text says nothing about methods of preserving stored grain against insects. Farmers’ storage practices are described in Section 9.14.

docs.title: 3.3.8 Rites of the farming year
docs.text:
Throughout the text practical instruction is interwoven with ritual. The first ploughing of the season, the first sowing and the bringing in of the harvest are all accompanied by offerings and observances, and auspicious lunar days and nakṣatras are prescribed for each operation. The text also describes a festival associated with the month of Pauṣa, the Puṣyayātrā (Majumdar and Banerji 1960; Sadhale 1999). Rites of this kind are typical of agrarian societies, and similar harvest festivals are still celebrated across eastern India. Agricultural festivals more generally are discussed in Chapter 2.

These rites were not decoration. For the author they were as much part of farming as ploughing and weeding: success depended on correct timing, and correct timing was understood in astral terms. A modern reader may separate the observational from the ritual parts of the text. Its author did not.

Cross-Reference: The nakṣatra calendar

The Kṛṣi-Parāśara, like all Indian agricultural texts, times its operations by lunar months, lunar days (tithi) and the twenty-seven or twenty-eight lunar mansions (nakṣatra). The structure of this calendar, its relation to the solar year and the seasons, and the history of the pañcāṅga are treated in Volume 12, Khagola Jyotiṣa. Because the lunar months drift against the solar year and the nakṣatra positions have shifted with the precession of the equinoxes, a nakṣatra named in a medieval text cannot be turned into a fixed modern calendar date without calculation.

docs.title: 3.4 Rain Forecasting in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā
docs.text:
The fullest Sanskrit account of rain forecasting is not in a farming manual but in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā of Varāhamihira, a sixth-century astronomer-astrologer associated with Ujjain in the Avanti region. The Bṛhatsaṃhitā is a compendium of the “natural” branch of astral science (saṃhitā): omens, portents, the signs of good and bad harvests, gems, animals, architecture and the care of trees. Varāhamihira repeatedly cites earlier authorities, and his chapters on rain record a body of lore that was already old in his time. The standard English translation is that of Bhat (1981), whose chapter numbering is used here.

Eight consecutive chapters deal with forecasting rain (Table 3.1). Two other chapters touch farming directly: chapter 54, on finding groundwater (dakārgala), treated in Chapter 8, and chapter 55, on the care of trees (vṛkṣāyurveda), treated in Chapter 4.

Table 3.1. The rain-forecasting chapters of Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā (chapter numbers as in (Bhat 1981)). Ch. Title Subject 21 Garbhalakṣaṇa Signs of the “conception” of the clouds in the cool season 22 Garbhadhāraṇa The sustaining of the cloud-embryos and the signs that they will yield rain 23 Pravarṣaṇa The first rains, and the measurement of rainfall 24 Rohiṇīyoga Forecasts from observations when the moon is in conjunction with Rohiṇī 25 Svātiyoga Forecasts from observations when the moon is in Svāti 26 Āṣāḍhīyoga Forecasts from observations at the Āṣāḍha full moon 27 Vātacakra Forecasts from the direction of the wind 28 Sadyovarṣaṇa Signs of immediate rain

docs.title: 3.4.1 The “pregnancy” of the clouds
docs.text:
The central idea of these chapters is that the rains of the monsoon are “conceived” months earlier, in the cool season, and “born” when their time comes. The conception season begins in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa (November–December). An “embryo” (garbha) formed when the moon stands in a particular nakṣatra is said to be delivered as rain about 195 days later, when the moon is again in that nakṣatra (Bhat 1981). Six and a half months after the cool season brings us to the beginning of the rains, so the scheme links each day of winter to a day of the coming monsoon.

The forecaster was to watch the sky on the days of conception. Favourable signs include gentle winds from the north, north-east or east, a clear sky with soft, glossy clouds, haloes around the sun and moon, and mild thunder and lightning. Unfavourable signs, such as meteors, dust storms, thunderbolts and planetary eclipses, are said to destroy the embryo. An embryo accompanied by all five signs of wind, rain, lightning, thunder and cloud is expected to bring abundant rain. If heavy rain falls during the period of pregnancy itself, the embryo is thought to be lost, “miscarried” before its time (Bhat 1981).

The scheme is elegant and internally consistent, and it reflects an awareness that the seasons are connected. It is also, in its working detail, a calendrical construction. There is no known physical mechanism by which the weather on a given winter day determines the rain on a particular day half a year later, and there is no established evidence that forecasts made by this method have useful skill.

docs.title: 3.4.2 Measuring the rain
docs.text: The chapter on the first rains (pravarṣaṇa) contains one of the clearest pieces of quantitative method in the whole tradition. Rain is to be collected in a round vessel one hasta (cubit) across, and the amount is to be expressed by weight: fifty palas of collected water make one āḍhaka (Bhat 1981). A vessel of fixed aperture is the essential principle of every rain gauge. Varāhamihira uses the measurement to judge whether the first rain of the season is good or poor, as one input to his forecasts. It is not described as part of a continuous record kept over many years.

docs.title: 3.4.3 Conjunctions, wind and immediate signs
docs.text:
The next three chapters prescribe observations at particular moments of the lunar calendar: when the moon passes Rohiṇī, when it passes Svāti, and at the full moon of Āṣāḍha, just before the main rains. The appearance of the sky, the direction of the wind and the presence of clouds or rain at these moments are read as signs for the season. The chapter on the “wheel of winds” (vātacakra) forecasts the year’s rain from the direction of the wind on the Āṣāḍha full moon (Bhat 1981).

The last chapter of the group, on immediate rain (sadyovarṣaṇa), is the most down-to-earth. It lists signs that rain will come soon: the look of the sky at sunrise and sunset, the colour and movement of the clouds, and the behaviour of animals, such as ants carrying their eggs and frogs calling (Bhat 1981). These are the kinds of short-range signs that farmers everywhere have used, and they are closest to what modern observers would accept as genuine indicators of approaching rain.

docs.title: 3.5 The Arthaśāstra and the Recording of Rain
docs.text:
Rain measurement in India is attested still earlier in the Arthaśāstra, the treatise on statecraft ascribed to Kauṭilya. In its present form the text is composite and dates from roughly 50 BCE to 300 CE; the attribution to a minister of Candragupta Maurya around 300 BCE is traditional (Olivelle 2013). The Arthaśāstra is discussed as a whole in Volume 18, Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra; only its rain lore concerns us here.

In Book 2 the royal storehouse is to be equipped with a rain gauge (varṣamāna), a vessel with a mouth one aratni (cubit) wide (2.5.7; (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013)). The chapter on the superintendent of agriculture (sītādhyakṣa, 2.24), who managed the crown’s own farmland, then states the normal rainfall of different regions in the volume measure droṇa. The arid jāṅgala country is given sixteen droṇas, the wet ānūpa country half as much again; Aśmaka thirteen and a half, Avanti twenty-three; for the western regions (Aparānta), the Himalayan regions and lands watered by channels the amount is said to be unlimited (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013). The ancient droṇa cannot be converted reliably into millimetres of rain, so these figures cannot be compared directly with modern data. What matters is the practice: rain was measured at state storehouses, and normal amounts for different regions were known well enough to be written down.

The same chapter connects the forecasting of rain with the positions and movements of Jupiter and Venus and with changes in the appearance of the sun. It advises the superintendent to plan sowing according to the expected rain, choosing crops that need more or less water (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013). Here administrative record-keeping and astral forecasting stand side by side, as they do in Varāhamihira. The rest of the chapter on the superintendent is summarised in Section 2.11.1.

docs.title: 3.6 Folk Forecasting: Khanā, Ghāgh and Bhaḍḍarī
docs.text:
Alongside the Sanskrit texts, every farming region of India had, and still has, a stock of rhymed sayings about weather, seasons and crops. They were transmitted orally, among cultivators rather than scholars, and they were written down only in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries by local scholars and colonial collectors. Because they were oral, they are hard to date, and many versions of each saying exist. The examples below are described rather than quoted. No reliable critical edition exists from which a fixed wording could be cited, and inventing “typical” sayings would be no better than inventing verses.

Khanā. In Bengal the best-known body of such sayings is the Khanār vacan, “the sayings of Khanā”. Legend makes Khanā a learned woman astrologer, sometimes connected with the household of Varāhamihira himself, whose tongue was cut out because her predictions surpassed those of the men around her. The sayings ascribed to her are short Bengali couplets on the timing of ploughing and sowing, the signs of rain and drought, the right season for particular crops, the care of cattle and the management of the household. As recorded, their language is that of early modern Bengali; their origins may be older, but they cannot be dated. Similar collections exist in neighbouring regions, such as the sayings attributed to Ḍāk in Assam and Bengal.

Ghāgh and Bhaḍḍarī. In the Hindi-speaking north, weather and farming sayings are attributed to Ghāgh and to Bhaḍḍarī. Ghāgh is a figure of legend placed by different traditions in different centuries and regions. Bhaḍḍarī (Bhaḍalī in Gujarati and Rajasthani usage) is likewise legendary and is associated especially with weather prognostication. The sayings attributed to both deal with the signs of rain in the sky and in animal behaviour, the qualities of good and bad bullocks, the right moment for sowing, and the conduct of a sensible farmer. They circulate in Bhojpuri, Awadhi, Braj and Rajasthani forms.

It is notable that in Bengal the emblematic authority on weather and farming is a woman. Whatever the historical reality behind the legend, it reflects the fact that agricultural knowledge was carried by women as well as by men. Women did much of the work of seed selection, storage, transplanting and post-harvest processing (see Chapters 9 and 14).

These sayings differ from the Sanskrit texts in voice rather than in substance. They mix astral rules (rain on a particular nakṣatra, the weekday on which a month begins) with local observations of wind, cloud, dew, the behaviour of birds and insects, and the flowering of plants. Their value lies less in any single prediction than in what they show of farmers’ attention to their environment and of the way knowledge was condensed into memorable form.

docs.title: 3.7 What Could Such Forecasting Do?
docs.text:
A fair evaluation of this material must distinguish several kinds of rule that are mixed together in the texts, because they differ greatly in what they could achieve.

Calendrical and astrological rules predict the year’s rain from the planet that rules the year, from the cloud assigned to the year by arithmetic, or from the position of the moon on certain days. These rules have no physical basis. The number of the year cannot affect the monsoon, and a forecast derived from it can be right only by chance.

Long-range rules link observations in one season to rain in another, as in the doctrine of the pregnancy of the clouds. They rest on a sound intuition: the seasons are connected, and the state of the atmosphere in one season does influence the next. But the specific links proposed, from a particular winter day to a particular monsoon day, have no known mechanism. Modern long-range forecasting depends on large-scale patterns of ocean temperature and atmospheric pressure across the whole tropics, which no ground-level observer could have detected.

Short-range signs, such as rising humidity, the build-up of clouds, shifts of wind, haloes and the behaviour of insects, frogs and birds, can carry real information about weather in the next few hours or days. Farmers who read them well had a practical advantage. Such signs are local and short-lived, however. They can tell a farmer that rain is coming this afternoon, but not whether the monsoon will fail next year.

Measurement stands apart. The rain gauges of the Arthaśāstra and the Bṛhatsaṃhitā are genuine empirical instruments, and the regional figures of the Arthaśāstra show that measurements were used to describe normal conditions. There is no evidence, however, that continuous records were kept and analysed over long periods to test the forecasting rules.

The monsoon’s variability was a matter of life and death, and the failure of the rains brought repeated famines. Systematic seasonal forecasting began only in the 1880s, when H. F. Blanford of the newly founded India Meteorological Department issued forecasts based partly on Himalayan snowfall. In the early twentieth century his successor Gilbert Walker searched worldwide weather records for statistical predictors of the monsoon and in the process identified the Southern Oscillation, later understood as part of the El Niño system. The colonial famines of the late nineteenth century, when the rains failed and grain continued to be exported, showed that forecasting alone could not prevent catastrophe (Davis 2001). Even today seasonal monsoon forecasts have limited skill.

Debate: Did Indian rain lore anticipate monsoon science?

For: the texts treat rain as part of a seasonal system, measure rainfall with standard vessels, and record observations of wind and cloud; some short-range signs they list are physically meaningful.

Against: the core predictive rules are astrological; the long-range links have no mechanism and no demonstrated skill; there is no evidence of the systematic testing of predictions against records that defines a forecasting science.

Assessment: the texts deserve to be read as a serious attempt to bring order to the most important uncertainty in farmers’ lives. They are part of the history of meteorology, as similar weather lore is in Europe and China. They did not anticipate the physical understanding of the monsoon, and nothing is gained by claiming that they did.

docs.title: 3.8 Other Agricultural Treatises
docs.text: The Kṛṣi-Parāśara is not alone. A small number of other works, in Sanskrit and in the regional languages, deal wholly or partly with agriculture and plant care; their dates, as far as they can be established, are given in Table 1.2 (Chapter 1). Those concerned mainly with trees and gardens are discussed further in Chapter 4.

docs.title: 3.8.1 The Kāśyapīya Kṛṣisūkti
docs.text: The Kāśyapīya Kṛṣisūkti, “Kāśyapa’s verses on agriculture”, is attributed to the sage Kāśyapa. Like the Kṛṣi-Parāśara it is a Sanskrit verse text, but it comes from the south of India. Its date is uncertain; its editor proposes the later first millennium CE, but the evidence is slight (Ayachit 2002). The text gives particular attention to rice, the dominant crop of the river deltas and tank-irrigated lands of the peninsula, and to the management of water. It places agriculture within a framework of royal responsibility and religious merit, in which the ruler is expected to promote cultivation. Ayachit’s translation made the text accessible, but it has received far less scholarly study than the Kṛṣi-Parāśara. Its relation to the irrigation history of south India (see Chapter 8) remains to be worked out.

docs.title: 3.8.2 The Lokopakāra
docs.text: The Lokopakāra (“For the benefit of the people”) of Cāvuṇḍarāya, written in Kannada around 1025 CE, is an early encyclopaedic work in Kannada. It brings together practical knowledge on topics such as astrology and omens, house-building, water-finding, cookery, perfumes, remedies and the care of plants, and an English translation was published by the Asian Agri-History Foundation (Ayangarya 2006). Its plant-care section belongs to the vṛkṣāyurveda tradition and is described in Section 4.1.5. The Lokopakāra matters for the history of agricultural knowledge because it shows Sanskrit technical material being recast in a regional language for a lay readership.

docs.title: 3.8.3 The Mānasollāsa
docs.text: The Mānasollāsa, also called Abhilaṣitārthacintāmaṇi, was composed in 1131 CE at the court of the Western Cālukya king Someśvara III. It is an encyclopaedia of royal life in five sections of twenty chapters each, covering the acquisition and protection of the kingdom and the king’s enjoyments and pastimes (Shrigondekar 1925). Several parts concern plants and animals: the laying out of gardens, with plant-care instructions of the vṛkṣāyurveda type; horses and elephants; dogs and hunting; birds; fishing; and a celebrated section on cookery. The text describes the agriculture and husbandry of the court rather than of the village, but it shows how much practical knowledge of plants and animals was expected of a cultivated king. Its material on animals is used in Chapters 15 and 17, and its cookery in Chapter 14.

docs.title: 3.8.4 Other sources
docs.text: Agricultural material is also scattered through the Purāṇas, notably the Agni Purāṇa, which has chapters on the care of trees and of animals; through the dharmaśāstra literature on land, tillage and its rules; and through inscriptions recording irrigation works and land grants. From the thirteenth century onward, Persian sources from the Sultanate and Mughal courts add much on crops, revenue and gardens; they are discussed in Chapter 18. Agricultural verse also exists in the regional languages, though it has received little critical study. In Tamil, the Ēr eḻupatu (“Seventy on the plough”), traditionally ascribed to the poet Kampaṉ, praises the plough and the cultivating Veḷḷāḷar; in Malayalam, the Kṛṣigīta, a verse work of uncertain, probably early modern date, presents the rice farming of Kerala as teaching given by Paraśurāma. Both are works of praise and of caste and regional identity as much as manuals, and their dates and attributions are traditional. For most of Indian history, however, agricultural knowledge was transmitted by practice and by word of mouth rather than in writing. The treatises are a small and socially narrow window onto it.

docs.title: 3.9 Farming Books Elsewhere
docs.text:
It can be helpful to set the Indian treatises beside agricultural writing from other pre-modern societies, provided the comparison is descriptive rather than competitive.

In the Roman world, Cato, Varro and above all Columella, whose De re rustica in twelve books was written in the first century CE, wrote for owners of estates worked largely by enslaved labourers. Columella covers soils, vines, olives, livestock, bees and gardens, and the management of the estate’s workforce. In China, Jia Sixie’s Qimin yaoshu (“Essential techniques for the common people”), compiled in the sixth century, is a long and systematic manual of field crops, vegetables, trees, animal husbandry and food processing, including fermentation; it quotes many earlier works. In al-Andalus, Ibn al-ʿAwwām of Seville compiled his Kitāb al-filāḥa (“Book of agriculture”) in the twelfth century, drawing on earlier Arabic, Greek and Andalusi sources; it is especially rich on irrigated gardens and fruit trees. The Byzantine Geoponika, compiled in the tenth century, is an anthology of older Greek agricultural writing.

Beside these, the Indian works have a distinctive profile. The Kṛṣi-Parāśara is very short and addressed to a single householder. The Indian texts are composed in verse for memorisation, closely tied to astral science and ritual, and concerned with rice and the monsoon rather than with the vine and the olive. The tree and garden texts discussed in the next chapter are, by contrast, closely modelled on medicine. Each tradition reflects its own ecology, economy and learned culture. None of these works records the whole agricultural knowledge of its society, and the cultivators whose practice they describe, enslaved estate workers in Italy, peasants in China and India, mostly left no writings of their own.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The Kṛṣi-Parāśara is a short Sanskrit verse manual, attributed by tradition to the sage Parāśara, probably composed in Bengal or eastern India around 950–1100 CE or somewhat later. After praising agriculture, it forecasts the year’s rain and then gives a householder’s rules for cattle, manure, the plough, seed, the cultivation of rice, the harvest and the rites of the year. Its rain lore draws on the older tradition recorded in Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā and the Arthaśāstra, which also measured rainfall; the oral sayings of Khanā, Ghāgh and Bhaḍḍarī carry the same mixture of astral rule and local observation into the vernaculars. Measurement and short-range signs had real value; the astrological and long-range rules did not. The Kāśyapīya Kṛṣisūkti, the Lokopakāra and the Mānasollāsa show that agricultural writing in India was limited in volume but varied in region, language and audience.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: The text and translation of Majumdar and Banerji (1960) remains the basic edition of the Kṛṣi-Parāśara; Sadhale (1999) offers a convenient translation with notes. Varāhamihira’s rain chapters can be read in Bhat (1981), and the Arthaśāstra’s chapter on the superintendent of agriculture in Kangle (1965) and Olivelle (2013). Ayachit (2002) translates the Kāśyapīya Kṛṣisūkti and Ayangarya (2006) the Lokopakāra. Gopal and Srivastava (2008) sets these texts in the wider history of early Indian agriculture, and Randhawa (1980) provides a broad survey.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Vṛkṣāyurveda: The Science of the Life of Trees
docs.text:
Vṛkṣāyurveda, “the science of the life of trees”, is the Sanskrit name for a body of knowledge about growing and tending trees, shrubs, creepers and garden plants. Its name and much of its method come from medicine (āyurveda). Plants are treated as living bodies that must be nourished, can fall ill, and can be cured. The tradition is represented by a single chapter in an encyclopaedia, a few chapters in the Purāṇas, one surviving specialised treatise, sections of medieval encyclopaedias and anthologies, and a late compilation. Its literature is therefore small. This chapter describes the texts, the ideas about plant life on which they rest, and the main topics they treat. It deals separately with the fermented liquid manure called kuṇapajala, with the literary and horticultural notion of plant “cravings” (dohada), and with the marvels the texts claim to produce. What the gardens produced, and what Indian culture made of their flowers, scents and betel, is the subject of Chapter 5. Plant classification is treated more fully in Chapter 6, and medicinal plants in Chapter 12 and in Volume 13, Āyurveda.

The word itself is old. The Arthaśāstra (2.24.1) requires the superintendent of agriculture to know the science of agriculture and the science of plant life (vṛkṣāyurveda), or to be assisted by people who do (Section 2.11.1). Nothing survives of any treatise of that period, but the term shows that a recognised body of knowledge about the care of plants existed by the early centuries CE.

docs.title: 4.1 The Texts
docs.text: The principal sources are the Bṛhatsaṃhitā (ch. 55), the Agni Purāṇa, Surapāla, the Lokopakāra, the Mānasollāsa, the Upavanavinoda and the Viśvavallabha; their approximate dates are given in Tables 1.1 and 1.2 (Chapter 1). For several of them the dates are disputed.

docs.title: 4.1.1 Bṛhatsaṃhitā, chapter 55
docs.text: The oldest surviving systematic account is chapter 55 of Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā (6th century), titled Vṛkṣāyurveda (Bhat 1981). It is short, but most of the topics of the later texts are already present in it. It recommends planting trees by houses, gardens and water bodies, and describes the preparation of the soil. It lists trees that can be raised from cuttings, gives seasons for transplanting, and prescribes the spacing of trees and a watering schedule. It then sets out the symptoms of disease and their treatment, ways of making a barren tree bear, and treatments of seeds before sowing (Section 4.3). Varāhamihira’s chapter is the model on which several later texts drew, directly or indirectly. For the Bṛhatsaṃhitā more generally, and for its rain-forecasting chapters, see Chapter 3; for chapter 54 on finding groundwater, see Chapter 8.

docs.title: 4.1.2 The Agni Purāṇa and other Purāṇas
docs.text: The Agni Purāṇa, an encyclopaedic Purāṇa of uncertain and composite date, contains a short chapter on the care of trees. Much of it parallels the Bṛhatsaṃhitā. Chapter numbers differ between editions and are not given here. Several Purāṇas also praise the planting of trees as a meritorious act and prescribe rites for consecrating new gardens and trees. A widely quoted verse of the Matsya Purāṇa (chapter 154 in the usual numbering, within the story of Pārvatī and Śiva), spoken by the goddess Pārvatī when she adopts an aśoka sapling as her son, ranks a single tree as the equal of ten sons. Such passages tell us more about the religious value placed on tree-planting than about techniques. They help explain why wealthy patrons founded gardens and groves, and why treatises on their care were written (see also Chapter 11).

docs.title: 4.1.3 Planting as merit and as policy
docs.text:
The planting of useful trees was also an act of public policy long before any surviving treatise: Aśoka’s second Rock Edict and seventh Pillar Edict record the planting of medicinal herbs, roadside banyans and mango groves (Chapter 11). Later kings, queens, merchants and temple authorities continued the practice, and inscriptions of many periods record the gift of gardens, groves and roadside trees together with tanks and wells. The vṛkṣāyurveda texts served people who undertook such works. Their praise of tree-planting as a source of religious merit, which can seem conventional, reflects a real social institution.

Folk practice carried the same values in other forms. In many parts of India a pīpal (aśvattha, Ficus religiosa) and a neem (Azadirachta indica) are planted side by side and their union is celebrated as a “marriage” of the two trees. The tulasī plant is ceremonially married to Viṣṇu in the annual tulasī-vivāha. Such customs express the idea that trees are persons with kinship and life-cycles of their own.

docs.title: 4.1.4 Surapāla’s Vṛkṣāyurveda
docs.text:
The only surviving independent treatise of any length is the Vṛkṣāyurveda of Surapāla, edited and translated by Nalini Sadhale as the first of the Agri-History Bulletins of the Asian Agri-History Foundation (Sadhale 1996). Surapāla describes himself as a physician (vaidya) in the service of a king named Bhīmapāla. This king has not been securely identified, and the text is usually dated, with some uncertainty, to the tenth or eleventh century CE. A Pāla connection in eastern India has been suggested but is not proven. The text is a verse work of a few hundred stanzas. Its standpoint is a physician’s. It covers the praise of trees and the merit of planting them, the choice of land, the classification of plants, seeds and their treatment, planting, watering, nourishment, the protection of plants from external harm, the diagnosis and cure of their diseases, a series of “marvels”, and the layout of gardens.

Two features make Surapāla’s text especially important. First, it shows how thoroughly the categories of human medicine were carried over to plants, as discussed below. Second, it contains the classic account of kuṇapajala (Section 4.3.6). What it does not contain is listed in Section 1.5; for its contents the reader should rely on Sadhale’s translation.

docs.title: 4.1.5 The Lokopakāra and the Mānasollāsa
docs.text: Two encyclopaedic works of the eleventh and twelfth centuries, described in Section 3.8, include plant-care sections in the vṛkṣāyurveda manner. The Kannada Lokopakāra of Cāvuṇḍarāya (c. 1025 CE) gives one of its chapters to the care of trees and garden plants, which its English translation makes accessible (Ayangarya 2006). The chapter follows the order already familiar from Varāhamihira: the choice and preparation of the ground, the trees auspicious near a house, the treatment of seeds and cuttings, planting, watering by season, nourishing applications of dung, oil-cake, milk and similar substances, the protection of trees against insects and disease by pastes and fumigation, and procedures for making trees flower or fruit out of season or bear fruit of unusual size, colour or taste. Much of this is shared with Surapāla, and it is not known whether either author drew on the other or both on a common source. The Lokopakāra is the earliest surviving treatment of the subject in a Dravidian language, and it carries the knowledge of the Sanskrit garden texts to readers who did not read Sanskrit. Its terms for plants and operations are partly Kannada, which makes it a valuable witness to the vocabulary of gardeners in the Deccan. The Mānasollāsa of Someśvara III (1131 CE) treats the laying out and tending of a garden among the king’s enjoyments (Shrigondekar 1925).

docs.title: 4.1.6 The Upavanavinoda
docs.text: The Upavanavinoda, “Delight of the garden”, is a section on arbori-horticulture in the Śārṅgadharapaddhati, an anthology of Sanskrit verse on many subjects compiled by Śārṅgadhara in 1363 CE. This Śārṅgadhara is not the author of the medical Śārṅgadhara-saṃhitā. G. P. Majumdar edited and translated the section in 1935, with notes on the plants named (Majumdar 1935). The Upavanavinoda covers much the same ground as Surapāla, from the praise of trees and the choice of soil to planting, watering, nourishment, diseases and marvels. The two texts share a good deal of material, including a description of kuṇapajala. As an anthology section, it gathers older verses rather than presenting the views of a single author.

docs.title: 4.1.7 The Viśvavallabha
docs.text: The Viśvavallabha of Cakrapāṇi Miśra, composed in Mewar in the later sixteenth century, is a late compilation; its author is associated with the court of Mahārāṇā Pratāp, and Nalini Sadhale has translated it (Sadhale 2004). It is a short verse work in a sequence of chapters that moves from water to plants. It begins, as Varāhamihira’s dakārgala does, with the signs of underground water — trees, termite mounds, soils and stones — and with the digging of wells and tanks (Section 8.10). It then turns to the garden: the kinds of land, the choice of trees for particular places, the treatment of seeds before sowing, planting and the spacing of trees, watering, manures and nourishing liquids, the protection of plants from pests and disease, and a closing set of marvels like those of Surapāla.
