docs.title: 6.7.2 Buddhist monastic rules
docs.text: Early Buddhism did not regard plants as sentient beings within the round of rebirth. Its monastic rules nevertheless protect them. The Pāli Vinaya prescribes a penance for a monk who destroys vegetation (bhūtagāma); according to the story attached to the rule, it was introduced after lay people complained that monks who cut trees were harming “one-faculty life”, reflecting a widespread belief that trees are alive. The explanation attached to the rule lists five kinds of propagule (bījagāma) — plants propagated from roots, from stems, from joints, from cuttings, and from seeds — a classification by mode of propagation that would have been familiar to any gardener. Schmithausen (1991) has argued that early Buddhist texts reflect an older Indian view in which plants were regarded as at least borderline sentient, and that Buddhist doctrine gradually defined them out of the class of beings that can be reborn while monastic practice continued to treat them with restraint.

docs.title: 6.7.3 Tamil grammar
docs.text: The Tamil grammar Tolkāppiyam, in its chapter on usage (Marapiyal), classifies beings by the number of their senses, from one to six, the sixth being the mind, which humans possess. Grasses (pul) and trees (maram) are placed among the one-sensed beings, having touch alone. The same chapter, as usually interpreted, distinguishes pul from maram according to whether the hard part of the stem is on the outside or the inside, so that palms, whose stems lack an inner core of heartwood, are grouped with the grasses rather than with the trees. The scheme is independent in its language and categories, though it shares the sense-based principle with Jain thought; its relationship to Jain and Sanskrit sources is a matter of scholarly debate.

docs.title: 6.8 Folk and Tribal Classifications
docs.text:
Most of India’s plant knowledge has never been written in Sanskrit. Every Indian language has its own everyday categories of plant life: in Hindi, for example, peṛ (tree), jhāṛī (bush), bel (creeper) and ghās (grass); in Tamil, maram (tree), ceṭi (small plant or shrub), koṭi (creeper) and pul (grass). These life-form terms, together with a large number of names for individual kinds of plant, correspond closely to what ethnobiologists working across the world have described as the typical structure of folk classifications: a small number of broad life-form categories, a large number of “generic” names for the kinds that matter locally, and finer distinctions for the most important ones, such as crop varieties (Berlin 1992). The finest distinctions are usually drawn where livelihoods depend on them — among rice landraces, cultivated millets, fodder grasses, or the trees that yield fruit, timber and leaf fodder (Chapter 9).

Adivasi and other forest-dwelling communities hold detailed knowledge of wild plants for food, medicine, fibre, dyes, poisons and ritual. Jain (1991), compiled from decades of ethnobotanical fieldwork by S. K. Jain and his colleagues, records a vast number of such vernacular names and uses across India. Two cautions apply. First, such compilations record names and uses, not the full classificatory systems of the communities concerned, which have been studied in depth for only a few groups. Second, sweeping generalisations about the “classification system” of a whole community should be treated with caution unless they rest on published fieldwork. Tribal knowledge of plants, sacred groves and land is treated on its own terms in Volume 23, Jana–Jāti, and sacred groves in Chapter 11.

docs.title: 6.9 Indian Plant Knowledge and European Botany
docs.text: From the sixteenth century European physicians, merchants and administrators in India depended on Indian informants to learn the names and uses of plants. The Portuguese physician Garcia da Orta’s Colóquios dos simples e drogas da Índia (Goa, 1563), a dialogue on the drugs of India, drew openly on conversations with Indian and other Asian physicians and traders.

docs.title: 6.9.1 Hortus Malabaricus
docs.text:
The most important single work of this encounter is Hortus Indicus Malabaricus, published in twelve volumes at Amsterdam between 1678 and 1693 under the direction of Hendrik Adriaan van Rheede tot Drakenstein, the Dutch East India Company’s commander in Malabar. It describes and illustrates, with large copperplate engravings, the plants of the Malabar coast, mostly with their uses. Its content rested on Indian knowledge. The principal informant was the Ezhava physician Itty Achuden of the Kollatt family, whose testimony in Malayalam is printed in the first volume, and three Konkani brahmin physicians, Ranga Bhat, Vinayaka Pandit and Appu Bhat, who drew on palm-leaf manuscripts; the Carmelite missionary Matthaeus of St Joseph and Dutch and other European scholars took part in the work of description and editing. Plant names are given in Latin and in Indian languages, including Malayalam in its own script (Manilal 1980).

Grove (1995) has argued that the arrangement and descriptions of Hortus Malabaricus owe much to the Ezhava physicians’ own ways of grouping plants, so that a south Indian folk-medical classification passed, through the book, into European botany. Whatever weight one gives to that argument, the book’s influence is not in doubt: Linnaeus and his successors used it as a primary source on tropical Asian plants, and a number of Malayalam plant names survive, latinised, in modern scientific names. The work stands as an example of how “European” botany of the period was built on Asian expertise that was often unacknowledged in later accounts.

docs.title: 6.9.2 The colonial botanists
docs.text:
In the late eighteenth century the East India Company established the botanic garden at Calcutta (1787). William Roxburgh (1751–1815), its superintendent from 1793, worked first in the Northern Circars and then at Calcutta; his Plants of the Coast of Coromandel and his posthumously published Flora Indica were built on years of observation, on drawings by Indian artists whom he employed, and on the vernacular names supplied by local informants. William Jones, the Orientalist, urged botanists to retain Sanskrit plant names where they could. Whitelaw Ainslie’s Materia Indica (1826) recorded drugs with their names in several Indian languages. J. D. Hooker’s Flora of British India (1872–1897) provided the first comprehensive Linnaean flora of the subcontinent (Arnold 2000).

By the end of the century the Linnaean system had become the official language of plant knowledge in India. George Watt’s Dictionary of the Economic Products of India (1889–1893) organised a vast amount of information about useful plants by Latin binomial, but recorded under each entry the vernacular names, uses and trade data gathered from district officers and local informants across the country (Watt 1889). K. R. Kirtikar and B. D. Basu’s Indian Medicinal Plants did the same for medicinal plants, giving Sanskrit and vernacular names for each species (Kirtikar and Basu 1935). These works made Indian names searchable through Latin binomials, and they remain indispensable for anyone trying to identify a plant named in a Sanskrit or vernacular source. They also fixed particular identifications, sometimes on slender evidence, which later writers have repeated as if they were certain; the modern identification of a Sanskrit plant name is often only as good as the colonial dictionary on which it ultimately rests.

docs.title: 6.10 Indian Schemes and Linnaean Taxonomy
docs.text:
Carl Linnaeus’s Species Plantarum (1753) established the consistent use of two-word names (genus and species) and arranged plants in an explicitly “artificial” system based on the number and arrangement of stamens and pistils. Before Linnaeus, European botanists had used descriptive Latin phrase-names, often several words long, which functioned in much the same way as descriptive Sanskrit synonyms: a name was also a short description. Within a few decades the “natural” systems of Antoine-Laurent de Jussieu (1789) and Augustin Pyramus de Candolle grouped plants by overall similarity in many characters; after Darwin, classification was reinterpreted as a record of descent; and present-day systems, such as that of the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group, are based largely on molecular evidence of evolutionary relationship.

Set against this history, the Indian schemes look less like rivals and more like answers to different questions. The life-form classes of Manu, Caraka and Suśruta are comparable to the broad life-form categories found in folk classifications everywhere and to the trees, shrubs and herbs of ancient Greek botany: they sort plants by habit and life history, not by relationship. The physicians’ groupings by action and by taste, like the nighaṇṭu chapters, are deliberately functional and bring unrelated plants together. The Jain, Buddhist and Tamil schemes classify plants among living beings for moral and philosophical purposes. None of them aimed at a single, universal, hierarchical system of names, and none needed one, because knowledge was transmitted within communities of practitioners who could show each other the plants.

The Linnaean system’s strength is precisely that it is detachable from use and locality: a binomial name refers to the same species in Kerala, Kashmir and Uppsala. That strength was a product of European science’s particular needs — to catalogue plants arriving from all over the world in herbaria far from where they grew — and of colonial and commercial networks. Indian names, by contrast, carry information about use, property and local recognition that a binomial does not. The two are complementary tools, and the practical task today, in pharmacognosy, ethnobotany and the documentation of traditional knowledge (Chapter 20), is to connect them reliably: to establish, plant by plant and region by region, which species a given Sanskrit or vernacular name actually refers to.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Indian traditions classified plants for many purposes. The Vedic hymns supplied a basic vocabulary (oṣadhi, vanaspati, vīrudh, vṛkṣa) and the Upaniṣads the idea of plants as “sprout-born” living beings. Manu and the physicians Caraka and Suśruta defined a small set of life-form classes based on visible flowering, fruiting and habit, but the physicians’ working categories were the part used and the plant’s action and taste. The nighaṇṭus collected descriptive synonyms whose richness created lasting problems of identity. Jain, Buddhist and Tamil thinkers placed plants in classifications of living beings by their senses, with real consequences for diet, monastic life and attitudes to farming. Folk and tribal classifications, still only partly documented, follow the life-form and generic structure found across the world. In the colonial period Indian knowledge, transmitted through informants such as Itty Achuden, entered European botany through Hortus Malabaricus and was later recast in Linnaean terms by Roxburgh, Watt and their successors. The Indian schemes are best understood as functional and philosophical classifications in their own right, not as precursors of Linnaeus.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Olivelle (2005) for Manu’s account of plants; Zimmermann (1987) on land, plants and medicine; Meulenbeld (1999) on the nighaṇṭu literature and its dating; Tatia (1994) and Dundas (2002) for the Jain classification of living beings; Sivarajan and Balachandran (1994) on the plant sources of Āyurvedic drugs and the “controversial drugs”; Schmithausen (1991) on plants in early Buddhism; and Manilal (1980) on Hortus Malabaricus and its Indian contributors.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Soil, Tillage and Implements
docs.text:
Farmers everywhere know their soils intimately, and Indian farmers were no exception. Yet the written record of that knowledge is thinner and more scattered than is often supposed. No surviving Sanskrit text is a treatise on soils in the way the Bṛhatsaṃhitā has chapters on rain or on finding groundwater. What we have instead is a vocabulary of land spread across Vedic hymns, grammar, lexicons, statecraft, medicine and architecture; a handful of practical instructions on manure in the agricultural texts; and a much larger body of practice—names for soils, ways of feeding and protecting them—that was recorded mainly by colonial officials, ethnographers and agronomists from the nineteenth century onwards. This chapter keeps these layers apart. It first sets out what the texts say about land, then what farmers did to keep it fertile and in place, how salinity became a large problem in the canal era, and how modern soil science classifies India’s soils. The second half of the chapter turns from the soil to the work done on it: the plough and its history, the implements used to prepare the seedbed, to sow, weed, reap, thresh and winnow, the draught animals and village artisans on whom these tools depended, the mechanisation of the twentieth century, and the division of field work by caste and gender.

The Kṛṣi-Parāśara does not classify soils at all (Chapter 3), and no Sanskrit text matches its colour words for soils with the soil orders of modern science.

docs.title: 7.1 Words for Land in Early Texts
7.1.1 Vedic vocabulary
docs.text:
The Ṛgveda already distinguishes cultivated land from the rest of the landscape. The field is kṣetra, and a whole hymn (RV 4.57) is addressed to the “Lord of the Field” (kṣetrasya pati) together with the plough, the ploughshare and the furrow (sītā) (Jamison and Brereton 2014). The word urvarā denotes arable or fertile land; winning or possessing urvarā is among the goods for which the poets pray, alongside cattle, sons and water. The earth as a whole (bhūmi, pṛthivī) is celebrated at length in the Pṛthivī Sūkta of the Atharvaveda (AV 12.1; Section 2.7), which praises the earth’s fertility, its plants and its waters; but it is a hymn, not a description of soils.

Barren and saline ground also has a name. Ūṣa is saline earth, and land impregnated with it is ūṣara. In the Brāhmaṇa accounts of setting up the sacred fires, saline earth is one of the materials ritually gathered and laid down, along with sand, gravel and the earth thrown up by moles—an indication that these different kinds of earth were recognised and named, even if the context is ritual rather than agricultural. In later Sanskrit ūṣara becomes the standard word for land on which nothing will grow, and the word survives in north Indian usage as usar (Section 7.7).

docs.title: 7.1.2 Grammar and lexicon
docs.text:
Pāṇini (c. 4th c. BCE) records a productive way of naming fields after the crops for which they are suited. His rules on secondary derivatives (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.2.1–4) form words such as vraiheya and śāleya (“a field fit for vrīhi / śāli rice”), yavya (“fit for barley”), tilya or tailīna (“fit for sesame”), māṣīṇa (“fit for black gram”) and maudgīna (“fit for green gram”). The grammar thus preserves a classification of land by use: what mattered was what a field would grow.

The Sanskrit lexicon Amarakośa (first millennium CE; its date is uncertain, though often placed around the sixth century) gathers land-words in its section on the earth. It glosses urvarā as land rich in every kind of crop, gives ūṣa as saline earth and ūṣara for land containing it, and lists terms for desert (maru, dhanvan), dry ground (sthala) and the field (kṣetra, kedāra). Like Pāṇini, it reflects the vocabulary of educated speakers rather than a farmers’ manual, but it shows that fertile, saline, desert and dry land were standard categories.

docs.title: 7.1.3 The Arthaśāstra
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra (composite, c. 50 BCE–300 CE; see Volume 18, Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra) approaches land as an administrator does. In Kangle’s and Olivelle’s translations, the village accountant (gopa) is to record the land of each village by category: cultivated and uncultivated (kṛṣṭa, akṛṣṭa), dry land and wet, embanked fields (sthala, kedāra), gardens and orchards, groves, enclosures, forest, house sites, shrines, irrigation works, cremation grounds and so on (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013). The distinction between sthala, land depending on rain, and kedāra, bunded fields that hold water (above all for rice), runs through later Indian agrarian vocabulary.

The chapter on the superintendent of agriculture (sītādhyakṣa, Book 2, chapter 24) adds a finer, practical grading of micro-sites. As Kangle renders it, land struck by river foam (the edges of a river bed) suits creeper fruits such as gourds; the margins of overflow channels suit long pepper, grapes and sugarcane; the surroundings of wells suit vegetables and root crops; the edges of moist beds suit green herbs; and the ridges between beds suit fragrant and medicinal plants. This is a classification by moisture and position in the landscape, the kind of judgement every gardener makes, and it is one of the few passages in early Sanskrit prose that matches particular crops to particular ground. The chapter does not set out a system of manures; its other contents are summarised in Section 2.11.1.

docs.title: 7.2 Land, Ecology and Medicine: Jāṅgala and Ānūpa
docs.text:
The most developed classification of land in Sanskrit comes from medicine, not agriculture. Āyurvedic texts divide country (deśa) into jāṅgala, ānūpa and sādhāraṇa. Jāṅgala land is dry and open, with sparse thorny trees, hard soil, clear skies and wind; it is considered healthy, and its animals (antelope, deer and game birds) yield the light meats the physicians prized. Ānūpa land is marshy and well watered, with dense vegetation, rivers and lakes, heavy air and the diseases of phlegm and wind. Sādhāraṇa is the balanced, intermediate type. Francis Zimmermann’s classic study showed that this is an ecological theory linking landscape, animals, food and bodily humours (Section 1.6; (Zimmermann 1987)). Caraka uses the scheme when advising where medicinal plants should be gathered and where patients fare best (Sharma 1981).

The plant-science texts borrowed the same frame. Surapāla’s Vṛkṣāyurveda (c. 10th–11th c.) describes land as ānūpa, jāṅgala and sādhāraṇa, judges ground by its colour and other qualities, and names trees suited to each kind; it also explains the ailments of trees as disorders of vāta, pitta and kapha, with treatments to match (Sadhale 1996). The Upavanavinoda of the Śārṅgadharapaddhati (1363) has a comparable section on judging ground for a garden (Majumdar 1935). These works apply Āyurvedic categories to plants and to the land they grow in; they do not classify soils themselves into vāta, pitta and kapha types. The Vṛkṣāyurveda tradition, including its fermented plant-feeds such as kuṇapajala, is treated in Chapter 4.

Classifying land by what it does

Across the early sources land is classified by use and by water: what it will grow (Pāṇini’s crop-fields), whether it holds water (sthala and kedāra), where it lies in relation to a river or well (the Arthaśāstra), whether it is saline (ūṣara), and whether the country as a whole is dry or marshy (jāṅgala, ānūpa). This is closer to a modern “land capability” assessment than to a soil taxonomy, and it is better described in those terms than as an anticipation of pedology.

docs.title: 7.3 Judging the Ground: Tests in Bṛhatsaṃhitā and Vāstu Texts
docs.text:
The physical tests of soil that do appear in Sanskrit belong to architecture. Varāhamihira’s chapter on building (vāstuvidyā, Bṛhatsaṃhitā 53 in Bhat’s numbering) and the later vāstu manuals tell the builder how to examine a house site (Bhat 1981). A pit is dug and then refilled with the same earth: if earth is left over, the site is excellent; if it just fills the pit, it is middling; if it falls short, the site is poor. A loose soil that cannot be packed back is thus judged inferior, a sensible test of compaction and bearing capacity for a building. A pit may also be filled with water and checked after an interval to see how much has drained away. Beyond these tests, ground is judged by colour, smell and taste, and by the plants growing on it; Varāhamihira assigns soils of different colours and tastes as suitable for the houses of the different varṇas, white for brahmins, red for kṣatriyas, yellow for vaiśyas and dark for śūdras, a reminder that these tests were embedded in a social hierarchy as well as in practical judgement.

Two cautions follow. First, these are tests of a building site, not of agricultural fertility; they should not be presented as “traditional soil testing for crops”. Second, they do not amount to a systematic analysis of agricultural soils. Farmers certainly looked at, handled and smelled their soil, and in saline tracts a salty crust or taste was an obvious warning; but these were the ordinary judgements of experience, and they are best described as such.

Varāhamihira’s separate chapter on finding underground water (dakārgala, Bṛhatsaṃhitā 54) also reads the ground, using plants, termite mounds, the colour of soil and stones as signs of water at a given depth. It is discussed in Chapter 8.

docs.title: 7.4 Farmers’ Soil Vocabularies
docs.text:
Every farming region of India has its own names for soils, usually based on texture, colour, moisture behaviour and the crops they carry, and many of these entered English through revenue settlements and district gazetteers. A few are especially well established.

  • In the Ganga–Yamuna Doab and much of north India, cultivators distinguish matiyār (stiff clay), dumaṭ or domaṭ (loam) and bhūr (light sand), terms that colonial settlement officers adopted for assessing revenue.

  • In Bundelkhand, the heavy black soils are mār and kābar, the lighter brown soils paṛuā, and the thin, stony upland soils rākaṛ.

  • The black cotton soils of the Deccan were known to British observers as regur, a word taken from Telugu (regaḍa); in Tamil Nadu the black-soil country of the south is called karisal.

  • In Tamil literature the agricultural lowland of paddy fields is the marutam landscape, one of the five tiṇai of Saṅgam poetry (Chapter 2).

Such vocabularies are local and practical. A word like mār carries knowledge of how the soil behaves—that it cracks when dry, holds moisture for a winter crop, and becomes unworkable when wet—which no colour term alone conveys. They do not map neatly onto Sanskrit words or onto modern soil orders, and attempts to force them into a single pan-Indian scheme lose exactly the local precision that makes them valuable.

docs.title: 7.5.1 Manure in the agricultural texts
docs.text: The Kṛṣi-Parāśara, a late text probably from Bengal, is the clearest early Sanskrit witness to deliberate manuring. It treats cow dung as the essential fertiliser: dung is to be accumulated in a pit or heap through the cold season, dried and broken up, and carried to the field to be laid down in small heaps before sowing, with the text insisting that crops without manure do not prosper (Majumdar and Banerji 1960; Sadhale 1999). This fits its wider concern with the cattle shed and the welfare of cattle, which are the source of both draught power and manure (Chapter 3). The Vṛkṣāyurveda texts go further in prescribing special preparations for trees and gardens, including the fermented kuṇapajala; those recipes belong to horticulture and are treated in Chapter 4.

docs.title: 7.5.2 Manuring in practice
docs.text:
For the field crops of ordinary farmers the evidence comes mainly from the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, when officials and agronomists described what they saw. The most important single witness is the agricultural chemist John Augustus Voelcker, consulting chemist to the Royal Agricultural Society of England, whom the Secretary of State sent to India in 1889 to advise on the application of agricultural chemistry. He toured the provinces until 1891, and his Report on the Improvement of Indian Agriculture (1893) is the most careful contemporary assessment of Indian farming practice (Voelcker 1893). Voelcker concluded that Indian cultivators managed their land with considerable skill; that their mixed cropping, rotations and weeding were in many respects as good as British practice; that their implements were in general suited to their soils, cattle and means; and that the main obstacles to higher yields were not ignorance but shortages of water, manure, fuel and credit. The shortage of manure he traced above all to the burning of cattle dung as fuel for want of firewood. He also urged the government to employ trained scientists, a recommendation that bore fruit in the research institutions described in Section 19.4. Later chapters refer back to this account. The practices he and others recorded include the following.

Farmyard manure. Dung, urine-soaked litter and household sweepings were collected in pits and carried to the fields, often by women, who also made the dung cakes that competed with the fields for the same material. The best-manured land was usually the land closest to the village. Folding livestock. In the Deccan and the south, herders of sheep and goats were paid in grain or cash to pen their flocks overnight on a farmer’s field before sowing, so that the dung and urine were deposited directly on the soil. Such arrangements linked settled cultivators and mobile pastoralists in a long-standing exchange (Chapter 13). Tank silt. Where tanks were common, the silt that accumulated on the tank bed was dug out in the dry season and carted to the fields, at once restoring the tank’s storage and returning fine soil and organic matter to the land (Chapter 8). Green manure and leaf manure. Crops such as sunn hemp (Crotalaria juncea) and dhaiñcā (Sesbania species) were grown and ploughed in, especially before rice, and green leaves and twigs lopped from trees and shrubs (for example Pongamia pinnata) were trampled into puddled rice fields in the south and west. Oilcakes. The cake left after pressing oilseeds in the village oil mill (Chapter 14) was used as cattle feed and as manure for valuable crops such as sugarcane and tobacco; neem cake was valued as well for its insect-deterring properties (Schmutterer 1995). Ash and burning. Ash from household fires and burnt crop residues was spread on fields. In the Konkan and along the Western Ghats, the rāb method of preparing rice nurseries involved burning layers of branches, leaves, dung and grass on the seedbed before sowing. Legumes, rotation and fallow. Pulses were grown in rotation or as mixed crops with cereals, and land was rested when it could be spared. Farmers valued pulses because cereals did well after them; the biological explanation, nitrogen fixation by root-nodule bacteria, is a nineteenth-century discovery and should not be read back into the practice. Rotations and mixed cropping are discussed in Chapter 9.

Albert Howard drew on these practices of collecting and rotting wastes when he developed the “Indore process” of composting, a well-documented instance of Indian farm practice shaping a modern method (Section 10.7).

Debate: Sustainable by design?

It is tempting to describe these practices as a balanced system that kept Indian soils fertile for millennia. The reality was more uneven. Manure was scarce and unequally distributed; the fields of landholders near the village received it, while distant and poorer fields often did not. Many soils were farmed at low yields precisely because nutrients were not replaced, and the burning of dung for fuel was a response to a shortage of wood that had its own ecological history (Chapter 11). The practices recorded here are best understood as ingenious responses to constraints, not as a finished science; their value for today’s agriculture has to be tested, not assumed (Chapter 10).

docs.title: 7.6 Holding Soil and Water in Place
docs.text:
On the plains the commonest conservation structure was the earthen field bund. Bunds hold rainwater on the field long enough to soak in, keep rice fields flooded, and stop topsoil washing away in heavy monsoon storms. In the black-soil country of the Deccan, bunds and small embankments across gentle slopes conserved the moisture on which the post-monsoon crop depended. In the Thar the khadin, an earthen embankment built across a slope to pond runoff, turns the silt and moisture left behind into a cultivable field (Chapter 8).

In the hills the characteristic solution is the terrace. Bench terraces with earth or dry-stone risers are cut into slopes throughout the Himalaya, from Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand to Sikkim, and along parts of the Western Ghats. In the North-East, the Angami Nagas build irrigated rice terraces on steep hillsides, and the Apatani of the Ziro valley in Arunachal Pradesh farm a levelled, bunded and canal-fed valley floor in which rice is grown together with fish. The zabo system of the Chakhesang Nagas links protected forest above, water-harvesting ponds and cattle yards with rice fields below, so that runoff carries manure down to the crops (Agarwal and Narain 1997). These are the work of communities whose knowledge is discussed further in Volume 23, Jana–Jāti.

Shifting cultivation (jhūm in the North-East, with many local names elsewhere) handles fertility in a different way: forest is cleared and burned, cropped for one or two years, and then left to regrow for a long fallow during which the soil recovers. Where fallows are long it can be a stable system; where population pressure or land loss shortens them, soils degrade. Colonial and post-colonial states often condemned it wholesale. It is treated in Chapter 10.

docs.title: 7.7 Saline and Alkaline Land: Ūṣara, Usar and Reh
docs.text:
Saline and alkaline soils occur naturally in the semi-arid parts of north and west India, where evaporation draws dissolved salts to the surface and leaves a white or grey crust. Villagers in the Ganga plain call such land usar (from Sanskrit ūṣara) and the salt efflorescence reh. Some communities made use of it: saline earth was a source of salt and saltpetre, and specialised castes such as the Nonias of north India worked it. For cultivation, however, usar was largely written off, used at most for grazing.

The problem became much larger in the nineteenth century. The great canals of the Doab and Punjab (Chapter 8) delivered water without adequate drainage; in many tracts the water table rose, land became waterlogged, and reh spread over fields that had previously been cultivated. Colonial officials recognised the problem by the 1870s, and historians of the canal regime have treated waterlogging and salinisation as among its most serious ecological costs (Kumar 1983; Ludden 1999). Farmers’ remedies—flushing salts with water where drainage allowed, adding manure, growing tolerant crops—were limited, and large-scale reclamation of sodic soils with gypsum and drainage is a twentieth-century development. Salinity in irrigated land remains a major problem in north-western India today.

docs.title: 7.8 Modern Soil Science and the Indian Soil Groups
docs.text:
Scientific soil survey in India began under colonial rule and was developed after independence by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research and its soil survey institutions. The broad grouping now taught in Indian schools and used in general surveys is summarised in Table 7.1. Internationally, these soils are also described in the categories of the United States Department of Agriculture’s Soil Taxonomy (for example, many black soils as Vertisols), but the correspondence between the two systems is approximate.

Table 7.1. The major soil groups of India in the standard modern classification (simplified). Group Main occurrence and origin Characteristic properties and uses Alluvial Indo-Gangetic and Brahmaputra plains, coastal plains and deltas; river-deposited sediments Generally fertile, from sandy to clayey; the basis of the rice and wheat agriculture of the plains Black (regur) Deccan plateau of Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and adjoining areas; mainly weathered basalt Clay-rich, swelling when wet and cracking deeply when dry; retain moisture; cotton, sorghum, pulses and post-monsoon crops Red and yellow Much of peninsular and eastern India; weathered crystalline rocks Usually light-textured and low in nutrients; millets, pulses, groundnut, and rice where irrigated Laterite High-rainfall uplands: Western Ghats, Odisha, parts of the North-East Strongly leached, rich in iron and aluminium; plantation crops such as cashew, tea, coffee and rubber, with manuring Arid (desert) Rajasthan and adjoining dry regions Sandy, low in organic matter; productive where water is available Saline and alkaline Patches in dry regions, poorly drained irrigated land and coasts Salt crusts and sodic conditions; require drainage and reclamation Peaty and marshy Waterlogged coastal tracts, e.g. Kuttanad in Kerala and parts of the Sundarbans High in organic matter, often acidic Forest and mountain Himalaya and other hill ranges Thin and variable, depending on slope and vegetation

This grouping is a modern scientific construction based on parent material, climate and laboratory analysis. It is useful to know it, both because it describes the ground on which Indian agriculture actually takes place and because it shows how the old local vocabularies relate to the landscape: regur, karisal, mār and kābar all name variants of the black soils, while bhūr and dumaṭ describe textures within the alluvium. But there is no basis for equating particular Sanskrit colour words with particular modern soil orders, and no evidence that the Sanskrit texts possessed a soil taxonomy comparable to this one.

docs.title: 7.9 The Plough
docs.text:
Cross-Reference: Field work elsewhere in this volume

The Kalibangan field and the Vedic hymns to the plough are discussed in Chapter 2; the plough passage and the farming rites of the Kṛṣi-Parāśara in Chapter 3; water-lifting devices in Chapter 8; seeds and mixed cropping in Chapter 9; draught breeds in Chapter 13; and husking, grinding and grain storage in Chapter 14. The sections that follow concentrate on the implements and the work done with them.

docs.title: 7.9.1 The Indian ard
docs.text:
Until well into the twentieth century almost all ploughing in India was done with an ard: a plough that cuts a furrow and stirs the soil but, having no mouldboard, does not turn it over. The common form was made by the village carpenter, almost entirely of wood. A pointed body carried the share at its tip; a single handle rose from it for the ploughman to grip and to press the point into the ground; and a long pole ran forward from the body to the yoke (Figure 7.1a). The share, a pointed iron bar or small iron blade fixed to the point of the body, was the one part that had to be renewed regularly by the smith. The yoke lay across the necks of a pair of bullocks, in front of the zebu’s hump, against which the animals pushed. In many wet-rice tracts and on heavy soils buffaloes replaced bullocks, and in western Rajasthan a plough was often drawn by a single camel. The whole implement was cheap, could be made and mended in the village, and was light enough to carry on the shoulder to a distant field.

Figure 7.1. Two Indian field implements, schematic and not to scale. (a) The wooden ard: the body, tipped with an iron share, runs in the soil; the handle rises from it, and the pole joins it to a yoke carried on the necks of a pair of bullocks (Section 7.9 and Table 7.2). (b) The multi-tube seed drill of the Deccan: tines on a bullock-drawn frame open the rows, and seed dropped into the bowl runs down bamboo tubes into them (Section 7.11).

Because the ard does not invert the soil, a field was ploughed several times, often in different directions, until the clods were broken and the surface reduced to a fine tilth; criss-cross ploughing of this kind is what the Early Harappan field at Kalibangan preserves. How often a field was ploughed depended on the crop, the soil and the farmer’s means. Land for wheat or sugarcane was usually worked more thoroughly than land for rain-fed millets, and the farmer who could plough often, and at the right moment, was the farmer who owned his own bullocks. In the rice country of the east and south the plough was also driven through standing water to churn the field into soft mud before transplanting. This puddling buries weeds, levels the field and reduces the loss of water through the soil.

Ploughs differed from region to region in weight, length of pole and shape of body and share, according to the soil and the animals available: light ploughs for the small cattle of the eastern rice country and for narrow hill terraces, and, on the black soils of the Deccan, where the ordinary plough was used sparingly (Section 7.10), occasionally a heavy plough drawn by several pairs to break the ground deeply and root out persistent weeds. In shifting cultivation the burnt clearing was sown with a digging stick and worked with the hoe, and the plough had no part (Chapter 10). Table 7.2 lists some common field implements with representative regional names.

Table 7.2. Some common implements of Indian field work, with representative names. Names vary greatly from region to region; those given are examples, not a complete list. Implement Representative names Use Plough Sanskrit lāṅgala, sīra, hala; Hindi hal; Tamil ēr, kalappai Cuts furrows and stirs the soil without turning it over Ploughshare Sanskrit phāla; Hindi phāl Iron point or blade fixed to the wooden body Yoke Sanskrit yuga; Hindi juā Joins the pair of draught animals and carries the pole Plough-pole Sanskrit īṣā Joins the body of the plough to the yoke Levelling plank Hindi pāṭā, Punjabi suhāgā; Bengali mai Breaks clods, levels and firms the surface, covers broadcast seed Blade harrow Marathi and Hindi bakhar; Telugu guntaka Shallow working of black soils; cutting weeds; loosening the surface Spade, mattock Sanskrit kuddāla; Hindi kudāl, phāvṛā; Tamil maṇveṭṭi Digging, earthwork, bunds and channels Hand hoe Hindi khurpā, khurpī Weeding and loosening soil around plants Sickle Sanskrit dātra, lavitra; Hindi hãsiyā, darāntī Reaping Threshing floor Sanskrit khala; Hindi khalihān; Tamil kaḷam Hard, dung-plastered floor on which the crop is threshed Winnowing basket Sanskrit śūrpa; Hindi sūp; Tamil muṟam Separating grain from chaff and dust Cart Sanskrit anas (Vedic), śakaṭa; Hindi gāṛī; Tamil vaṇṭi Carrying manure, silt, harvest and goods

docs.title: 7.9.2 Archaeological evidence
docs.text:
The ploughed field at Kalibangan and the terracotta plough model from Banawali (Section 2.4) show that the ard was in use in the north-west by the third millennium BCE. No metal ploughshare is known from Harappan sites, and the working point of the Harappan plough was presumably of hard wood. The cutting tools of the earliest farmers were blades of flint and chert; at Neolithic Mehrgarh the excavators reported a sickle made of such blades set with bitumen in a wooden haft. Harappan metal tools of copper and bronze include axes, chisels and knives (Kenoyer 1998).

Iron changed the farmer’s equipment, though more slowly than was once believed. Iron sickles, hoes and axes are found at sites of the first millennium BCE in the Ganga plain and in the megalithic burials of the Deccan and the south. Iron ploughshares are rarer in the early levels, and when they became common is debated (Chapter 2) (Allchin and Allchin 1982; Singh 2008). For the medieval centuries the sources say little about field implements; the technical changes that historians of the period emphasise, such as the spread of the geared water-wheel, lie in water-lifting and in crops rather than in tillage (Chapter 8) (Habib 2008).

docs.title: 7.9.3 Words for the plough
docs.text:
The Ṛgveda has two words for the plough, sīra and lāṅgala, together with the share (phāla), the yoke (yuga), the pole (īṣā), the goad (aṣṭrā), the furrow (sītā) and the ploughman (kīnāśa) (Jamison and Brereton 2014). Lāṅgala has often been regarded as a loanword into Vedic from a non-Indo-European language of the subcontinent; an Austroasiatic origin was proposed by Jean Przyluski, but the question remains open. In later Sanskrit hala becomes the ordinary word, and the plough becomes the emblem of Balarāma, Kṛṣṇa’s elder brother, called Haladhara and Halāyudha, “plough-bearer” and “he whose weapon is the plough”. In parts of north India women keep a day associated with him, Hal Ṣaṣṭhī (Hal Chhaṭh), on which custom requires them to avoid food grown on ploughed land.

The parts of the plough were familiar enough to serve as a metaphor: the Buddha’s spiritual plough in the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta (Chapter 2) names the yoke and plough (yuganaṅgala), the pole (īsā), the binding strap (yotta), and the share and goad (phāla, pācana) (Sutta Nipāta 1.4, v. 77). The Amarakośa, in its section on the vaiśya, gives lāṅgala, hala, godāraṇa (“that which tears the earth”) and sīra as synonyms for the plough, explains īṣā as the shaft of the plough and sītā as the track it leaves, and gives dātra and lavitra for the sickle. In Tamil the plough is ēr, and the ploughing praised in the Tirukkuṟaḷ’s chapter Uḻavu is the work of the uḻavar, the ploughmen of the marutam landscape.

The administrative texts treat implements as stores to be managed, as in the Arthaśāstra’s rules for the crown farms (Section 2.11.1). The Kṛṣi-Parāśara, centuries later, names the parts of the plough and gives their dimensions; its passage is discussed in Chapter 3.

docs.title: 7.10 Preparing the Seedbed: Planks, Harrows and Hoes
docs.text:
After the plough, or in place of it, came lighter operations to break clods, level the field, kill weeds and conserve moisture. The most widespread implement for this was the levelling plank, a heavy beam of wood (Hindi pāṭā, Punjabi suhāgā) dragged across the field by a pair of bullocks while the driver stood on it to add his weight. The plank crushes clods, smooths the surface and presses it firm, which slows the drying of the soil beneath; drawn over a field after broadcast sowing, it also covers the seed. In Bengal a ladder-like frame, the mai, served the same purpose, and in puddled rice fields plank or ladder levelled the mud so that water would stand evenly.

On the black soils of the Deccan, Malwa and Gujarat the characteristic implement was not the plough but the blade harrow, called bakhar in Marathi and Hindi and guntaka in Telugu: a horizontal iron blade fixed between two wooden legs and drawn by bullocks so that it slides just below the surface, cutting the roots of weeds and loosening the top layer without bringing up moist soil from below. Black soils swell when wet and crack deeply as they dry, and so partly till themselves; what the farmer needed was to break the crust, control weeds and prepare a shallow seedbed. In many black-soil districts the blade harrow was therefore worked over the field repeatedly each season, while deep ploughing was done only at intervals of some years. Narrower versions of the same blade were used to weed between the rows of growing crops (Section 7.12).

Hand tools did the work that animals could not. The spade or mattock (Sanskrit kuddāla; Hindi kudāl and phāvṛā; Tamil maṇveṭṭi, the “mamoty” of Anglo-Indian usage) built and repaired bunds, cut channels, dug manure pits and lifted silt from tank beds (Section 7.5), and it was the main tillage tool on plots too small, steep or stony for a team. The small hand hoe, the khurpā or khurpī, was the most widely used implement of all for weeding and for loosening soil around plants.

docs.title: 7.11 Sowing
docs.text:
The simplest method of sowing was broadcasting: scattering seed by hand over the prepared field and covering it with the plank. Small millets, many pulses and much rice in the east were sown in this way, as are the relay crops sown into standing rice before its harvest (Chapter 9). Seed could also be dropped by hand into the furrow behind the plough, so that the next furrow covered it, or fed through a bamboo tube tied to the plough, which delivered it to the moist bottom of the furrow; in the Punjab the two methods are called kerā and porā. Placing seed deep mattered most for crops sown on stored moisture after the rains, when the surface had already dried.

The fullest development of this idea was the multi-tube seed drill of the Deccan and other parts of south and west India (Figure 7.1b). A wooden frame carries several tines, each with a hollow bamboo tube behind it; the tubes join at the top in a wooden bowl, into which the sower, walking behind, drops seed by hand, so that it runs down into the rows opened by the tines. A pair of bullocks draws the drill. Often a second, single-tube drill followed to sow a different crop in some of the rows, which is how the alternate-row mixtures of the Deccan, such as sorghum with pigeon pea, were laid out (Chapter 9). Row sowing saves seed, places it at an even depth, and leaves lines between which the crop can be weeded with a bullock hoe. The drill has many regional names and forms.

European observers in the late eighteenth century wrote admiring accounts of these drills, several of which were collected by Dharampal (1971). It is sometimes claimed that the Indian drill was the model for the seed drill of the English agriculturist Jethro Tull (1701). There is no good evidence of such a transmission, and seed drills were invented more than once: a seeding plough with a funnel and tube appears on Mesopotamian seals, and multi-tube drills were used in China from the Han period. The Indian drill is best appreciated in its own right, as an implement well suited to the dry farming of the black-soil country.

In dibbling, a hole is made with a pointed stick and a few seeds are dropped in and covered. It is slow but economical of seed, suits ground that cannot be ploughed, and is the main method of sowing in shifting cultivation. Transplanting, finally, was the defining operation of wet-rice farming. Seed was sown thickly in a nursery bed; after some weeks the seedlings were pulled, tied in bundles, carried to the puddled field and pressed by hand, a few at a time, into the mud. The Kṛṣi-Parāśara describes this sequence (Chapter 3). Finger millet was also transplanted in parts of the south, as were tobacco, chillies and many vegetables. Transplanting needs much labour in a short time, and in most of India it has been done largely by women (Section 7.16).

docs.title: 7.12 Weeding and Interculture
docs.text:
The Tirukkuṟaḷ names weeding, with manuring and guarding the crop, among the farmer’s essential tasks, and the Kṛṣi-Parāśara insists on timely weeding (Chapters 2 and 3). In practice most weeding was done by hand. Workers squatted in the field and worked through it with the khurpī, cutting weeds below the surface and loosening the soil; in rice fields weeds were pulled and pressed back into the mud to rot. This slow, back-breaking work was done mostly by women and hired labourers, and in many regions it was one of the main sources of wage work for women from landless households.

Where crops were sown in lines, bullocks could do part of the work. Light bullock hoes, essentially narrow blade harrows set to pass between the rows, were drawn through the standing crop to cut weeds and loosen the surface. This interculture was one of the main advantages of drill sowing, and the drill, the blade harrow and the bullock hoe together made up a coherent system of dry farming.

Broadcast rice in parts of eastern and central India was treated in a striking way. When the crop was some weeks old and the field held water, it was ploughed across with the ordinary plough and then levelled. This operation, called biāsī in Chhattisgarh and neighbouring regions (“beushening” in older English writing), uproots weeds and thins and redistributes the rice plants, which recover in the soft mud; it substitutes for transplanting where labour or water is too scarce for a nursery.

docs.title: 7.13.1 Reaping
docs.text: Grain crops were reaped with the sickle, a curved iron blade on a short wooden handle, its edge often finely toothed, used by a reaper who squats or bends low and grasps a handful of stalks before cutting. Cereals were generally cut low, because straw was valuable as fodder, thatch and fuel; pulses and some other crops were pulled up by hand. The crop was tied in sheaves, dried in the field and carried to the threshing floor by head-load or cart. Households without enough labour of their own hired reapers, who in much of India were paid in kind with a share of the sheaves they cut, and in many villages the poor were allowed to glean the fields afterwards. In the twentieth century the wheat and rice harvests of Punjab and Haryana came to depend on labourers who migrated seasonally from eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.

docs.title: 7.13.2 Threshing
docs.text: The threshing floor (Sanskrit khala, Hindi khalihān, Tamil kaḷam) was a patch of level ground beaten hard and plastered with cow dung and water, which dried to a smooth, clean surface. The Kṛṣi-Parāśara gives rules and rites for preparing and using it (Chapter 3). Wheat, barley, sorghum and many other grains were threshed by treading. The sheaves were spread in a circle around a stout wooden post in the middle of the floor (Sanskrit methi or medhi); a line of bullocks, tied abreast to the post, was driven round and round over the crop, while workers with forks turned the straw, until the grain had been trodden out and the straw broken. In the wheat country the broken straw, bhūsā, was itself a valued fodder. Rice was often threshed by beating handfuls of stalks against a plank, a stone or the floor, or by treading; pulses, mustard and other small seeds were beaten out with sticks.

docs.title: 7.13.3 Winnowing
docs.text: On a day with a steady breeze a worker stood on a stool or platform and poured the threshed mixture slowly from a basket held at head height, so that the heavier grain fell to the floor while the wind carried the chaff aside. The grain was then cleaned further in the winnowing basket (Sanskrit śūrpa, Hindi sūp, Tamil muṟam), a shallow basket of split bamboo or reed, open at one end, in which grain is tossed so that chaff, dust and small stones are separated from it. The śūrpa appears among the implements of the Vedic ritual (Chapter 14), and Gaṇeśa is called Śūrpakarṇa, “he whose ears are like winnowing baskets”. Husking and grinding are discussed in Chapter 14, and the storage of grain and seed in Chapters 9 and 14.

docs.title: 7.13.4 Dividing the harvest
docs.text: The threshing floor was also where the harvest was divided. Before the grain left the floor, shares were measured out to the landholder, the tenant or sharecropper, and the village artisans and servants—carpenter, smith, potter, barber, washerman and others—who were paid in grain at harvest for their services through the year (Wiser 1936). Under the Mughal revenue system one form of crop-sharing consisted precisely in dividing the heaps of grain on the threshing floor between the cultivator and the state (Habib 1999).

docs.title: 7.14 Draught Animals, Carts and Village Artisans
docs.text:
The basic unit of power on the Indian farm was the pair of bullocks. The plough, the plank, the blade harrow, the drill, the cart, the leather bucket of the well (Chapter 8) and the oil press (Chapter 14) were all built for a pair, and several of the best-known Indian cattle breeds were valued above all for draught (Chapter 13). A pair had to be fed all year, although much of its work was concentrated into a few weeks of ploughing, sowing and threshing. Holdings were commonly described in terms of ploughs, and the household with its own pair was in a different position from the one without. Smallholders who could not keep a pair joined with neighbours, borrowed or hired a team, or paid for ploughing in labour, and so often ploughed and sowed late. Landless labourers owned no draught animals at all.

The bullock cart is as old as the plough in the subcontinent: terracotta models of carts with solid wheels are common at Harappan sites (Kenoyer 1998). The Vedic ox-cart is the anas, distinct from the horse-drawn chariot (ratha); the common later word is śakaṭa. Most later carts had spoked wheels made by the carpenter and fitted with iron tyres by the smith. On the farm the cart carried manure and tank silt to the fields and the harvest to the threshing floor and market. Over long distances the grain trade depended, until the railway age, on the pack-bullock caravans of the Banjārās, which also supplied armies (Habib 1999).

The village carpenter and smith made and maintained almost the whole stock of implements. The carpenter shaped plough, yoke, plank, harrow frame, drill and cart from local wood; the smith forged and sharpened the share, the harrow blade, the sickle, the hoe and the spade, and before each season shares and sickles were brought to him to be re-pointed. In much of India these artisans were paid not for each job but with a customary share of grain from each household at harvest, an arrangement Wiser (1936) described as part of the north Indian jajmānī system. Rope-makers, potters and leather-workers supplied the rest: ropes and tethers, pots, and the leather of buckets, straps and whips. The leather-workers’ trade, indispensable to an agriculture of bullocks, was also a mark of their exclusion (Chapter 18).

docs.title: 7.15.1 Colonial attempts at improvement
docs.text:
From the first half of the nineteenth century British officials, missionaries and improving landholders tried to introduce European ploughs and harrows, and the experimental farms of the later nineteenth century tested many imported designs. Most of these trials failed. Heavy iron ploughs needed larger animals than most Indian cultivators possessed, cost far more than a wooden plough, and could not be repaired in the village. Voelcker (Section 7.5.2) saw a place for light improved implements introduced with care for particular purposes, but not for wholesale replacement.

In the early twentieth century provincial agricultural departments promoted light iron ploughs, some with small mouldboards for burying weeds or green manure, and Indian manufacturers began to make them. The best known was Laxmanrao Kirloskar, who began making iron ploughs in the first decade of the century and soon afterwards established his works at Kirloskarwadi, in what is now Maharashtra. Adoption was slow and uneven, and the wooden plough remained the ordinary implement of most Indian farmers until the 1960s, and in many regions long after.

docs.title: 7.15.2 Tractors, threshers and combines
docs.text:
After independence a Central Tractor Organisation used tractors to reclaim land overgrown with deep-rooted grasses in central and northern India, but the mechanisation of ordinary farming began with the Green Revolution of the late 1960s and 1970s (Chapter 20). Tractor manufacture in India began around 1960, and in the irrigated regions of Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh tractors bought with institutional credit spread rapidly, for ploughing and seedbed preparation and, with a trailer, for haulage in place of the bullock cart. In the rice regions small two-wheeled power tillers came into use. By the early twenty-first century India had become one of the world’s largest producers and markets for tractors, and many small farmers hired a tractor and driver for each operation.

Mechanical threshers spread in the wheat country at the same time. They did in hours what treading did in days and produced the chopped bhūsā that farmers wanted for fodder, but they also caused many serious injuries to hands and arms caught in the feeding chutes, and the Dangerous Machines (Regulation) Act of 1983 was passed to regulate their safety. Combine harvesters, which reap and thresh in one operation, became common in Punjab and Haryana from the 1980s, often owned by contractors who moved with the harvest from region to region. Because combines leave standing stubble and loose straw, and the interval between the rice harvest and wheat sowing is short, many farmers in the north-west took to burning the rice residue in the field, which contributes to severe air pollution across the region in late autumn. Machines that sow wheat directly through the residue have been promoted as an alternative; the problem remains unsolved.

docs.title: 7.15.3 The effects of mechanisation
docs.text:
A review of the evidence by Hans Binswanger in 1978 found little clear evidence that tractors had substantially raised yields or cropping intensity in South Asia, and concluded that their main effect had been to replace bullocks and human labour (Binswanger 1978). Others have argued that in irrigated areas the speed of tractor ploughing helps farmers fit two crops into a year. The distributional effects are less disputed. Mechanisation reduced the demand for the labour of attached ploughmen, harvest workers and the women who had threshed and winnowed, and it favoured larger farmers and the contractors who hired out machines. It also changed the place of cattle in the farm economy (Chapter 13). In rain-fed regions, on small and scattered holdings and in the hills, the bullock and the wooden plough remained in use much longer, and in some places they still are.

Debate: Were India’s implements “primitive”?

Colonial writers often called the Indian plough a primitive implement that merely scratched the soil, and the judgement recurs in modern development writing. Those who studied it closely, Voelcker above all, took a different view: the ard, the plank, the blade harrow and the drill formed a set of cheap, locally repairable tools matched to small cattle, thin purses and soils that often did not need deep inversion. Neither view should be pressed too far. The old implements were well adapted to the constraints under which most cultivators worked, but they were also limited by them: they demanded great quantities of human and animal labour, the timing of operations depended on access to a team, and the poorest households had no team at all. They are best judged against those constraints, and contempt and nostalgia are equally out of place.

docs.title: 7.16 Who Did Which Work
docs.text:
The tools of field work were divided by caste and by gender. Ploughing was the central operation of the farming year, yet it was hedged with restrictions. Following the Manusmṛti’s disapproval of the plough (Section 2.9), in much of India brahmins, and in some regions other high-caste landholders, did not handle the plough themselves. The work fell to tenants and attached ploughmen, often from castes treated as untouchable or from Adivasi communities: the halvāhā of north India, whose name means “ploughman”, and the Dubla hāli farm servants of south Gujarat studied by Breman (1974) are examples (Chapter 18).

Women were almost everywhere in South Asia barred by custom from ploughing, and in many regions from touching the plough at all; Agarwal (1994) discusses this taboo and the use made of it in arguments against women’s independent rights in land. Ester Boserup argued that societies using the plough tended to restrict women’s field work more than those that cultivated with the hoe (Boserup 1970), and Alberto Alesina, Paola Giuliano and Nathan Nunn found that descendants of societies that traditionally used the plough hold less equal views about women’s roles today (Alesina et al. 2013). Both are broad comparative arguments, which India, with its great regional variety, fits only in part.

Exclusion from the plough did not mean exclusion from the field. Transplanting and weeding rice were in most regions largely women’s work, and the songs women sang while transplanting form a large oral literature in many Indian languages. Women did much of the harvesting, gleaning, threshing, winnowing and cleaning of grain, carried head-loads and manure, and made the dung cakes that competed with the fields for it (Section 7.5); in shifting cultivation they often did much of the hoeing and sowing. Most of this work was done with hand tools—the khurpī, the sickle and the sūp—rather than with the animal-drawn implements controlled by men. Mechanisation has altered this division without abolishing it: threshers, combines, rice mills and herbicides took over many tasks for which poor women had been paid, while the work that remains unmechanised, above all transplanting and weeding in small fields, is still largely theirs.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Early Indian texts classify land by fertility and salinity (urvarā, ūṣara), by the crop it will bear (Pāṇini), by whether it holds water (sthala, kedāra), by micro-site (the Arthaśāstra) and by the dry or marshy character of a country (jāṅgala, ānūpa); the physical soil tests of Sanskrit are tests of building sites. The Kṛṣi-Parāśara gives the clearest early instructions on manuring with cow dung, but most of what we know about fertility management, bunds and terraces comes from farmers’ practice recorded since the nineteenth century. Canal irrigation spread waterlogging and reh, and modern soil science’s groups have no exact counterpart in the Sanskrit sources. The soil was worked with the ard, a wooden plough with an iron share, and a set of cheap, locally made implements — plank, blade harrow, seed drill, hoes, sickle, threshing floor and winnowing basket — maintained by village carpenters and smiths paid in grain. Colonial attempts to replace them largely failed; tractors, threshers and combines spread with the Green Revolution. Throughout, field work was divided by caste and gender: ploughing was barred to brahmins by custom and to women almost everywhere, while transplanting, weeding and much of the harvest fell to women and to labourers of low status.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Zimmermann (1987) on jāṅgala and ānūpa; Kangle (1965) and Olivelle (2013) for the Arthaśāstra; Sadhale (1999) for the Kṛṣi-Parāśara; Voelcker (1893) for Indian farming practice and implements in the late nineteenth century; Agarwal and Narain (1997) for terraces and water-harvesting structures; and Habib (2008) for the history of agricultural technology in medieval India.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Water: Tanks, Canals, Wells and Communities
docs.text: Indian agriculture has always had to manage a seasonal abundance of water and a long seasonal scarcity. Over most of the subcontinent the bulk of the year’s rain falls in the few months of the south-west monsoon, and much of it runs off quickly; the rest of the year is dry, and the monsoon itself is uncertain in its timing and amount (see Volume 19, Vāṇijya and Samudra, on the monsoon, and Chapter 3 on rain forecasting). Almost every Indian irrigation technique is a way of holding monsoon water back—in a tank, behind a weir, in the soil, or underground—or of lifting stored water from a well or river when it is needed. This chapter surveys those techniques and the institutions that sustained them, from the earliest textual references to the colonial canals and the recent decline and partial revival of community systems. The emphasis is on what can be documented in texts, inscriptions, surviving works and field studies.

docs.title: 8.1.1 Before and in the Veda
docs.text:
The Harappan cities were careful managers of water: Mohenjo-daro had a very large number of brick-lined wells and covered drains, and Dholavira in Kachchh had large stone-cut reservoirs for storing seasonal runoff (Kenoyer 1998; Possehl 2002). Whether Harappan farmers practised canal irrigation on any scale is debated; much of their agriculture probably relied on rainfall and on the flooding of rivers (Chapter 2).

The Ṛgveda knows both natural and artificial water. A hymn to the Waters speaks of waters that are heavenly or that flow, khanitrimā uta vā yāḥ svayaṃjāḥ, “those that are dug and those that arise of themselves” (RV 7.49.2; (Jamison and Brereton 2014)). The well (avata) appears in the same collection: one late hymn (RV 10.101), addressed to the priests as if they were farmers, uses the image of a well with a strap and bucket, drawing water that does not run dry, alongside the yoking of ploughs. The word kulyā, a channel or ditch, also occurs in Vedic texts. These references show that dug channels and wells were familiar, but they do not describe irrigation systems, and nothing in the Vedic corpus supports claims of large-scale hydraulic works.

docs.title: 8.1.2 Buddhist and Jain traditions
docs.text: Early Buddhist and Jain texts are set in a landscape of rice fields divided by bunds and fed by channels. A well-known story in the later Buddhist commentarial tradition tells how the Śākyas and the Koliyas, neighbouring peoples on either side of the river Rohiṇī, quarrelled over the waters of a weir across the river during a drought, and how the Buddha made peace between them. Whatever its historicity, the story assumes that dividing river water between communities was a familiar cause of conflict.

docs.title: 8.1.3 The Arthaśāstra
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra (composite, c. 50 BCE–300 CE) gives the earliest sustained treatment of irrigation as a matter for the state; for the text as a whole, see Volume 18, Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra. Its key term is setu, which covers dams, embankments and the reservoirs they create. In the chapter on settling the countryside (Book 2, chapter 1) the king is told to have irrigation works built, either with water available on the spot (sahodaka) or with water brought from elsewhere (āhāryodaka), and to help others who build them by providing land, roads, timber and implements (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013). In Book 7, when weighing one strategic advantage against another, the text judges a work with its own water source better than one depending on water brought from elsewhere, and among the former, the one that irrigates the larger crop.

Several other passages concern water. The chapter on the superintendent of agriculture (2.24) fixes a water rate graded by the way the water reaches the field (Section 2.11.1), and the rain gauge and regional rainfall norms are discussed in Section 3.5. In Book 3, the rules on property and damage grant remissions of tax for a number of years to those who construct new irrigation works or restore abandoned ones, the remission being longer for new works; they treat privately built works as property; and they impose fines on those who breach embankments or obstruct another’s water. Whether these rules describe actual Mauryan administration or the ideal of later theorists is uncertain, but they show that by the early centuries CE, Sanskrit political thought treated irrigation works as both a royal responsibility and a form of property.

docs.title: 8.1.4 Merit and patronage
docs.text: From the Dharmaśāstra and Purāṇic literature onward, the building of wells, tanks, stepwells and gardens is classed as pūrta, a work of public merit that, with sacrificial and charitable works (iṣṭa), earns religious reward. Thousands of inscriptions across India record the digging or repair of a tank or well by a king, queen, merchant, temple, village assembly or individual, often with a grant of land or revenue for its upkeep. This ideology of merit was one important reason why so much hydraulic infrastructure was built by patrons outside the central state; it does not mean that the resulting water was shared equally (Section 8.5).

docs.title: 8.2 The Sudarśana Lake at Girnar
docs.text:
The best-documented early irrigation work in India is the Sudarśana lake at Girnar, near Junagadh in Saurashtra, known from inscriptions on the same boulder that carries a set of Aśoka’s major rock edicts. The Sanskrit inscription of the Western Kṣatrapa ruler Rudradāman, dated to year 72 of the Śaka era (150 CE), records that the lake had been constructed under Candragupta Maurya by his provincial governor, the vaiśya Puṣyagupta, and that under Aśoka the Yavana king Tuṣāspha had furnished it with conduits. A great storm had then burst the dam and emptied the lake. Rudradāman, the inscription says, had it rebuilt, stronger than before, from his own treasury and without oppressing the people with taxes, forced labour or levies, through his minister Suviśākha, a Pahlava who governed the province (Singh 2008). The lake was breached again three centuries later; an inscription of the Gupta emperor Skandagupta on the same rock records its repair in the mid-fifth century by Cakrapālita, son of the provincial governor.

These records are valuable precisely because they are not idealised prescriptions. They show a single reservoir maintained for more than seven centuries under three successive powers—Maurya, Kṣatrapa and Gupta—and the provincial officials who served them, with all the risks of breaching and neglect that such works faced. They also show irrigation as royal propaganda: Rudradāman’s boast of having avoided forced labour (viṣṭi) is a reminder that such labour was the normal way in which large works were built.

A second early record comes from Odisha. The Hāthīgumphā inscription of the Kaliṅga king Khāravela (1st c. BCE) says that he brought into his capital a canal first opened by a “Nanda king” long before; the interval is read differently by different scholars, so the age of the canal is uncertain.

docs.title: 8.3.1 What a tank is
docs.text:
Across the drier parts of the peninsula, from Tamil Nadu through Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana into the Deccan, the characteristic irrigation work is the tank: Tamil ēri, Kannada kere, Telugu cheruvu. A tank is made by throwing an earthen embankment across a shallow valley or the line of a seasonal stream. Monsoon runoff collects behind the bund; one or more sluices let water out to the fields below as the crop requires; and a surplus weir carries off excess water in heavy rain so that the bund is not overtopped. In many areas tanks are arranged in chains or cascades along a drainage line, so that the surplus of one feeds the next (Figure 8.1). Tanks also serve for drinking water, bathing, washing, cattle, fish and the recharge of nearby wells, and the silt deposited on their beds is a valued manure (Chapter 7).

Figure 8.1. The south Indian tank (Tamil ēri, Kannada kere, Telugu cheruvu), schematic and not to scale. (a) Tanks built in a chain along a drainage line: each earthen bund holds back runoff, sluices release water to the fields below, and surplus weirs pass excess water on to the next tank. (b) A section through one bund. After the descriptions in Section 8.3.

docs.title: 8.3.2 Tanks in inscriptions
docs.text: The epigraphic record of tanks in south India is enormous. Pallava, Pāṇḍya, Cōḻa, Cālukya, Hoysala, Kākatīya and Vijayanagara inscriptions record the construction and repair of tanks, the grant of land whose income was to pay for annual desilting and bund repair, and disputes over water. In Karnataka and Andhra, grants known as daśabandha (Telugu dasavanda, “one-tenth”) rewarded those who built or maintained tanks with a share of the land or produce they irrigated. Large tanks associated with particular rulers include the great reservoir at Gaṅgaikoṇḍacōḻapuram, the capital built by the Cōḻa king Rājendra I in the eleventh century. Such works were important, but most tanks were small, local and anonymous.

docs.title: 8.3.3 The Uttaramērūr inscriptions
docs.text:
The most detailed evidence for the local management of tanks comes from two inscriptions of the Cōḻa king Parāntaka I, of 919 and 921 CE, at Uttaramērūr near Kanchipuram. They set out the rules by which the sabhā, the assembly of this brahmadeya (a village granted to brahmins), was to choose its executive committees (vāriyam). Candidates were nominated by ward and chosen by lot, slips bearing their names being drawn from a pot (kuḍavōlai). Among the committees were an annual committee, a garden committee and a tank committee (ēri-vāriyam) responsible for the village’s tanks (Singh 2008).

The inscriptions are justly famous as evidence of elaborate local self-government, but they are sometimes described too generously as a “village democracy”. Eligibility was limited to men of a certain age who owned taxable land and a house on their own site and had Vedic learning; the assembly was that of brahmin landholders, and the cultivators and labourers who worked the land had no voice in it. The tank committee managed water on behalf of landholders.

docs.title: 8.3.4 Cōḻa and Vijayanagara landscapes
docs.text:
Under the Cōḻas (9th–13th c.) the Kāvēri delta was irrigated mainly by channels taking off from the river and its branches, while the drier uplands around it depended on tanks. Inscriptions show temples acting as major investors in, and managers of, irrigation, receiving endowments of land and lending money for tank works.

Kathleen Morrison’s archaeological study of the region around Vijayanagara, the capital of the empire of that name (14th–16th c.), shows how varied irrigation could be within a single landscape (Morrison 1995). Close to the Tungabhadrā river, weirs (anicuts) diverted water into long channels that fed irrigated fields; away from the river, reservoirs behind embankments held runoff; and on the uplands, dry farming and small run-off fields persisted. Morrison argues that agricultural intensification around the city was achieved through this mix of strategies, each with different costs and risks, rather than through a single type of “hydraulic” system directed by the state.

docs.title: 8.4 The Grand Anicut on the Kāvēri
docs.text:
In south India a weir across a river that diverts water into irrigation channels is called an anicut (from Tamil aṇaikkaṭṭu). The most celebrated is the Grand Anicut, Tamil Kallaṇai (“stone dam”), near Tiruchirappalli at the head of the Kāvēri delta, which regulates how the river’s water is divided between the Kāvēri proper and its northern branch, the Kollidam (Coleroon). Tradition attributes the original work to the early Cōḻa king Karikāla (early centuries CE), and later Cōḻa-period traditions credit him with embanking the Kāvēri. No contemporary inscription confirms the attribution, and the date of the earliest structure is not known; but an old masonry weir certainly existed at the site before the colonial period (Figure 8.2).

Figure 8.2. The Grand Anicut (Kallaṇai) on the Kāvēri near Tiruchirappalli. Tradition attributes the original weir to the Cōḻa king Karikāla; the structure seen today is largely the product of nineteenth-century rebuilding and later works. Photo: Beckamrajeev, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The structure visible today is largely the work of the nineteenth century. In the 1830s and 1840s the Madras engineer Arthur Cotton studied the old weir, built a new regulating work (the Upper Anicut) across the Kollidam upstream, and rebuilt and raised the Grand Anicut itself, with further modifications by later engineers. Cotton is said to have learned from the old anicut how to found a masonry weir on a sandy river bed, and he went on to build the great anicut across the Godāvarī at Dowleswaram (begun 1847), which transformed irrigation in the Godāvarī delta; a similar work on the Kṛṣṇā followed in the 1850s. The Grand Anicut thus belongs to two histories at once: a long Tamil tradition of river diversion, and the colonial irrigation engineering that built on it.

docs.title: 8.5 Tanks, Caste and Community
docs.text:
Tanks are often presented as the model of community water management, and in an important sense they were. Their upkeep depended on collective labour by the villagers who used them, known in Tamil as kuṭimarāmattu (roughly, “maintenance by the cultivators”): desilting the bed, repairing the bund, clearing the channels. Water was distributed through village functionaries such as the Tamil nīrkaṭṭi, who opened sluices and turned water from field to field in an agreed order, often paid in grain at harvest. Rules for sharing in scarcity, closing the sluices, and timing the crop were made and enforced locally.

But “community” did not mean equality. David Mosse’s study of tank systems in the Ramanathapuram and Sivaganga region of Tamil Nadu shows that tanks were embedded in political systems of kingship, temple honour and caste rank (Mosse 2003). Rights to water, the order in which fields received it, and the duty to perform the labour of maintenance were tied to caste status: dominant landholding castes controlled tanks and took the first and best water, while the actual digging, desilting and watering were frequently done by Dalit labourers and by low-ranked service castes, including the water-turners themselves. Mosse also shows that the colonial state, by treating tanks as revenue-producing property and taking over their maintenance, weakened the older political arrangements that had sustained them, without creating effective new ones.

Exclusion from water was also enforced in everyday life. Across much of India, Dalits were barred from using village wells and tanks used by the upper castes, and separate wells were the norm. In 1927 B. R. Ambedkar led a large assembly of Dalits to drink from the public Chavdar tank at Mahad in Maharashtra, a landmark of the movement against untouchability. Any account of traditional water management that celebrates community must also record whom the community excluded.

Water institutions

Most Indian irrigation systems were neither purely state works nor purely “community” works. Kings and temples financed large tanks and channels; village assemblies and dominant landholders managed them; customary officials—the nīrkaṭṭi in Tamil Nadu, the kohli of the Kangra kuhls, the watermen of the Maharashtra phads—regulated day-to-day distribution; and the heavy labour fell largely on lower castes. These institutions were often durable and effective, and also hierarchical.

docs.title: 8.6 Kashmir: Suyya’s Works
docs.text: One of the few accounts of a named hydraulic engineer in pre-modern India comes from Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī, the Sanskrit chronicle of the kings of Kashmir completed in 1148–49. In its fifth book Kalhaṇa describes the works of Suyya, a man of humble origins who served King Avantivarman (r. c. 855–883). According to Kalhaṇa, the valley suffered from floods because the Vitastā (Jhelum) was choked by rocks where it leaves the valley, and Suyya had the bed cleared—famously, by throwing money into the river so that villagers would dig out the obstruction while searching for coins. He is said to have built stone embankments, moved the confluence of the Vitastā and the Sindhu, reclaimed land from the marshes, protected villages with circular dykes, and fixed the allotment of irrigation water to villages; Kalhaṇa adds that the price of rice fell greatly as a result (Stein 1900). The town of Sopore (Suyyapura) is named after him. The account is a court chronicle written three centuries after the events, and its details cannot be checked independently, but it is a rare literary description of drainage and river training in medieval India.

docs.title: 8.7 Stepwells
docs.text:
The stepwell—Sanskrit vāpī, Gujarati vāv, Hindi and Rajasthani bāolī or bāvaḍī—is a well reached by a long flight of steps descending through a series of landings and pavilions to the water, so that people can reach the water whatever its level. Stepwells are concentrated in Gujarat and Rajasthan, where groundwater lies deep and fluctuates greatly with the seasons.
