The form is attested in the later first millennium CE (the Chand Baori at Abhaneri in Rajasthan is commonly dated to the eighth or ninth century), and the great Gujarati examples date from the eleventh to the sixteenth century (Jain-Neubauer 1981).

The Rani-ki-Vav at Patan, built in the later eleventh century and traditionally associated with Queen Udayamatī in memory of the Caulukya king Bhīma I, is the most elaborate, with hundreds of sculptures on its walls; it was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2014. The stepwell at Adalaj near Ahmedabad bears an inscription of 1499 recording its construction by a queen, Rūḍādevī, wife of a local Vāghelā chief. Many other stepwells were built under the Gujarat Sultanate and the Mughals, and the type was shared across religious communities.

Stepwells were primarily for drinking water, bathing and rest rather than irrigation, although some fed gardens. They were also social spaces, especially for the women who drew water, and cool places of retreat in the hot season. Their elaborate architecture made them works of conspicuous merit for their patrons, among whom queens and merchants are prominent. The stepped tank at Mohenjo-daro known as the “Great Bath” is a different kind of structure, and no stepwell of the Harappan period is known.

docs.title: 8.8 Regional Systems
docs.text:
India’s diversity of terrain and rainfall produced a correspondingly diverse set of local irrigation and water-harvesting systems. Many were documented systematically for the first time in the survey Dying Wisdom, edited by Anil Agarwal and Sunita Narain (Agarwal and Narain 1997), which did much to draw attention to them; some are summarised in Table 8.1, and Figure 8.3 locates them and the other works named in this chapter. Community water harvesting in tribal regions is treated more fully in Volume 23, Jana–Jāti.

Figure 8.3. Some irrigation works and water systems named in this chapter: the Sudarśana lake at Girnar; the stepwells of Patan, Adalaj and Abhaneri; the canal heads and towns of the north (Haridwar for the Ganges Canal, Hisar and Delhi for the Sultanate and Mughal canals); Mahad, where Ambedkar led the Chavdar tank satyagraha; the reservoirs and channels of Vijayanagara; the tanks of Uttaramērūr and Gaṅgaikoṇḍacōḻapuram; the Grand Anicut and Cotton’s anicut at Dowleswaram; and representative areas of the regional systems of Table 8.1. The kuhls of Kangra and the zabo of Nagaland lie outside the frame. Positions are plotted by latitude and longitude; the coastline is simplified, islands other than Sri Lanka are omitted, and no rivers or political boundaries are shown. Table 8.1. Selected regional water systems of India. System Region Principle Ēri, kere, cheruvu Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana Tanks behind earthen bunds, often in cascades; sluices release water to fields Ahar–pyne South Bihar Channels (pyne) lead river and runoff water to embanked reservoirs (ahar) that irrigate rice Phad Tapi basin, north-western Maharashtra Weirs (bandhara) divert river water to channels serving blocks of land (phad) planted to a common crop Kuhl Kangra and other valleys of Himachal Pradesh Gravity channels from mountain streams, maintained by irrigators under a watermaster (kohli) Zabo Phek district, Nagaland Protected forest, ponds, cattle yards and rice terraces linked by runoff channels Bamboo drip Khasi and Jaintia hills, Meghalaya Spring water carried and divided through bamboo pipes, notably to betel-leaf and black pepper gardens Kuṇḍ or kuṇḍī Thar desert, western Rajasthan Covered cistern fed by a prepared catchment, mainly for drinking water Johad Eastern Rajasthan Earthen embankment that impounds runoff and recharges wells Khadin Jaisalmer region, Rajasthan Embankment across a slope; ponded water and silt make a cultivable bed for a winter crop Surangam Kasaragod (Kerala) and Dakshina Kannada (Karnataka) Horizontal tunnels dug into laterite hillsides to draw out groundwater

docs.title: 8.8.1 Ahar–pyne of south Bihar
docs.text: The plains of south Bihar slope northward towards the Ganga, and their rivers run full in the monsoon and dry soon after. The ahar–pyne system exploits this. Pynes are channels that take water from the rivers in flood, or collect runoff, and lead it to ahars, reservoirs embanked on three sides with the fourth open to the slope. Water stored in the ahars, and the moisture in their beds, carries the rice crop through the end of the monsoon. Maintenance depended on landlord investment and on collective labour; the decline of both after the abolition of zamindari in the 1950s is widely blamed for the system’s deterioration (Agarwal and Narain 1997).

docs.title: 8.8.2 Phad of Maharashtra
docs.text: In the valleys of the Panjhra and neighbouring rivers of the Tapi basin, farmers built stone weirs (bandhara) to divert river water into main canals and smaller distributaries. The land commanded by each system was divided into blocks (phad), each of which grew a single crop in a given season, such as sugarcane or a grain crop, so that water could be delivered efficiently to the block as a whole. Water distribution and maintenance were organised by the irrigators through appointed watermen.

docs.title: 8.8.3 Kuhls of Kangra
docs.text: In the Kangra valley of Himachal Pradesh, gravity-flow channels called kuhls divert water from Himalayan streams to terraced rice fields. Mark Baker’s study shows that each kuhl is managed by the households it serves, under a watermaster (kohli) who organises the annual repair of headworks after the monsoon and the rotation of water between villages and fields; customary rules were written down by colonial settlement officers in the late nineteenth century and still carry weight (Baker 2005). Baker also traces how these institutions have adapted, or failed to adapt, to the spread of off-farm employment and state intervention.

docs.title: 8.8.4 The North-East
docs.text: In the zabo (“impounding water”) system of the Chakhesang Nagas of Kikruma and neighbouring villages, rainwater falling on protected forest above the fields is led into ponds, passes through cattle yards where it picks up manure, and is then channelled onto rice terraces, with fish sometimes reared in the fields. In the Khasi and Jaintia hills of Meghalaya, water from springs and streams is carried in bamboo pipes and progressively divided through smaller pipes and channels until it arrives, at a much reduced flow, at the base of individual plants, chiefly in betel-leaf and black pepper gardens. The system is often called “bamboo drip irrigation”; it shares the principle of delivering small quantities of water to each plant with modern drip irrigation, though it was developed independently (Agarwal and Narain 1997).

docs.title: 8.8.5 Rajasthan: kuṇḍs, johads and khadins
docs.text:
The Thar and its margins have very low and erratic rainfall, and water harvesting there aims first at drinking water. A kuṇḍ or kuṇḍī is an underground cistern, usually lined and covered with a dome, fed by a carefully prepared and often plastered catchment sloping towards it. In eastern Rajasthan, johads are crescent-shaped earthen embankments that hold monsoon runoff; their main benefit is often the recharge of downstream wells. From the 1980s the voluntary organisation Tarun Bharat Sangh, led by Rajendra Singh, revived the building of johads in Alwar district, an effort that became a model for water-harvesting campaigns elsewhere.

The khadin, associated by tradition with the Paliwal Brahmins of the Jaisalmer region, is a long earthen embankment built across the lower slope of a rocky catchment. Monsoon runoff collects behind it, depositing fine silt; when the water has soaked in or been drained, the moist bed is sown with a winter crop such as wheat or gram. The khadin is as much a soil-making device as a water-harvesting one (Chapter 7).

docs.title: 8.8.6 Surangam of the laterite coast
docs.text: In Kasaragod district of northern Kerala and the adjoining Dakshina Kannada district of Karnataka, farmers dig horizontal tunnels, called surangam or suranga, into laterite hillsides until they reach water-bearing strata; the water then flows out by gravity into a pit or tank, and is used for drinking and for areca nut and coconut gardens. The technique resembles the qanāt of Iran in principle, though a surangam is usually a single tunnel without the vertical shafts of a qanāt. How old the tradition is, and whether it is connected to West Asian practice, is not known; many existing tunnels are relatively recent.

docs.title: 8.9 Lifting Water
docs.text:
Where water lay below the level of the field—in a well, a river or a low tank—it had to be lifted. Irfan Habib’s survey of medieval Indian technology distinguishes several devices and traces their history (Habib 2008); the three main types are shown in Figure 8.4.

The swing-beam lever. The simplest device, a pivoted pole with a bucket at one end and a counterweight at the other (the shaduf of Egypt), is known in north India as ḍheṅklī or ḍhekulī, in Anglo-Indian usage in the south as the picottah, and by many other local names. Worked by one or two people, it lifts water a short height from shallow wells, tanks or streams. The rope-and-bucket lift. In western and northern India, a large leather bucket (charas in north India, mhoṭ or moṭ in Marathi) was drawn up from a deep well on a rope passing over a pulley by a pair of bullocks walking down an inclined ramp, then emptied into a channel. It could lift water from considerable depths but required continuous work by two men and two animals. The water-wheel. Sanskrit texts from the early centuries CE mention the araghaṭṭa and the ghaṭīyantra, “pot-machine”. In Habib’s reconstruction these were wheels carrying pots, either fixed to the rim or tied to a chain or garland of rope, turned directly by human or animal effort. The fully developed “Persian wheel” (Hindi rahaṭ), in which animals walking in a circle drive the pot-garland through right-angled gearing, spread in north India in the Sultanate period.

The emperor Bābur, writing in the 1520s, described the two methods he found in Hindustan: a wheel with a rope of pots, turned by an animal through a gear, in the Lahore and Dipalpur region; and the bullock-drawn bucket in the region of Agra and Bayana (Thackston 1996). In the Mughal period well irrigation of these kinds, rather than canals, watered most irrigated land in north India (Habib 1999).

Figure 8.4. Three ways of lifting water, schematic and not to scale. (a) The swing-beam lift, in which a counterweight balances a pot on a pivoted pole, raises water a short height from a shallow well, tank or stream. (b) The rope-and-bucket lift: a pair of bullocks walking down a ramp draws a large leather bucket up a deep well over a pulley. (c) The geared Persian wheel: an animal walking in a circle turns a horizontal wheel whose gearing drives a vertical wheel carrying a garland of pots. After Habib (2008) and the descriptions in Section 8.9.

Water-lifting was hard and continuous labour. A well with a charas could keep a team of men and bullocks occupied through the day in the dry season, and access to a well, which was expensive to dig and line, was itself a mark of a household’s standing. Wells were usually owned by landholding families, and their use, like the use of tanks, was governed by caste rules.

docs.title: 8.10 Finding Water: Varāhamihira’s Dakārgala
docs.text:
The fifty-fourth chapter of Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā (6th c. CE; Bhat’s numbering) is the dakārgala, a manual for finding groundwater for wells (Bhat 1981). Varāhamihira begins from the idea that water runs beneath the earth in channels (śirā) like the veins of the body, and that these can be located by surface signs. Most of the chapter is a list of such signs and their meanings: a particular tree, such as a jambū or an udumbara, growing in a dry place; an anthill beside a tree; the presence of certain creatures; the colour and texture of the soil; and the kind of stones met in digging. For each sign the text states in which direction from it, and at what depth (measured in puruṣa, a unit based on a man’s height), water will be found, and sometimes whether it will be sweet or brackish. It distinguishes ordinary country from desert regions, where the indications and depths differ.

The chapter is a remarkable document of systematic observation and of the importance attached to well-digging in Varāhamihira’s world. It is also a text of its time: the rules are stated as certainties, are mixed with astrological and omen material elsewhere in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā, and have not been tested as a set. That some plants indicate shallow groundwater is a reasonable general observation; that the particular depths and directions given in the text are reliable has not been shown. The dakārgala theme was continued in later works, among them the Viśvavallabha of Cakrapāṇi Miśra (16th c., Mewar), which also deals with water-finding (Section 4.1).

docs.title: 8.11 Canals of the Sultanate and Mughal Periods
docs.text: Canals drawing water from the great rivers of the north were built in the Delhi Sultanate. The most important builder was Fīrūz Shāh Tughluq (r. 1351–1388), whose canals from the Yamuna and the Sutlej carried water to his new city of Hisar and irrigated land along their courses (Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982). These canals fell into disrepair after his reign. Under Shāh Jahān, the Persian noble ʿAlī Mardān Khān re-excavated and extended the old Yamuna canal in the 1640s to bring water to the emperor’s new capital at Shāhjahānābād (Delhi); inside the Red Fort the water ran through the marble channel known as the Nahr-i Bihisht, “stream of paradise”. ʿAlī Mardān Khān is also credited with a canal bringing water from the Ravi to Lahore. These canals served cities and gardens first, but they also irrigated land along the way; their remains were later the starting point for British canal building in the Yamuna region (Habib 1999). Mughal water gardens are treated in Chapter 18.

docs.title: 8.12.1 From restoration to new canals
docs.text:
British irrigation in India began by restoring older works. The Western Yamuna Canal, on the line of the Tughluq and Mughal canals, was reopened in the early nineteenth century, and an Eastern Yamuna Canal followed. In the south, Arthur Cotton’s work on the Kāvēri, Godāvarī and Kṛṣṇā (Section 8.4) turned the deltas of the Madras Presidency into heavily irrigated rice country. In the north, the Ganges Canal, designed by Proby Cautley to take water from the Ganga at Haridwar into the Doab, was opened in 1854 and is often described as the largest irrigation canal of its time.

In Punjab, where large rivers cross dry plains, canal building after the 1880s created the “canal colonies”: wholly new agricultural settlements on former pasture and waste in the doabs between the Punjab rivers. The colonies made western Punjab one of the most productive wheat and cotton regions of Asia. Imran Ali has argued that they also served imperial interests—land was granted to favoured landholding castes, retired soldiers and loyal notables, while the “menial” castes who did much of the agricultural labour were largely excluded from proprietary grants, and the pastoral peoples who had used the land lost it (Ali 1988). David Gilmartin has set the canal colonies within a longer history of the Indus basin, in which the state’s control of water reshaped both the environment and the relationship between the state and the communities who used the rivers (Gilmartin 2015).

docs.title: 8.12.2 Costs and critics
docs.text: Canal irrigation brought gains in output and some protection against drought, but also serious costs. Seepage from unlined canals and the lack of drainage raised water tables; land became waterlogged and, as saline groundwater rose and evaporated, encrusted with reh (Chapter 7). Waterlogging was linked by contemporaries to an increase in malaria in canal tracts. Historians of the canal regime, notably Elizabeth Whitcombe in her work on the United Provinces, have documented these effects (Whitcombe 1972; Kumar 1983). Canal water was sold at rates set to make the works pay, and the government distinguished between “productive” works expected to earn a return and “protective” works built mainly against famine. Critics then and since have argued that investment went where it would yield revenue rather than where need was greatest, and that older systems such as the tanks of the south were neglected (Davis 2001; Ludden 1999). The Indian Irrigation Commission of 1901–03 reviewed the whole field after the famines of the late 1890s.

docs.title: 8.12.3 Independent India
docs.text: After independence, irrigation expanded rapidly through large multipurpose dams and canal systems, and, from the 1960s and 1970s onward, through private tubewells powered by electricity and diesel. Groundwater pumped by individual farmers has since become the main source of irrigation in much of the country, a shift whose consequences for aquifers are discussed in Chapter 20.

docs.title: 8.13 Decline and Revival of Tanks
docs.text:
Through the twentieth century, many tanks and other community systems decayed. The reasons were several. Colonial and post-colonial states took over formal responsibility for larger tanks but often did not maintain them; the authority of the local elites who had organised collective labour weakened with land reforms and changing village politics; the spread of private wells and tubewells gave the wealthier farmers an alternative and reduced their interest in common works; tank beds silted up and their catchments and supply channels were encroached upon by fields, roads and buildings, especially around growing towns. In many places the result was a vicious circle, in which a poorly maintained tank supplied less water, which further reduced the incentive to maintain it.

From the 1980s these trends provoked a revival of interest. Dying Wisdom and the work of voluntary organisations such as Tarun Bharat Sangh popularised traditional water harvesting (Agarwal and Narain 1997), and state and national programmes have funded the rehabilitation of tanks, often through water-users’ associations. Results have been mixed. Physical repairs are easier to fund than the social arrangements that kept systems working, and attempts to recreate “community management” have had to deal with the same inequalities of caste, land and gender that shaped the old systems (Mosse 2003). The lesson of the historical record is not that traditional systems were ideal and need only to be restored, but that their success depended on institutions—of authority, obligation and sharing—that have to be rebuilt in forms that are fair under present conditions.

Cross-Reference: Related chapters

Rain forecasting and the rain gauge: Chapter 3. Tank silt as manure, usar and reh: Chapter 7. Rice and other irrigated crops: Chapter 9. Groundwater and modern water policy: Chapter 20. Community water harvesting in tribal regions: Volume 23, Jana–Jāti.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Indian irrigation is, above all, the storage and lifting of monsoon water. The Arthaśāstra already treats irrigation works as a royal duty and a form of property, and the Sudarśana lake was maintained for more than seven centuries. Peninsular India relied on tanks, built by many kinds of patron and managed by village institutions; the river deltas on channels from anicuts such as the Grand Anicut; and other regions on a wide variety of local systems. Water was lifted by lever, leather bucket and wheel. Sultanate, Mughal and above all colonial canals expanded irrigation in the north at the cost of waterlogging and salinity, while community systems declined. Throughout, the management of water was bound up with caste and power, a fact that any revival must confront.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Agarwal and Narain (1997) for regional water-harvesting systems; Mosse (2003) on tanks, caste and the state in Tamil Nadu; Baker (2005) on the kuhls of Kangra; Morrison (1995) on Vijayanagara; Habib (2008) on water-lifting devices; Jain-Neubauer (1981) on stepwells; and Gilmartin (2015) on the Indus canals.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Crops and Seeds
docs.text: The fields of the subcontinent have never grown a single, fixed set of crops. Some plants were brought into cultivation within South Asia; many more arrived from south-west Asia, Africa, China, Southeast Asia and, after 1500, the Americas, and were then reshaped by generations of farmers into local varieties suited to particular soils, rains and tastes. This chapter surveys the principal crops: cereals, pulses, oilseeds, sugarcane, cotton, spices, fruits and vegetables. It then turns to the reckoning of seasons, to rotation and mixed cropping, and to the selection, treatment, storage and exchange of seed. Archaeobotanical evidence for the beginnings of farming is treated in Chapter 2; the processing of grain, oil and sugar in Chapter 14; and pests, livestock integration and trees on farms in Chapter 10.

docs.title: 9.1 A Region of Domestication and of Introduction
docs.text:
The Russian botanist N. I. Vavilov (1887–1943) placed the Indian region among the handful of world “centres of origin” of cultivated plants that he defined in the 1920s and 1930s. He credited it with rice, several pulses, sugarcane, the Old World cottons, the cucumber, a number of tropical fruits and several spices (Vavilov 1951). Vavilov’s method was to locate the regions where a crop showed the greatest varietal diversity and to treat these as its homeland. Later work showed that a centre of diversity need not be a centre of origin; a crop may become most varied far from where it was first domesticated, and several “centres” turned out to be broad zones rather than points (Harlan 1971). Vavilov’s scheme is therefore best read as a landmark in the history of crop science rather than as a current account of where crops began.

The present picture comes mainly from archaeobotany, whose evidence is set out in Chapter 2: in Dorian Fuller’s synthesis South Asia was not one centre but several, combining crops introduced from south-west Asia (from about 7000 BCE at Mehrgarh), from Africa (from about 2000 BCE) and from East Asia with local wild plants brought into cultivation in Gujarat, the southern Deccan, the Ganga plain and the north-west (Fuller 2006, 2011). The cultivated landscape that emerges is a mosaic of local domesticates and introductions, and it has stayed that way ever since. Table 9.1 summarises the probable origins of the principal crops by name.

Table 9.1. Probable origins of some major crops grown in India. “Origin” refers to the region where the crop was first domesticated, as far as current evidence allows; several entries remain under study (Fuller 2006, 2011; Achaya 1998). docs.title: 9.2 Grain Classes in the Texts
docs.text:
Sanskrit texts do not describe crops in the categories of modern botany, but they do group them. The earliest lists are ritual. Barley (yava) is the grain of the Ṛgveda, where the word can also mean grain in general; rice (vrīhi) is first named in the Atharvaveda, and wheat (godhūma) only in later Vedic texts. The Yajurveda’s camaka litany (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 18), in which the sacrificer asks for each good thing “and for me”, names among its foods rice, barley, beans (māṣa), sesame, mung, khalva, the millets priyaṅgu, aṇu and śyāmāka, wild rice (nīvāra), wheat and lentil. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad gives a compact list of ten cultivated grains:

Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.13

daśa grāmyāṇi dhānyāni bhavanti vrīhiyavās tilamāṣā aṇupriyaṅgavo godhūmāś ca masūrāś ca khalvāś ca khalakulāś ca “There are ten cultivated grains: rice and barley, sesame and beans, millet and panic, wheat, lentils, khalva and khalakula.”

The last two terms are of uncertain identity; they are usually taken to be pulses (Olivelle 1998). The word grāmya (“of the village”) sets these cultivated grains against āraṇya, wild foods gathered from the forest, such as nīvāra.

Pāṇini (c. 4th century BCE) has rules forming adjectives for a field suited to a particular grain, such as vraiheya (a field fit for vrīhi), śāleya (for śāli) and maudgīna (for mung): evidence that farmers matched land and crop in their everyday vocabulary. The Arthaśāstra’s chapter on the director of agriculture (Section 2.11.1) sorts crops by sowing time, a classification discussed in Section 9.12.

The fullest classical scheme is medical. The chapter on food and drink in the Caraka-saṃhitā (Sūtrasthāna 27) arranges foods in twelve groups (varga). The first two are grains: śūkadhānya, “awned grains”, the cereals (rice, barley, wheat and others); and śamīdhānya, “pod grains”, the pulses (mung, urd, horsegram, lentil, chickpea, pigeon pea and others), with sesame also treated in this group. In Caraka’s list of things that are best of their kind (Sūtrasthāna 25), red śāli rice is the most wholesome of the awned grains and mung of the pulses (Sharma 1981). The Suśruta-saṃhitā’s corresponding chapter (Sūtrasthāna 46) distinguishes śāli, ṣaṣṭika and vrīhi rices, then a class of “lesser grains” (kudhānya) comprising millets such as kodrava, śyāmāka and priyaṅgu, and then the pulses (Bhishagratna 1907). These are dietetic categories, concerned with how foods act on the body; they are not crop manuals, but they preserve a valuable record of which grains were known and how they were ranked (see Volume 13, Āyurveda).

Tamil literature offers a different, landscape-based frame. In the Saṅgam poems and the tiṇai scheme of the Tolkāppiyam, the marutam tract is the land of wet paddy fields (nel), while the hill country (kuṟiñci) is the land of dry millet (tiṉai) fields guarded against parrots; crops are part of a whole poetic ecology rather than a dietetic list (Chapter 2).

docs.title: 9.3.1 Origins
docs.text: Asian rice (Oryza sativa) has two main lineages, japonica, securely domesticated in the Yangtze basin of China, and indica, the dominant rice of India, whose history is debated. In Fuller’s model, local wild rice (Oryza rufipogon and O. nivara) was long cultivated in the middle Ganga plain before japonica arriving from the east hybridised with it after about 2000 BCE; early dates claimed for domesticated rice at Lahuradewa and elsewhere remain contested (Section 2.5; (Fuller 2011)). Rice cultivation spread through the Ganga plain in the first millennium BCE and became the staple of eastern and southern India.

docs.title: 9.3.2 Classical rice types
docs.text:
The texts distinguish rices by season, duration and quality. Śāli was the prestigious rice, generally a transplanted crop harvested in early winter (hemanta); Caraka names many kinds, among them raktaśāli (red), mahāśāli (“great”), kalama, dīrghaśūka (long-awned) and sugandhaka (fragrant) (Sharma 1981). Vrīhi usually denotes rainy-season rice ripening in autumn, rated in the medical texts as heavier and less wholesome than śāli. Ṣaṣṭika, “sixty-day” rice, was a quick-maturing type valued in diets for convalescents. Nīvāra, wild rice, was the food of forest ascetics in the epics and in Kālidāsa. Lexicons such as the Amarakośa add further names. The names do not map neatly onto modern varieties, and it would be a mistake to treat the medical texts’ lists as a census of rice diversity; they record the rices known to particular authors in particular regions.

Regional agrarian vocabularies preserve similar distinctions. In Bengal, rice crops are named by their seasons: āus (sown with the early rains and harvested in late summer or autumn), āman (the main transplanted crop, harvested in early winter) and boro (grown in the dry season on residual or lifted water). The Kṛṣi-Parāśara, which probably comes from eastern India and is centred on rice, gives instructions for raising seedlings, transplanting, weeding, draining the field and harvesting; the south Indian Kāśyapīya Kṛṣisūkti likewise devotes most of its agricultural material to rice (Majumdar and Banerji 1960; Sadhale 1999; Ayachit 2002). These texts are discussed in Chapter 3.

docs.title: 9.3.3 Landraces
docs.text:
Before the twentieth century, rice in India was grown as a very large number of landraces: farmer-maintained varieties adapted to particular water regimes, from upland fields watered only by rain to deep-water and floating rices of the deltas and the saline-tolerant rices of coastal Kerala, Goa and the Sundarbans. Grain colour (white, red, black), aroma, cooking quality, duration and ritual use all mattered to farmers. The rice scientist R. H. Richharia (1909–1996), director of the Central Rice Research Institute at Cuttack and later of a rice research institute at Raipur, reportedly assembled a very large collection of landraces from the Chhattisgarh region, and argued for breeding from local varieties rather than relying on imported high-yielding lines. Precise totals for the number of rice varieties “once grown” in India circulate widely but are not based on any agreed count.

Several regional landraces now carry Geographical Indication registrations, among them Navara and Palakkadan Matta in Kerala, Kalanamak in eastern Uttar Pradesh and Joha in Assam. The decline of landrace diversity after the Green Revolution, and the movements to conserve it, are discussed in Section 9.14.4 and Chapter 20.

docs.title: 9.4 Wheat and Barley
docs.text: Barley and wheat are the oldest crops of the subcontinent. At Mehrgarh, naked six-row barley dominates the early plant remains, with smaller amounts of wheat (Meadow 1996). In the Harappan civilisation, both were winter-sown staples of the Indus plains; Harappan sites also yield a distinctive short, round-grained bread wheat, often classed as Indian dwarf or “shot” wheat (Triticum aestivum subsp. sphaerococcum) (Weber 1999; Possehl 2002). In the Ṛgveda, yava is the grain that is ploughed, sown, reaped and threshed; later Vedic ritual uses barley in many offerings, and wheat gradually rises in importance in the first millennium BCE. In the north and north-west, barley and wheat have remained the main winter crops, sown after the monsoon on the moisture left in the soil or with well and canal water, and harvested in spring. Barley, which tolerates poorer and more saline soil, was long the grain of the less prosperous.

docs.title: 9.5 Millets
docs.text:
“Millet” is not a botanical group but a name for many small-grained grasses. India grows two kinds. The first are millets domesticated within South Asia, among them kodo (Paspalum scrobiculatum, Sanskrit kodrava), little millet (Panicum sumatrense), browntop millet (Urochloa ramosa) and Indian barnyard millet (Echinochloa frumentacea); śyāmāka refers to one or more of these small millets. At Rojdi in Saurashtra, small millets were the main crops in the Harappan period, a reminder that Harappan farming was not uniform (Weber 1991). The second are introductions. Foxtail millet (Setaria italica, usually identified with priyaṅgu) and broomcorn or proso millet (Panicum miliaceum, cīnaka, a name that itself suggests a connection with China) were domesticated in northern China. Sorghum (jowār), pearl millet (bājrā) and finger millet (rāgi, nācanī) are African domesticates that reached India around 2000 BCE (Fuller 2006). Some reported early finds of finger millet in India have been questioned on identification, but the African origin of all three is not in doubt.

Millets became the staple grains of the drier Deccan, Rajasthan, Gujarat and the southern uplands, and of many hill and forest communities. The medical texts rank them as kudhānya, “lesser grains”; in social terms, millet was often the food of the poor while rice and wheat were the grains of status, a ranking that shaped diets for centuries. In the twentieth century, irrigated rice and wheat displaced millets over large areas. Interest has revived because millets suit rain-fed farming on light soils, and the United Nations General Assembly, on India’s proposal, declared 2023 the International Year of Millets. The nutritional profile of millets varies a great deal by species; claims for them should be made species by species and from current nutritional data, not from tradition.

docs.title: 9.6 Pulses
docs.text:
Pulses (Caraka’s śamīdhānya; dvidala or vaidala, “split” grains, in other texts) are central to Indian food and farming. Several were domesticated within the subcontinent: mung (Vigna radiata, mudga), urd or black gram (V. mungo, māṣa), horsegram (Macrotyloma uniflorum, kulattha), moth bean (V. aconitifolia) and pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan, āḍhakī), whose wild relative grows in the Eastern Ghats (Fuller 2011). Lentil (masūra), chickpea (caṇaka), pea (kalāya) and grass pea (Lathyrus sativus, khesārī) came from south-west Asia; cowpea and the hyacinth bean from Africa. Grass pea is hardy and drought-tolerant, but heavy dependence on it in times of scarcity causes lathyrism, a crippling neurological disease, and its history shows how a “famine crop” can harm the poorest who rely on it.

Pulses are legumes, and their roots carry nodules in which bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen. That growing legumes improves the following crop was known empirically to many farming peoples, in India as in the Roman world; the mechanism was demonstrated in Europe in the 1880s. Indian farmers commonly sowed pulses with cereals or after them, as discussed in Section 9.13. No surviving Sanskrit text, however, sets out a theory of rotation for soil fertility.

docs.title: 9.7.1 Oilseeds
docs.text: Sesame (Sesamum indicum, tila) was domesticated in South Asia from a wild relative and is found at Harappan sites (Fuller 2006). Its importance is preserved in language: Sanskrit taila, “oil”, means literally “that which comes from tila”. Sesame and its oil are prominent in ritual, especially in offerings to the dead. Mustards and rapeseed (Brassica species; sarṣapa, with white mustard called siddhārtha) became the oil crops of the northern plains and Bengal. Linseed (Linum usitatissimum, atasī, umā) is a south-west Asian domesticate; in India it was grown mainly for oil. Safflower (kusumbha) gave both an oil and a red dye. Castor (eraṇḍa), an African plant, supplied lamp oil and medicine. The coconut (nārikela) was the oil and food palm of the coasts, and niger (Guizotia abyssinica), an Ethiopian domesticate, was an oilseed of hill and forest farmers. Groundnut, now one of India’s main oilseeds, is an American crop (Section 9.11). The oil press (ghāṇī) and the castes who worked it are discussed in Chapter 14.

docs.title: 9.7.2 Flax and cotton
docs.text: Flax is the oldest plant fibre known to have been worked by humans; linen was woven in south-west Asia well before cotton, and Sanskrit kṣauma is often, though not certainly, understood as linen. Cotton, however, has a genuinely ancient history in South Asia. Mineralised cotton fibres preserved in a copper bead from a Neolithic burial at Mehrgarh, dated to around the sixth to fifth millennium BCE, are among the earliest evidence of cotton use anywhere (Moulherat et al. 2002), and cotton textiles are known from Mohenjo-daro (Kenoyer 1998). The Old World “tree cottons” (Gossypium arboreum, and the related G. herbaceum, whose earliest domestication may lie further west) were the cottons of India for millennia; cotton was independently domesticated in the Americas, and American upland cotton was promoted in India by colonial authorities in the nineteenth century. Since 2002 most of India’s cotton has been grown from hybrids carrying a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt cotton), whose history and controversies are discussed in Section 20.9. Herodotus’ report of Indian trees that bore wool shows how Indian cotton struck the Greek world. Spinning, weaving and the cotton trade are treated in Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru.

docs.title: 9.8 Sugarcane
docs.text:
The noble canes (Saccharum officinarum) were domesticated in New Guinea; the thin, hardy canes long grown in northern India (S. barberi) are thought to be hybrids between these and the wild S. spontaneum. Sugarcane (ikṣu) is named in the Atharvaveda and is a familiar crop in Sanskrit and Pali literature. What India gave the world was less the plant than the technology of making solid sugar. Indian texts of the early centuries CE distinguish grades of sugar product: the Arthaśāstra’s list of storehouse goods includes phāṇita, guḍa, matsyaṇḍikā, khaṇḍa and śarkarā, from thickened juice to crystalline sugar (Kangle 1965). Sanskrit śarkarā lies behind Persian shakar, Arabic sukkar and English “sugar”, and khaṇḍa behind “candy”. Chinese sources record that the Tang court sent envoys to Magadha in the seventh century to learn the method of sugar-boiling (Mazumdar 1998).

The Arthaśāstra ranks sugarcane as the least desirable crop for the state farms (Section 2.11.1). In the twentieth century the Sugarcane Breeding Institute at Coimbatore (founded 1912) crossed noble canes with S. spontaneum to produce hardier hybrid varieties that were grown far beyond India (Section 19.5.2). Jaggery-making and sugar-refining are treated in Chapter 14.

docs.title: 9.9 Spices
docs.text:
The Western Ghats are the home of black pepper (Piper nigrum, marica) and cardamom (Elettaria cardamomum, elā). Long pepper (Piper longum, pippalī), also a plant of the Indian region, was the older and more prized pepper in classical Indian pharmacology and was also traded westward. Ginger (Zingiber officinale; fresh ārdraka, dried śuṇṭhī) and turmeric (Curcuma longa, haridrā) are tropical Asian crops propagated from rhizomes; both have long histories of cultivation in South Asia. Not every “Indian spice” is Indian: true cinnamon is from Sri Lanka, while the Sanskrit tvak covers cassia barks as well; cloves are from the Moluccas and reached India by trade; cumin and coriander came from south-west Asia and the Mediterranean.

Black pepper was the principal Indian export to the Roman world, shipped from Malabar ports such as Muziris; the trade is treated in Volume 19, Vāṇijya and Samudra. Before the sixteenth century, the pungency of Indian cooking came from pepper, long pepper, ginger and mustard. The chilli (Capsicum) is a New World plant brought by the Portuguese in the sixteenth century; within a century or two it had become indispensable across the subcontinent.

docs.title: 9.10 Fruits and Vegetables
docs.text:
The mango (Mangifera indica, āmra), native to the region of north-eastern South Asia and Myanmar, is the fruit most celebrated in Indian literature. Other fruits of long South Asian cultivation include the jackfruit (panasa), jamun (jambū), Indian jujube or ber (badarī), Indian gooseberry (āmalakī), wood-apple (kapittha) and bael (bilva). Citrus fruits originated in the broad region of the eastern Himalayan foothills, north-east India, southern China and Myanmar. Bananas (kadalī) were domesticated in New Guinea and Southeast Asia but reached India early. Pomegranate (dāḍima) and grape (drākṣā) came from Iran and Central Asia, and the tamarind from tropical Africa, all in antiquity.

Among vegetables, the cucumber was domesticated in South Asia from a wild form of the Himalayan foothills, and the brinjal (vṛntāka) was domesticated in South or Southeast Asia. Gourds (bottle gourd alābu, ash gourd kūṣmāṇḍa, bitter gourd kāravella), yams, taro and leafy greens formed the everyday vegetable supply, much of it grown in kitchen gardens rather than fields. Many of the vegetables now thought typically Indian are later arrivals: the potato, tomato and chilli from the Americas, and cauliflower and cabbage from Europe in the colonial period. Medicinal plants are treated in Chapter 12 and Volume 13, Āyurveda.

docs.title: 9.11 Crops from the Americas and the Islamic World
docs.text:
The sixteenth century opened a new phase. Through Portuguese ports on the west coast and through overland trade, American crops entered India: maize, chilli, potato, tomato, tobacco, groundnut, pineapple, papaya, guava, custard apple, cashew, sweet potato and cassava among them (Achaya 1998; Randhawa 1980). They spread at very different speeds. Chilli and tobacco were adopted quickly; tobacco was being smoked at the Mughal court by the early seventeenth century, and Jahāngīr records in his memoirs that he tried to forbid it (Thackston 1999). Maize became a hill crop of the Himalaya and of parts of the north. The pineapple was known at the Mughal court. Cashew was planted along the western coast and later became a plantation and export crop. The potato and tomato became important only in the nineteenth century, when colonial administrators and missionaries encouraged them, and groundnut became a major field crop of the Deccan and Gujarat in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Cassava was promoted in Travancore in the nineteenth century and became a food of the poor in Kerala.

Debate: Pre-Columbian maize in India?

It is occasionally claimed that maize was grown in India before 1492, mainly on the basis of carved motifs on medieval temples that resemble maize cobs. Most archaeobotanists and art historians reject this: the motifs are more plausibly read as conventional ornaments (such as strings of pearls held by figures), and no maize remains have been found in any securely dated pre-Columbian Indian context.

A second current of introductions came through the Islamic world and the courts of the Sultanates and the Mughals. Persian and Central Asian fruits such as melons, grapes and new varieties of apricot and peach were cultivated in royal gardens, often with grafting; Bābur’s memoirs survey the plants of Hindustan, which he found wanting in the fruits of his homeland, and Jahāngīr describes fruits and grafts in his (Thackston 1996, 1999). The Mughal revenue system reorganised the agrarian calendar into two harvests and recorded crops in great detail (Section 9.12). In the colonial period, tea, coffee, rubber, cinchona and many other plantation crops transformed hill landscapes, with profound social and ecological effects. These histories are treated in Chapter 18.

docs.title: 9.12 Seasons and the Crop Calendar
docs.text:
Indian farmers grew crops in two main seasons long before the familiar terms kharīf and rabī existed. Those terms are Arabic in origin (kharīf, “autumn”; rabīʿ, “spring”) and entered Indian usage through Persian revenue practice under the Sultanates and the Mughals, which assessed land revenue harvest by harvest. Abū’l-Faẓl’s Āʾīn-i Akbarī tabulates revenue rates crop by crop for the rabī and kharīf harvests of the provinces (Abū’l-Faẓl 1873; Habib 1999). A third, minor summer season is called zāid (“additional”). These are not classical Sanskrit categories, and the Sanskrit agricultural texts do not use them. Figure 9.1 sets the three seasons and their main crops against the six seasons of the Sanskrit texts.

Figure 9.1. The two main crop seasons of northern India, with the minor summer season, set against the six seasons (ṛtu) of the Sanskrit texts. The kharīf crops are sown with the onset of the south-west monsoon and harvested in autumn; the rabī crops are sown after the rains on stored soil moisture or with well and canal water and harvested in spring. The terms are Perso-Arabic (Section 9.12). Months are approximate and vary from region to region; much of peninsular India, and the Tamil coast with its north-east monsoon rains in October to December, follows different calendars, and Bengal and Assam name their rice crops by season (āus, āman, boro; Section 9.3). Each ṛtu corresponds to a pair of lunar months, so its boundaries move against the solar months shown here.

Sanskrit texts reckon agricultural time in other ways. The year is divided into six seasons (ṛtu): vasanta (spring), grīṣma (summer), varṣā (rains), śarad (autumn), hemanta (early winter) and śiśira (late winter). The Taittirīya Saṃhitā already observes that the crop ripens twice a year (Section 2.7). Crops are also named by their seasons: vrīhi and ṣaṣṭika by the rains, śāli by early winter, barley by spring. The Arthaśāstra’s director of agriculture classifies crops by sowing time: early-sown crops (pūrvavāpa) such as śāli and vrīhi rice, kodo, sesame and millets; middle-sown crops (madhyavāpa) such as mung and urd; and late-sown crops (paścādvāpa) such as safflower, lentil, horsegram, barley, wheat, pea, linseed and mustard (Kangle 1965). In effect this is the monsoon-sown and winter-sown division under other names. The text also advises sowing crops that need more or less water according to the rainfall of the year. Detailed calendars tied to the lunar mansions (nakṣatra) appear in the Kṛṣi-Parāśara and in regional farmers’ sayings; they are discussed in Chapter 3 and, for the calendar itself, in Volume 12, Khagola Jyotiṣa.

docs.title: 9.13 Rotation, Mixed and Relay Cropping
docs.text:
The strongest evidence for how Indian farmers combined crops comes not from Sanskrit texts but from observers of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Voelcker (Section 7.5.2) singled out mixed cropping, the alternation of cereals with pulses and the keeping of fields free of weeds as matters in which British agriculture had little to teach Indian cultivators (Voelcker 1893), and Howard (Section 10.7) found mixed cropping one of the most striking features of their practice (Howard 1940). These observers had their own agendas (Voelcker defending the cultivator against official blame, Howard building a case against chemical fertilisers), but their descriptions are detailed and based on fieldwork.

Practices that these and later observers describe include:

  • Rotation, alternating cereals with pulses or oilseeds on the same land from one season or year to the next; for example, a monsoon cereal followed by chickpea, lentil or another winter pulse.

  • Mixed cropping, sowing two or more crops together in the same field, either mixed in the seed or in alternate rows. Examples include sorghum or pearl millet with pigeon pea and other pulses on the black soils of the Deccan; wheat or barley mixed with chickpea in the north; and lines of mustard sown through fields of wheat.

  • Relay cropping, sowing a second crop into a standing crop before it is harvested. In parts of eastern and central India, lentil, grass pea or linseed seed is broadcast into rice shortly before the rice harvest, so that it germinates on the residual moisture (the practice is called utera in Chhattisgarh and paira in Bihar and Odisha).

  • Intercropping of long- and short-duration crops, such as the classic Deccan combination of sorghum with pigeon pea: the cereal is harvested at the end of the rains, after which the slower pigeon pea grows on through the winter on stored soil moisture.

  • Composite multi-crop systems in particular regions, such as the akkaḍi sālu rows of Karnataka, in which lines of pulses and oilseeds are sown through finger millet, and the bārahnājā (“twelve grains”) of the Garhwal and Kumaon hills.

The advantages farmers sought were several: insurance against the failure of any one crop in an uncertain monsoon, a spread of labour and harvest over the year, food and fodder of several kinds from one field, and, in the case of pulses, a benefit to the following crop. Agronomists have since studied these systems experimentally. Results depend heavily on the crops, soils and rainfall concerned, and general statements that mixed cropping always controls pests or yields more than sole cropping are not supported. The sources also contain no figures on the extent of these practices, and none are given here.

docs.title: 9.14.1 Selection
docs.text: Every farming household that saved its own seed practised selection, choosing the heads, pods or fruits from which next season’s seed would come. The Kṛṣi-Parāśara has a short section on seed. As Majumdar and Banerji and Sadhale render it, the text advises gathering seed in the months of Māgha or Phālguna (late winter), drying it thoroughly in the sun, and keeping it so that it is not mixed with other seed; mixed or uneven seed, it says, gives a poor crop (Majumdar and Banerji 1960; Sadhale 1999). Many farmers’ practices of seed testing (floating seed in water and discarding what floats, or germinating a sample on a damp cloth before sowing) are recorded in modern surveys of farming practice; they are sensible tests, but they are not classical prescriptions.

docs.title: 9.14.2 Treatment before sowing
docs.text:
The earliest detailed prescriptions for treating seed are in the Arthaśāstra’s chapter on the director of agriculture (2.24; Section 2.11.1). As Kangle translates it, grain seeds are to be exposed to mist by night and heat by day for seven nights, and pulse seeds for a shorter period; cuttings of sugarcane and similar plants are to have their cut ends smeared with honey, ghee and hog’s fat mixed with cowdung; bulbous roots are to be smeared with honey and ghee; and hard-coated seeds (asthibīja) with cowdung (Kangle 1965). Whether these instructions describe practice on the royal farms or a learned author’s ideal is uncertain, as with much of the Arthaśāstra (see Volume 18, Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra).

The Vṛkṣāyurveda texts give many recipes for treating seeds of trees and garden plants before sowing, often with milk, ghee, honey and dung, and these are discussed in Chapter 4 (Sadhale 1996; Majumdar 1935).

docs.title: 9.14.3 Storage
docs.text:
Stored seed in a hot, often humid climate faces moisture, moulds, insects and rodents. Farmers’ storage practices, recorded across India in colonial and modern surveys, include:

  • drying seed thoroughly in the sun before storage;

  • storing it in earthen pots or jars with sealed mouths, in bins built of mud or of woven bamboo plastered with mud and dung, or in bundles and containers of straw;

  • mixing dried neem leaves, ash or sand with stored grain and seed;

  • keeping small seed lots in the kitchen roof or above the hearth, where smoke and warmth keep them dry;

  • in some dry regions, storing grain in lined underground pits.

Several of these practices are reasonable responses to the threats they address. Neem leaf and kernel contain compounds that deter or disrupt many storage insects (Schmutterer 1995), and keeping seed dry is the single most important factor in preserving its viability. Their effectiveness in any particular case depends on how they are carried out.

docs.title: 9.14.4 Exchange, landraces and conservation
docs.text:
Seed moved constantly: between neighbours, as part of marriage gifts, at fairs, along trade routes, and through the borrowing of seed from landlords and moneylenders at high rates of interest, a recurring source of indebtedness. In many communities, selecting and storing seed has been women’s work, and women’s knowledge of varieties has been an important, if little recorded, part of agricultural expertise. The result of continual selection and exchange was a large stock of landraces in every major crop: genetically diverse, locally adapted populations, rather than uniform varieties.

From the 1960s, the spread of high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice, bred for response to irrigation and chemical fertiliser, replaced landraces over large areas (Chapter 20). Collections of traditional varieties were made, partly in response, by national and international gene banks: the National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources in New Delhi, the International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics near Hyderabad (for sorghum, millets, chickpea, pigeon pea and groundnut) and the International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines, among others. Alongside these ex situ collections, farmers’ movements and non-governmental organisations have tried to keep landraces in cultivation. Examples include the Beej Bachao Andolan (“Save the Seeds” movement) in the Garhwal hills; the women’s groups of the Deccan Development Society in Telangana, which have promoted millet-based farming; Navdanya, founded by Vandana Shiva; and community seed banks in Odisha and elsewhere. Figures for their holdings vary widely between sources. The law on plant varieties and farmers’ rights, and the debates over patents on seeds and traditional knowledge, are discussed in Chapter 20 (Shiva 1991, 2001).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: India’s crops have mixed origins. Wheat, barley, lentil and linseed came from south-west Asia; sorghum, pearl millet and finger millet from Africa; maize, chilli, potato, groundnut and tobacco from the Americas. Rice, several small millets, mung, urd, horsegram, pigeon pea, sesame, tree cotton, black pepper and cardamom have South Asian or partly South Asian origins, as archaeobotany has shown in revising Vavilov’s “centres”. Sanskrit texts group crops by ritual use, by sowing season (as in the Arthaśāstra’s early-, middle- and late-sown crops) and by dietetic value (Caraka’s awned grains and pod grains, Suśruta’s “lesser grains”); the categories kharīf and rabī come from Sultanate and Mughal revenue practice. The best evidence for rotation, mixed and relay cropping comes from colonial observers and later fieldwork. Seed was selected, treated (as the Arthaśāstra prescribes), stored with care, and exchanged, producing a large landrace diversity that the Green Revolution reduced and that gene banks and seed-saving movements now try to conserve.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Fuller (2006) is the standard synthesis of crop origins in South Asia. Achaya (1998) is a reference for the history of individual crops and foods. Randhawa (1980) gathers a great deal of material on the history of Indian agriculture, though it should be used critically. Voelcker (1893) remains the best contemporary description of Indian cropping practice in the late nineteenth century, and Habib (1999) covers crops and seasons in the Mughal period.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Agroecology: Pests, Livestock, Trees and Fallows
docs.text: “Agroecology” is a modern word for the study of farms as ecological systems: how crops, weeds, pests, livestock, trees, soil and water interact, and how farming practices shape those interactions. Applied to the Indian past, it is a useful lens, but it is also easily misused. Pre-modern farming in India, as everywhere, used no synthetic fertilisers or pesticides because none existed; that does not make it “organic farming” in the modern sense, nor does it make it sustainable or benign by definition. This chapter examines what the texts and the historical record actually show about the protection of crops and trees from pests, the integration of crops and livestock, the growing of trees on farms, shifting cultivation, the farming systems of the Himalaya and the North-East, and the making of manure. It ends with the ethical ideals often invoked in discussions of Indian ecological thought, and with their limits. Soils are discussed in Chapter 7, water in Chapter 8, forests and sacred groves in Chapter 11, and modern natural-farming movements in Chapter 20.

docs.title: 10.1 Protecting Crops and Trees in the Texts
10.1.1 Tree medicine
docs.text:
The fullest classical discussions of plant protection concern trees and garden plants rather than field crops, and are found in the Vṛkṣāyurveda tradition (Chapter 4). Varāhamihira’s chapter on trees in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā (chapter 55, 6th century CE) describes the signs of disease in trees and prescribes a simple course of treatment: the diseased part is cut away, the wound is dressed with a paste of viḍaṅga (Embelia ribes), ghee and mud, and the tree is sprinkled with milk and water (Bhat 1981). Surapāla’s Vṛkṣāyurveda (c. 10th–11th century CE) develops this into a fuller system. Following the logic of human medicine, it classifies the disorders of trees by the three doṣas and by external causes such as insects, frost, wind, fire and lightning, and its remedies include pastes applied to wounds, fumigation (dhūpana) with burning plant and animal substances, and sprinkling or watering with various liquids, among them the fermented preparation kuṇapajala (Sadhale 1996). The Upavanavinoda, a section of Śārṅgadhara’s anthology of 1363, follows the same pattern for the trees and flowering plants of the pleasure garden (Majumdar 1935).

These texts are valuable evidence of how learned gardeners thought about plant health: by analogy with the human body, through the categories of Āyurveda, and with close attention to symptoms such as yellowing leaves, failure to fruit and insect attack. They are not field manuals of crop protection, and the Kṛṣi-Parāśara as edited gives no recipes against pests.

docs.title: 10.1.2 Pests as calamities
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra treats rats as one of the great calamities against which a king must guard, alongside fire, flood, disease, famine, wild animals and snakes, and among the measures it lists is the release of cats and mongooses (Kangle 1965). Locust swarms, birds and wild animals in standing crops were a constant concern of farmers, and literature preserves the human side of crop protection. In the fourth canto of the Raghuvaṃśa, Kālidāsa pictures the women who guard the rice fields, sitting in the shade of the sugarcane and singing of the king’s fame; the Tamil poems of the hill country repeatedly describe girls on raised platforms in the millet fields, driving off parrots with rattles and slings. Field-watching from platforms, by day against birds and by night against deer, wild pigs and elephants, was work for women, children and the poor, and it remained a major part of the farming year in forest-edge villages into modern times.

docs.title: 10.2 Farmers’ Pest Practices
docs.text:
Most pest management in Indian agriculture was never written down in Sanskrit. It was carried in farmers’ practice and has been recorded, unevenly, in colonial reports and modern surveys. The commonly described practices include:

  • Neem. Leaves of the neem tree (Azadirachta indica, nimba) mixed with stored grain and seed; neem cake, the residue of oil pressing, worked into the soil; and, in more recent practice, water extracts of leaves or seed kernels sprayed on crops.

  • Ash and dust. Wood ash dusted on vegetable crops, especially cucurbits, against leaf-eating beetles and other insects; ash or fine sand mixed with stored pulses.

  • Smoke and fire. Smoke from smouldering heaps at the edge of fields, and fires lit at night, to drive off or attract and kill flying insects.

  • Birds as allies. Poles or branches set up in fields as perches for insect-eating birds such as drongos, and the retention of trees and hedges that shelter birds. Bird perches are now also recommended in integrated pest management programmes.

  • Border and trap crops. Rows of a different crop sown around or through the main crop, which may attract pests away from it or harbour their enemies; mixed cropping in general (Chapter 9).

  • Timing and choice of variety. Adjusting sowing dates to avoid periods of heavy pest attack, and keeping landraces known to withstand local pests and diseases.

  • Field sanitation and physical removal. Hand-picking of caterpillars and egg masses, removal of infested plants, and the burning or burial of crop residues.

Of these, neem has been studied most thoroughly. The seed kernel contains limonoids, of which azadirachtin is the most important, that act on many insects as feeding deterrents, as disrupters of moulting and growth, and as deterrents to egg-laying; their toxicity to mammals is low, though not nil, and they break down quickly in sunlight (Schmutterer 1995). Neem preparations are therefore genuinely useful, but their effect varies with the insect, the crop, the part of the tree used and the preparation; they act more slowly than synthetic insecticides; and they are not harmless to all beneficial insects. The disputes over patents on neem-based products are discussed in Chapter 20.

For the other practices, systematic evidence of effectiveness is patchy. Some, such as perches for insectivorous birds, rest on sound ecological reasoning and have experimental support in particular settings; others are untested, and each has to be judged on the evidence for it.

Health and Safety Note

Several plants used as traditional pest repellents are toxic to people and animals, among them tobacco, the latex of Calotropis (arka) and the seeds of Datura. Neem oil taken by mouth has caused serious poisoning in infants. Nothing in this chapter is a recipe; preparations of this kind should be handled only in line with current agricultural safety advice.

docs.title: 10.3 Crops and Livestock Together
docs.text:
Indian farming was, for most of its history, mixed farming: crops and animals depended on each other. Cattle and, in wet-rice areas, buffaloes pulled the plough, the cart, the water-lift and the cane-crusher. Their dung was the main manure of the fields, and also a fuel and a building material. In return, the fields fed them: straw of rice and wheat, the stalks (stover) of sorghum and pearl millet, the haulms of pulses and groundnut, and oil cake from the press. In dry regions sorghum stover could be as important a product as the grain, and farmers chose varieties with an eye to fodder as well as food. Trees on farms were lopped for leaf fodder in the dry season (Section 10.4).

The integration was never complete or frictionless. Much of the dung that might have manured the fields was dried into cakes and burnt for want of fuel wood, a shortage Voelcker regarded as a central constraint on Indian agriculture (Chapter 7). Grazing land and fallows were contested between cultivators and herders; and the care of animals followed lines of caste and gender. Women did much of the work of collecting dung, making dung cakes and cutting fodder. The removal of dead cattle and the working of hides fell to communities treated as untouchable, whose labour was essential to the agrarian economy and whose status was degraded by it (Chapter 13) (Ambedkar 1948; Wiser 1936).

Relations between settled farmers and mobile pastoralists also had a cooperative side: herders were paid to pen their flocks overnight on harvested fields, an exchange of manure for grazing described in Chapter 13.

In some wetland regions, fish were part of the same system. The Apatani of the Ziro valley in Arunachal Pradesh raise fish in their irrigated rice terraces; in the brackish coastal fields of Kerala, pokkāḷi rice grown in the monsoon season alternates with prawn and fish culture in the saline season; and in the khazan lands of Goa, reclaimed estuarine fields are managed with sluice gates for both salt-tolerant rice and fish. These are cases where a farming system makes use of seasonal changes in water and salinity rather than fighting them.

docs.title: 10.4 Trees on Farms: Agroforestry
docs.text: Growing trees and crops on the same land, now studied under the name of agroforestry, is very widespread in India (Nair 1993). The classical texts encourage the planting of trees, especially by roads, wells and tanks, as a meritorious act (Chapter 4), but the farming systems described below are known mainly from historical observation and modern study.

docs.title: 10.4.1 Homegardens
docs.text: The homegardens of Kerala are the best-studied example. Around each house, on plots that are often small, are grown together coconut and areca palms, jackfruit, mango, tamarind, banana, black pepper trained on trees, tubers such as yams and colocasia, vegetables, spices and medicinal plants, frequently with a cow, goats or poultry. The garden supplies food, fodder, fuel, timber and cash crops in a layered structure that resembles, in some respects, a forest (Kumar and Nair 2004). The homegarden is not a fixed “traditional” form: cassava, cocoa, rubber and other introductions of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries have been absorbed into it, and many gardens have been simplified as land has been subdivided or turned over to a single cash crop. Homestead gardens of other kinds are found across India, from the bamboo- and fruit-tree groves around Bengal villages to the kitchen gardens of north Indian households.

docs.title: 10.4.2 Trees in fields
docs.text: In the arid west of Rajasthan, the khejri tree (Prosopis cineraria) is deliberately kept in farmers’ fields. Crops such as pearl millet, moth bean and cluster bean are grown beneath it; its leaves are lopped for fodder, its pods (sāṅgarī) are eaten as a vegetable, and its wood is used for fuel. Khejri is a leguminous tree, and farmers in the region regard the soil under it as better for crops. It is protected with particular strictness by the Bishnoi community (Section 10.8 and Chapter 11). Elsewhere farmers retain or plant other useful trees in and around fields: the babul (Vachellia nilotica) on the black soils of the Deccan and Gujarat, valued for timber, pods and gum; the palmyra palm on field bunds in Tamil Nadu, tapped for sap and used for leaves and timber; the mahua (Madhuca longifolia) of central India, whose flowers are food and the source of a distilled liquor and whose seeds yield oil; and the tamarind, mango and neem in almost every region. Trees on bunds and boundaries mark property, provide shade for workers and animals, and break the wind; they also shade and compete with crops, and farmers manage them by lopping and spacing.

docs.title: 10.4.3 Tree crops under shade
docs.text: In the Western Ghats, several plantation crops are grown under a canopy of shade trees. In Kodagu (Coorg) and Chikmagalur, coffee is grown beneath retained forest trees and planted shade trees, on which pepper vines are trained; cardamom is grown under forest cover in the hills of Kerala, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. Coffee is not a traditional Indian crop: tradition credits the Sufi Baba Budan with bringing coffee seeds from Yemen in the seventeenth century, but plantations developed under British and Indian planters in the nineteenth century, often on land taken from forest. These shaded systems retain much more tree cover than open plantations do, and they have attracted the attention of conservationists, but their history is also one of forest clearance and of a plantation workforce recruited under harsh conditions.

docs.title: 10.5 Shifting Cultivation
docs.text:
Shifting cultivation (swidden, slash-and-burn) is practised in the hills of north-east India, where it is called jhūm, and has been practised in the Eastern Ghats (poḍu), in central India (bewar among the Baiga and other names elsewhere) and in the Western Ghats (kumri). A patch of forest or secondary growth is cut, the vegetation is dried and burnt, and the cleared land is cropped for one or two seasons, usually with a mixture of crops sown together: upland rice, millets, maize, pulses, vegetables, cotton, sesame and tubers. The plot is then left fallow so that the vegetation and the soil can recover, and the cultivators move on to another patch, returning after a cycle of years.

The ecology of shifting cultivation depends on the length of that cycle. Burning releases nutrients from the vegetation into the soil as ash; the fallow allows trees and bamboo to regrow, rebuilds soil organic matter and suppresses weeds; and the mixture of crops spreads risk and provides a varied diet. P. S. Ramakrishnan’s long-term studies of jhūm in Meghalaya showed that when cycles are long the system can sustain itself, but that as cycles are shortened by growing population, loss of land and other pressures, soil fertility declines, weeds increase and yields fall (Ramakrishnan 1992). Shifting cultivation is thus neither inherently destructive nor inherently sustainable; its effects depend on the cycle, the terrain and the wider pressures on the land.

Colonial forest departments were hostile to shifting cultivation, which they saw as a waste of timber and a challenge to state control of forests. From the late nineteenth century it was banned or restricted in many reserved forests; in the Central Provinces, the Baiga were confined to a reserved tract in which alone bewar was permitted (Gadgil and Guha 1992). These restrictions were part of the broader colonial transformation of forest rights (Chapter 11). Hostility continued after independence, when shifting cultivation was often described in official documents as primitive and wasteful and cultivators were encouraged to adopt settled terraces or plantations. More recent research has tended to stress the knowledge embodied in shifting cultivation, its crop diversity and the importance of secure land rights for those who practise it, while recognising that shortened cycles can cause real degradation (see also Volume 23, Jana–Jāti).

docs.title: 10.6 Farming in the Hills: The Himalaya and the North-East
docs.text: Hills and mountains cover a large part of India, from Kashmir and Ladakh along the Himalaya to Arunachal Pradesh, and south through the hills of Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram, Tripura and Meghalaya. Farming there contends with slope and erosion, short growing seasons at altitude, cold, heavy monsoon rain on the eastern ranges and, until recently, isolation from markets. Hill peoples answered these conditions with a range of systems that combine terraces, valley-floor rice, shifting cultivation, orchards, forest and livestock. Several have been described already: terraces in general (Section 7.6), the kuhls of Kangra, the zabo of the Chakhesang Nagas and the bamboo pipes of Meghalaya (Section 8.8), shifting cultivation (Section 10.5) and the transhumant herders of the western Himalaya (Chapter 13). The Apatani valley, the alder fallows of the Angami Nagas, the bamboo flowering and famines of Mizoram and the meltwater irrigation of Ladakh are treated in Volume 23 (Jana–Jāti). This section describes some of the other hill systems: the mixed farming of the central Himalaya, Kashmir, the orchards of the western Himalaya, Sikkim, and the rice valley of the Brahmaputra.

docs.title: 10.6.1 Terraces, forest and livestock in the central Himalaya
docs.text:
In Garhwal and Kumaon (Uttarakhand) and the adjoining hills of Himachal Pradesh, villages farm narrow bench terraces cut into the slopes. Two kinds of land are distinguished. Low terraces in the valleys and on gentle lower slopes, irrigated by small channels (gūl) led from streams, carry rice in the monsoon and wheat in the winter. The much larger area of upland terraces depends on rain alone and carries millets, pulses and other monsoon crops, followed where moisture allows by wheat or barley. Local terminology, such as talāun for the irrigated and upraun for the rain-fed land, records the distinction.

The fertility of these terraces has depended on the forest. Farmers lop oak (banj, Quercus leucotrichophora) and other trees for winter fodder, gather fallen leaves for bedding in the cattle sheds, and carry the mixture of dung and leaf litter down to the fields as manure, so that a village’s terraces are sustained by a much larger area of forest and grassland around them. Much of this work, from lopping and carrying fodder to spreading manure, is done by women. The link between forest, livestock and field explains why the reservation of Himalayan forests by the colonial forest department from the late nineteenth century, which restricted lopping, grazing and burning, was resented so strongly, and why protest in these hills, culminating in Chipko, took the form it did (Guha 1989); see Section 11.10.

On the rain-fed terraces the characteristic practice is the mixed sowing known as bārahnājā (“twelve grains”; Section 9.13). A single field may carry finger millet (maṇḍuā), barnyard millet (jhaṅgorā), foxtail millet, amaranth (rāmdānā), horse gram (gahat), rice bean, black soybean (bhaṭ), cowpea and other pulses and vegetables, sown together or in close succession; at higher altitudes buckwheat and naked barley take their place. The crops ripen at different times, differ in their tolerance of drought and pests, provide grain, pulses, greens and fodder from the same land, and spread the risk of failure. From the late 1980s farmers in the Henwal valley of Tehri Garhwal, among them Vijay Jardhari, organised the Beej Bachao Andolan (“save the seeds movement”) to collect and exchange local seeds and to defend mixed cropping against single cash crops promoted by development agencies. Since the 1970s large-scale migration of men to the plains and to the army has left many outlying terraces abandoned, and crop raiding by monkeys and wild boar (Section 16.11) has hastened their abandonment.

Grain from these terraces was traditionally ground in water mills (gharāṭ), in which a small stream led down a wooden chute turns a horizontal paddle wheel coupled directly to the upper millstone. Thousands of such mills once stood on the streams of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh, usually owned by a family or a village and paid for with a share of the flour. Most were abandoned as diesel and electric mills spread, but since the 1990s improved designs with metal wheels, which can also drive small generators and other machines, have been promoted by government and voluntary agencies as a source of local, renewable power.

docs.title: 10.6.2 Kashmir: rice, saffron and floating gardens
docs.text:
The Kashmir valley, a flat alluvial basin drained by the Jhelum at about 1,600 metres, has been a land of irrigated rice since at least the period of Kalhaṇa’s chronicle, which records the drainage and irrigation works of Suyya in the ninth century (Section 8.6). Channels led from the side streams water terraced and level rice fields; maize, pulses and oilseeds were grown on the higher, unirrigated land. The fullest description of the agriculture of the valley before modern changes is The Valley of Kashmir (1895) by Walter Lawrence, who as settlement commissioner surveyed its land revenue. It records the cultivators’ varieties of rice, their calendar and their methods of irrigation and manuring, and is frank about the heavy exactions of the state and its officials under which they worked (Lawrence 1895).

Kashmir’s most famous crop is saffron (Crocus sativus; Sanskrit kuṅkuma). It is grown on the karewa, the raised plateaus of old lake deposits, above all around Pampore south-east of Srinagar. The saffron crocus is sterile and does not set seed; it is propagated by its corms, which are planted in well-tilled beds and left in the ground for several years. The flowers appear in October and November, and the three red stigmas of each flower are picked by hand and dried, so that a kilogram of saffron represents the labour of picking very large numbers of flowers. Kalhaṇa already counts saffron among the characteristic products of the valley in the description of Kashmir that opens his chronicle (Stein 1900), and the Āʾīn-i Akbarī describes the saffron fields (Section 18.7). How and when the plant reached Kashmir is uncertain. In recent decades the saffron area has shrunk under the pressure of urban building on the karewa and of irregular rainfall.

On the Dal and other lakes around Srinagar, cultivators grow vegetables on floating gardens (rādh): mats of reeds and water plants are cut, bound together, anchored with poles and covered with weed and mud dredged from the lake bed, and on them are grown cucumbers, melons, tomatoes and other vegetables. The gardens can be cut into sections and towed from place to place. They are one of the few Indian examples of a farming system built on the water itself, comparable in principle to the floating gardens of Myanmar’s Inle lake and of Bangladesh.

docs.title: 10.6.3 Orchards of the western Himalaya
docs.text: Fruit growing in the western Himalaya is old — the walnuts, apricots and almonds of Kashmir and Ladakh, the grapes of Kinnaur — but the orchard economy that now dominates much of Himachal Pradesh is modern. Small apple orchards were planted by Europeans in Kullu and around Shimla in the late nineteenth century. In 1916 Samuel Evans Stokes, an American who had settled at Kotgarh near Shimla, introduced varieties of the American Delicious apple, which proved well suited to the hills; from the middle of the twentieth century, as roads reached the valleys, apples became the main cash crop of Shimla, Kullu and Kinnaur districts. The change brought prosperity to many villages, but also dependence on a single crop, on market prices and on heavy spraying, and pressure on forests for packing cases until cardboard replaced wood.

docs.title: 10.6.4 Sikkim and the eastern Himalaya
docs.text:
In Sikkim and the Darjeeling hills the characteristic cash crop is large cardamom (Amomum subulatum), a native plant of the eastern Himalaya, distinct from the small cardamom of the Western Ghats (Section 9.9). It is grown in moist ravines and on shaded slopes under a canopy of trees, especially the Himalayan alder (Alnus nepalensis), whose roots fix nitrogen and whose leaf litter enriches the soil. Ecologists have described the alder–cardamom system as an efficient form of agroforestry that combines a valuable crop with continuous tree cover on steep land. Mandarin oranges, ginger, maize and terraced rice complete the farming of the lower and middle hills. From the late twentieth century the cardamom gardens suffered heavily from virus diseases, known locally as chirke and foorkey, and from the ageing of plantations, and production in Sikkim declined; replanting with healthy suckers and seedlings has been the main remedy.

Sikkim has also become a test case for organic farming policy. In 2003 the state government resolved to convert its agriculture to organic methods; chemical fertilisers and pesticides were progressively withdrawn, and in 2016 Sikkim was declared fully organic. Supporters point to the state’s small consumption of chemicals even before conversion, to the protection of its rivers and biodiversity and to the market value of an organic label; critics have pointed to lower yields of some crops, dependence on food from outside the state, and difficulties in certification and marketing. Independent, published assessments are still few, and the experiment is too recent for firm conclusions, and the general evidence on organic and natural farming is discussed in Chapter 20.

docs.title: 10.6.5 The Brahmaputra valley
docs.text:
The Brahmaputra valley of Assam is a rice country shaped by the river’s floods, which bring silt to the fields but can also destroy crops and villages. Assamese cultivators match their rice crops to the levels of the land and to the seasons of the flood. Āhu rice is sown in spring and harvested in summer, before or between floods. Sāli, the main crop, is transplanted during the monsoon and harvested in early winter. Bao, deep-water rice, is broadcast on low-lying land and grows with the rising water, its stems elongating as the flood deepens, to be harvested after the water falls. Boro rice is grown in winter on low wet land and harvested before the floods, now mostly with pumped water. The great Assam earthquake of 1950 raised the beds of many rivers with landslide debris and worsened the floods of the following years; from the mid-1950s the government built long earthen embankments along the Brahmaputra and its tributaries, which protected some land but, when breached, caused sudden and severe flooding and deprived the fields behind them of the silt that floods once brought. Among the many local varieties are glutinous bora rices used in festival foods, aromatic joha rices, and the komal sāul (“soft rice”) prepared from a glutinous variety, which can be eaten after soaking in cold water without cooking.
