Unboiled milk can transmit tuberculosis, brucellosis and other infections, and poorly stored grains and oilseeds can carry fungal toxins. Illicitly distilled liquor has repeatedly caused mass poisoning in India through methanol contamination, and mustard oil adulterated with the seed oil of the weed Argemone mexicana has caused outbreaks of epidemic dropsy. The consumption of pañcagavya is discussed, with a safety note, in Chapter 13.

docs.title: 14.5 Dairying Communities and Modern Cooperatives
docs.text:
In most of India milk was produced in small quantities by farming households, and the daily work of milking, setting, churning and making ghee fell mostly to women. Alongside them were castes and communities for whom cattle and dairying were a hereditary occupation and an element of identity: the Ahīr, Gvālā and Yādava groups of the north, who claim descent from Kṛṣṇa’s cowherd clan; the Gollas of Andhra and Karnataka; the Gavlīs of Maharashtra; the pastoral Rabārī, Maldhārī and Gujjar communities of the west and north-west; and the Toda of the Nilgiris, whose buffalo dairies are graded temples and whose dairymen are priests (Chapter 13). In towns, confectioners (the Halvāī of the north, the Moirā of Bengal) turned milk and sugar into sweets.

Modern organised dairying owes most to a cooperative. In the Kaira (Kheda) district of Gujarat, milk producers who sold to a private dairy at Anand holding the contract for Bombay’s milk supply complained of low and uncertain prices. With the encouragement of Vallabhbhai Patel and under the leadership of Tribhuvandas Patel, they formed the Kaira District Cooperative Milk Producers’ Union in 1946. Verghese Kurien, a dairy engineer who came to Anand in 1949, became its manager; the union learned to make milk powder from buffalo milk, and its products were sold under the brand name Amul. Its structure — village societies owned by the producers, which collect and test milk twice daily and pay according to fat content, federated into a district union that runs the processing plant — became known as the “Anand pattern”.

The National Dairy Development Board, set up at Anand in 1965 with Kurien as chairman, spread this pattern through Operation Flood, launched in 1970. The programme used the proceeds of sale of dairy commodities donated by the European Economic Community through the World Food Programme to build cooperative dairies in milk-producing districts and to link them to the cities in a national milk grid; by the end of the twentieth century India had become the largest milk producer in the world. Critics argued that donated commodities competed with local producers, and that urban consumers and better-off producers benefited more than the landless and women (George 1985). Its importance is nevertheless beyond dispute: it brought very large numbers of small producers, many of them households owning only one or two animals, into an organised market on their own terms.

docs.title: 14.6.1 Curd and Sour Gruels
docs.text: The simplest and most widespread fermentation is the setting of curd. Each household kept a little curd from one day to inoculate the next day’s milk — the practice microbiologists call back-slopping — so that household cultures of lactic acid bacteria were carried on, and sometimes given to new households, for long periods. Sour gruels made by fermenting rice water or cooked grain, called kāñjika or dhānyāmla in Sanskrit, are used in Āyurvedic preparations and as a sour base in cooking. In eastern India cooked rice left overnight in water (Odia pakhāḷa, Bengali pāntābhāt) is eaten in the hot season; in north India a sour fermented drink of black carrot and mustard (kāñjī) is made in winter; in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu fermented gruels of finger millet (ambali, kūḻ) are everyday foods of the poor.

docs.title: 14.6.2 Fermented Batters and the History of Idli
docs.text:
The steamed cakes (idli) and griddle pancakes (dosa) of south India are made from a batter of rice and black gram (Tamil uḷuntu, Hindi uṛad) soaked, ground and left to ferment overnight. Their early history calls for caution. Achaya noted that the Kannada Vaḍḍārādhane of Śivakoṭyācārya (920 CE) mentions iḍḍalige, and that the Lokopakāra of Cāvuṇḍarāya (c. 1025 CE) describes its preparation from black gram soaked in buttermilk, ground and seasoned — without rice, and without any mention of fermenting the batter; the Mānasollāsa (1131 CE) describes an iḍḍarikā also made from black gram (Achaya 1994, 1998; Shrigondekar 1925). Achaya therefore suggested that the fermented, steamed rice-and-pulse idli is a later development, and speculated that the technique might have come from Indonesia, where comparable fermented and steamed foods were made, at a time when south Indian dynasties had close contact with Southeast Asia. The early texts may simply not record a fermentation that cooks took for granted; the question is open.

Other fermented batters are regional: the ḍhokḷā of Gujarat, the appam of Kerala (traditionally leavened with palm toddy), the seli roṭī of the Nepali-speaking Himalaya. The jalebī, a fermented wheat batter fried and soaked in syrup, takes its name and probably its origin from the West Asian zalābiya (Achaya 1998). In the eastern Himalaya and the North-East, fermented soybean (kinema in Sikkim and Darjeeling, akhunī in Nagaland), fermented bamboo shoot, fermented leafy vegetables (gundruk) and fermented fish are central to diet and identity, with histories of their own largely outside the Sanskrit textual tradition.

docs.title: 14.6.3 Fermented Drinks and Alcohol
docs.text:
Alcoholic drinks have a long and well-documented history in India. The Vedic texts distinguish soma, the pressed plant juice of the great sacrifices, from surā, a fermented drink made from grain. Surā was offered in certain rites, notably the Sautrāmaṇī, and yet the texts already regard it with suspicion as a source of disorder. The Arthaśāstra places the manufacture and sale of liquor under a state superintendent (surādhyakṣa) who controls where it may be drunk and by whom; it names several kinds of drink — medaka, prasannā, āsava, ariṣṭa, maireya and madhu (the last made from grapes) — and describes the preparation of a ferment or starter (kiṇva) (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013). Caraka’s madya group lists many drinks by source and quality, and self-fermented medicinal preparations (āsava, ariṣṭa) remain part of Āyurvedic pharmacy (Sharma 1981).

At the same time Dharmaśāstra counts the drinking of surā among the gravest sins for brahmins (Olivelle 2005), and Buddhist and Jain ethics forbid intoxicants to monks and lay followers alike; for Jains, honey and fresh butter are also forbidden, along with alcohol and meat, because of the minute life believed to arise in them. The resulting pattern is not one of a “dry” civilisation but of drink regulated by caste, sect, gender and occasion. Palm toddy (tāḍī), the fermented sap of the palmyra, date and coconut palms, was tapped and sold by specialist castes — the Īḻavas of Kerala, the Nāṭārs of Tamil Nadu, the Īḍigas of Andhra and Karnataka, the Bhaṇḍārīs of the Konkan and others — many of whom were held to be of low rank precisely because of this work, and whose nineteenth- and twentieth-century reform movements often included a rejection of it. Many Adivasi communities brew rice beer (hanḍiyā in Jharkhand and Odisha, and many named beers in the North-East) with starter cakes of rice and plants, and distil a spirit from mahua flowers (Madhuca longifolia); these drinks have ritual and social roles that colonial and later excise laws often criminalised. When distillation began in India is debated; distilled spirits were certainly being made in the medieval period (see Chapter 18).

docs.title: 14.7.1 Pounding, Grinding and Parching
docs.text:
Grain must be freed from its husk and, for many uses, ground. The saddle quern, a flat lower stone on which grain is rubbed with a hand-held upper stone, is found at Neolithic and Harappan sites (Kenoyer 1998); the wooden mortar and pestle (ulūkhala and musala) and the winnowing basket (śūrpa) appear among the implements of the Vedic ritual, where rice for the offering cakes is husked before the fire. The rotary hand-mill (cakkī), two round stones of which the upper is turned by a peg handle, became the standard flour mill of the household in historical times; in the Himalaya, small water-driven mills (gharāṭ) ground the grain of whole villages. Husking rice with the pestle or, in Bengal and the east, with the foot-operated lever pounder (ḍhẽkī), and grinding wheat or millet at the hand-mill, were among the heaviest and most constant tasks of women. In Maharashtra the songs women sang at the grindmill (ovī) form a large oral literature. Power-driven rice and flour mills in the twentieth century relieved this labour, but also deprived many poor women who had husked rice for wages of their livelihood.

Several old preparations involve parching. Saktu (Hindi sattū) is flour of roasted barley or, later, of roasted gram, eaten mixed with water; the Ṛgveda (10.71.2) compares the wise who refine speech with their minds to men cleaning saktu through a sieve (Jamison and Brereton 2014). Parched or popped grain (lāja) is offered into the fire in the Hindu wedding rite and remains a common food as puffed rice (muṛī, kurmurā, pori). Flattened rice (pṛthuka; Hindi ciūṛā, Marathi pohe, Tamil aval) is made by soaking or parboiling paddy, heating it and pounding it flat while warm; it needs no further cooking, and the gift of a handful of flattened rice by the poor brahmin Sudāmā to his friend Kṛṣṇa in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa has made it the emblem of the humble offering.

docs.title: 14.7.2 Parboiling and Malting
docs.text: In much of eastern and southern India paddy is parboiled before husking: it is soaked, steamed or boiled, and dried, and only then milled. Parboiled grain is harder, breaks less in pounding and milling, keeps well, and has a texture and flavour preferred where it is eaten. Twentieth-century nutritional research found a further effect: some of the B vitamins, notably thiamine, migrate during parboiling into the grain, so that parboiled rice loses less of them in milling than polished raw rice. When the practice began is not known. Germinated grain was also used: sprouted, dried and ground finger millet (“ragi malt”) is a traditional food for infants in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, and malted grain was used in brewing, though early Indian brewing practice is imperfectly known.

docs.title: 14.7.3 Storage
docs.text: Grain was stored in large jars, in bins of unbaked clay or of wickerwork plastered with mud and dung (koṭhī), in underground pits in the drier regions and in granaries raised on posts in the wetter ones, often with neem leaves mixed in against insects (Chapter 12). The large buildings at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa long described as state granaries are now often interpreted as other kinds of public building (Kenoyer 1998; Possehl 2002). The storage of seed, as distinct from food grain, is treated in Chapter 9.

docs.title: 14.8 Oil Pressing
docs.text:
The commonest cooking and lamp oils of India were pressed from sesame (tila, from which comes the general Sanskrit word for oil, taila), mustard and rapeseed (sarṣapa), linseed (atasī), safflower (kusumbha), castor (eraṇḍa, used for lamps and as a purgative rather than for food) and, on the coasts, coconut (nārikela). Sesame was domesticated in South Asia and is found at Harappan sites (Fuller 2006). Groundnut, an American crop, became an important oilseed only from the nineteenth century (Chapter 9). The oil-cake left after pressing was fed to cattle and used as manure (Chapter 7).

The village oil mill, Hindi ghāṇī or kolhū, is a large mortar, usually cut from a tree trunk or built of stone, in which a heavy wooden pestle is turned by a bullock walking in a circle; the pestle grinds the seed against the side of the mortar, and the oil is drawn off while the cake remains. The same type of machine, with appropriate changes, was used to crush sugarcane. The ghāṇī is simple and can be made and repaired by village carpenters; the blindfolded bullock circling it all day became a proverbial figure of drudgery. The same mortar and pestle are also worked by machine (Figure 14.1).

Figure 14.1. An oil press (ghāṇī) with a stone mortar and a wooden pestle, here turned by a mechanical drive rather than by a bullock. The operator pushes the seed paste back towards the pestle, and the oil runs from a spout into the vessel below. Photo: Etan Doronne, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Oil-pressing was the hereditary occupation of particular castes: the Telī of north and central India, the Ghāñcī of Gujarat, the Gāṇiga of Karnataka, the Vāṇiyar (Vāṇiya Ceṭṭiyār) of the Tamil country, among others. Many of these communities also traded in oil and grain, and some rose to prosperity. Their ritual status was generally low. The Manusmṛti groups the oil-presser with the butcher, the tavern-keeper and the brothel-keeper as persons from whom a brahmin should not accept gifts (Olivelle 2005), and in Jain ethics the operation of mills and presses is one of the occupations forbidden to lay followers because of the destruction of small life it involves. In some regions the oil-pressers were divided according to whether they themselves worked the press or only traded in oil, the latter claiming higher standing.

In the twentieth century power-driven expellers and, later, solvent extraction and refining largely displaced the bullock ghāṇī, despite Gandhian programmes that promoted improved bullock presses for rural employment. “Wood-pressed” oils have recently returned as a premium product; the claims made for their nutritional superiority are largely untested.

docs.title: 14.9 Sugar and Jaggery
docs.text:
Sugarcane as a crop, the graded Sanskrit vocabulary of sugar products and the derivation of English “sugar” and “candy” from Sanskrit śarkarā and khaṇḍa are discussed in Chapter 9. The processing followed a sequence that remained recognisable into the twentieth century. Cane was cut and crushed in a press — at first a mortar-and-pestle mill of the kolhū type, later mills with two or three vertical wooden or iron rollers turned by bullocks — and the juice (ikṣurasa) was boiled in shallow iron pans over a furnace fed with the dried crushed cane (bagasse). Scum was skimmed off, often with the help of vegetable clarifying agents, and the juice thickened in stages: to a syrup or treacle (phāṇita); to a mass that set on cooling into blocks or balls of jaggery (guḍa, Hindi guṛ); and, when the thickened mass was allowed to crystallise and the molasses drained away, to a coarse granular sugar (khaṇḍa, khāṇḍsārī) and, by further purification, to white crystalline sugar (śarkarā). Large clear crystals grown slowly on threads in a concentrated syrup give rock-sugar (miśrī).

This knowledge travelled: the Tang court’s mission to Magadha to learn sugar-boiling (Chapter 9) was followed by Chinese developments of its own (Mazumdar 1998). The Hindi word cīnī for white sugar is usually taken to refer to China, suggesting that the exchange later ran in the other direction as well. Jaggery was also made from the sap of the date palm (Bengali nalen guṛ) and the palmyra (Tamil karuppaṭṭi). Bengal and the Gangetic plain were great sugar-producing regions in the Mughal and colonial periods (Chapter 18); in the twentieth century vacuum-pan factories took over refined sugar, while jaggery and khāṇḍsārī remained village industries.

docs.title: 14.10 Preservation
docs.text:
Much Indian food processing aimed at carrying food through the dry season or the monsoon. The main methods were:

  • Drying. Grains and pulses were sun-dried before storage. Pastes of pulses were shaped into small cakes and dried (vaḍī, Kannada sanḍige, Tamil vaṭakam) or rolled into thin wafers (pāpaḍ) for frying later. Unripe mango was sliced and dried and ground (āmcūr). Fish were sun-dried and salted on every coast and along the great rivers (Bengali śuṭkī, Tamil karuvāṭu), and dried meat (Sanskrit vallūra) is named in the lexicons.

  • Salting. Salt, from sea pans on the coasts and from inland lakes and rock deposits, was used for fish, for limes and other fruits, and in most pickles. Salt was taxed by states from the Arthaśāstra onwards, and the British salt monopoly was the target of Gandhi’s Salt March of 1930.

  • Pickling. Fruits and vegetables — mango, lime, gooseberry (āmalaka), bamboo shoot and many others — were preserved with salt, oil, spices and sometimes sour agents and the sun. The common modern word acār is Persian, but salted and spiced preserves of fruits are older.

  • Cooking in fat and sugar. Ghee, oil and sugar syrup were themselves preservatives: sweets made with khoa or chhena keep only briefly, but sweets fried in ghee and soaked in syrup, or sugar-based sweets with little water, keep for days or weeks, and preserves of fruits in syrup (murabbā, a word of Arabic origin that came through Persian) became popular under the Indo-Islamic courts.

These are empirical methods. Their effect can be described in modern terms — drying, salt and sugar lower the water available to micro-organisms, and acid and oil exclude many of them — without implying that they were designed on that basis; and in a monsoon climate their limits were real.

docs.title: 14.11 Texts on Food and Cookery
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads already make food a theme of philosophical reflection: in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad Bhṛgu first perceives that brahman is food (annaṃ brahmeti vyajānāt, 3.2; Chapter 2). Practical cookery, however, is recorded mainly in much later works and in incidental descriptions in poetry, narrative, temple inscriptions and travellers’ accounts (Achaya 1994).

The richest early account is the section on food in the Mānasollāsa of the Cālukya king Someśvara III (1131 CE), the encyclopaedia of royal enjoyments described in Chapter 3 (Shrigondekar 1925). It describes the king’s meal: rice, pulses and vegetables; meat, including pork, game and fish, roasted, fried or cooked in sauces; breads and fried cakes; sweets of milk, grain, jaggery and ghee; and drinks. Its frank treatment of meat at a Hindu court is a useful corrective to the assumption that “traditional” Indian food was everywhere vegetarian. A little earlier the Kannada Lokopakāra of Cāvuṇḍarāya (c. 1025 CE), a compendium of useful knowledge, includes a section on cookery as well as on plants (Ayangarya 2006).

Several later Sanskrit works are devoted to cookery or dietetics, though their dates and authorship are often uncertain. The Pākadarpaṇa is attributed to Nala, the epic king who, in the Mahābhārata, served in disguise as charioteer and cook to King Ṛtuparṇa; the attribution is legendary and the text is probably medieval. The Kṣemakutūhala of Kṣemaśarman, usually placed in the sixteenth century, combines cookery with Āyurvedic dietetics. The Bhojanakutūhala of Raghunātha, generally assigned to the later seventeenth century in Maharashtra, is a compilation on foods and their qualities drawn from earlier dietetic and culinary sources. K. T. Achaya summarises the contents of all three (Achaya 1994); they are described here from his account.

The Indo-Islamic courts produced their own culinary literature. The Niʿmatnāma, an illustrated Persian book of recipes compiled for the sultans of Malwa at Mandu around 1500, records the dishes, perfumes and remedies of a cuisine that combined Persian and Indian elements; it has been translated by Norah Titley (Titley 2005). The Āʾīn-i Akbarī describes Akbar’s kitchen and gives recipes for the imperial table, from vegetarian dishes to pulāʾo and meat preparations (Abū’l-Faẓl 1873). Through such kitchens, and the cooks and confectioners of the Sultanate and Mughal cities, much of what is now thought of as “Indian” food took shape.

docs.title: 14.12 Food, Purity and Caste
docs.text:
Food in India has never been only nourishment; it has also been a principal medium through which caste rank was expressed and enforced. The Dharmaśāstras set out at length whose food a brahmin may and may not accept, and treat the acceptance of food from those of low status as polluting (Olivelle 2005). In practice, rules of commensality — who may eat with whom, who may cook for whom, from whose hands one may take water — were among the most closely watched boundaries between castes, and anthropologists working in twentieth-century villages found that the ranking of castes could be reconstructed from the transactions of food among them (Marriott 1968).

A central distinction in north India was between kaccā food, cooked in water (boiled rice, lentils), which was highly vulnerable to pollution and was normally accepted only from one’s own caste or a higher one, and pakkā food, fried in ghee or oil, which was less vulnerable and could be accepted more widely — one reason why ghee-fried foods were served at feasts where several castes were present, and why brahmin cooks were widely employed. At the bottom of the order, Dalit communities were excluded from shared wells and kitchens, and the eating of beef or of the flesh of dead cattle, forced on some by poverty and by the work of removing carcasses, was made a mark of their exclusion (Chapters 13 and 18). Vegetarianism itself carried caste meanings: it was a mark of high status for brahmins and many trading castes, and was adopted by groups seeking higher rank, while the majority of Indians, then as now, ate meat or fish when they could.

These rules were never uniform. They varied by region and sect, were relaxed in some devotional movements and pilgrimage centres — the shared food of the Jagannātha temple at Puri is the classic example — and were challenged by Buddhist, Jain, Sikh, Bhakti, Islamic and modern reform movements. The common kitchen (laṅgar) of the Sikh gurdwaras, at which all sit together to eat, was a deliberate rejection of caste commensality. Urban life has weakened the rules in public, though they remain powerful in marriage and the home.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Dairy products were central to Indian food and ritual from the Vedic period, and medical and lexical texts record a graded vocabulary of milk products. Acid-curdled cheeses and the chhena sweets of Bengal appear to be comparatively recent, possibly owing something to Portuguese example; the twentieth century brought the Anand cooperative of 1946 and Operation Flood from 1970. Fermentation produced curd, sour gruels, batters whose early history remains uncertain, and alcoholic drinks regulated by state, caste and sect. Grain was pounded, ground, parched, flattened and parboiled, mostly by women; oil was pressed in the bullock ghāṇī by castes of low ritual rank; Tang China sought India’s sugar-making knowledge; and drying, salting, pickling and cooking in fat and sugar carried food through the year. Cookery texts from the Mānasollāsa to the Āʾīn-i Akbarī record court cuisines, while rules of purity made food an instrument of caste. The knowledge was real and largely unwritten; the medical virtues claimed for it belong to Volume 13 and to critical evaluation.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Achaya (1994) is the standard historical survey of Indian food, and Achaya (1998) a reference work on individual foods and terms. Mazumdar (1998) places Indian sugar technology in an Asian context. Shrigondekar (1925) edits the Mānasollāsa, and Abū’l-Faẓl (1873) translates the Āʾīn-i Akbarī. On dietetics see Sharma (1981) and Volume 13.

docs.title: Chapter 15: Elephants and Horses: Hastyāyurveda and Aśvaśāstra
15.1 Two Royal Animals
docs.text:
Of all the animals discussed in this volume, the elephant and the horse were the least connected with the peasant economy and the most closely connected with kings. Both were instruments of war and emblems of sovereignty; both had their own bodies of specialised knowledge, preserved in Sanskrit treatises on their selection, care, training and medicine; and both were sources of great expense to the states that maintained them. Their histories in India are nevertheless almost opposite. The Asian elephant is native to the subcontinent, and Indian kings obtained their elephants by capturing them from the wild rather than by breeding them. The horse was not native to most of South Asia, did not thrive in much of its climate, and for over two thousand years Indian rulers depended heavily on horses imported from Central Asia, Iran and Arabia. These contrasting histories shaped the knowledge traditions examined in this chapter (Trautmann 2015; Digby 1971).

Warfare with elephants and cavalry is treated in Volume 20 (Yuddha and Dhanurveda); this chapter concentrates on the animals themselves and on the knowledge of their keepers.

docs.title: 15.2 Elephants in Early India
docs.text: Elephants appear on the seals of the Indus civilisation, and their bones are found at Harappan sites, but there is no clear evidence that Harappans tamed them (Kenoyer 1998; Possehl 2002). The capture, taming and use of elephants for riding, work and war appear in the historical record in the Ganga valley in the first millennium BCE. Thomas Trautmann has argued that the military use of captive elephants was an Indian development, which spread from India to Southeast Asia, to the Achaemenid and Hellenistic kingdoms of the west and ultimately to Carthage (Trautmann 2015). Greek writers record that Seleucus I, after his war with Candragupta Maurya around 303 BCE, received five hundred elephants as part of the settlement, and that these animals played a part in the wars of his successors.

docs.title: 15.2.1 Capture Rather Than Breeding
docs.text:
Trautmann’s central observation is that Indian kings, with few exceptions, did not breed elephants in captivity. An elephant takes some fifteen to twenty years to reach working maturity, and a female in calf or nursing a calf cannot work; it was cheaper to capture adult animals from the wild and train them. The supply of war elephants therefore depended on the preservation of wild elephant populations and of the forests in which they lived. This, Trautmann argues, gave Indian kings a direct interest in protecting forests and forest peoples, who were the capturers and first trainers of elephants (Trautmann 2015).

The Arthaśāstra reflects exactly this interest. It provides for elephant forests (nāgavana) at the frontiers of the kingdom, under a superintendent with a staff of guards, and treats the killing of an elephant there as a capital offence. Its chapters on the superintendent of elephants describe the stables, the rations, the staff — physicians, trainers, grooms, cooks, guards — and the classes of trained elephant: those under training (damya), those trained for war (sāṃnāhya), those for riding (aupavāhya) and the vicious (vyāla) (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013). Like the rest of the Arthaśāstra, these chapters describe an administrative ideal; their dating follows that of the text as a whole (c. 50 BCE–300 CE in Olivelle’s analysis).

docs.title: 15.3 The Literature of Elephant Science
docs.text: The body of Sanskrit knowledge about elephants is called gajaśāstra or hastividyā; its medical branch is hastyāyurveda or gajacikitsā. Its two best-known texts are the Hastyāyurveda ascribed to the sage Pālakāpya and the much shorter Mātaṅgalīlā of Nīlakaṇṭha.

docs.title: 15.3.1 Pālakāpya’s Hastyāyurveda
docs.text:
The Hastyāyurveda is a large work in prose and verse, printed in 1894 in the Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series (Pālakāpya 1894). It is framed as a dialogue between the sage Pālakāpya and King Romapāda of Aṅga, whose capital was Campā in the eastern Ganga plain. In the legend Pālakāpya was born of an elephant mother and grew up among elephants in the forest; when Romapāda’s men captured the wild herd, the sage followed it to the court and there taught the king the knowledge of elephants and their diseases.

The work is divided into four sections (sthāna) with a total of 160 chapters:

  • Mahārogasthāna, on the major diseases;

  • Kṣudrarogasthāna, on the minor diseases;

  • Śalyasthāna, on surgery, chiefly the extraction of foreign bodies such as arrows and spear-heads and the treatment of wounds;

  • Uttarasthāna, the “later section”, on matters such as feeding, bathing, oiling, regimen by season and general care.

Disease is explained, as in human Āyurveda, through the three doṣas and the other categories of Āyurvedic physiology, and the treatments — oils, decoctions, purgation, enemas, fumigation, bleeding, surgery and dietary regimen — correspond closely to those of human medicine (Volume 13). The work also contains a great deal of mythology, auspicious and inauspicious marks, and ritual.

The date of the Hastyāyurveda is uncertain. The legend of Pālakāpya is old, and elephant physicians are mentioned in the Arthaśāstra; but the text as printed is a compilation that presupposes developed Āyurvedic doctrine, and it is best placed somewhere in the first millennium CE, with the possibility of later additions (Meulenbeld 1999). Older claims that it is a work of the third century BCE or earlier have no basis.

docs.title: 15.3.2 The Mātaṅgalīlā
docs.text:
The Mātaṅgalīlā (“The Sport of Elephants”) of Nīlakaṇṭha, a short work of uncertain date, probably from Kerala, was translated by Franklin Edgerton under the title The Elephant-Lore of the Hindus (Edgerton 1931). It is a compact handbook in verse that summarises the tradition: the myth that the first elephants were born from the shell of the cosmic egg from which the sun emerged, and the legend that elephants once had wings and flew until they were cursed by a sage whose tree they had broken; the auspicious marks of good elephants; the classes of elephant — in the commonest scheme, bhadra, manda and mṛga, with a mixed class (saṅkīrṇa) — distinguished by build, proportions and temperament; the stages of life; the signs and stages of musth (mada); the methods of capture; and the qualities of a good elephant-keeper. Edgerton’s translation remains the most accessible introduction to the subject for readers without Sanskrit. It should not be confused with the Hastyāyurveda, which is a different and much larger work. Figure 15.1 sets the divisions of the two texts beside the working classes of the Arthaśāstra’s stables.

Figure 15.1. Three ways of ordering knowledge about elephants: the four sections of Pālakāpya’s Hastyāyurveda, the classes of elephant in the Mātaṅgalīlā (with literal glosses of their names), and the working classes of the Arthaśāstra’s elephant stables. After Pālakāpya (1894), Edgerton (1931) and Kangle (1965); see Section 15.3.

docs.title: 15.3.3 Other Sources
docs.text: Elephant lore is also found in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā (on the marks of elephants), in Purāṇas such as the Agni Purāṇa, which has chapters on the treatment of elephants and horses, and in the Mānasollāsa (Section 3.8), whose sections on royal pleasures include the training and sports of elephants (Shrigondekar 1925). A number of later elephant treatises survive in manuscript, many of them unpublished.

docs.title: 15.4.1 Methods of Capture
docs.text: The texts and later observers describe several methods of capture. Elephants were driven into concealed pits; noosed from the backs of trained elephants; lured by tame females used as decoys; or, in the largest operations, driven by lines of beaters into a stockade — the kheddā of Bengal, Assam and Mysore. The British officer G. P. Sanderson, who conducted kheddā operations for the Mysore government in the 1870s, left a detailed account of the method and of the skills of the forest people on whom it depended (Sanderson 1878). The capturers and first trainers were very often members of forest communities, a fact that the Sanskrit texts acknowledge only indirectly.

docs.title: 15.4.2 The Mahout
docs.text: The trained elephant was managed by a rider and keeper — in Sanskrit hastipaka, hastyārohaka or mahāmātra, whence the modern “mahout” (Hindi mahāvat). The keeper controlled the animal with voice commands, pressure of the feet behind the ears and the goad (aṅkuśa). The Mātaṅgalīlā lists the qualities of a good keeper: knowledge of the elephant’s nature and moods, patience, courage and kindness (Edgerton 1931). In practice the craft was learned by apprenticeship, often within families or communities of hereditary mahouts, and much of it was never written down. Mahouts in Kerala, Karnataka, Assam and Sri Lanka still use command vocabularies inherited from these traditions.

docs.title: 15.4.3 Musth
docs.text:
All the elephant texts give careful attention to musth (mada), the periodic state in adult males marked by secretion from the temporal glands, dribbling of urine and heightened aggression. The texts describe its stages and its signs and prescribe changes of diet and restraint during it; they also treat the flow of mada as a sign of vigour and therefore of value in a war elephant. Modern research has shown that musth is associated with greatly raised levels of testosterone and plays an important part in the reproductive competition of bulls (Sukumar 2003). The traditional descriptions of its outward signs are accurate observations; their physiological explanations are those of Āyurveda.

Health and Safety Note

The treatments described in the elephant and horse treatises are reported here as historical evidence of what the texts prescribe. Several involve purgatives, bleeding, cautery or substances that are toxic in quantity, and none has been tested by modern veterinary science. They are not a guide to the care or treatment of animals. Sick animals should be seen by a qualified veterinarian; the care of captive elephants in particular is a specialised field governed in India by law and by veterinary guidelines.

docs.title: 15.5 Elephants, Kings and Empires
docs.text:
In the ideal of the Indian army as four-limbed (caturaṅga) — infantry, cavalry, chariots and elephants — the elephant was the most prestigious arm and the king’s own mount (Figure 15.2). The Delhi Sultans, whose cavalry came from the Persianate north-west, quickly adopted the elephant as well, obtaining animals by capture, purchase and tribute from Bengal, Odisha and the forests of central India; Simon Digby showed how the control of the supply routes for war-horses and elephants shaped the politics of the Sultanate (Digby 1971). The Mughals maintained very large elephant establishments, and the Āʾīn-i Akbarī records Akbar’s elephant stables in detail — the classes of elephants, their rations and the numbers of attendants assigned to each (Abū’l-Faẓl 1873; Gommans 2002). Bābur, a newcomer from Central Asia, recorded in his memoirs his first impressions of the Indian elephant and its uses (Thackston 1996).

Elephants also served in ceremony and religion. They carried kings and images in procession, were kept by temples, and in Kerala remain central to temple festivals (pūram); the Dasarā procession at Mysore is another famous example. Ivory was worked into a variety of objects from early times (see Volume 17).

Figure 15.2. The building known as the “Elephant Stables” in the royal centre of Vijayanagara (Hampi), Karnataka, 15th–16th centuries: a row of domed chambers, each large enough for an elephant, on either side of a central pavilion. Photo: iMahesh, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 15.6 The Elephant in Religion and Art
docs.text: The elephant’s place in Indian religion and art is older and wider than its use in war. In Vedic and epic mythology Indra rides the white elephant Airāvata, born from the churning of the ocean, and elephants of the quarters (diggaja) support the world at its eight directions. The elephant-headed Gaṇeśa, remover of obstacles, became from the Gupta period onwards one of the most widely worshipped deities of India. The motif of Gajalakṣmī, the goddess Lakṣmī lustrated by two elephants pouring water over her from pots held in their trunks, appears on early Buddhist monuments such as the railings of Bharhut and Sanchi and on coins, and remained a symbol of prosperity and royal fortune. In Buddhist tradition Queen Māyā dreamed of a white elephant entering her side before the Buddha’s birth, and the Jātaka stories include tales in which the Bodhisattva is born as an elephant. The great rock-cut elephants of Mamallapuram and the elephant friezes of temple plinths across the south show how closely the animal was tied to the image of royal and divine power.

docs.title: 15.7 Colonial Capture and Protection
docs.text: Under colonial rule the capture of wild elephants continued on a large scale, now organised by forest departments and private contractors for the army, the timber industry and sale. Two methods were especially important: the kheddā stockade drive, practised in Mysore, Assam and Bengal, and melā shikār in Assam, in which riders on trained elephants pursued and noosed wild animals. Large numbers of captured elephants died in the process or soon afterwards. At the same time the government recognised that unrestricted killing threatened the supply: the Madras presidency protected wild elephants by law in 1873, and the Elephants’ Preservation Act of 1879 extended protection more widely, while still permitting capture under licence and the killing of animals declared dangerous (Rangarajan 2001; Sukumar 2003). Working elephants hauled timber in the forests of the Western Ghats, Assam and Burma well into the twentieth century. The great elephant fairs, of which the Sonepur fair at the confluence of the Gaṇḍak and the Ganga in Bihar was the most famous, were for long the main markets for captive elephants; the sale of elephants has since been restricted by wildlife law.

docs.title: 15.8 Elephants Today
docs.text: The Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) is classified as endangered. India holds the largest share of the remaining wild population, but its range has been greatly reduced and fragmented by agriculture, roads, mining and settlement, and conflict between elephants and farmers — crop raiding on one side, the killing of elephants on the other — is now among the most serious conservation problems in the country (Sukumar 2003). The Government of India launched Project Elephant in 1992 to protect elephant habitat and corridors. Large numbers of elephants also live in captivity, in temples, with private owners and in forest departments, where their welfare — chaining, inadequate exercise, unsuitable diets, the stress of festivals — has become a matter of legal and public concern. Raman Sukumar’s ecological work has combined field biology with the history of the human–elephant relationship and is the starting point for modern study (Sukumar 2003).

docs.title: 15.9.1 Archaeology and the Ṛgveda
docs.text: No securely identified domestic horse has been found at Mature Harappan sites. Claims for horse remains at a few Harappan and late Harappan sites have been disputed by specialists, and the earliest widely accepted evidence for domestic horses in South Asia belongs to the second millennium BCE (Meadow 1996; Possehl 2002). Claims that Harappan terracotta figurines represent horses have not been accepted. In the Ṛgveda, by contrast, the horse (aśva) and the light chariot with spoked wheels are everywhere: in the racing and warfare of gods and men, in the hymns to the sacrificial horse (Ṛgveda 1.162 and 1.163), and in the names of deities such as the Aśvins (Jamison and Brereton 2014). The contrast is one of the main pieces of evidence in the debate over the relationship between the Indus civilisation and the speakers of Vedic Sanskrit (see Volume 1).

docs.title: 15.9.2 The Horse Sacrifice
docs.text:
The aśvamedha, the horse sacrifice performed by a king claiming paramount sovereignty, is described at length in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa and the ritual sūtras. A consecrated stallion was allowed to wander for a year, guarded by armed men, and then sacrificed. Several historical kings, from the Śuṅga Puṣyamitra to the Gupta Samudragupta, claimed to have performed it. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad opens with a meditation that identifies the sacrificial horse with the cosmos (Olivelle 1998):

Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.1.1

uṣā vā aśvasya medhyasya śiraḥ “The dawn, clearly, is the head of the sacrificial horse.”

The passage goes on to identify the horse’s eye with the sun, its breath with the wind and its body with the year. It is a ritual and contemplative identification. The Ṛgveda already gives the Sun a chariot drawn by seven mares (1.50.8), an image that later mythology and temple art developed; the number seven belongs to a widespread pattern of Vedic symbolism and is not an observation of the colours of sunlight.

docs.title: 15.10 Horses and the Horse Trade
docs.text: Much of the subcontinent is poorly suited to breeding horses: the humid climate of the south and east, the lack of suitable grazing, and diseases took a heavy toll, and Indian-bred horses were generally regarded as inferior to imported ones. The arid north-west — Sindh, Punjab, Rajasthan, Kathiawar — and the Deccan plateau were partial exceptions, and these regions developed their own horse-breeding traditions (Gommans 2002). For the most part, however, Indian states obtained cavalry horses by import: overland from Central Asia and Afghanistan through the passes of the north-west, and by sea from the Persian Gulf and Arabia to the ports of Gujarat, the Konkan, Malabar and the Coromandel coast (Digby 1971). Late-thirteenth-century observers, among them Marco Polo, described the large sums spent by south Indian kings on imported Arabian horses, many of which soon died; in the sixteenth century the horse trade through Goa was a vital interest of the Vijayanagara kings. Sanskrit horse texts reflect this situation in their lists of horses by country of origin, which name the north-western regions (Sindhu, Kamboja, Bāhlīka/Balkh) and Persia among the best sources.

docs.title: 15.11.1 Śālihotra and the Horse Texts
docs.text:
In Sanskrit tradition the founder of horse science (aśvaśāstra, aśvāyurveda) is the sage Śālihotra, and the name became so closely associated with horse medicine that in Hindi and Urdu a horse doctor is still called a sālotrī. The epic tradition also associates expert knowledge of horses with Nakula, one of the five Pāṇḍavas. A number of works circulate under Śālihotra’s name, in different recensions; like the Hastyāyurveda, they presuppose developed Āyurvedic doctrine, and in their surviving forms they are medieval. Older claims that Śālihotra wrote in the third century BCE or earlier rest on tradition alone. Other horse treatises include the Aśvacikitsita ascribed to Nakula, the Aśvavaidyaka of Jayadatta, and horse sections in the Agni Purāṇa and in Someśvara’s Mānasollāsa (Shrigondekar 1925; Meulenbeld 1999).

Śālihotra material was adapted into Persian from the Sultanate period onwards, and Persian versions known as Sālotar circulated widely; illustrated Persian horse books were produced at Mughal and regional courts. These works combined Indian material with the hippology of the Islamic world, which had its own rich tradition. The English word “farrier”, which is sometimes said to derive from Śālihotra, in fact comes through French from Latin ferrarius, “worker in iron”, and has nothing to do with Indian horse science.

docs.title: 15.11.2 Contents of the Horse Treatises
docs.text:
The horse treatises cover broadly similar ground:

  • the mythical origin of horses — from the churning of the ocean, which produced the divine horse Uccaiḥśravas, and the legend that horses once had wings;

  • the classification of horses by place of origin, colour, build and temperament, and their auspicious and inauspicious marks, among which the position of hair whorls (āvarta) is particularly important — a feature shared with Arab and Persian hippology;

  • judging age by the teeth, and the qualities of a good horse for war, riding and display;

  • stable construction, grooming, feeding and exercise, and regimen by season;

  • the diseases of horses, explained through the doṣas, and their treatments by oils, decoctions, fumigation, bleeding, cautery and surgery.

Like the elephant texts, they record a long experience of keeping horses and contain accurate descriptions of external signs. Their medical theory is Āyurvedic, and their treatments are of historical interest only (see the safety note above).

docs.title: 15.12 The Horse in Indian Art and Culture
docs.text:
Because horses were costly and associated with kings and warriors, they became potent symbols. The Sun god Sūrya is shown driving a chariot drawn by seven horses, and the thirteenth-century Sun temple at Konark in Odisha was conceived as his colossal stone chariot, with carved wheels and rearing horses. Equestrian figures of warriors and heroes appear on memorial stones (vīrakal) of the Deccan and the south, and the terracotta horses offered to village guardian deities such as Aiyaṉār in Tamil Nadu, and in the Bankura region of Bengal, are among the best-known forms of Indian folk art. Rajput and Mughal painting produced a rich tradition of equestrian portraits, and Mughal and Deccani artists painted individual horses from the royal stables with the same care as they gave to the emperors’ elephants. The great animal fairs at Pushkar and Sonepur (Section 13.10) were also horse markets.

The keeping of horses also involved specialist communities: grooms (sāīs), horse-dealers, farriers and horse-doctors, whose skills, like those of mahouts, were learned within families. Many of the dealers who brought horses from Central Asia and Afghanistan in the Mughal period were Afghans and Central Asians, while the grooms and keepers in Indian stables were drawn from local service communities (Gommans 2002).

docs.title: 15.13 Horse Breeds and Horse Cultures
docs.text:
Several distinctive horse and pony breeds are recognised in India today: the Marwari of Rajasthan and the Kathiawari of Gujarat, both with their characteristic inward-curving ear tips; the Manipuri pony, ridden in the Manipuri game of sagol kangjei, from which British officers in Manipur and Cachar learned modern polo in the mid-nineteenth century; and the hill ponies of the Himalaya — Spiti, Zanskari and Bhutia. Their histories are poorly documented before the modern period, and claims that particular modern breeds descend from horses named in Sanskrit texts cannot be verified. The Marathas, whose light cavalry dominated eighteenth-century warfare, bred horses in the Bhīmā valley of the Deccan (the Bhīmthaḍī horse), a breed that has become rare (Gommans 2002).

Under colonial rule the army established stud farms to breed remounts; the estate at Pusa in Bihar, where the agricultural research institute was founded in 1905, had earlier been a government stud. Modern veterinary education in India began in the late nineteenth century, partly to serve the army’s horses and the cattle of the countryside (see Chapter 13).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Elephants and horses were the animals of kings. The elephant, native and wild-caught, gave rise to a knowledge tradition — Pālakāpya’s Hastyāyurveda, the Mātaṅgalīlā, the Arthaśāstra’s elephant forests — rooted in the forest and in the skills of capturers and mahouts, and its supply depended on preserving the forests where elephants lived. The horse, largely imported and expensive, gave rise to the aśvaśāstra literature ascribed to Śālihotra, which travelled into Persian as Sālotar and met the hippology of the Islamic world. Both traditions are medieval in their surviving texts, both applied the framework of Āyurveda to animals, and both preserve careful observation alongside myth and ritual. Today the elephant is an endangered species whose survival depends on reconciling it with farmers; the Indian horse breeds are a small but distinctive heritage.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Trautmann (2015) is the essential historical study of elephants and kings; Edgerton (1931) translates the Mātaṅgalīlā; Sukumar (2003) covers elephant biology and conservation. For horses and the horse trade see Digby (1971) and Gommans (2002); for the medical literature, Meulenbeld (1999).

docs.title: Chapter 16: Wild Animals: Hunting, Protection and Conservation
16.1 Wild Animals beside the Field
docs.text:
The farmers whose knowledge this volume describes never worked in a landscape empty of wild animals. Deer and antelope grazed their crops, wild pigs rooted in their fields, elephants raided their millet and paddy, wolves, leopards and tigers took their goats and cattle, and monkeys stripped their orchards. Wild animals were also food, a source of skins, horns, ivory and medicines, objects of worship and fear, and the quarry of kings. The history of wild animals in India is therefore part of agrarian history: the expansion of cultivation over thousands of years was also the contraction of wild habitat, and the long story of hunting, from the ritual and royal hunts of the texts to the colonial war on “vermin”, was in large part a story about who controlled the land and its produce.

This chapter follows the larger wild mammals of South Asia from rock art and the Harappan seals, through texts on medicine, statecraft and ethics, to the royal, Mughal and colonial hunt and the rise of modern wildlife protection. Elephants are treated in Chapter 15, birds (including falconry) in Chapter 17, and forests, sacred groves and the Bishnoi in Chapter 11; this chapter refers to them rather than repeating them.

One caution runs throughout. Texts that forbid killing, kings who protected particular animals and communities that revere particular species are an important part of this history, but they are not evidence of an ancient “conservation policy” in the modern sense. They coexisted, often in the same courts and the same centuries, with enthusiastic hunting and with the steady clearance of forest for the plough.

docs.title: 16.2 Early Evidence: Rock Art, Seals and Names
16.2.1 Hunters in Rock Art
docs.text: The oldest images of Indian wild animals are the rock paintings of central India, above all those of the rock shelters of Bhimbetka near Bhopal, a World Heritage Site. Their dating is debated, but the earliest layers are generally assigned to the Mesolithic. They show deer, wild cattle, boar, elephants, rhinoceros and big cats, often in scenes of hunting with bows, spears and traps, and later layers add horses, riders and armed warriors (Singh 2008). The animal bones from Mesolithic and early Neolithic sites, and from the earliest levels at Mehrgarh, show that hunting of gazelle, deer, wild cattle, wild pig and the onager long continued alongside the first herding and farming (Chapter 2).

docs.title: 16.2.2 The Harappan Seals
docs.text: The square stamp seals of the Mature Harappan civilisation (c. 2600–1900 BCE) are carved with animals. The most frequent is the one-horned animal usually called the “unicorn”, which is not a real species; but the seals also show, with great naturalism, the zebu bull, the water buffalo, the elephant, the rhinoceros and the tiger (Kenoyer 1998; Possehl 2002). On a famous seal from Mohenjo-daro a seated, horned figure is surrounded by an elephant, a tiger, a rhinoceros and a buffalo, with deer or antelopes below the seat. John Marshall identified the figure as a “proto-Śiva” in his aspect as Paśupati, lord of animals; that identification is now widely doubted, and the meaning of the scene is unknown. The presence of these animals on seals does not mean that they were domesticated; it does show that the rhinoceros and the tiger lived in or near the Indus plains and that they mattered to the people who made the seals.

docs.title: 16.2.3 Names in the Vedic and Later Texts
docs.text:
The Ṛgveda knows many wild animals, mostly as images in hymns: the lion (siṃha), an image of terrifying strength; the wolf (vṛka), the archetypal enemy of the herds; the bear (ṛkṣa); the wild boar (varāha); the monkey (kapi); and the elephant, called the “beast with a hand” (mṛga hastin) (Jamison and Brereton 2014). The word mṛga originally meant any wild beast, as opposed to domestic animals (paśu); only later did it come to mean above all the deer and antelope, so that the king of beasts, the lion, is mṛgarāja or mṛgendra, and hunting itself is mṛgayā, “the pursuit of wild animals”. The tiger (vyāghra) is not mentioned in the Ṛgveda but appears in the Atharvaveda and later Vedic texts, and its skin is spread for the king in the royal consecration; scholars have often linked its arrival in the texts with the movement of Vedic culture east into the forested Ganga valley, though the argument from silence is not conclusive.

Some of the commoner Sanskrit and Tamil names are listed in Table 16.1. Identifications are often uncertain, because the same word could denote different animals in different periods and regions.

Table 16.1. Some names of wild mammals in Sanskrit and Tamil, with their usual identifications. Term Identification Notes mṛga wild animal; deer General sense “wild beast” in early texts; later chiefly deer and antelope. siṃha, mṛgendra lion The Asiatic lion, once widespread in north-western and central India. vyāghra; Tamil puli tiger Absent from the Ṛgveda; prominent from the Atharvaveda onwards. dvīpin, citraka leopard; cheetah Dvīpin is usually the leopard; citraka (“spotted”) can mean the leopard or the cheetah, and is the source of Hindi cītā. hastin, gaja; Tamil yāṉai elephant See Chapter 15. khaḍga, gaṇḍa rhinoceros The Indian one-horned rhinoceros. mahiṣa buffalo Wild and domestic water buffalo are not always distinguished. gavaya, gaura wild cattle Identifications (gaur, gayal, nilgai) are uncertain and disputed. varāha, sūkara; Tamil paṉṟi wild pig Also the boar incarnation of Viṣṇu. vṛka wolf The enemy of the herds in Vedic imagery. ṛkṣa, bhalluka; Tamil karaṭi bear Chiefly the sloth bear. kapi, vānara, markaṭa monkey Including langurs and macaques. kṛṣṇasāra, eṇa, hariṇa; Tamil māṉ antelope, deer Kṛṣṇasāra is the blackbuck, whose range was held to define land fit for Vedic ritual. śṛgāla, gomāyu jackal A stock figure of cunning in the fables. tarakṣu hyena The striped hyena.

The blackbuck had a special place. The Manusmṛti (2.23) defines the land fit for sacrifice as the country where the black antelope roams by nature (Olivelle 2005), and the skin of the black antelope was used in Vedic ritual and by students and ascetics. A wild animal thus served as the boundary marker of a ritual geography — a reminder that the open plains of northern and western India, the jāṅgala of the medical texts, were once antelope country.

docs.title: 16.3 Animals in Āyurvedic Classification
docs.text:
The fullest systematic classification of wild animals in classical Sanskrit is found not in a work of natural history but in the dietetic chapters of the medical compendia, because meat was an important part of Āyurvedic diet and therapy. Caraka’s chapter on food and drink (Sūtrasthāna 27) groups the animals whose flesh may be eaten into eight classes according to their habitat and manner of feeding (Table 16.2) (Sharma 1981). Suśruta (Sūtrasthāna 46) divides meats first into those of dry-land (jāṅgala) and wet-land (ānūpa) animals and then subdivides each (Bhishagratna 1907).

Table 16.2. The eight classes of animals whose meat is discussed in the Caraka-saṃhitā (Sūtrasthāna 27), with examples. After Sharma (1981) and Zimmermann (1987). Class Meaning Examples prasaha those that seize their food Predators such as the lion, tiger, leopard, wolf, hyena and jackal, and birds such as hawks, crows and vultures. bhūmiśaya those that lie in the ground Burrowing animals such as the porcupine and the monitor lizard. ānūpa marsh animals Large animals of wet country: buffalo, rhinoceros, boar, elephant. vāriśaya water-dwellers Fish, tortoises, crabs. vāricara those that move on water Water birds: geese, ducks, cranes. jāṅgala dry-land animals Deer and antelope. viṣkira scatterers Birds that scratch and scatter their food: quails, partridges, peafowl, junglefowl. pratuda peckers Birds that peck: pigeons, parrots and others.

Francis Zimmermann’s study of these chapters showed that they rest on an ecological picture of the subcontinent (Zimmermann 1987). Each kind of land (deśa) has its characteristic animals, and the qualities of an animal’s flesh reflect those of its habitat: the meat of the antelope and the deer of the dry, open jāṅgala is light, wholesome and the best for general use, whereas that of the heavy, slow animals of the marshy ānūpa is heavy and productive of phlegm. The ideal landscape of Āyurveda was a dry savanna rich in game (Chapter 1). The scheme is dietetic, not zoological — it groups the lion with the crow because they feed alike — but it rests on careful attention to where and how animals live. The therapeutic uses of meats and of other animal products in Āyurveda are discussed in Volume 13 (Āyurveda).

Health and Safety Note

The medical texts prescribe the meat, fat, horn, bile and other products of many wild animals. These prescriptions are described here as historical evidence. Many of the animals concerned are now protected by law, and the hunting of them and the possession of or trade in their parts are criminal offences under the Wild Life (Protection) Act; illegal trade in animal parts for medicine is one of the main threats to species such as the tiger, rhinoceros and pangolin. Nothing in this chapter is a recommendation to use any animal product as medicine.

docs.title: 16.4 Mṛgayā: Hunting as Royal Sport and Royal Vice
16.4.1 The Arthaśāstra
docs.text:
The literature of statecraft treated the hunt with a mixture of approval and suspicion. The Arthaśāstra (composite, c. 50 BCE–300 CE) provides for an enclosed game forest (mṛgavana) for the king’s recreation, stocked with animals whose claws and teeth have been removed or which have otherwise been rendered harmless, and for forests in which animals are given safety; killing or injuring animals in protected forests is fined (Chapter 11, Section 11.3) (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013).

In its discussion of the vices (vyasana) of the king, the Arthaśāstra stages a debate on whether hunting or gambling is the worse. An earlier teacher holds that hunting is worse, because it exposes the king to robbers, enemies, wild beasts, forest fires, falls, losing his way, hunger and thirst, and so to the loss of life. The text’s own view is that gambling is worse, and it credits hunting with real benefits: exercise, the reduction of phlegm, bile, fat and sweat, practice in hitting moving and stationary targets, and knowledge of the behaviour of animals when angry or afraid (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013). Hunting is thus treated as a kind of military training, a theme taken up in Volume 20 (Yuddha and Dhanurveda).

docs.title: 16.4.2 The Law Books and the Epics
docs.text:
The Manusmṛti (c. 2nd century CE) is less indulgent. Among the ten vices of a king that arise from desire, it names hunting first, and it counts hunting with drinking, gambling and women as the four most ruinous of them (Olivelle 2005). Its argument that meat cannot be obtained without injury to living creatures applies to the hunt as to the slaughterhouse, though Manu still permits meat in many circumstances.

The epics are full of hunting, and many of their decisive misfortunes begin with it. In the Rāmāyaṇa, King Daśaratha as a young man, hunting by night beside the Sarayū, shoots at a sound he takes for an elephant drinking and kills the son of a blind ascetic couple; the dying father’s curse, that Daśaratha too will die grieving for a son, is fulfilled when Rāma goes into exile. In the Mahābhārata, Pāṇḍu shoots a deer in the act of mating, which turns out to be a sage who had taken that form, and is cursed to die if he ever approaches his wives. In these stories the hunt is a royal privilege whose excess brings disaster.

docs.title: 16.4.3 Hunting in Kāvya
docs.text:
Kālidāsa’s Abhijñānaśākuntala opens with a hunt. King Duṣyanta, in his chariot, pursues a blackbuck which flees, turning its neck to look back at the chariot, until hermits of Kaṇva’s forest stop him: the deer belongs to the hermitage and must not be killed (Chapter 11). In the second act the king’s general praises hunting in terms that closely echo the Arthaśāstra — it takes off fat, makes the body light and fit, teaches how animals behave in fear and anger, and gives the archer practice at moving targets — while the jester, worn out by the chase, complains of its hardships.

Classical Tamil poetry, by contrast, knows hunting mainly as the life of the hill people of the kuṟiñci landscape, who hunted boar and deer, gathered honey and guarded their millet fields against parrots and elephants (Chapter 2). Across south India, hero-stones (naṭukal, vīragal) commemorate men who died defending cattle from raiders or fighting tigers and boar, and the dynastic emblem of the Hoysaḷas of Karnataka showed their legendary founder Saḷa killing a tiger (or, in some versions, a lion).

docs.title: 16.4.4 The Mānasollāsa
docs.text: The most detailed Sanskrit account of the royal hunt is in the Mānasollāsa of Someśvara III (Section 3.8; (Shrigondekar 1925)). Its fourth book, on the king’s entertainments (vinoda), treats hunting at length among the other pleasures of the court: the varieties of hunting, the keeping and training of hunting dogs and the methods used for particular kinds of game. It describes an ideal of courtly life rather than particular hunts. Falconry and the Śyainikaśāstra are discussed in Chapter 17 (Section 17.3).

docs.title: 16.5 The Ethics of Killing: Aśoka, Buddhists and Jains
16.5.1 Aśoka
docs.text: The edicts of Aśoka (r. c. 268–232 BCE), whose provisions on animals and trees are summarised in Chapter 11 (Section 11.4), are the earliest datable Indian texts to criticise hunting. The Eighth Rock Edict states that in the past kings went out on pleasure tours (vihārayātrā) in which there was hunting and other such amusements, but that Aśoka, ten years after his consecration, set out for Sambodhi — the place of the Buddha’s enlightenment — and since then has made tours of dhamma instead, meeting ascetics and brahmins and instructing the people of the countryside (Singh 2008). The First Rock Edict adds that where once many hundreds of thousands of animals were killed each day for the royal kitchen, only three are now killed — two peafowl and a deer, and the deer not always — and that even these will cease. The edicts present the giving up of the royal hunt as a mark of a reformed king; they did not forbid others to hunt.

docs.title: 16.5.2 Buddhist Teaching
docs.text:
The first of the five precepts of the Buddhist lay follower is to refrain from taking life (pāṇātipātā veramaṇī). The discourses list trade in living beings and in meat among the wrong livelihoods for a lay disciple (Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.177). The position on meat was more nuanced: monks, who lived on alms, were allowed to accept meat unless they had seen, heard or suspected that the animal had been killed specifically for them; the monastic code forbade them the flesh of certain animals, including humans, elephants, horses, dogs, snakes and the large carnivores — lions, tigers, leopards, bears and hyenas. Some later Mahāyāna texts, such as the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, condemn meat-eating outright.

The Jātaka stories of the Buddha’s former births, many of them older folk tales, frequently cast the Bodhisattva as an animal who sacrifices himself for others (Cowell 1895). In the Nigrodhamiga Jātaka (no. 12) the Bodhisattva is a king of deer who offers his own life in place of a pregnant doe chosen for the royal kitchen, and so moves the king of Benares to grant safety to deer and then to all creatures; in the Mahākapi Jātaka (no. 407) a monkey king makes a bridge of his own body for his troop to escape the king’s archers; in the Chaddanta Jātaka (no. 514) a six-tusked elephant king allows a hunter to saw off his tusks. Several of these stories were carved at Bharhut and Sanchi and painted at Ajanta. They are moral fables, not natural history, but they show a sustained effort to imagine animals as moral subjects, and the hunter in them is usually the villain. The Pañcatantra, by contrast, a collection of animal fables for the instruction of princes, probably composed in the early centuries CE and later carried through Middle Persian into Arabic as Kalīla wa Dimna, uses its lion king and scheming jackal ministers as types of human character; it is evidence of attitudes to power rather than of zoological knowledge (Olivelle 1997).

docs.title: 16.5.3 Jain Teaching
docs.text:
Jainism made non-injury (ahiṃsā) the first and most comprehensive of its vows. Jain doctrine classifies living beings by their number of senses and distinguishes mobile (trasa) from immobile (sthāvara) beings (Tatia 1994). The mendicant renounces all injury; the layperson renounces at least the intentional killing of mobile beings, which rules out hunting, fishing and occupations that involve killing. Jain communities have maintained animal shelters (pāñjarāpoḷ, “pinjrapole”) for aged, injured and unwanted animals, especially in Gujarat and Rajasthan, and Jain teachers sought, with varying success, to persuade rulers to proclaim days on which no animal might be killed (amāri). Jain sources credit the twelfth-century Caulukya king Kumārapāla of Gujarat, a patron of the scholar Hemacandra, with such prohibitions, and record that the Śvetāmbara monk Hīravijaya obtained from Akbar orders forbidding slaughter on certain days, including the Jain festival of Paryuṣaṇa. The scope and enforcement of such orders are hard to judge.

Scholarly Note: Ideals and Practice

The ethic of non-injury was real and influential. It shaped the diet of large sections of Indian society, inspired royal proclamations from Aśoka to Akbar, and sustains today the animal shelters of Jain communities and the protective practices of groups such as the Bishnoi. But it did not end hunting. Kings who patronised Buddhist and Jain monks continued to hunt; the Arthaśāstra and the Mānasollāsa treat the hunt as a royal art; and the killing of animals that damaged crops or took livestock was accepted almost everywhere. The relation between ideal and practice in this field is a long negotiation, not a story of a lost conservationist golden age (Alsdorf 2010).

docs.title: 16.6 Hunting and Gathering Peoples
docs.text:
Alongside the royal hunt there was the hunting of those for whom it was a livelihood. Many communities of forest and hill — among them the Chenchus of the Nallamala hills, the Bhils and Gonds of central India, the Santals of the Chotanagpur plateau and the Irulas of Tamil Nadu — lived wholly or partly by hunting, trapping and gathering. Specialist hunting and trapping castes, such as the Pārdhīs of western and central India and the Baheliyas of the north, served villages and courts as catchers of birds and animals (Chapter 17). The Sanskrit texts rank the hunter (vyādha, lubdhaka) low, and under colonial rule many such groups were classified as “criminal tribes” under the Act of 1871.

Royal and colonial hunters depended on their knowledge of tracks, calls and seasons: the trackers, beaters and trappers of the shikār, the capturers of elephants and cheetahs, and the informants of colonial naturalists came mostly from these communities and were rarely named (Rangarajan 2001). Some communal hunts survive in modified form, such as the annual ritual hunts (sendra) of the Santals, now contested by forest officials. In the 1970s the Irulas, traditional catchers of snakes and rats, formed a snake catchers’ cooperative that extracts venom for the manufacture of antivenom. Forest peoples also worship the animals they live among, as with tiger deities such as Vāghobā in Maharashtra, or seek protection from them, as from the Sundarbans goddess Bonbibi, invoked by Hindu and Muslim honey-gatherers and fishers against the tiger. These traditions are treated more fully in Volume 23 (Jana–Jāti).

docs.title: 16.7.1 The Ring Hunt and the Royal Chase
docs.text:
The Turkish and Mongol traditions brought by the Delhi Sultans and the Mughals placed the hunt at the centre of royal life. The historian Baranī presents the long hunting expeditions of Sultan Balban (r. 1266–1287) as exercises that kept his cavalry in readiness, much as the Arthaśāstra had treated hunting as training. The most spectacular form of the Central Asian hunt was the qamargha, a ring hunt in which thousands of beaters, sometimes whole armies, gradually closed a circle many miles across, driving the game into an ever smaller space where the ruler and his nobles killed it. Abū’l-Faẓl records that in 1578 Akbar, during a great qamargha near Bhera in the Punjab, was overcome by a spiritual experience and ordered the hunt stopped and the trapped animals released — an episode he presents as a sign of the emperor’s spiritual elevation. The Āʾīn-i Akbarī justifies Akbar’s hunting as more than pleasure, an occasion for learning about the condition of the country and its people, and describes a variety of methods used at court, among them hunting with trained cheetahs and with tame decoy antelopes (Abū’l-Faẓl 1873).

Bābur, who came to India from Kabul in 1526, recorded the animals of his new country with a naturalist’s curiosity, among them the rhinoceros, which he hunted in the jungles near Peshawar — evidence of how far west the species still ranged in the early sixteenth century (Thackston 1996). His great-grandson Jahāngīr (r. 1605–1627) was the most passionate hunter of the dynasty and the most careful recorder of animals. His memoirs note the game he and his household killed, with tallies broken down by species; record with pride that the empress Nūr Jahān shot tigers from an elephant’s howdah; and contain detailed observations of animal behaviour and of rare animals brought to the court (Thackston 1999). Near Lahore, at Sheikhupura, he built a tower over the grave of a favourite antelope, Mansraj, and forbade the hunting of deer in the area; the Hiran Minar still stands. Mughal painting is a major source for the appearance of wild animals in the period (Chapter 17).

Mughal and later princely courts also kept menageries of local and exotic animals, a tradition continued by the public zoological gardens of the nineteenth century, such as that at Alipore in Calcutta (1876).

docs.title: 16.7.2 The Cheetah
docs.text:
The cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) once ranged across the open plains and scrublands of northern, western and central India and the Deccan, where it hunted blackbuck and gazelle. Its history in India has been reconstructed by Divyabhanusinh (1995). Trained cheetahs were used for coursing antelope from before the Mughal period, and the practice reached its height at the Mughal court. The animal, hooded, was carried on a cart or on horseback close to a herd of blackbuck, unhooded and released for a short, explosive chase; when it brought down its prey it was rewarded with a share of the meat. Akbar kept very large numbers of cheetahs, ranked in grades with their own keepers, and the Āʾīn-i Akbarī describes their management in detail (Abū’l-Faẓl 1873). Jahāngīr records as a remarkable event the birth of a litter of cheetah cubs in captivity in his own establishment, observing that this had not happened before even though his father had kept so many (Thackston 1999).

That remark points to the heart of the problem. As with the elephant (Chapter 15), coursing cheetahs were not bred but captured from the wild, generally as adults that had already learned to hunt, so that every hunting establishment was a continuous drain on the wild population. Divyabhanusinh argues that this long-standing capture, combined with the shrinking of the grasslands and of the blackbuck herds on which the cheetah depended and with the bounties paid on it as a predator in colonial times, drove it to extinction. By the early twentieth century Indian princes who wanted to continue coursing had to import cheetahs from Africa. The last reliable records of wild cheetahs in India date from the late 1940s — a widely reproduced photograph shows three young cheetahs shot by the Maharaja of Koriya in 1947 — and the species was declared extinct in India in 1952. The Asiatic cheetah now survives only in Iran, in very small numbers (Divyabhanusinh 1995).

docs.title: 16.8 Colonial Shikār and the War on “Vermin”
docs.text:
British rule transformed the scale and meaning of hunting (Rangarajan 2001). The shikār — the hunting of tigers from elephant back or from platforms (machān) over a tethered bait, with lines of beaters driving the animal towards the guns — became a central ritual of colonial and princely power. Viceroys, governors and visiting royalty were entertained with great tiger shoots, such as the one held for King George V in the Nepal Terai in 1911; British officers hunted wild boar on horseback with spears (“pig-sticking”) as a test of nerve and horsemanship, contested in competitions such as the Kadir Cup near Meerut; and Indian princes competed in the size of their tiger tallies, some of which ran into hundreds.

Alongside the sport went a systematic campaign of extermination. From the 1870s the colonial government paid rewards for killing tigers, leopards, wolves, bears, wild dogs and other animals classed as “vermin” or “dangerous animals”. Officials justified the bounties as protection for human life and livestock — wolves, tigers and leopards did kill large numbers of people and animals in some districts — and as a means of extending and securing cultivation. Mahesh Rangarajan’s study of the bounty records shows that tens of thousands of tigers and well over a hundred thousand leopards and wolves were killed for reward in the half-century after 1875 (Rangarajan 2001); his study of the Central Provinces traces how the campaign against “dangerous” animals was tied to the colonial drive to extend settled cultivation into forest country (Rangarajan 1996). At the same time, the Arms Act of 1878 restricted the ownership of guns by Indians, and some historians have argued that the combination of disarmed villagers and protected game reserves left cultivators more exposed to crop damage in some areas.

The consequences can be traced species by species. The Asiatic lion, once found across much of north-western, northern and central India, was shot out of nearly all its range during the nineteenth century, surviving only in the Gir forest of Saurashtra. The Indian rhinoceros, which Bābur had still found near Peshawar, had by the late nineteenth century vanished from the Indus basin and most of the Ganga plain, surviving in the floodplains of the Brahmaputra, north Bengal and the Nepal Terai. The cheetah disappeared. The swamp deer (barasiṅghā), the wild buffalo, the gaur and the blackbuck lost much of their range to cultivation, drainage and guns. Clearance for cultivation, plantations and railways probably did more lasting damage than hunting, but the two worked together.

Colonial law began to protect some animals while their numbers were falling. The Elephants’ Preservation Act of 1879 restricted the killing of wild elephants — valuable to the state as working animals, much as they had been to the kings of the Arthaśāstra — and the Wild Birds and Animals Protection Act of 1912 provided for closed seasons and protection of specified species. Forest departments regulated hunting through licences and game rules in reserved forests, which had the effect of reserving the animals for officials and sportsmen while excluding local hunters (Chapter 11, Section 11.9).

docs.title: 16.9 The Beginnings of Conservation
docs.text:
Modern wildlife conservation in India grew partly out of the hunting culture itself. The Bombay Natural History Society, founded in 1883, brought together hunters, naturalists and collectors; its Journal published notes from all over the subcontinent, and its Mammal Survey of India in the 1910s and 1920s documented the distribution of species. Many early conservationists were hunters alarmed at the decline of game.

Princely states created and protected some of the most important wildlife areas. The Nawabs of Junagadh protected the last lions of Gir from about the beginning of the twentieth century, restricting their shooting to rare, closely controlled occasions; a well-known story credits the Viceroy Lord Curzon, who declined an invitation to shoot a lion around 1900, with encouraging this policy. Princely hunting preserves became the cores of several later national parks: Travancore created a game sanctuary around the Periyar lake in 1934, and Jaipur’s preserve at Ranthambhore later became a tiger reserve. Such preserves often protected animals at the expense of neighbouring cultivators. In Assam, the Kaziranga area was declared a reserved forest in 1908, largely to protect the rhinoceros, and later became a game sanctuary; it became a national park in 1974 and a World Heritage Site in 1985.

In 1936 the United Provinces established India’s first national park in the sub-Himalayan forests of the Ramganga valley, named the Hailey National Park after the Governor, Sir Malcolm Hailey. Among those who helped to define its boundaries was Jim Corbett (1875–1955), born at Naini Tal, who had become famous for hunting man-eating tigers and leopards in Kumaon and Garhwal at the request of the government and the villagers who suffered from them. His books, beginning with Man-Eaters of Kumaon (1944), joined accounts of these hunts to a deep knowledge of the forest, and in later life he turned from shooting to photography and to warning of the tiger’s decline (Corbett 1944). After independence the park was renamed, first Ramganga and then, in the 1950s, Corbett National Park.

docs.title: 16.10.1 From the Board for Wildlife to Project Tiger
docs.text:
The Indian Board for Wild Life was constituted in 1952 to advise the central and state governments, and new sanctuaries and national parks were declared in the following decades, including the Gir sanctuary in 1965. But the 1950s and 1960s were a period of rapid decline. The clearing of forest and grassland for agriculture, the spread of firearms, the trade in skins and the opening of former princely preserves all reduced wildlife populations. The General Assembly of the International Union for Conservation of Nature, meeting in New Delhi in 1969, drew attention to the plight of the tiger; tiger hunting was banned in India in 1970.

The Wild Life (Protection) Act of 1972 provided for the first time a national legal framework. It prohibited the hunting of animals listed in its schedules, regulated trade in wild animals and their products, and set out procedures for declaring sanctuaries and national parks. Later amendments tightened it and, in 2002, created conservation and community reserves (Chapter 11). India joined the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) in 1976. In the early 1970s the tiger replaced the lion as India’s national animal.

Project Tiger was launched on 1 April 1973, with nine tiger reserves — among them Corbett, Kanha, Manas, Ranthambhore, Similipal and the Sundarbans — under the direction of Kailash Sankhala, with the strong personal support of the Prime Minister, Indira Gandhi. A count in 1972 had put the number of tigers in India at fewer than two thousand. The project’s model was a core area free of human use within a buffer zone of regulated use.
