The pugmark census of its early decades was shown by the ecologist K. Ullas Karanth and others to be unreliable, and was replaced by camera trapping and statistical sampling. In 2005 it emerged that the Sariska Tiger Reserve in Rajasthan had lost all its tigers to poachers, a shock that led to the report of a Tiger Task Force and to the creation of the National Tiger Conservation Authority in 2006. The official all-India estimates since 2018, based on camera trapping, have put the number of tigers at around three thousand or more; the figures have been welcomed as evidence of recovery and also questioned on methodological grounds.

Project Elephant followed in 1992 (Chapter 15, Section 15.8). The campaign against a hydroelectric dam in Kerala’s Silent Valley, in which the lion-tailed macaque became a symbol, ended with the declaration of a national park there in 1984.

docs.title: 16.10.2 The Lions of Gir and the Question of Translocation
docs.text:
The Asiatic lion (Panthera leo leo, formerly P. l. persica) has recovered under protection from a very small population in the early twentieth century to several hundred animals, according to the censuses of the Gujarat Forest Department, and lions now range well beyond the Gir protected area into the farmland and coasts of Saurashtra. Recovery has brought conflict over livestock and the resettlement of many families of the Maldhārīs, pastoralists who lived with their buffaloes and cattle in settlements inside Gir, from the 1970s onwards.

Because the whole wild population lives in one region, conservation biologists have long argued that a second population should be established elsewhere, as an insurance against epidemic disease or natural disaster; an outbreak of canine distemper virus that killed a number of Gir lions in 2018 lent weight to the argument. From the 1990s the Kuno–Palpur sanctuary in Madhya Pradesh was prepared as a second home for the lion, and villages were relocated out of it. The Gujarat government, which regarded the lion as a symbol of the state, resisted the transfer. In 2013 the Supreme Court ordered that lions be translocated to Kuno, but the order was not carried out.

Debate: The Cheetah at Kuno

On 17 September 2022 eight cheetahs brought from Namibia were released into enclosures in the Kuno National Park, Madhya Pradesh, followed in 2023 by twelve from South Africa, under a government plan to establish the species in India seventy years after its extinction. Supporters argue that the cheetah can serve as a flagship for India’s neglected grasslands and open forests and restores a lost member of the fauna. Critics, including several Indian and international biologists, have questioned whether Kuno and the proposed additional sites are large enough and hold enough prey for a free-ranging population; whether African cheetahs, a different subspecies from the extinct Asiatic animal, can be called a “reintroduction”; whether conflict with leopards, people and livestock outside the park can be managed; and whether the project diverted attention and resources from the translocation of lions to Kuno ordered by the Supreme Court. Several imported adults and cubs born in India died in the first years, which supporters attributed to the expected difficulties of any introduction and critics to flaws in design. The outcome remains uncertain.

docs.title: 16.11 Wild Animals and Farmers
docs.text:
For most Indian farmers the most important fact about wild animals is the damage they do. Crop raiding is as old as agriculture: the Tamil poems of the hill country already picture watchers guarding millet against elephants, boar and parrots, and the watch-platform (machān), the night fire, the drum and the sling remain familiar in the fields. Today the most serious crop raiders are elephants, wild pigs, nilgai (Boselaphus tragocamelus, the “blue bull”, which many villagers will not kill because its name associates it with the cow), several species of deer, and rhesus and bonnet macaques. Elephants, which raid paddy, sugarcane, banana and stored grain and can destroy houses, kill people in India every year and are themselves killed by electrocution, poisoning and trains; conflict with farmers is now one of the main obstacles to their conservation (Sukumar 2003). Livestock predation by lions in Saurashtra, tigers and leopards in central India and the Himalaya, wolves in the Deccan grasslands and snow leopards in the high mountains imposes heavy costs on herders, who are often among the poorest people in their regions.

Responses combine guarding, trenches, walls and electric fences, early-warning systems for elephants, and compensation schemes run by state forest departments, often criticised for low payments and long delays. Section 62 of the Wild Life (Protection) Act allows the central government to declare an animal vermin in a specified area for a specified period, and this power has been used in recent years at the request of states — in 2015–16, for example, by notifications of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change for wild pigs and nilgai in parts of Bihar and for rhesus macaques in parts of Himachal Pradesh — each time provoking controversy. Research by Vidya Athreya and colleagues in the sugarcane country of western Maharashtra showed that leopards live and breed in dense rural landscapes far from any forest, mostly unseen (Athreya et al. 2013), and that capturing “problem” leopards and releasing them elsewhere tended to increase attacks on people rather than reduce them (Athreya et al. 2011). Such findings have encouraged a shift from removal towards coexistence.

Some agricultural landscapes are themselves important habitats. The blackbuck, chinkara and nilgai of the north-western plains, the wolves and Indian foxes of the Deccan, and many birds live among fields and on the grazing commons that official classifications long labelled “wastelands”. Where communities such as the Bishnoi protect wild animals on religious grounds, blackbuck and chinkara graze close to the fields (Chapter 11, Section 11.8).

docs.title: 16.12 Conservation and Displacement
docs.text:
The protected-area model adopted in India, as in much of the world, rested on the idea that wildlife is best protected by removing people. Villages were relocated out of national parks and tiger reserves — from Kanha, Sariska, Kuno and many other areas — and the rights of those who remained to graze, collect forest produce or cultivate were curtailed. Pastoral groups such as the Maldhārīs of Gir and the Van Gujjars of the Rajaji area in the Uttarakhand foothills, and Adivasi communities in central and southern India, bore much of the cost. Relocation has sometimes been voluntary and fairly compensated, in other cases coercive and impoverishing (Rangarajan 2001; Gadgil and Guha 1992).

The Forest Rights Act of 2006 (Chapter 11, Section 11.11) recognised the rights of forest dwellers within protected areas and laid down that “critical wildlife habitats” could be made inviolate only through a defined process with the informed consent of the people affected. The relationship between that Act and the Wild Life (Protection) Act remains contested in courts and in practice.

Debate: Inviolate Areas or Shared Landscapes?

One school of conservationists, many of them field biologists working on large mammals, argues that wide-ranging, conflict-prone animals need large areas free of human use, as the tiger’s recovery in some reserves shows. Another, represented by ecologists and historians such as Madhav Gadgil and Mahesh Rangarajan and by advocates of forest rights, argues that exclusion has been unjust to forest dwellers, has made them hostile to conservation, and ignores the long coexistence of people and wildlife in Indian landscapes; they emphasise community-managed reserves, the knowledge of local people and the protection of wildlife outside parks (Gadgil and Guha 1992; Rangarajan 2001). Most participants accept both that some areas need strict protection and that conservation cannot succeed without the support of those who live with wild animals; the disagreement is about the balance.

These questions of the rights and knowledge of forest communities are treated more fully in Volume 23 (Jana–Jāti).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Wild animals have been part of the Indian agrarian world since the hunters of the rock shelters and the seal-carvers of the Indus cities. Vedic and classical texts named many wild mammals, and Āyurveda classified them by habitat and manner of feeding. Hunting (mṛgayā) was both a royal art, praised as training in the Arthaśāstra and by Kālidāsa and elaborated in the Mānasollāsa, and a royal vice in Manu and the epics, while Aśoka, the Buddhists and the Jains made the renunciation of killing a moral ideal that coexisted with the hunt rather than replacing it. The Mughals raised cheetah coursing to its height; capture, the loss of grasslands and colonial bounties drove the cheetah to extinction in India by about 1950. Colonial shikār and the war on “vermin” devastated tigers, leopards and wolves, and the lion and rhinoceros survived only in refuges. Conservation grew from naturalists’ societies, princely preserves and the first national park (1936), and after independence the Wild Life (Protection) Act of 1972 and Project Tiger built a network of protected areas — at heavy cost to farmers living with crop raiders and predators and to forest dwellers displaced from parks.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Rangarajan (2001) is the best introduction to the history of wildlife in India, and Rangarajan (1996) studies forests, hunting and bounties in the Central Provinces in detail. For the cheetah see Divyabhanusinh (1995); for the Āyurvedic classification of animals and landscapes Zimmermann (1987); for Mughal hunting and natural history Thackston (1999); for elephants and human–elephant conflict Sukumar (2003); and for the ecological history of Indian land use Gadgil and Guha (1992).

docs.title: Chapter 17: Birds, Insects, Reptiles and Aquatic Life
17.1 Knowledge of Smaller and Wilder Creatures
docs.text: Beyond the cattle of the farm and the elephants and horses of the court lay a much larger world of animals that Indians observed, named, hunted, protected, used and wrote about: birds, insects, snakes and other reptiles, frogs, fishes, shellfish, turtles, crocodiles and river dolphins. Knowledge about them was rarely gathered into a single treatise. It is scattered across Vedic hymns, the Arthaśāstra and the edicts of Aśoka, medical and gemmological texts, the omen literature, court poetry and the memoirs of Mughal emperors — and, above all, it lived in the practice of fowlers, falconers, silk-rearers, lac-cultivators, honey-hunters and fisherfolk, most of whose knowledge was never written down. This chapter surveys these sources, separating, as far as possible, what was observed from what was conventional or mythical.

docs.title: 17.2 Birds in Vedic and Classical Literature
17.2.1 Vedic Birds
docs.text:
Birds appear in the Ṛgveda chiefly as images and messengers. The falcon or eagle (śyena) brings the soma from heaven (Ṛgveda 4.26–27); a pigeon (kapota) that has entered the house is treated as a messenger of Nirṛti, the goddess of destruction, in a hymn to avert its evil (10.165); pairs of ruddy shelducks (cakravāka) and geese (haṃsa) appear in similes (Jamison and Brereton 2014). In a famous riddle hymn two birds sit on one tree:

Ṛgveda 1.164.20

dvā suparṇā sayujā sakhāyā samānaṃ vṛkṣam pari ṣasvajāte tayor anyaḥ pippalaṃ svādv atty anaśnann anyo abhi cākaśīti “Two birds, companions joined together, embrace the same tree. One of them eats the sweet fig; the other, not eating, looks on.”

The verse, taken up again in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad (3.1.1), was read in later tradition as an image of the individual self and the witnessing self. Its value here is as a reminder that birds in Vedic poetry are usually symbols; the ornithological content is incidental. The Vedic haṃsa, for example, is often a solar or spiritual image rather than a particular species.

docs.title: 17.2.2 Poetic Conventions and Real Birds
docs.text: Classical Sanskrit poetry developed a repertoire of bird conventions (kavisamaya): the haṃsa that can separate milk from water; the pair of cakravākas condemned to spend each night apart and calling to each other across the river; the cātaka that drinks only raindrops falling from the clouds; the cakora that feeds on moonlight; the peacock (mayūra) that dances at the approach of rain clouds, declared India’s national bird in 1963; the kokila (koel) whose call announces spring. Some of these conventions rest on real observation. The haṃsa of the poets is most probably the bar-headed goose, a winter visitor that leaves the plains for Central Asia in spring — the “departure of the geese for Mānasa” of the poets. The ruddy shelduck does live in pairs and calls loudly at dusk. The pied cuckoo, often identified with the cātaka, arrives in northern India with the monsoon. Others — the milk-separating swan, the moon-drinking cakora — are poetic fancies. K. N. Dave’s Birds in Sanskrit Literature is the standard attempt to identify the birds named in the texts, and shows both how rich the vocabulary is and how uncertain many identifications remain (Dave 1985).

docs.title: 17.2.3 Protected Birds
docs.text: Lists of birds also appear in administrative and legal contexts. Aśoka’s fifth Pillar Edict (c. 242 BCE; Chapter 11) exempts from killing, among other creatures, parrots, mynas, ruddy shelducks, wild geese and pigeons (Singh 2008). The Arthaśāstra, in its chapter on the superintendent of slaughterhouses, likewise protects a list of birds and animals, including geese, cranes, ruddy shelducks, peacocks, parrots and mynas, mostly birds valued for their beauty, their song or their auspiciousness (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013). These are early examples of legal protection for named animals; their selection reflects royal, religious and aesthetic preferences rather than ecological criteria.

docs.title: 17.3 Omens, Hunting and Court Natural History
17.3.1 Bird Omens
docs.text: The interpretation of omens from the calls, flight and behaviour of birds and animals (śakuna) was an important branch of Indian divination. Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā devotes a group of chapters to it, describing how the direction, time and quality of a bird’s cry predict success or failure on a journey or undertaking (Bhat 1981); later handbooks of śakuna elaborated the system. The omen literature preserves a great many bird names and some acute observations of behaviour, but its purpose was divination, not natural history.

docs.title: 17.3.2 The Mṛgapakṣiśāstra
docs.text: Modern accounts often cite a Mṛgapakṣiśāstra (“Treatise on Beasts and Birds”) ascribed to a Jain author named Haṃsadeva and dated to the thirteenth century, which describes the appearance, habits and temperament of many animals and birds. The work is known only through a twentieth-century publication with an English version; its manuscript basis has not been properly described, and its date and authenticity are uncertain. Some scholars regard it as a late compilation. Until a critical study is available it should not be used as evidence for medieval Indian zoology.

docs.title: 17.3.3 Falconry and Fowling
docs.text: Hawking was a royal sport across the Persianate and Indian worlds. A Sanskrit treatise on falconry, the Śyainikaśāstra, edited and translated by Haraprasad Shastri (Shastri 1910), is ascribed to a king Rudradeva of Kumaon; it classifies hunting birds, describes their training and care and treats hunting as a royal pleasure with its own ethics. Falconry flourished at the courts of the Delhi Sultans and the Mughals, whose falconers (mīr-shikār) formed a specialised service. Fowling with nets, snares, decoys and lime was practised by specialist communities — the Pārdhī of western and central India, the Bahelia of the north and many others — whose knowledge of bird behaviour was intimate and largely unwritten, and who were stigmatised under colonial law as “criminal tribes”.

docs.title: 17.3.4 Jahāngīr and the Painters
docs.text: The Mughal emperor Jahāngīr (r. 1605–1627) recorded in his memoirs many careful observations of animals and birds: he noted, for example, the breeding behaviour of a pair of sarus cranes kept at court, including the sharing of incubation between male and female, and described birds and animals brought to him from distant lands (Thackston 1999). He had his painters, above all Ustād Manṣūr, record birds, animals and flowers with a precision unmatched in earlier Indian art. These paintings and notes are among the most valuable documents of pre-modern natural history in India.

docs.title: 17.4.1 Modern Ornithology
docs.text: Scientific ornithology in India took shape in the colonial period, notably through Allan Octavian Hume, who founded the journal Stray Feathers (1872), and through the Bombay Natural History Society, founded in 1883. Sálim Ali (1896–1987) made the study of Indian birds a field of Indian science; his Handbook of the Birds of India and Pakistan, written with S. Dillon Ripley, remains a standard reference (Ali and Ripley 1968). Ali and his successors drew extensively on the knowledge of local hunters, trappers and villagers, often without acknowledgement in print (Rangarajan 2001).

docs.title: 17.4.2 Birds and Agriculture
docs.text: Farmers have always had an ambivalent relationship with birds. Parrots (śuka) are listed among the six traditional agricultural calamities (īti) — excessive rain, drought, locusts, rats, parrots and the incursions of neighbouring kings — and bird-scaring from crop platforms was, and is, the work of children and the poor. At the same time birds such as owls, egrets, drongos and mynas eat rodents and insects in the fields. In recent decades India has witnessed one of the most rapid declines of any bird group recorded: the collapse of the populations of Gyps vultures, which once disposed of the carcasses of cattle across the subcontinent, caused by residues of the veterinary drug diclofenac in carcasses (Oaks et al. 2004). The drug was banned for veterinary use in India in 2006. The vulture collapse illustrates how closely wild birds were bound to the agrarian economy of cattle described in Chapter 13.

docs.title: 17.4.3 Village Heronries and Bird Refuges
docs.text: Some of India’s best-known bird sites owe their survival to villagers. At Kokkare Bellur in Karnataka, painted storks and spot-billed pelicans nest every year in the trees of the village itself, and the villagers have long tolerated and protected them, valuing the droppings that accumulate under the nesting trees as manure; the village name itself refers to the storks (Kannada kokkare). At Vedanthangal in Tamil Nadu, a tank whose trees support a large colony of waterbirds, the local cultivators protected the birds by custom, and the colonial government recognised their protection in the nineteenth century; the site later became a bird sanctuary. Such places show a practical bargain between farmers and birds, in which the manure from heronries enriched the fields and tank water downstream. Elsewhere the relationship was one of royal sport: the wetlands of Keoladeo at Bharatpur in Rajasthan were developed by the rulers of Bharatpur as a duck-shooting preserve, at which enormous bags were recorded in the colonial period, before becoming a national park in 1982 and a World Heritage Site. The sarus crane, the tallest flying bird, still nests in the wet fields and village ponds of the Gangetic plain and Gujarat, where it is widely regarded as a symbol of marital fidelity and left unharmed.

docs.title: 17.5.1 Silk
docs.text: The Sanskrit word for silk, kauśeya, derives from kośa, “cocoon”. The Arthaśāstra distinguishes kauśeya from cīnapaṭṭa, “Chinese cloth”, showing that both local and imported silks were known (Kangle 1965). India is unusual in having several native silk-producing moths. Besides the mulberry silkworm (Bombyx mori), domesticated in China and introduced to India, wild or semi-domesticated species yield tasar silk (Antheraea mylitta and related species, on trees such as Terminalia), eri silk (Samia ricini, reared on castor) and the golden muga silk of Assam (Antheraea assamensis). Microscopic study of fibres from Harappa and Chanhu-daro has shown that silk from wild Antheraea moths was being used in the Indus civilisation in the third millennium BCE (Good et al. 2009). Rearing tasar and eri has long been the work of tribal and peasant communities in central and north-eastern India. Mulberry sericulture expanded in Bengal in the Sultanate and Mughal periods and was promoted in Mysore by Tipu Sultan in the late eighteenth century. The textile side of the story belongs to Volume 17.

docs.title: 17.5.2 Lac
docs.text: Lac (lākṣā; Hindi lākh, whence English “lac” and ultimately “lacquer”) is the resinous secretion of the scale insect Kerria lacca, which encrusts the twigs of host trees such as palāśa (Butea monosperma), kusum (Schleichera oleosa) and ber (Ziziphus mauritiana). It yields both a red dye (the source of alaktaka, the red colour with which women decorated their feet) and the resin used for varnish, sealing, ornaments, bangles and, in modern times, shellac. A hymn of the Atharvaveda (5.5) is addressed to lākṣā as a healing substance for wounds (Whitney 1905), and the Mahābhārata’s “house of lac” (lākṣāgṛha), built to burn the Pāṇḍavas, shows that its flammability was well understood. Lac cultivation — inoculating host trees with brood lac and harvesting the encrusted twigs — is an old practice of the forest communities of present-day Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and West Bengal, and India remains the world’s leading producer.

docs.title: 17.5.3 Bees and Honey
docs.text: Honey (madhu) is prominent in Vedic ritual and imagery, and the medical texts distinguish several kinds of honey according to the insects that produce them: Suśruta lists eight (Bhishagratna 1907). Three species of honeybee are native to the subcontinent: the giant rock bee (Apis dorsata), which builds huge open combs on cliffs and tall trees; the Asian hive bee (Apis cerana), which nests in cavities and has long been kept in log, pot and wall hives in Kerala, the Himalaya and the North-East; and the dwarf bee (Apis florea); there are also stingless bees. Honey-hunting from rock-bee colonies is a specialised and dangerous skill of forest communities such as the Jēnu Kuruba (“honey Kuruba”) of Karnataka and the Kurumba of the Nilgiris, who combine climbing technique, smoke and ritual with detailed knowledge of the bees’ seasonal movements. Modern apiculture with movable-frame hives was introduced in the twentieth century, and the European honeybee (Apis mellifera) later still.

docs.title: 17.5.4 Pollinators
docs.text: The greatest service insects render to agriculture is pollination. Many Indian crops — mustard and other oilseeds, pulses such as pigeon pea, cucurbits, many fruit trees, and cardamom and coffee in the hills — depend wholly or partly on bees and other insects to set seed and fruit. Wild bees, flies, wasps, beetles, butterflies and moths, as well as the honeybees, do this work, and the hedgerows, field margins, trees and fallows of mixed farming landscapes sustain them. Farmers and beekeepers have long observed the connection between flowering crops and honey; the rock-bee colonies of the Western Ghats and the cardamom and coffee plantations below them are linked in this way. The texts of the vṛkṣāyurveda tradition, concerned with making trees flower and fruit (Chapter 4), do not describe pollination by insects, which was first understood in Europe in the eighteenth century. In modern India, as elsewhere, the intensive use of insecticides, the loss of uncultivated land and the simplification of cropping systems are causes of concern for pollinator populations, and the deliberate placing of hives in orchards and oilseed fields to improve pollination has become part of agricultural extension.

docs.title: 17.6 Insects in Medicine, Lore and the Fields
docs.text:
The anthill (valmīka) has a special place in Indian lore. The poet Vālmīki is said to have been so absorbed in austerity that an anthill grew over him; in south India anthills (termite mounds) are worshipped as the dwelling of snakes; and Varāhamihira’s chapter on finding underground water (dakārgala) uses anthills near particular trees as signs of water below (Bhat 1981) (see Chapter 8). Termite-mound earth is used in some regions as a soil amendment and in building.

Locusts (śalabha) appear among the agricultural calamities mentioned above, and swarms periodically devastated crops in north-western India; the colonial and modern states organised locust warning services. The medical texts classify stinging and biting insects (kīṭa) among venomous creatures and describe the effects of their bites, including those of mosquitoes (maśaka) (Bhishagratna 1907). These classifications are of real historical interest, but they do not amount to a theory of insect-borne disease; that mosquitoes transmit malaria was established by Ronald Ross, working in India, in 1897–1898.

docs.title: 17.7.1 Serpents in Religion
docs.text: No group of animals has a larger place in Indian religion than the snakes. Serpent beings (nāga) appear in the Vedic texts, in the epics — the Mahābhārata opens its narrative frame with Janamejaya’s great snake sacrifice — and in Buddhist and Jain art and story: the serpent king Mucalinda shelters the meditating Buddha with his hoods, and the twenty-third Jain tīrthaṅkara, Pārśvanātha, is shown beneath a canopy of snake hoods. Viṣṇu reclines on the cosmic serpent Śeṣa, and Śiva wears snakes as ornaments. In village religion snakes are worshipped above all as guardians of fertility, of water and of the household: in the month of Śrāvaṇa, at the height of the monsoon when snakes are driven from their holes, women offer milk and flowers at anthills and serpent images on Nāgapañcamī; in south India stones carved with entwined serpents (nāgakal) are set up beneath sacred trees, often by women seeking children; and in Kerala the serpent groves (sarpakkāvu) attached to households and temples are among the best-known sacred groves (Chapter 11). The association of snakes with anthills and termite mounds, noted above, is part of the same complex of belief.

docs.title: 17.7.2 Snake Charmers and the Law
docs.text: Snake charming was the hereditary occupation of several itinerant communities, among them the Kalbeliyā (Sapera) of Rajasthan, who caught snakes, displayed them to the music of the gourd pipe (pūṅgī or bīn), and sold amulets and remedies against snakebite. The Wildlife (Protection) Act of 1972, which protected Indian snakes and forbade keeping them, made the occupation illegal, and many such families lost their livelihood without any alternative being provided. The Kalbeliyā songs and dances, which developed from their performances, were inscribed on UNESCO’s list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2010. Their case illustrates a recurring tension in Indian conservation between protecting animals and protecting the communities whose way of life depended on them (Chapter 16).

docs.title: 17.7.3 Snakes in the Medical Texts
docs.text:
The medical texts give snakes careful attention because of the danger they pose. The Kalpasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā, devoted to poisons, classifies venomous snakes into groups that are recognisable to a modern reader: the hooded snakes (darvīkara), corresponding broadly to the cobras; the snakes marked with circular patches (maṇḍalin), broadly the vipers; and the striped or banded snakes (rājimant), among which the kraits are usually placed; together with non-venomous snakes and hybrids (Bhishagratna 1907). It describes the signs of bites by each group, distinguishes the effects of their venoms by the language of the doṣas, and lays down first aid and treatment: the binding of the limb above the bite, incision and suction, cautery, and a great range of antidotes and incantations. Caraka’s chapter on poisons covers similar ground (Sharma 1981). The classification by external appearance reflects long observation, and the recognition that the bites of hooded snakes and of vipers produce different effects is accurate; the treatments, as far as they have been examined, are not effective, and some, such as incision and tight tourniquets, are now known to do harm.

Snakebite

Snakebite is a medical emergency. The only effective treatment for envenoming is antivenom, given in a hospital by trained staff, together with supportive care. The victim should be kept still and taken to hospital at once. Cutting, sucking or burning the wound, tight tourniquets, herbal applications, incantations and visits to traditional healers are ineffective and can cause harm or fatal delay. Nothing in this chapter describes a usable remedy.

docs.title: 17.7.4 Snakebite and Agriculture
docs.text:
Snakebite is, above all, an occupational hazard of farming. Four species — the spectacled cobra (Naja naja), the common krait (Bungarus caeruleus), Russell’s viper (Daboia russelii) and the saw-scaled viper (Echis carinatus), often called the “big four” — cause most serious bites in India. Most victims are farmers and agricultural labourers bitten in the fields during the monsoon and harvest seasons, or people bitten at night while sleeping on the floor of their homes, where kraits come in search of rodents. A nationally representative mortality study estimated that snakebite killed about 58,000 people a year in India on average between 2000 and 2019, mostly in rural areas and among the poor (Suraweera et al. 2020), which makes it one of the gravest health burdens of agricultural work in the country. Delay in reaching hospital, often caused by first resorting to traditional healers, is a major factor in these deaths. Polyvalent antivenom against the big four is produced in India from venom collected in large part by the Irula snake-catchers’ cooperative of Tamil Nadu (Chapter 16).

Snakes are also farmers’ allies. The Indian rat snake (Ptyas mucosa), which is not venomous, and many other snakes feed largely on rats and mice in fields and granaries, and their killing on sight removes one of the main natural checks on rodents — themselves one of the traditional calamities of agriculture.

docs.title: 17.7.5 Monitor Lizards, Turtles and Tortoises
docs.text: The Manusmṛti (5.18) lists the five-nailed animals that may be eaten: the porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard (godhā), the rhinoceros, the tortoise and the hare (Olivelle 2005). The monitor lizard was hunted for meat and for its skin, which was used for drum-heads and leather, and is still hunted illegally; the Bengal monitor and other Indian monitors are now protected. Tortoises and freshwater turtles were eaten in many regions and protected in others: several temple tanks keep sacred turtles, and the tortoise appears in myth as the kūrma incarnation of Viṣṇu. On the coast of Odisha, at Gahirmatha and the mouth of the Rushikulya river, olive ridley sea turtles come ashore in their thousands to nest together in mass arrivals (arribadas) that are among the largest in the world; their protection from fishing trawlers, in whose nets many drown, has been a long-standing concern of conservationists and a point of conflict with fishing communities.

docs.title: 17.7.6 Frogs
docs.text: The Ṛgveda contains a famous hymn to the frogs (7.103), in which the croaking of the frogs at the coming of the rains, after lying silent through the dry season, is compared to the chanting of brahmins at a year-long rite (Jamison and Brereton 2014); whether its tone is reverent, humorous or both has been debated. In the twentieth century Indian frogs became an export commodity: large bullfrogs were caught in paddy fields for the trade in frogs’ legs to Europe and the United States, until India banned the export in 1987, in part because the depletion of frogs was thought to increase insect pests in the rice fields. The episode is a small but clear example of the connection between the wildlife of the fields and the health of the crops.

docs.title: 17.8.1 Fish in Texts and Edicts
docs.text: Fish were a major source of food in much of India, particularly in Bengal, Odisha, Assam, the coasts and the river valleys, as well as being the subject of religious restrictions in others (Achaya 1994). The Arthaśāstra expects fishermen to pay dues to the state for the use of boats and waters, under the superintendent of shipping (Kangle 1965). Aśoka’s fifth pillar edict forbids the catching and sale of fish on certain days of the month and protects some kinds of fish altogether (Singh 2008). The Mānasollāsa of Someśvara III (1131) includes fishing among the pleasures of a king and names many kinds of fish, with the baits and methods appropriate to each (Shrigondekar 1925). Among the freshwater fishes most valued in the east were the carps — rohita (rohu, Labeo rohita) above all — and the hilsa (ilīśa); the rearing of carp in village ponds, stocked with fry collected from rivers in the monsoon, is an old practice of Bengal and neighbouring regions.

docs.title: 17.8.2 Inland Fisheries and Fish Culture
docs.text: Inland fisheries — in rivers, floodplain lakes, tanks, ponds and estuaries — were as important as sea fishing for most Indians who ate fish. Village tanks were commonly leased for fishing, and the right to fish them was often a source of income for temples and village bodies as well as a matter of dispute between communities. In Bengal and Assam, floodplain wetlands (bil, bhēṛī) were managed for fish, and in the twentieth century the wetlands east of Calcutta developed a remarkable system in which the city’s sewage is led into shallow ponds where it is purified by sunlight and algae while supporting large fish harvests, with vegetables grown on the embankments and rice downstream; the East Kolkata Wetlands were designated a wetland of international importance under the Ramsar Convention in 2002. In the coastal backwaters of Kerala and the khazan lands of Goa, fish and prawns are trapped in tidal fields between rice crops (Chapter 10). Since the 1970s, scientific carp culture, using induced breeding of the major Indian carps (rohu, catla and mrigal) developed by Indian fisheries scientists, has transformed inland aquaculture.

docs.title: 17.8.3 Lagoons, Migratory Fish and Temple Fish
docs.text:
Some of India’s most productive fisheries lie in coastal lagoons. The largest, Chilika in Odisha, is a brackish lagoon whose fish, prawns and crabs have long supported the fishing villages around its shores, which held customary rights to particular fishing grounds. From the 1980s and 1990s the spread of commercial prawn culture in the lagoon, backed by outside investors and landholders, brought bitter conflict with the traditional fishing communities, while the silting of the lagoon’s mouth threatened its ecology until a new channel to the sea was cut in 2000. The lagoon is also home to a small population of Irrawaddy dolphins.

The hilsa (Tenualosa ilisha), the most prized fish of Bengal, lives in the sea and the estuaries and migrates far up the rivers to spawn during the monsoon. Its runs once reached well up the Ganga and its tributaries; barrages and dams, among them the Farakka barrage on the Ganga, have blocked or reduced these migrations, and river catches upstream have declined. The mahseer (species of Tor), the great game fish of Himalayan and peninsular rivers, has suffered from dams, dynamite fishing and pollution. In several places, however, fish have long been protected by religious custom: at riverside temples in the Western Ghats — the stretch of the Tuṅgā at Śṛṅgeri is a well-known example — and at shrines in the Himalayan foothills, the fish in the temple waters are fed by pilgrims and may not be caught. Such temple pools have served, in effect, as refuges for mahseer and other fish whose populations have collapsed elsewhere, and conservationists have drawn attention to them as examples of the protective effect of sacred sites, comparable to the sacred groves of Chapter 11.

docs.title: 17.8.4 The Fish in Myth
docs.text: The oldest version of the Indian flood story, in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.8.1), tells how Manu rescued a small fish that grew and in return warned him of the coming flood and towed his boat to safety; in the Purāṇas the fish becomes the first incarnation (avatāra) of Viṣṇu. Modern suggestions that the sequence of avatāras encodes biological evolution are a reading imposed on the myth, not a meaning found in the texts.

docs.title: 17.8.5 Pearls, Conch and Coral
docs.text:
Pearls (muktā) were among India’s most famous products. The pearl banks of the Gulf of Mannar, between south India and Sri Lanka, were fished from antiquity: the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st century CE) mentions the pearl fishery near Korkai in the Pāṇḍya kingdom, and the Arthaśāstra lists the sources of pearls, beginning with the Tāmraparṇī river (Kangle 1965). The pearl-divers of this coast were mainly Paravar fishermen, most of whom became Catholic Christians in the 1530s under Portuguese influence. Gemmological texts — the Bṛhatsaṃhitā’s chapter on pearls, the Ratnaparīkṣā ascribed to Buddhabhaṭṭa, edited with other Sanskrit lapidaries by Finot (1896) — grade pearls by size, shape, lustre and colour with much practical knowledge, but also list mythical “sources” of pearls such as elephants’ heads, serpents, clouds and bamboo, alongside the oyster.

The sacred conch (śaṅkha, the shell of Turbinella pyrum) has been fished in the Gulf of Mannar and worked into bangles, ladles and trumpets since Harappan times (Kenoyer 1998); the conch-cutters of Bengal (śāṅkhārī) were a well-known craft caste. Coral (pravāla, vidruma), by contrast, was largely red Mediterranean coral imported through the Red Sea trade, though the reefs of the Gulf of Mannar, Lakshadweep and the Andaman Islands were well known to local fishermen.

docs.title: 17.8.6 River Dolphins, Crocodiles and Turtles
docs.text: The Ganges river dolphin (Platanista gangetica), an almost blind dolphin of the Ganga–Brahmaputra system, is probably the creature called śiśumāra or śuśuka in some Sanskrit texts, though the identification is not certain (śiśumāra also names a crocodile-like constellation). It was declared India’s national aquatic animal in 2009 and is endangered by dams, pollution and fishing nets. The gharial and the mugger crocodile were common in the rivers; the makara, the composite water-monster that serves as the mount of the river goddess Gaṅgā and decorates temple doorways, draws on them and on fishes, though it is a creature of art rather than natural history. Freshwater turtles and tortoises were eaten, protected in some temple tanks, and given cosmic meaning in the tortoise (kūrma) incarnation of Viṣṇu.

docs.title: 17.9 Fishing Communities and Their Knowledge
docs.text:
The real repository of Indian knowledge about the sea and rivers is the practice of the fishing communities: the Koḷī of the Konkan and Gujarat coasts, the Mukkuvar of Kerala and Kanyakumari, the Paravar and Paṭṭiṉavar of the Tamil coast, the Kaivarta and Jalia castes of Bengal and Odisha, the Mallāh and Nishād of the Ganga, and many others. Their knowledge covers the seasons and movements of fish shoals, the relation of catches to winds, currents, tides and the moon, the location of fishing grounds and submerged rocks, the construction of boats, nets and traps, and the reading of the sea’s colour and of birds working over shoals. On the Kerala coast fishermen exploited the chākara, the calm, fish-rich mud banks that form near the shore during the monsoon. Customary institutions regulated access to fishing grounds and settled disputes in many coastal villages (Agrawal 2001).

Most of these communities occupied a low place in caste hierarchies, and their knowledge was seldom recorded by the literate. Since the mid-twentieth century mechanised trawling, the motorisation of boats, coastal pollution and the decline of river fisheries have transformed their livelihoods; seasonal bans on trawling during the monsoon breeding season, adopted by coastal states from the late 1980s, owed much to the campaigns of traditional fishworkers. Fisheries and the maritime world are treated more fully in Volume 19.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Indian knowledge of birds, insects and aquatic animals is spread across poetry, law, medicine, divination and court memoirs, and lived above all in the practice of specialist communities. Snakes, central to Indian religion and classified with real care in the medical texts’ chapters on poison, remain a grave hazard of agricultural work, for which antivenom, not traditional remedy, is the only effective treatment; frogs, monitor lizards and turtles have their own histories of use and protection. Vedic and classical poetry used birds mainly as symbols and developed conventions, some grounded in observation and some fanciful; Aśoka and the Arthaśāstra protected lists of birds and animals; the omen literature, falconry treatises and Jahāngīr’s memoirs and paintings record real observation; the Mṛgapakṣiśāstra is too uncertain to be relied upon. India’s native silk moths, its lac insect and its honeybees supported old industries in which tribal and forest communities were the experts. Fishes, pearls, conch and coral were important in diet, trade and ritual, and the knowledge of fisherfolk, though rarely written, was the most detailed of all.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Dave (1985) on birds in Sanskrit literature; Ali and Ripley (1968) for Indian birds; Good et al. (2009) on early silk; Thackston (1999) for Jahāngīr’s observations; Rangarajan (2001) for the history of wildlife in India.

docs.title: Chapter 18: Agrarian Society and Change: Caste, Land Grants, the Indo-Islamic World and Colonial Rule
18.1 Texts and Agrarian Society
docs.text: The treatises discussed in the earlier chapters of this volume — the Kṛṣi-Parāśara, the Vṛkṣāyurveda texts, the elephant and horse books — describe how fields, gardens and animals should be managed. They say much less about who did the work, on whose land, for whose benefit, and under what compulsion. Yet agricultural knowledge in India, as everywhere, was embedded in a social order: in rules about who might plough and who might own land, in the obligations of tenants and labourers, in revenue systems that decided how much of the harvest the cultivator kept, and in political changes that brought new crops, new irrigation devices and new markets. This chapter sketches that history from the early centuries CE to the mid-twentieth century. It does not attempt a complete agrarian history of South Asia, for which readers should turn to Ludden (1999), the two volumes of the Cambridge Economic History of India (Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982; Kumar 1983) and, for the Mughal period, Habib (1999). Its aim is to place the knowledge traditions of this volume within the society that produced and used them.

docs.title: 18.2 Who Worked the Land: Varṇa, Caste and Agricultural Labour
18.2.1 Agriculture in the Normative Texts
docs.text:
In the normative literature agriculture belongs, together with cattle-keeping and trade, to vārttā, the livelihood assigned to the vaiśya. The Arthaśāstra defines vārttā in exactly these terms and treats it as one of the four branches of knowledge a king must master (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013). In practice, already in the Mauryan and post-Mauryan periods much of the actual cultivation was in the hands of śūdras. The Arthaśāstra, in its chapter on settling the countryside, recommends founding villages consisting mostly of śūdra cultivators, and its crown farms under the superintendent of agriculture (sītādhyakṣa) were worked by slaves, hired labourers and convicts as well as by sharecroppers (Kangle 1965). Sharma (1980) traced how the śūdra, originally a servile category, came over the first millennium CE to be identified above all with the peasantry.

The Pali canon gives a complementary picture. Its gahapati, the landed householder, appears as a substantial farmer who employs dāsas (slaves) and kammakaras (hired workers) on his fields (Chakravarti 1987). The well-known story of the brahmin Kasibhāradvāja, who was supervising a ploughing with hundreds of ploughs when the Buddha came for alms, shows a large landholder directing the labour of others; the Buddha’s reply turns ploughing into a metaphor for spiritual practice (Sutta Nipāta 1.4, vv. 76–82; Section 2.10).

The Manusmṛti’s advice that brahmins and kṣatriyas should avoid the plough (Section 2.9) had lasting effects. In much of India it became a taboo against brahmins personally handling the plough. It did not prevent brahmins from holding land; it meant that brahmin and other high-caste landholders had their land ploughed by tenants and labourers of lower status. The prestige of not ploughing, and the stigma attached to manual labour in the fields, were an enduring part of the agrarian order.

docs.title: 18.2.2 Peasants, Labourers and Agrestic Servitude
docs.text:
From the early medieval period onwards, caste and agrarian position were closely linked, though never identical. In most regions a set of locally dominant cultivating castes — for example the Veḷḷāḷar of the Tamil country, the Reḍḍi and Kamma of Andhra, the Kuṇbī of Maharashtra, the Jāṭ of the north-west — held or controlled land, often alongside brahmin and temple holdings. Beneath them were tenants and labourers, many of whom belonged to castes that were treated as untouchable. In the wet-rice regions of the far south, the agricultural labour of the paddy fields was performed largely by groups such as the Pallar and Paṟaiyar in Tamil Nadu and the Pulayar and Cherumar in Kerala, who were held in hereditary agrestic servitude: they were attached to land and to masters, could be transferred with the land, and in Malabar were bought and sold. Colonial legislation (the Indian Slavery Act of 1843) withdrew legal recognition from slavery, but forms of bonded and attached labour persisted long afterwards.

Detailed studies of particular regions show how such relationships worked and changed. Breman (1974) studied the hāli system of south Gujarat, in which Dubla farm servants were bound to Anāvil brahmin landowners, and showed how a relationship described by landowners in the language of patronage became, under commercial pressure, one of exploitation without protection. Prakash (1990) examined the kamiyā labourers of south Bihar and the way colonial officials came to define them as “bonded” labour. In the north Indian village of Karimpur, William Wiser described the jajmānī system, in which service castes (carpenters, blacksmiths, potters, barbers, washermen, leather-workers and others) received shares of the harvest from landholding patrons in return for customary services (Wiser 1936). Wiser presented these exchanges as a stable reciprocity; later scholarship has emphasised the inequality and coercion within them.

The handling of dead cattle, of hides and of leather — indispensable to an agrarian economy that ran on bullocks and leather buckets — was assigned to castes such as the Cāmār and Mādiga and was a central marker of their exclusion. B. R. Ambedkar argued that the stigma attached to beef-eating and to the handling of dead cattle was a key element in the origin of untouchability (Ambedkar 1948); the history of cattle and caste is discussed further in Chapter 13. In irrigated regions, rights to water were also structured by caste: Mosse (2003) shows how the management of south Indian tanks encoded caste hierarchy in the allocation of water, the duties of tank servants and the honours of temple festivals (see Chapter 8).

docs.title: 18.2.3 Women’s Work and Women’s Knowledge
docs.text:
The agricultural treatises were written by men and address the male householder. Yet women’s labour has been central to Indian agriculture: in transplanting and weeding rice, in harvesting and threshing, in seed selection and storage, in the kitchen garden, in dairying and the care of animals, and in processing grain. Many of the work songs of the paddy fields are women’s songs. Much of the practical knowledge of seeds and of food processing discussed in Chapters 9 and 14 was carried by women. Their rights over land, however, were limited: under most customary and textual regimes women inherited land rarely, and only in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries did Indian law begin to give daughters equal rights in agricultural property (the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act of 2005 made daughters coparceners). Agarwal (1994) has argued that independent land rights for women are among the most important determinants of their welfare and status in rural South Asia.

Scholarly Note: Reading the Agricultural Texts Socially

When the Kṛṣi-Parāśara advises the farmer to inspect his cattle shed or to supervise the sowing, it addresses a householder who commands the labour of others. Its knowledge is real, but it is managerial knowledge. The knowledge of the ploughman, the transplanter and the herder — much of which never reached writing — has to be recovered from ethnography, oral tradition and the observations of outsiders. Both kinds of knowledge belong in a history of Indian agriculture.

docs.title: 18.3 Land Grants and Agrarian Expansion, c. 300–1200 CE
docs.text:
The most abundant documents of Indian agrarian history for the first millennium and a half CE are inscriptions recording grants of land, mostly on copper plates. Kings and local rulers granted villages or plots to brahmins (brahmadeya, agrahāra), to temples (devadāna) and to Buddhist and Jain monasteries, often with rights to the revenue and sometimes with exemption from the entry of royal officials. The grants specify boundaries — trees, tanks, streams, anthills, fields of named cultivators — and so preserve a precise if fragmentary picture of the rural landscape (Singh 2008).

Historians have interpreted the spread of land grants in different ways. One influential view, associated with R. S. Sharma and with D. D. Kosambi’s earlier work, saw in them the fragmentation of royal authority and the subjection of the peasantry (“Indian feudalism”); others have stressed instead the integration of new regions and peoples into state society, the extension of cultivation into forest and frontier land, and the role of brahmin settlements and temples in agricultural colonisation (Kosambi 1956; Singh 2008). What is not in doubt is that this period saw a great expansion of settled, plough-based and especially rice-based agriculture — in Bengal and Odisha, in the Deccan, and in the river deltas of the south — often at the expense of forest and of forest peoples, many of whom were absorbed as peasant castes.

In the Tamil country, the inscriptions of the Pallava and Cōḻa periods show villages governed by assemblies: the ūr of non-brahmin landholders and the sabhā of brahmin settlements, grouped into localities (nāṭu). The famous inscriptions of Uttaramērūr (10th century) set out rules for the committees of a brahmin village assembly, including one for the tank. Temples were great landholders and creditors, financing irrigation and receiving produce (Singh 2008). In the Vijayanagara period (14th–16th centuries), as Morrison (1995) has shown for the region around the capital, the state, temples and local elites invested in reservoirs, canals and terraced fields, intensifying agriculture in a semi-arid landscape.

docs.title: 18.4 Agriculture under the Delhi Sultanate
docs.text:
The establishment of the Delhi Sultanate in the early thirteenth century brought northern India into close connection with the Persianate world of Central and West Asia. Its agrarian significance lay in three areas: revenue, irrigation and technology (Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982; Habib 2008).

The Sultanate assigned the revenue of territories (iqṭāʿ) to military commanders in return for service. ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn Khaljī (r. 1296–1316), according to the historian Baranī, demanded half of the produce as land revenue in the Doab around Delhi, assessed by measurement, and sought to reduce the share taken by village intermediaries. Muḥammad bin Tughluq (r. 1325–1351) raised the revenue demand in the Doab, with disastrous results in a period of drought, and later attempted to extend cultivation through a special department and state loans. Fīrūz Shāh Tughluq (r. 1351–1388) built canals from the Yamuna and the Sutlej and laid out gardens around Delhi (Section 8.11).

The period also saw the spread of new techniques and products, above all the geared “Persian wheel”, whose right-angled gearing let animals drive the older pot-wheel efficiently (Section 8.9; (Habib 2008)). Sericulture expanded, especially in Bengal; sugar refining and the distillation of spirits developed; and new fruits and garden plants arrived with the Persianate court culture.

docs.title: 18.5.1 Revenue, Measurement and the Crops of an Empire
docs.text:
The Mughal empire (1526–1857, effectively to the early eighteenth century as a major power) was above all an agrarian state. Its revenue system, as reformed under Akbar in 1580 by Rāja Ṭoḍar Mal and others, assessed the land revenue on the basis of measured land and of cash rates fixed for each crop, derived from averages of past yields and prices (the zabṭ or dahsāla system). The great administrative survey of the empire, the Āʾīn-i Akbarī of Abū’l-Faẓl (completed in the 1590s), records these crop rates for the provinces season by season, together with prices, wages and lists of fruits, vegetables and flowers (Abū’l-Faẓl 1873). Read as a source of agricultural history, it shows a diverse agriculture: many varieties of rice, wheat, barley and millets; pulses and oilseeds; cotton, sugarcane, indigo, opium poppy and hemp; vegetables and spices. It also shows what was not yet there: the crops of the Americas — maize, chillies, tobacco, groundnut — were absent or marginal at the end of the sixteenth century and spread in the seventeenth and later centuries (tobacco reached Akbar’s court only at the very end of his reign) (Habib 1999).

Irfan Habib’s study of the Mughal agrarian system remains the fundamental work (Habib 1999). It distinguishes the resident peasant (khud-kāsht) from the non-resident cultivator (pāhī-kāsht), describes the zamīndārs with hereditary rights over the land revenue of villages, and argues that the high revenue demand, levied largely in cash, pushed peasants towards cash crops and markets and, in bad years, into flight and revolt. The famine of 1630–1632 in Gujarat and the Deccan, described by Dutch and English observers and by Mughal chroniclers, showed how drought, war and the revenue demand could combine with terrible effect. Habib’s interpretation has been debated — some historians see more regional variation and more peasant prosperity — but the documentary picture of a commercialised agriculture embedded in a revenue state is generally accepted (Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982).

docs.title: 18.5.2 Cash Crops and Regional Specialisation
docs.text: By the seventeenth century several regions were known for specialised production for distant markets: indigo from Bayana near Agra and from Sarkhej near Ahmedabad; cotton and cotton textiles from Gujarat, the Coromandel coast and Bengal; raw silk from Bengal; sugar from Bengal and the Gangetic plain; pepper from Malabar. European trading companies bought these products in large quantities, and their records, together with those of Indian merchants, show how closely the peasant producer was tied to merchant credit (Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982). Trade and crafts are treated in Volumes 17 and 19.

docs.title: 18.5.3 The Village Order in the Deccan
docs.text: Records from the Deccan of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, under the Deccan sultanates and the Marathas, give an unusually clear picture of the internal organisation of the village. Hereditary rights and offices were called watan. The village headman (pāṭīl) and the accountant (kulkarṇī) held their offices and associated lands by inheritance, collected the revenue and represented the village to the state. Cultivators with permanent hereditary rights in their fields (mirāsdārs) were distinguished from tenants and outsiders who cultivated on temporary terms (upari). A group of village servants and artisans — traditionally reckoned as twelve, the bārā balutedār, including the carpenter, the blacksmith, the potter, the barber, the washerman, the leather-worker and the Mahār, who served as watchman, messenger and remover of dead cattle — received fixed shares of the harvest (balutā) from each cultivating household in return for their customary services. The balutā system is the Deccan counterpart of the north Indian jajmānī relations described above: it bound the village together in a web of reciprocal obligations, but on profoundly unequal terms, and it fixed the Mahār and other Dalit servants in the most degraded tasks. B. R. Ambedkar, himself born into a Mahār family, made the abolition of the Mahār’s hereditary watan service one of his early political causes in the 1920s and 1930s.

docs.title: 18.6 Gardens and Horticulture in the Indo-Islamic World
docs.text: Gardens were not new to India. Sanskrit literature knows the royal pleasure garden (udyāna, upavana) and its pavilions, ponds and flowering trees, and the arbori-horticultural chapters of the Bṛhatsaṃhitā, Surapāla and the Upavanavinoda were written for such gardens (Chapter 4). Someśvara’s Mānasollāsa (1131) includes garden pleasures among the enjoyments of a king (Shrigondekar 1925). But the Persianate garden brought by the Sultans and Mughals had a distinctive form and ideology, and it transformed the landscape of northern India (Moynihan 1979; Wescoat and Wolschke-Bulmahn 1996).

docs.title: 18.6.1 The Chahār Bāgh
docs.text:
The classic Persianate garden is the chahār bāgh, the “fourfold garden”: a walled rectangle divided into four by raised walkways and water channels meeting at a central pool or pavilion, often further subdivided. Running water, fountains and cascades were essential; so were shade trees, fruit trees and flowers planted in the sunken beds. The form carried associations with the gardens of paradise in Islamic tradition, whose four rivers it was sometimes understood to evoke, as well as with royal power over land and water (Moynihan 1979).

Bābur (r. 1526–1530), the founder of the Mughal dynasty, was a passionate maker of gardens. His memoirs, the Bāburnāma, complain that Hindustan lacked running water and walled gardens, and describe how he laid out gardens at Agra soon after his conquest, using water-wheels to raise water from the Yamuna (Thackston 1996). The same memoirs contain careful descriptions of the animals, birds, trees and fruits of India — the mango, the banana, the jackfruit, the rhinoceros, the parrots — written with a naturalist’s eye and a newcomer’s frankness. They are among the most important pre-modern descriptions of Indian natural history.

docs.title: 18.6.2 Mughal Gardens and the Science of Water
docs.text:
Under Bābur’s successors the garden became one of the chief arts of the empire. In Kashmir, the gardens of the Dal lake — the Shālīmār Bāgh begun under Jahāngīr and the Nishāt Bāgh built by his brother-in-law Āṣaf Khān — exploited the mountain slope to create terraces with cascades and channels fed by springs. In Lahore, Shāh Jahān’s Shālīmār garden (1640s) was supplied by a canal. The tomb gardens of Humāyūn in Delhi and of Mumtāz Maḥal (the Taj Mahal) in Agra applied the chahār bāgh plan on a monumental scale. Behind these works lay real hydraulic skill: the lifting of water by wheels, the regulation of channels, the construction of tanks and the management of gradients (Wescoat and Wolschke-Bulmahn 1996). Garden-making also stimulated horticulture — the cultivation and grafting of fruit trees, the introduction of Central Asian melons and grapes, and the planting of avenues and orchards. The pineapple, brought by the Portuguese from the Americas, was known at the Mughal court by Jahāngīr’s time.

Jahāngīr’s observations of plants and animals, and the natural-history painting of his court, are discussed in Chapters 16 and 17.

Two Garden Traditions

The Sanskrit Vṛkṣāyurveda tradition and the Persianate garden tradition met in India. The first emphasised the care, nourishment and treatment of individual trees and plants; the second, the geometry of the garden as a whole and the control of running water. Gardeners (mālī) and water engineers working for Mughal, Rajput and Deccani patrons drew on both, and the gardens of Rajput palaces such as Amber and Udaipur combine the two.

docs.title: 18.7 Persian Writing on Fields, Crops and Gardens
docs.text: From the thirteenth to the nineteenth century Persian was the language of government over much of India, and a large body of Persian writing bears on agriculture: revenue manuals and village accounts, the great survey of the Āʾīn-i Akbarī, memoirs and chronicles, regional histories and topographies, and a few manuals of agriculture and gardening. Little of it is agricultural instruction in the manner of the Kṛṣi-Parāśara or the Vṛkṣāyurveda texts. Its value lies mostly elsewhere: in administrative records that measured, counted and priced, and so preserved a picture of what was grown, where, and with what yield, more detailed than anything in the Sanskrit sources. Its limits are those of the revenue office. Like the Sanskrit treatises, it sees agriculture from above, and the knowledge of the cultivator appears in it only indirectly.

docs.title: 18.7.1 The Āʾīn-i Akbarī as an agricultural record
docs.text:
Akbar’s revenue reforms required uniform measures, and Abū’l-Faẓl’s account of them in the Āʾīn-i Akbarī is in effect a description of how land and harvests were to be known (Abū’l-Faẓl 1873; Habib 1999). Length was measured in the imperial yard (gaz-i Ilāhī); fields were measured with the surveyor’s jarīb, which, the Āʾīn records, was changed in the 1570s from a hempen rope, which shrank and stretched with the damp, to lengths of bamboo joined by iron rings; and the unit of area, the bīgha, was fixed at sixty by sixty gaz.

The Āʾīn classifies land not by soil but by the regularity of its cultivation. Polaj is land cultivated for every harvest and never left fallow; parautī is land left out of cultivation for a time so that it may recover its strength; chachar has lain fallow for three or four years; and banjar has been uncultivated for five years or more. Polaj, and parautī when it was cropped, paid the full revenue; chachar and banjar were assessed at reduced rates that rose year by year to the full rate, an arrangement meant to encourage the reclamation of waste. The scheme is a revenue classification, but it rests on the cultivator’s own distinction between land in continuous use and land resting under fallow (Chapter 10), and the word banjar is still the ordinary term for uncultivated land in the revenue records of northern India.

For land of the polaj class the Āʾīn gives, crop by crop, the yield per bīgha of good, middling and bad land. The average of the three was taken as the standard yield, and one-third of it as the state’s share. Converted into money at local prices, these shares produced the cash rates (dastūr) per bīgha for each crop in each assessment circle, and the ten-year averages of 1580 became the dahsāla rates (Section 18.5; the fiscal system is discussed in Volume 19). The crops covered run from wheat, barley, gram and other pulses, rice, sorghum and the millets, oilseeds and cotton to the high-value crops — sugarcane, indigo, opium poppy, betel leaf, melons and vegetables — each with its own rate. As a by-product of taxation, the Āʾīn thus preserves the most detailed crop and yield statistics of any pre-modern Indian state.

Modern historians have used these figures in different ways. Shireen Moosvi built from them a statistical reconstruction of the output, revenue and income of the empire around 1595 (Moosvi 1987), and Irfan Habib mapped the distribution of crops, manufactures and resources in his Atlas of the Mughal Empire (Habib 1982). Both Moosvi and Habib (1999) concluded, with due caution about the figures, that yields per unit of land in the late sixteenth century were not very different from those recorded around 1900, while the area under cultivation was considerably smaller. The Āʾīn’s accounts of the twelve provinces note the characteristic produce of each, from the rice of Bengal to the saffron fields of Kashmir (Section 10.6). Its chapters on the imperial household describe the fruit-house, with the melons, grapes and other fruits brought from Kabul, Badakhshan and Samarqand and those now grown in India by gardeners from Iran and Central Asia; they list the fruits of India and their prices; the flowers of India, with their colours and seasons; and the perfumery, whose rose and other scents are discussed in Chapter 5. Other chapters regulate the imperial stables of elephants, horses, camels, oxen and mules, with the daily rations of each class of animal (Chapter 15). Taken together they are a record of the plants and animals of a sixteenth-century court as precise, in its way, as Bābur’s memoirs.

docs.title: 18.7.2 Manuals of agriculture and gardening
docs.text:
Persian writing on agriculture belongs to the wider Islamicate tradition of books on filāḥa (Persian falāḥat), “husbandry”. In Arabic that tradition goes back to the tenth-century Nabataean Agriculture of Ibn Waḥshiyya and includes the agronomists of al-Andalus, among them Ibn al-ʿAwwām of Seville (late twelfth century). In Persian, the Ilkhanid vizier Rashīd al-Dīn (d. 1318) wrote a work on agriculture and arboriculture, the Āthār wa aḥyāʾ, that took account of plants from India and China. Closest to India in time and milieu is the Irshād al-zirāʿa (“Guide to agriculture”), written in Herat in 1515 by Qāsim b. Yūsuf Abū Naṣrī Haravī. It describes the cultivation of grains, vegetables, flowers and fruit trees around Herat, the seasons of the agricultural year, grafting and the layout of the walled garden, and it shows how closely the Timurid chahār bāgh was tied to practical horticulture (Subtelny 1997). This was the world in which Bābur grew up, and his successors brought gardeners from Iran and Central Asia to India.

Manuals were also written in India. The best known is a short Persian treatise on cultivation, the Nuskha dar fann-i falāḥat (“Treatise on the art of agriculture”), which deals with fruit trees, flowers and vegetables and is ascribed to Dārā Shukoh (1615–1659), the eldest son of Shāh Jahān. An English translation by Razia Akbar was published by the Asian Agri-History Foundation (Akbar 2000), which also published Surapāla and the Kṛṣi-Parāśara (Section 1.7); the text’s sources, date and authorship still await critical study. Persian versions of Indian works on animals — the Sālotar books on horses derived from the Śālihotra tradition (Chapter 15) and works on hawks and hunting — show the same movement of knowledge between Sanskrit and Persian that is better known in medicine and astronomy. Earlier still, al-Bīrūnī’s Arabic account of India (c. 1030) had drawn extensively on Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā, the source of so much Indian rain lore (Chapter 3).

docs.title: 18.7.3 Revenue papers and the language of the fields
docs.text:
Below the level of the empire, revenue was assessed and recorded in village and district papers kept in Persian and in the regional languages. The best-studied series come from the Kachhwāhā state of Amber (later Jaipur) in eastern Rajasthan, whose arhsaṭṭā records, in Rajasthani, give for many villages the area under each crop and the revenue due from it from the later seventeenth century. S. P. Gupta and others have used them to reconstruct cropping patterns, the stratification of the peasantry, and the spread of new crops, among them tobacco and maize, in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries (Gupta 1986). Comparable records survive from the Deccan in Marathi, written in the Modi script and full of Persian terms (Section 18.5).

The administrative vocabulary of these records has outlived the states that created it. Kharīf and rabī for the two cropping seasons (Section 9.12), zamīndār and kāshtkār for landholder and cultivator, khasra for the field register, jamabandī for the record of rights and rents, girdāwarī for the seasonal inspection of crops and jarīb for the measuring chain are all Persian or Arabic words that remain in everyday use in the land records of northern India, alongside Indic terms that the Āʾīn itself used, such as banjar for waste. Colonial land administration inherited this apparatus and the village accountants (paṭwārī) who kept it, and built its own agricultural statistics upon it (Section 19.8).

docs.title: 18.7.4 Observers and chroniclers
docs.text: Persian poets and historians also wrote about Indian agriculture as observers. Amīr Khusrau (1253–1325), in his long poem Nuh Sipihr (1318), praised India’s flowers and fruits above those of Persia and Central Asia. The Moroccan traveller Ibn Baṭṭūṭa, who served the Delhi Sultan Muḥammad bin Tughluq in the 1330s and 1340s, wrote in Arabic of the fertility of the land, which gave two harvests a year. Bābur’s memoirs survey the plants and animals of Hindustan with a newcomer’s frankness (Section 18.6), and Jahāngīr’s record his own observations as a naturalist (Chapters 16 and 17). Later topographical histories, such as Sujān Rāy Bhaṇḍārī’s Khulāṣat al-tawārīkh (1695), describe the provinces of the empire and their produce. These works are uneven as evidence, but together with the revenue records they make the Persian archive the richest single source for the agriculture of India between the fourteenth and the eighteenth centuries (Habib 1999).

docs.title: 18.8.1 New Revenue Settlements
docs.text:
British rule, beginning with the East India Company’s acquisition of the revenue administration (dīwānī) of Bengal in 1765, reorganised the relationship between the state, landholders and cultivators (Ludden 1999; Kumar 1983). Three main systems emerged:

  • The Permanent Settlement of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha (1793) fixed the revenue in perpetuity and recognised the zamīndārs as proprietors of the land, leaving cultivators as their tenants; tenant protection came only gradually through later tenancy legislation.

  • The Ryotwari settlements of Madras and Bombay (from the early nineteenth century, associated with Thomas Munro) assessed revenue directly on individual cultivators (ryots), at rates that were for long very high.

  • The Mahalwari settlements of the North-Western Provinces and the Punjab (from 1822) assessed revenue on village or estate communities.

All three turned land into a saleable commodity, and debt and sale of land to moneylenders became a recurring source of rural conflict, as in the Deccan riots of 1875.

docs.title: 18.8.2 Commercial Crops and Their Costs
docs.text: Colonial rule intensified the production of crops for export. Indigo was grown in Bengal and Bihar under a system that compelled peasants to cultivate it on terms dictated by European planters; the Indigo Revolt of 1859–1860 in Bengal, and Gandhi’s Champaran campaign of 1917 in Bihar, were responses to it. Opium was grown under a government monopoly in Bihar and around Benares for export to China. The American Civil War (1861–1865) created a cotton boom in the Deccan, followed by collapse. Jute in eastern Bengal, tea in Assam and the hills (worked by indentured labourers recruited from central and eastern India), coffee in the south and wheat for export from the newly irrigated Punjab were further examples (Kumar 1983; Ludden 1999).

docs.title: 18.8.3 Famine
docs.text: The late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries were punctuated by catastrophic famines: Bengal in 1770, the Great Famine of 1876–1878 in the south and west, and the famines of 1896–1897 and 1899–1900. Davis (2001) has argued that the late-Victorian famines resulted from the interaction of El Niño droughts with colonial policies that prioritised revenue, exports and market principles over relief; Roy (2011) gives more weight to the droughts themselves and to the weakness of transport and credit. After the Famine Commission of 1880, the government adopted Famine Codes that organised relief works and food distribution, and famine mortality declined — until the Bengal famine of 1943, in which between two and three million people died in most estimates. Amartya Sen’s analysis of that famine, which showed that it occurred without a catastrophic decline in food availability and was driven by the collapse of the purchasing power (“entitlements”) of rural labourers, artisans and fishermen, has become a classic of economic thought (Sen 1981). In every famine the landless — agricultural labourers, many of them Dalits, and village artisans — died in disproportionate numbers.

docs.title: 18.8.4 Colonial Agricultural Science and Indian Practice
docs.text: The colonial state at first regarded Indian agriculture as backward and in need of improvement. Its more perceptive observers, above all Voelcker (Section 7.5.2), found Indian cultivators skilled and placed the obstacles in shortages of manure, water, credit and fuel. The departments, research institutes and colleges that grew out of this concern, from the Famine Commission of 1880 to the high-yielding varieties of the 1960s, are the subject of Chapter 19; colonial botany, veterinary science and forestry are treated in Chapters 6, 13 and 11 (Arnold 2000).

docs.title: 18.8.5 Plantations and Indentured Labour
docs.text: A different agrarian world grew up on the plantations. Tea was planted in Assam from the late 1830s and later in Darjeeling, the Dooars and the Nilgiris; coffee in Kodagu, Mysore and the Nilgiris; and indigo, before its decline, in Bengal and Bihar. Plantations needed large, disciplined labour forces in thinly populated regions, and planters recruited them from the Adivasi and low-caste populations of Chotanagpur, the Santal Parganas and the Central Provinces, often through contractors and under penal contracts that made leaving the estate a criminal offence. Mortality on the journey and in the early years on the estates was very high. The plantation economy thus brought into being a new class of wage labourers, uprooted from their own agrarian communities, whose descendants still form a large part of the population of the tea districts (Kumar 1983; Ludden 1999).

docs.title: 18.8.6 Peasant Movements
docs.text:
Colonial agrarian policy provoked resistance from cultivators, often in alliance with, and sometimes against, the nationalist movement (Ludden 1999). Among the best-known episodes are:

  • the Indigo Revolt in Bengal (1859–1860), in which cultivators refused to grow indigo for European planters;

  • the Deccan riots of 1875, directed against moneylenders who had acquired peasants’ land, which led to the Deccan Agriculturists’ Relief Act of 1879;

  • the Champaran (1917) and Kheda (1918) campaigns led by Gandhi, against compulsory indigo cultivation in Bihar and against revenue collection after crop failure in Gujarat;

  • the Eka and Kisan Sabha movements of tenants in Awadh in the early 1920s, and the rebellion of Muslim Mappila cultivators in Malabar in 1921, in which agrarian grievances against landlords were entangled with religious conflict;

  • the Bardoli satyagraha of 1928 in Gujarat against an increase in land revenue;

  • the founding of the All India Kisan Sabha in 1936, which gave peasant organisation a national form;

  • the Tebhāgā movement of sharecroppers in Bengal (1946–1947), who demanded two-thirds of the crop instead of half, and the armed peasant uprising in Telangana (1946–1951) against the landlords of the Nizam’s state.

The colonial state also legislated to protect cultivators from losing land to moneylenders — the Punjab Land Alienation Act of 1900, for instance, restricted the transfer of land from “agricultural tribes” to others — in ways that were shaped as much by political calculation as by concern for the peasantry. These struggles placed land reform at the centre of the agenda of independent India.

docs.title: 18.9 After Independence
docs.text: The independent Indian state inherited a stagnant agriculture, deep inequality in land and a recent memory of famine. In the early 1950s most states passed laws abolishing zamīndārī intermediaries; tenancy reform and ceilings on landholding followed, with very uneven implementation. Vinoba Bhave’s Bhūdān (“land gift”) movement, begun in 1951 in Telangana, sought voluntary donations of land for the landless. Large irrigation projects, community development programmes and agricultural universities were established. In the mid-1960s, after two severe droughts and dependence on food imports, India adopted the package of high-yielding varieties, fertiliser and irrigation known as the Green Revolution. Its scientific and institutional origins are described in Chapter 19, and its achievements and costs in Chapter 20.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The knowledge traditions of Indian agriculture were embedded in a society in which the right to own land, the duty to labour on it and the stigma of particular kinds of work were distributed by caste and gender. Normative texts assigned agriculture to the vaiśya but discouraged high castes from ploughing; much of the actual cultivation was done by śūdra peasants and by labourers held in various forms of servitude, many from castes treated as untouchable, and by women whose work was rarely recorded. Land grants of the first millennium CE document the expansion of settled agriculture. The Sultanate and Mughal states brought new revenue systems, canals, water-wheels, gardens and fruits, and left a Persian archive of measured fields and crop rates richer than any earlier record. Colonial rule turned land into a commodity, promoted export crops and presided over devastating famines.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Ludden (1999) is the best single survey. For the Mughal period see Habib (1999), Raychaudhuri and Habib (1982), Moosvi (1987) and Habib (1982), and for the Persian agricultural manuals Subtelny (1997); for the colonial period Kumar (1983); for caste and labour Sharma (1980), Breman (1974) and Prakash (1990); for women and land Agarwal (1994); for gardens Moynihan (1979) and Wescoat and Wolschke-Bulmahn (1996).

docs.title: Chapter 19: Science, Famine and the State: Agricultural Research in India, 1870–1970
19.1 From Revenue to Improvement
docs.text:
For most of Indian history the state took an interest in agriculture chiefly as the source of its revenue. The Arthaśāstra’s superintendent of agriculture ran crown farms and recorded rainfall; Sultanate and Mughal officials measured fields and fixed cash rates for each crop; the early East India Company settled the land revenue with zamīndārs and ryots (Chapters 3 and 18). Rulers also built canals and tanks, laid out gardens, kept studs and promoted particular crops, as Tipu Sultan promoted mulberry silk in Mysore. But there was no permanent institution whose business was to study crops, soils, pests and animals and to change the way cultivators worked.

Between about 1870 and 1970 that changed.
