docs.text: For guilds and traders, Chakravarti (2002); for the Gupta inscriptions, Fleet (1888); for weavers in medieval south India, Ramaswamy (1985); for caste in modern history, Bayly (1999); for Ambedkar’s critique, Ambedkar (1936); for anti-caste thought, Omvedt (2008); for the jajmānī debate, Wiser (1936) and Fuller (1989); for artisans and merchants in western India, Haynes (2012); on theory and practice in Sanskrit learning, Pollock (1985); on tacit knowledge, Polanyi (1958); on the Kashmir tālīm, Irwin (1973); on craft, training and development, Venkatesan (2009); on medieval technology, Habib (2008); on European accounts of Indian technology, Dharampal (1971); on the circulation of knowledge between India and Europe, Raj (2007).

docs.title: Chapter 14: Crafts in the Colonial Economy
docs.text: Between the mid-eighteenth and the mid-twentieth centuries, the Indian craft economy was transformed. The East India Company, from a trading company, became the ruler of Bengal and then of most of India; British factory goods, above all cotton cloth, flooded Indian markets; and many artisan industries declined, while others adapted and some new ones grew. Nationalists from the late nineteenth century onwards made the ruin of Indian crafts a central charge against British rule, and the spinning wheel became the symbol of the freedom movement. This chapter examines what happened, how historians have measured and debated it, and how a famous myth, that of the muslin weavers’ severed thumbs, arose.

docs.title: 14.1 India in the Eighteenth-Century World Economy
docs.text:
In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, South Asia was one of the world’s largest producers of manufactured goods, and its cotton textiles were exported in great quantities to Southeast Asia, West Asia, East Africa and, through the European companies, to Europe, West Africa and the Americas (Chaudhuri 1978; Riello and Roy 2009). Two sets of estimates are often quoted to show the scale of this economy:

  • Angus Maddison estimated that India accounted for about a quarter of world GDP around 1700, falling to about 16 per cent in 1820 and under 5 per cent by 1950 (Maddison 2001). These figures largely reflect the size of India’s population; they do not measure productivity or living standards.

  • Paul Bairoch estimated that the Indian subcontinent produced roughly a quarter of the world’s manufactures in 1750, falling to under 2 per cent by 1900, while Britain’s share rose from about 2 per cent to nearly a fifth (Bairoch 1982); his figures are given in Table 14.1.

Table 14.1. Bairoch’s estimates of shares of world manufacturing output (per cent) Year Indian subcontinent United Kingdom China 1750 24.5 1.9 32.8 1800 19.7 4.3 33.3 1830 17.6 9.5 29.8 1860 8.6 19.9 19.7 1880 2.8 22.9 12.5 1900 1.7 18.5 6.2

Source: Bairoch (1982). The figures for the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries are rough estimates, based largely on assumptions about population and per capita consumption of manufactures.

Both sets of figures are estimates, and economic historians use them with caution. They do show, however, that the relative position of Indian manufacturing changed dramatically in the nineteenth century, in part because Britain industrialised and in part because Indian handicraft industries declined.

docs.title: 14.2.1 From Trade to Rule
docs.text:
Until the mid-eighteenth century, the European companies bought Indian textiles in competition with Indian and other Asian merchants, through brokers who advanced money to weavers. After the battle of Plassey (1757) and the grant of the revenue administration (dīvānī) of Bengal in 1765, the English Company used its political power to secure cloth on its own terms. Its agents (gumāśtas) forced advances on weavers, bound them to deliver only to the Company, fixed low prices, and used peons to confine, fine and beat weavers who failed to deliver or tried to sell to others. Company regulations from the 1770s and 1780s gave legal backing to many of these practices (Hossain 1988). In south India, Prasannan Parthasarathi has shown how the Company’s new controls eroded the bargaining power that weavers had previously enjoyed (Parthasarathi 2001).

The great Bengal famine of 1769–70, which killed a large part of the population of the province in the first years of Company rule, fell heavily on weavers, spinners and other artisans, who depended on buying grain in the market. Famine and scarcity recurred throughout the colonial period, and artisans, who had no land to fall back on, were among the first to suffer.

These coercive practices were described at the time by critics of the Company, among them William Bolts, a former Company servant, whose Considerations on India Affairs (1772) is one of the most detailed contemporary accounts (Bolts 1772).

docs.title: 14.2.2 The Myth of the Severed Thumbs
docs.text:
A story widely repeated in India holds that the British cut off the thumbs of the muslin weavers of Dhaka to destroy their craft. The story is not supported by any documentary evidence. It appears to derive from a misreading of a passage in Bolts’s book, which describes the oppression of the winders of raw silk in Bengal (whom he calls “Nagaads”), and reports that some of them had cut off their own thumbs to escape being forced to wind silk for the Company (Bolts 1772). Over time, in nationalist writing and popular memory, this account of self-mutilation by silk-winders became a story of mutilation by the British of the weavers of Dhaka muslin.

The myth should be abandoned, not because the Company’s treatment of weavers was benign, but because the documented reality is serious enough. Weavers were coerced by advances, confined, fined and flogged; they lost the freedom to sell to the highest bidder; and their earnings fell (Hossain 1988; Parthasarathi 2001). The decline of the Dhaka muslin industry in the early nineteenth century had several causes: the loss of Mughal court patronage, the Company’s purchasing regime, British tariffs on Indian cloth, and above all the arrival of cheap machine-made cloth from Lancashire.

docs.title: 14.3 Tariffs and Machine-Made Cloth
docs.text:
By the late eighteenth century British manufacturers, having learned to print, dye and finally spin and weave cotton by machine, could compete with Indian cloth in Britain and in third markets. Indian cottons entering Britain had long faced heavy duties or prohibition. The historian H. H. Wilson, writing in the 1850s, remarked that in the early nineteenth century Indian cotton and silk goods could have been sold profitably in Britain at much lower prices than British goods, and that British manufactures had to be protected by duties of 70–80 per cent or by prohibition; Romesh Chunder Dutt, who quoted him, made the contrast between British protection at home and enforced free trade in India a central argument of his Economic History of India (1902) (Dutt 1902). British goods, by contrast, entered India at low duties after the end of the Company’s trading monopoly in 1813; the remaining cotton import duties were abolished in 1882, and when they were reimposed in the 1890s for revenue, an equivalent excise was levied on cloth from Indian mills.

Imports of British cotton cloth and yarn into India grew rapidly from the 1820s, and by the later nineteenth century Lancashire cloth dominated the market for ordinary cloth. Handloom weavers lost much of their market, especially for plain cloth; spinners, most of them women working at home, lost almost all of theirs as handloom weavers turned to cheap machine-spun yarn.

docs.title: 14.4 The Drain and the Weaver
docs.text: Nationalist economists connected the fate of Indian crafts with a broader critique of colonial rule. Dadabhai Naoroji argued that a large part of India’s revenue was transferred to Britain each year, without equivalent return, in the form of the salaries and pensions of officials, interest on debt, the costs of the army and the profits of British firms: the “drain” of wealth from India (Naoroji 1901). Romesh Chunder Dutt added a detailed history of land revenue, famine and the decline of manufactures. In their view, the ruin of the weaver was one part of a system that impoverished India for Britain’s benefit (Dutt 1902). Later economic historians have debated the size of the drain and its effects, but the critique shaped Indian economic thought and policy for decades, including the protection of handlooms and village industries after independence.

docs.title: 14.5 The Deindustrialisation Debate
docs.text:
The nationalist case, set out in Naoroji’s Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901) and in Dutt’s histories, was that British rule had “deindustrialised” India, destroying its manufactures and forcing artisans back onto the land. Later historians have debated the extent and causes of this decline.

  • Amiya Kumar Bagchi, using the surveys of Francis Buchanan-Hamilton for Gangetic Bihar in the 1810s and the census of 1901, argued that the share of the population dependent on industry roughly halved over the nineteenth century, a clear case of deindustrialisation (Bagchi 1976).

  • Morris D. Morris and others questioned the reliability of such comparisons and argued that handloom weaving survived on a larger scale than nationalists assumed (Morris 1963).

  • Tirthankar Roy has shown that many “traditional” industries adapted rather than disappeared: handloom weavers specialised in products the mills could not make cheaply, such as saris with complex borders, used mill yarn, adopted improved looms, and in some regions expanded their output in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries (Roy 1993, 1999).

  • The Cambridge Economic History of India surveys the evidence for the period as a whole (Kumar 1983).

The picture that emerges is of severe and uneven decline. Cotton spinning by hand collapsed; plain cloth weaving lost much of its market; iron smelting, paper-making and many other crafts dwindled; luxury crafts lost their courtly patrons. At the same time some handicrafts adapted and some new industries, such as carpets for export, grew; and from the 1850s Indian entrepreneurs built cotton mills in Bombay and Ahmedabad, so that by the early twentieth century India had a substantial modern textile industry of its own. Artisans who could not adapt fell into poverty, and many joined the ranks of landless labourers.

docs.title: 14.6 Other Crafts under Colonial Rule
docs.text:
The fate of crafts other than cotton weaving varied.

Iron and steel Village iron smelting declined steeply in the second half of the nineteenth century, as cheap imported iron and steel, carried by the railways, reached rural markets, and as forest laws restricted access to charcoal. Crucible steel production also ended. The first large modern steelworks in India, the Tata Iron and Steel Company at Jamshedpur, began production in 1911–12. Paper Hand-made paper was displaced by machine-made paper, both imported and, from the later nineteenth century, made in Indian mills. Shipbuilding Indian shipwrights built large ships for the East India Company and for Indian merchants at Bombay, Surat and on the Hughli in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries; the Wadia master-builders of Bombay built ships for the Royal Navy (Wadia 1955). The coming of iron and steam ships in the mid-nineteenth century, and the preference for British yards, ended this industry. Luxury crafts The decline of Indian courts and aristocracies after the Company’s conquests deprived many craftsmen of patrons. At the same time, new markets appeared among Europeans in India and abroad, for whom craftsmen produced “art wares” adapted to European taste: carved furniture, ivory and metal souvenirs, embroidered goods and shawls. New industries Some crafts expanded: carpet-weaving for export, the Firozabad glass bangle industry, and the brass industry of Moradabad grew in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, often using imported materials such as sheet brass and glass.

Tirthankar Roy’s study of several craft industries in the late colonial period, among them handloom weaving, silk, wool and leather, shows a pattern of change rather than simple decline: some branches of each industry collapsed, others adapted to new markets and new materials, labour relations became more commercial, and workshops employing wage labour grew at the expense of independent artisans (Roy 1999).

docs.title: 14.7 The Indian Cotton Mills
docs.text: Indian entrepreneurs answered British competition by building their own mills. The first successful cotton-spinning mill in Bombay was founded by Cowasji Nanabhai Davar in 1854, and Ranchhodlal Chhotalal opened the first mill in Ahmedabad in 1861. By the early twentieth century Bombay and Ahmedabad were great textile cities, with mills owned largely by Parsi, Gujarati Hindu, Jain and Muslim entrepreneurs. Their workforce included many people from weaving and other artisan castes who had lost their livelihoods, as well as migrants from agricultural communities. The mills competed with the handloom weavers for the market in coarse cloth, but they also supplied the weavers with yarn. In Ahmedabad, a dispute between millworkers and owners in 1918, in which Gandhi intervened, led to the foundation of the Textile Labour Association, a union based on Gandhian principles of arbitration, in which Anasuya Sarabhai played a leading role. The history of Indian textiles thus continued into the industrial age, with many of the same communities.

docs.title: 14.8 The Princely States
docs.text: Some princely states pursued their own policies towards crafts and industry. In Mysore, the state promoted sericulture and silk weaving, establishing a government silk-weaving factory in 1912, and the Mysore government’s industrial programme under the engineer-administrator M. Visvesvaraya (Dewan 1912–1918) included support for traditional as well as modern industries. Baroda under Sayajirao Gaekwad III (r. 1875–1939) founded the Kala Bhavan technical institute (1890), which taught both modern technology and the arts. Travancore, Hyderabad, Jaipur and other states maintained schools of art and crafts, museums and emporia. The princely states were not immune from the pressures of the colonial economy, but under some of them crafts and industry were deliberately fostered rather than left to decline.

docs.title: 14.9 Indigo and Cotton
docs.text:
Colonial rule also turned some craft materials into plantation and export crops. Indigo was grown in Bengal and Bihar under the control of European planters, who forced peasants to cultivate it on unfavourable terms. In 1859–60 the cultivators of Bengal rose in the “Indigo Revolt”; Dinabandhu Mitra’s play Nīl Darpaṇ (1860) dramatised their sufferings. In Champaran in Bihar, Gandhi’s first satyagraha in India (1917) was against the system that compelled tenants to grow indigo on part of their land. Synthetic indigo, marketed from 1897, ended the plantation industry in the following decades.

During the American Civil War (1861–65), when supplies of American raw cotton to Lancashire were cut off, cotton cultivation expanded rapidly in western India, and Bombay experienced a speculative boom that collapsed in 1865. Sven Beckert’s global history of cotton places the episode in a longer story, in which British and other states pressed India, Egypt and other regions to grow raw cotton for the mills of Europe while buying their cloth (Beckert 2014). India’s place in the world economy had been reversed: from the great exporter of cotton cloth it had become a supplier of raw cotton and a market for Lancashire.

docs.title: 14.10 Exhibitions, Art Schools and the Idea of “Indian Art Manufactures”
docs.text:
Paradoxically, the colonial state also became a collector and promoter of Indian crafts. Indian textiles, metalwork, jewellery and carvings were displayed at the Great Exhibition of 1851 in London and at many later exhibitions, and were acquired for the South Kensington Museum (later the Victoria and Albert Museum). George Birdwood’s The Industrial Arts of India (1880) praised Indian “art manufactures” as the products of a timeless village craftsman and deplored their corruption by European taste (Birdwood 1880). Schools of art were founded at Madras, Calcutta, Bombay and Lahore in the 1850s–1870s, partly to improve Indian design for the market; John Lockwood Kipling at Lahore and others collected and documented crafts. Abigail McGowan has shown how these colonial projects shaped the very idea of “Indian crafts” as a national heritage, an idea that nationalists then took up (McGowan 2009).

The Delhi Durbar of 1903, held to celebrate the accession of Edward VII, included a large exhibition of Indian art industries, organised by the economic botanist George Watt, whose catalogue surveyed the crafts of every province and lamented their decline under the influence of European taste and cheap imports (Watt 1903). From 1884 to 1917 the Journal of Indian Art, published in London, documented Indian crafts in illustrated articles, and provincial governments commissioned monographs on particular industries, such as cotton fabrics, silk, brass and copper ware, pottery, and wood-carving, in each province around 1900. These works, often written by district officers with the help of local informants, remain important sources, though they share the assumption that Indian crafts were static traditions in decline.

Ananda Coomaraswamy’s The Indian Craftsman (1909) drew on the British Arts and Crafts movement of William Morris and on his own studies of Ceylonese and Indian crafts to argue that the Indian craftsman, working within a guild and a religious tradition, embodied a way of life superior to industrial labour (Coomaraswamy 1909). His idealised picture paid little attention to caste hierarchy, but it gave Indian craft a philosophical dignity that strongly influenced later revivalists.

docs.title: 14.11 Svadeśī and Khādī
docs.text:
The Svadeśī movement in Bengal (1903–1908), launched in protest against Lord Curzon’s partition of the province in 1905, called for the boycott of British goods and the use of Indian ones. It encouraged handloom weaving and Indian enterprise, and its leaders included Surendranath Banerjea, Bipin Chandra Pal and Aurobindo Ghose in Bengal, and Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Lala Lajpat Rai elsewhere. Rabindranath Tagore composed songs for the movement and organised the tying of rākhīs as a symbol of unity on the day the partition took effect (Sarkar 1973).

Sumit Sarkar distinguished two strands in the movement: the boycott of foreign goods, and “constructive Svadeśī”, the effort to build Indian industries, crafts and institutions in their place (Sarkar 1973). Both touched the crafts directly. Manchester cloth was the main target of the boycott, and imports of British piece-goods into Bengal fell in the first years of the agitation. Volunteers picketed shops, and in some places women gave up imported glass bangles along with foreign cloth. Swadeshi stores opened in Calcutta and the district towns to sell Indian-made cloth, soap, matches, cutlery and other goods. Some of these, such as the store opened in Calcutta by Saraladevi Chaudhurani, sold goods made by women at home.

The movement raised the demand for Indian cloth, but its benefits were unevenly shared. Sarkar showed that much of the cloth sold as svadeśī came from the mills of Bombay and Ahmedabad, whose owners profited more from the boycott than Bengal’s handloom weavers did. Handloom weaving nonetheless revived in parts of Bengal, helped by the fly-shuttle (Section 4.4) and by weaving schools. New Bengali enterprises were also founded, among them the Banga Lakshmi Cotton Mills (1906). The National Council of Education and the Bengal Technical Institute, both founded in 1906 and merged in 1910, set out to train Indians in technology and the industrial crafts; together they were the forerunners of Jadavpur University. In the same years Abanindranath and Gaganendranath Tagore, with British admirers of Indian art, founded the Indian Society of Oriental Art (1907), which promoted an “Indian” art drawing on Mughal, Rajput and Ajanta painting and, later, on folk and craft traditions (Chapter 11).

The boycott also had a coercive side. Poor traders, many of them Muslim, who depended on selling cheap foreign cloth, were pressed or forced to give it up, and the burning of their goods caused bitterness. Rabindranath Tagore, who had at first composed songs for the movement, withdrew from it. In his novel Ghare Baire (The Home and the World, 1916) the forced burning of a poor trader’s foreign cloth is one of the episodes through which he criticised nationalist zeal (Volume 24). The arguments of the Svadeśī years about whether to boycott or to build, about mill and handloom, and about whom the movement served, were taken up again, on a much larger scale, in the Gandhian campaign for khādī.

M. K. Gandhi made hand-spinning and hand-woven cloth (khādī) the centre of the national movement from the early 1920s. In Hind Swaraj (1909) he had condemned machinery as a symbol of modern civilisation (Gandhi 1997); in practice he called for the boycott and burning of foreign cloth, spun daily himself, and founded the All India Spinners’ Association (1925) and the All India Village Industries Association (1934). For Gandhi, the spinning wheel offered rural people, especially women, supplementary income during the agricultural off-season, and it symbolised self-reliance and the dignity of manual labour. A spinning wheel was placed at the centre of the flag adopted by the Congress, and was replaced by the Aśokan wheel in the national flag of 1947. Khādī was, however, more expensive than mill cloth, and its economic impact was limited; its political and symbolic significance was immense. C. A. Bayly has shown how the politics of khādī drew on older Indian ideas about the moral and physical properties of cloth (Bayly 1986).

docs.title: 14.12 The Charkhā and the Making of Khādī
docs.text: The khādī movement was a craft programme as well as a political one. To make cloth by hand on a national scale, the movement had to recover skills that had almost disappeared. It had to organise spinners, carders and weavers, improve their tools, fix prices and wages, and guarantee to buyers that the cloth was what it claimed to be. This section looks at that practical work. Gandhi’s economic and political thought, and the arguments of his critics, are treated in Volumes 19 and 24.

docs.title: 14.12.1 Recovering a Lost Skill
docs.text: Gandhi recalled in his autobiography that when he praised the spinning wheel in Hind Swaraj in 1909, he had not yet seen one (Gandhi 1927). His ashram at Ahmedabad, founded in 1915, began by weaving on handlooms with mill-spun yarn, because neither a wheel nor a spinner could be found. In 1917 or soon after, Gangabehn Majmundar, a widow who had joined his work, found spinning wheels lying unused in the lofts of houses at Vijapur in the princely state of Baroda. She also found women there who were willing to spin again if someone supplied them with slivers (pūnī) of carded cotton and bought their yarn. At first the slivers came from a mill. Only later was a carder engaged, so that the whole process, from raw cotton to cloth, could be done by hand. Within a century, hand-spinning had declined so far in western India that a national movement had to search for it (Section 14.3); yet the skill had survived in the hands of older women, who taught it to the movement’s volunteers.

docs.title: 14.12.2 From Ashram to Organisation
docs.text:
During the Non-Cooperation Movement of 1920–22, khādī became the visible sign of commitment to the national cause. Foreign cloth was burned in public bonfires, and in September 1921, at Madurai, Gandhi gave up the shirt and cap for a loincloth and shawl. He explained that while khādī was scarce, those who could not obtain enough of it should make do with less. Congress office-holders were expected to wear khādī, and in 1924 the Congress briefly made the spinning of a monthly quota of yarn a condition of membership.

The All India Spinners’ Association (Akhil Bhāratīya Carkhā Saṅgh), founded in 1925, turned these commitments into an organisation. It bought cotton and distributed it to spinners, often as slivers, and paid for their yarn according to its count and evenness. It gave the yarn to weavers to be woven for a wage, and sold the cloth through its own shops (khādī bhaṇḍār) and at exhibitions held alongside the annual sessions of the Congress. It also certified producers and shops, so that buyers could trust that “khādī” was hand-spun as well as hand-woven, a guarantee that mill cloth sold under nationalist labels could not give. Lisa Trivedi has shown how the Association’s exhibitions, travelling displays, photographs and printed images created a shared visual language of the nation, in which the spinning wheel, the white cap and the hand-spun cloth stood for self-rule (Trivedi 2007). Some regions produced khādī of great fineness. At Ponduru in coastal Andhra, fine yarn is still spun from local cotton that, as in Dhaka, is cleaned with the jaw-bone of a fish (Section 4.7).

The economics were difficult. Spinning paid very little, and khādī cost more than mill cloth. In the mid-1930s Gandhi persuaded the Association to raise spinners’ wages towards a “living wage”, even though this raised prices and reduced sales. He also placed growing weight on self-sufficiency (svāvalambana): households and villages spinning for their own needs rather than for the market.

docs.title: 14.12.3 Improving the Wheel
docs.text:
The village spinning wheel had a single spindle driven by a cord from a large hand-turned wheel. The spinner turned the wheel with one hand and drew out the yarn with the other, and her output was small. The movement spent much effort on improving the tools. Maganlal Gandhi, a younger kinsman of Gandhi and the manager of the Sabarmati ashram until his death in 1928, worked on the wheel and on carding. In 1929 the Association offered a prize of one lakh rupees for a wheel that would allow a spinner to earn substantially more at home under stated conditions; it does not appear to have been awarded. Gandhi’s own contribution was the compact box wheel (peṭī carkhā; Figure 14.1), associated with his imprisonment at Yeravda in the early 1930s, which folded into a case small enough to carry on journeys. For schoolchildren and travellers the movement promoted the simple hand spindle (takalī), which became part of the curriculum of Gandhian basic education (Chapter 15).

Figure 14.1. A box spinning wheel (peṭī carkhā) of the 1920s or 1930s, opened out. The pair of wheels on the right drives, by a cord, the spindle on the left, where the spun yarn is wound (Textile Museum, George Washington University, Washington). Photo: Daderot, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons (cropped)

After independence the most important change was the multi-spindle Ambar charkhā. It was developed by E. Ekambaranathan of Tamil Nadu, whose name it carries, and adopted in the mid-1950s by the All India Khadi and Village Industries Board, the predecessor of the Commission. With four spindles and drafting rollers it greatly increased output. It needed evenly prepared slivers, which were made by machine, and this raised the question of how much machinery khādī could include while remaining khādī. Later models added more spindles. The debate, about where the line between hand and machine should be drawn, continues in handloom policy today (Section 15.2).

docs.title: 14.12.4 Meanings and Limits
docs.text:
Khādī had critics from the start. Rabindranath Tagore’s essay “The Cult of the Charka” (1925) questioned whether mechanical spinning could free the mind, and Gandhi replied in “The Poet and the Charkha” in Young India later that year (Bhattacharya 1997). Economists pointed to the low returns of hand-spinning, and B. R. Ambedkar rejected the idealisation of the village economy (Volume 19). Even among nationalists, wearing coarse, heavy khādī was a sacrifice. Emma Tarlo has shown how men and women negotiated it, and how khādī was refined over the following decades into finer and more varied cloths (Tarlo 1996). Its achievement was not economic. It brought very large numbers of people, many of them women, into the national movement through a daily act of making. It joined the politics of independence to the fate of the poorest craft workers, and it gave Indian handmade cloth a symbolic standing that it has kept. After independence khādī remained the customary dress of politicians. Until the Flag Code was amended at the end of 2021, the national flag itself had to be made of hand-spun, hand-woven khādī.

Modern Relevance: At Independence

At independence in 1947, millions of Indians still depended on handicrafts and handloom weaving, most of them in poverty. The new state created the All India Handicrafts Board (1952), the All India Handloom Board, and the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (1957), and reserved certain products for the handloom sector. The story of these institutions and of the craft revival they supported is taken up in the next chapter.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For the Company and the Bengal weavers, Hossain (1988); for south India, Parthasarathi (2001); for the global context, Parthasarathi (2011) and Riello (2013); for the deindustrialisation debate, Bagchi (1976) and Roy (1999); for the nationalist critique, Dutt (1902); for colonial and nationalist ideas of craft, McGowan (2009); for Svadeśī, Sarkar (1973); for the beginnings of khādī, Gandhi (1927); for khādī and the visual culture of the nation, Trivedi (2007).

docs.title: Chapter 15: Living Crafts: Revival, Protection and the Present
docs.text: India still has one of the largest populations of craftspeople and handloom weavers in the world. Their crafts survive in very different conditions: some prosper in national and international markets, some are sustained by government and voluntary support, and many are declining as younger people leave for other work. This chapter surveys the institutions and movements of the craft revival since independence, the design schools, the legal protection of craft names through Geographical Indications, the markets and enterprises that sell crafts today, and the problems that remain.

docs.title: 15.1.1 Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay and the Handicrafts Board
docs.text:
The central figure of the post-independence craft revival was Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay (1903–1988), a nationalist, socialist and feminist who had worked in the freedom movement and for refugee resettlement after Partition. As the first chair of the All India Handicrafts Board (1952), she directed surveys of crafts across the country, established emporia and marketing organisations, and promoted the recognition of master craftspeople; she was also a founder of the Crafts Council of India (1964) and a leading figure in the World Crafts Council. Her books, such as Handicrafts of India, describe crafts region by region (Chattopadhyay 1975), and her memoir Inner Recesses, Outer Spaces (1986) records her work (Chattopadhyay 1986). Pupul Jayakar, who organised exhibitions of Indian textiles and crafts in India and abroad, from the Museum of Modern Art exhibition of 1955–56 (Jayakar and Irwin 1956) to the Festivals of India of the 1980s, was another influential figure.

Kamaladevi’s work for crafts began with the refugees of Partition. The Indian Co-operative Union, which she founded in 1948, helped to resettle refugees from the North-West Frontier and western Punjab in a co-operative township at Faridabad, near Delhi. To sell the work of refugee and other craftspeople it opened a cottage industries emporium in New Delhi, which the government later took over as the Central Cottage Industries Emporium. At the Handicrafts Board she argued that the artisan should be treated as a creator and not as a source of cheap labour, and that craftspeople should be organised in co-operatives they controlled themselves. She travelled widely to find crafts on the edge of extinction, and many of the makers honoured by the early national awards were people she had sought out. Her approach also had limits that later writers have noted. By presenting crafts above all as national heritage, the programmes she inspired could cast artisans as custodians of tradition rather than as workers with interests of their own (Chapter 13). She received the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 1966.

docs.title: 15.1.2 Institutions
docs.text:
The state created a network of institutions for crafts and handlooms:

  • the All India Handicrafts Board (1952), later the office of the Development Commissioner (Handicrafts), and the All India Handloom Board;

  • the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (1957), for khādī and village industries;

  • state handicrafts and handloom development corporations and cooperative societies, with their emporia;

  • the Crafts Museum in New Delhi, founded in the 1950s and now the National Crafts Museum and Hastkala Academy;

  • the Weavers’ Service Centres, set up from the 1950s to provide designs and technical support to handloom weavers;

  • the National Institute of Design, Ahmedabad (1961), and later craft-design schools (Section 15.8);

  • national awards for master craftspersons (from the 1960s) and, from 2002, the Shilp Guru awards.

These institutions sustained many crafts through difficult decades. They have also been criticised for bureaucracy, for favouring cooperatives dominated by traders, and for promoting products designed for urban tastes rather than for the needs of artisans themselves.

docs.title: 15.1.3 Voluntary Organisations and Enterprises
docs.text: From the 1970s, voluntary organisations, designers and private enterprises became increasingly important. The Self-Employed Women’s Association (SEWA), founded by Ela Bhatt in Ahmedabad in 1972, organised home-based women workers, including embroiderers and other craftswomen, and helped them to market their work. Dastkar, founded in Delhi in 1981, has worked with craft groups across India and organised craft bazaars that bring artisans directly to urban buyers. Fabindia, founded in 1960 as an exporter of handloom textiles, became a large retailer of hand-made and hand-printed goods, and from the 2000s experimented with companies in which artisan suppliers hold shares. Anokhi, founded in Jaipur in 1970, worked with block-printers in Sanganer and Bagru and established a Museum of Hand Printing at Amber. In Kutch, organisations such as Khamir, founded after the 2001 earthquake, and Kala Raksha (Section 15.8) have worked with embroiderers, weavers and printers.

docs.title: 15.2 Artisans and New Technology
docs.text:
Artisans have never been simply “traditional”; they have adopted new tools, materials and designs whenever these served them. In the early twentieth century handloom weavers took up the fly-shuttle, which allowed one weaver to weave wider cloth faster, and the Jacquard attachment; colonial and princely governments and missionaries promoted improved looms. Weavers adopted mill-spun yarn, artificial silk and synthetic dyes. After independence, many weavers moved from handlooms to power looms, especially in towns such as Bhiwandi and Malegaon in Maharashtra and Surat in Gujarat, which became huge centres of power-loom weaving. Potters have adopted electric wheels and kilns, metalworkers electric blowers and lathes, embroiderers sewing machines, and printers screen-printing.

These changes raise difficult questions. When does a craft cease to be “hand-made”? Does technology that increases productivity help artisans, or does it hand the market to those with capital? Policy has often tried to protect a sharp boundary between handloom and power loom, while many weavers have moved across it in search of a living, and some of the most admired “traditional” textiles of the twentieth century were woven with tools, such as the fly-shuttle and the Jacquard, that had once been new.

docs.title: 15.3 Handloom Policy
docs.text:
Handloom weaving remains the largest single craft occupation in India. Since independence the state has tried to protect it from the competition of mills and power looms through cooperatives, subsidies on yarn, rebates on sales, and the reservation of certain products for the handloom sector under the Handlooms (Reservation of Articles for Production) Act of 1985. Enforcement of the reservation has been weak, and power looms producing imitations of handloom saris and fabrics have taken much of the market. Labelling schemes, such as the Handloom Mark (2006) and the India Handloom brand (2015), certify that products are genuinely hand-woven. Since 2015, 7 August, the anniversary of the launch of the Svadeśī movement in 1905, has been observed as National Handloom Day.

State governments have also promoted crafts through programmes such as Uttar Pradesh’s “One District One Product” scheme (2018), which identifies a characteristic product of each district, many of them crafts, for support with credit, training and marketing; and in 2023 the central government launched the PM Vishwakarma scheme of credit, training and toolkits for artisans in eighteen traditional trades (Chapter 2). Such schemes are recent, and their effects remain to be assessed.

Policy for handicrafts and handlooms has often swung between two views: that crafts are a heritage to be preserved, and that they are an economic sector to be modernised. Artisans themselves have generally wanted both: respect for their skills and traditions, and access to credit, raw materials, markets, education, social security and new technology on their own terms.

docs.title: 15.4 Craft and Education
docs.text:
Gandhi’s scheme of “basic education” (Nayī Tālīm), adopted at a conference at Wardha in 1937, proposed that children should learn through productive work, especially spinning and weaving, and that schools should become partly self-supporting through the sale of their products. The scheme was adopted by several provinces and, after independence, became the model for “basic schools”, but it was gradually abandoned in favour of conventional academic schooling. Its central idea, that manual skill is a form of knowledge to be valued in education, has been revived in recent discussions of school curricula and vocational training.

Artisan families themselves now face a choice between transmitting the craft to their children and giving them a formal education that may lead them away from it. Many craft organisations run schools, scholarships and training programmes, and some, such as the design schools for working artisans described below, try to combine the two.

docs.title: 15.5 Museums
docs.text: Museums have played an important part in the documentation and revival of Indian crafts. The Victoria and Albert Museum in London holds one of the largest collections of Indian textiles and decorative arts, formed largely in the colonial period; its 2015 exhibition The Fabric of India surveyed the whole history of Indian textiles (Crill 2015). In India, the Calico Museum of Textiles in Ahmedabad, founded in 1949 by Gautam and Gira Sarabhai, holds outstanding collections of historic textiles and has published a series of scholarly catalogues (Irwin and Hall 1971, 1973); the National Crafts Museum in Delhi combines collections with demonstrations by living craftspeople; and many state and private museums, such as the Anokhi Museum of Hand Printing at Amber, document particular crafts. Museums face the question of how to present craft objects: as anonymous “ethnographic” specimens, as works of art, or as the products of named individuals and communities with their own histories.

docs.title: 15.6 Geographical Indications
docs.text:
The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act was passed in 1999 and came into force in 2003. A Geographical Indication (GI) is a name identifying goods as originating in a particular place, where a given quality, reputation or other characteristic of the goods is essentially attributable to that origin. Registration prevents others from using the name for goods that do not come from the registered area or meet its specification. The first Indian GI was Darjeeling tea (2004); since then several hundred GIs have been registered, a large proportion of them handicrafts and handloom products.

Among the craft and handloom GIs are Pochampally ikat, Kancheepuram silk, Banaras brocades and saris, Chanderi fabric, Muga silk of Assam, Kashmir pashmina and the Kani shawl, Phulkari, Lucknow chikan, Madhubani paintings, Thanjavur paintings, Orissa paṭṭacitra, Bidrī ware, Channapatna toys, Kondapalli toys, Āṟanmuḷa mirrors, Kannauj perfume, the block prints of Sanganer, Bagru and Bagh, and Kolhapuri chappals.

Scholarly Note: What GIs Can and Cannot Do

A GI protects a name, not a technique or a design, and not the livelihood of the makers. It can prevent machine-made saris from Surat from being sold as “Kancheepuram silk”, and it can help to build a reputation for quality. But enforcement depends on producers’ organisations with the resources to take action; a registered GI may be held by an association dominated by traders rather than artisans; and a GI cannot by itself address the low earnings, poor working conditions and social stigma that lead young people to leave crafts. Its value depends on what producers and their organisations do with it.

docs.title: 15.7 Markets Today
docs.text:
Indian crafts reach their buyers through many channels: local markets and fairs, government emporia and craft bazaars (such as the Dilli Haat in Delhi, opened in 1994, and the Shilpgram centres), private shops and brands, exporters, and increasingly online platforms and social media, which allow some artisans to sell directly to customers. Craft tourism has grown in places such as Kutch, Raghurajpur, Pochampally and Swamimalai; Pochampally was named one of the “Best Tourism Villages” of the UN World Tourism Organization in 2021. Jaipur (2015) and Srinagar (2021) have been designated UNESCO Creative Cities of Crafts and Folk Art.

The structure of the market often works against the artisan. Between the maker and the final buyer stand contractors, traders, exporters and retailers, each taking a share; artisans who lack working capital must accept advances from traders who then fix the price. Hand production cannot compete with machines on price, and where buyers do not value the difference between hand-made and machine-made goods, artisans are squeezed. Power looms imitating handloom designs have taken much of the market for handloom saris, despite legal reservations for handloom.

docs.title: 15.7.1 Who Buys Crafts?
docs.text: The buyers of Indian crafts have changed several times. Village households once bought pots, cloth and tools from local artisans; courts and temples commissioned luxury goods; foreign merchants bought for export. Today, much of the market for handmade goods is among the urban middle classes in India and among buyers abroad, including the Indian diaspora, who buy crafts as expressions of taste, identity and support for artisans. Handloom saris, khādī and regional textiles are worn by many Indians as a statement of national or regional identity, and politicians often wear them in public. This market values “authenticity” and “tradition”, but it also demands novelty, consistency and convenience; artisans must negotiate between these expectations.

docs.title: 15.8 Design Schools and the Crafts
docs.text: Since independence, the professional designer has become one of the main intermediaries between India’s craftspeople and their markets. The institutions that trained designers grew out of a long argument about the relation between art, craft and industry, an argument that began in the colonial art schools (Chapter 14) and at Santiniketan (Chapter 11).

docs.title: 15.8.1 The Bauhaus in Calcutta
docs.text: In December 1922 the Indian Society of Oriental Art in Calcutta exhibited works by artists of the Bauhaus, the German school of art, architecture and design founded at Weimar in 1919. Among them were Paul Klee, Wassily Kandinsky, Lyonel Feininger and Johannes Itten, and their works were hung alongside paintings of the Bengal school. The exhibition was arranged through Stella Kramrisch, who had come to India at Rabindranath Tagore’s invitation. Partha Mitter treats it as the moment at which Indian artists first met the European avant-garde in their own city (Mitter 2007). The Bauhaus programme called for artists and craftsmen to work together in the workshop, with no barrier of rank between them. This had obvious affinities with Tagore’s experiments at Santiniketan and Sriniketan. At the time, however, its influence on Indian crafts was slight. Its lasting influence came forty years later, through design education.

docs.title: 15.8.2 The Eameses’ India Report
docs.text: In 1958, at the invitation of the Government of India and with the support of the Ford Foundation, the American designers Charles and Ray Eames spent several months travelling in India. Pupul Jayakar had a large part in bringing them. Their India Report, submitted in April 1958, argued that India faced rapid change, in which traditional ways of making and modern industrial production would collide. It called for a new kind of designer who understood both, and it recommended an institute for training, research and service in design (Eames and Eames 1958). The report’s famous praise of the humble brass loṭā as a model of good design was not nostalgia. The Eameses used the vessel to show how a form refined by generations of makers and users can answer many demands at once, of material, use, cost and beauty. They asked designers to approach every new product with the same seriousness.

docs.title: 15.8.3 The National Institute of Design
docs.text:
The National Institute of Design was set up in Ahmedabad in 1961 as an autonomous institution. Gira Sarabhai and Gautam Sarabhai, of the family that had founded the Calico Museum (Section 15.5), were its guiding figures, and the Ford Foundation gave support. Its early teaching drew on European modernist design education, including the foundation course of the Bauhaus and the methods of the Ulm School of Design, and on visiting teachers from Europe, America and Japan. It also sent its students to study crafts. The documentation of a craft became a regular exercise in Indian design education: recording, in a village or workshop, the materials, tools, processes, products, makers and markets of a living craft. Such studies, accumulated over decades, form an important archive of crafts as they were practised in the second half of the twentieth century.

In January 1979 the Institute hosted an international meeting, held by the United Nations Industrial Development Organization and the International Council of Societies of Industrial Design, which adopted the Ahmedabad Declaration on Industrial Design for Development. The Declaration called on designers in developing countries to serve basic needs and to build on local resources and skills rather than imitate the products of the industrial West. A National Institute of Design Act of 2014 declared the Institute an institution of national importance, and further campuses have since been opened in other states.

docs.title: 15.8.4 Designers in the Handloom Sector
docs.text: The Weavers’ Service Centres of the All India Handloom Board (Section 15.1) employed artists and designers to create new designs for handloom weavers and to record old ones. The painter K. G. Subramanyan, later a leading teacher at Baroda and Santiniketan, worked as a designer for the Board’s Bombay centre around 1960. In the 1980s the Weavers’ Service Centres, under the direction of Martand Singh, prepared a series of exhibitions of handwoven textiles called Vishwakarma. Weavers re-created historical designs and techniques from museum pieces and old samples for these shows, which were seen in India and at the Festivals of India abroad. These projects showed that skills thought to be lost could often be recovered when weavers were given the time, materials and payment to do so.

docs.title: 15.8.5 Crafts on Show: The Festivals of India
docs.text: In the 1980s the Festivals of India, a series of cultural festivals organised by the Indian government under the direction of Pupul Jayakar, presented Indian crafts abroad on an unprecedented scale. They began in Britain in 1982 and continued in the United States and France in the mid-1980s and later in the Soviet Union, Japan and other countries. Besides exhibitions of sculpture and painting, they brought living craftspeople and performers to work in public. The exhibition Aditi, designed by Rajeev Sethi and first shown in London in 1982, followed the cycle of life, from birth and childhood to marriage, through objects, with potters, painters, puppeteers and other makers working in the galleries. Other exhibitions paired international designers with Indian craftspeople to make new objects. The festivals opened export markets and made some master craftspeople known by name. They also revived an old problem. Saloni Mathur has described how, at the Colonial and Indian Exhibition in London in 1886, Indian artisans were brought to work before visitors as living exhibits of a timeless India (Mathur 2007). Critics of the 1980s festivals asked whether showing artisans at work, however respectfully, still presented them as specimens of “tradition” rather than as contemporary makers.

docs.title: 15.8.6 Surveys and Documentation
docs.text: Designers were not the only documenters. The Census of India of 1961 included a series of surveys of handicrafts, published as monographs on particular crafts and villages, which recorded processes, tools, communities and incomes across the country. The art magazine Marg, founded in Bombay in 1946 by the writer Mulk Raj Anand, published special numbers on regional crafts and textiles that brought them to a wide educated readership. Together with the catalogues of the Calico Museum, the reports of the handicrafts and handloom boards and the work of design students, these surveys make the crafts of the mid-twentieth century unusually well recorded.

docs.title: 15.8.7 New Schools
docs.text: From the 1980s the number of design schools grew. The National Institute of Fashion Technology was founded in New Delhi in 1986, and the Indian Institute of Crafts and Design in Jaipur followed in the 1990s. A different model put the artisan in the classroom. The design school opened by Kala Raksha in Kutch in 2005, led by Judy Frater, taught working artisans from embroidering, weaving, printing and other communities to design new work within their own traditions and to understand the markets they sold to. Frater later founded Somaiya Kala Vidya on the same principles. Its graduates are recognised as designers in their own right, not as executors of other people’s designs.

docs.title: 15.8.8 Design for Whom?
docs.text:
Collaboration between designers and artisans has been one of the main strategies of the revival. At its best it brings new products and markets to artisans while respecting their skills and their own design traditions; at its worst it treats them as anonymous labour executing the designs of others. The design schools have also changed how craft knowledge is judged. Ethnographic studies, such as Soumhya Venkatesan’s work on the Pattamadai mat-weavers (Chapter 13), show how the views of designers, officials and buyers about what counts as good craft can override the makers’ own (Venkatesan 2009). The language of “design intervention”, common in development programmes, assumes that a craft needs correcting from outside. Many designers and institutions now prefer to speak of collaboration, to name the artisans they work with, and to share authorship and income. The ideal set out in the India Report and the Ahmedabad Declaration, of design that starts from the knowledge already present in a community, is easier to state than to carry out.

Some artisans have become well-known artists in their own right. Mithilā painters such as Sita Devi, Ganga Devi and Dulari Devi, the Warli painter Jivya Soma Mashe, the Gond painter Jangarh Singh Shyam and the rogan painter Abdul Gafur Khatri (Chapter 12) have been recognised with national awards and international exhibitions. Their success has raised its own disputes: whether a painting made for the market by a named artist is still “folk” or “tribal” art, who may use a community’s styles and motifs, and how much of the price paid in a city gallery returns to the village. Jangarh Singh Shyam’s early death in Japan in 2001, where he had gone to paint for a museum, became for many critics a symbol of the inequalities of that market.

docs.title: 15.9 Fair Trade and Certification
docs.text: Since the 1970s, “alternative trade” organisations in Europe and North America have bought Indian crafts directly from producer groups on terms intended to give artisans a fair price, advance payment and long-term relationships. Indian organisations have joined international fair-trade networks, and certification schemes, such as those against child labour in carpet-weaving (Chapter 4) and the Handloom Mark, try to assure buyers of the conditions under which goods are made. Such schemes have helped some producer groups, but they reach only a small part of the craft sector, and certification adds costs that small producers find hard to bear.

docs.title: 15.10 Shocks and Resilience
docs.text: Craft economies are vulnerable to sudden shocks. The Gujarat earthquake of 2001 destroyed homes and workshops across Kutch; craft organisations and communities rebuilt, and the earthquake led to new initiatives such as the village of Ajrakhpur and the organisation Khamir. The lockdowns imposed during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 closed markets and fairs, cut off orders from exporters and left many artisans without income; online sales and relief from craft organisations helped some, but many artisans turned to other work. Craft communities have survived many such crises, but livelihoods that depend on long chains of intermediaries and on distant markets are the first to fail when those chains break.

docs.title: 15.11.1 Livelihoods and Status
docs.text: The most serious problem is that many craftspeople earn too little to live decently from their work. Surveys of handloom weavers and handicraft artisans conducted by the Government of India have repeatedly found low household incomes and high levels of debt. Young people from artisan families often prefer other occupations, both because they pay better and because craft work still carries the low status that caste attached to manual work. Any revival that does not improve artisans’ incomes and social standing will not last.

docs.title: 15.11.2 A Note on Numbers
docs.text: Figures for the number of artisans in India, the value of craft production and exports, or the number of Geographical Indications are often quoted, but they should be used with care. The most systematic counts are the All India Handloom Censuses conducted for the Ministry of Textiles, the most recent of them in 2019–20, and the surveys of handicraft artisans of the office of the Development Commissioner (Handicrafts). The handloom censuses count households and persons engaged in weaving and in “allied” work such as winding, warping and sizing, and distinguish full-time from part-time workers, so that totals change greatly according to which categories are added together; successive censuses have recorded a declining number of handloom workers, a large majority of them women. Handicraft surveys use different definitions again, and many artisans work part-time or seasonally, combine craft with agriculture or wage labour, or are counted as “helpers” rather than workers. This volume has therefore avoided precise statistics where reliable, sourced figures could not be given. Readers who need numbers should consult the census reports themselves and note how each figure was obtained.

docs.title: 15.11.3 Raw Materials
docs.text: Crafts depend on materials whose supply is often uncertain: the indigenous “desi” cottons suited to hand-spinning, now a small fraction of India’s cotton area, which since 2002 has been dominated by genetically modified Bt hybrids; the host trees of tasar and mugā silk; natural dye plants; sandalwood and other carving woods (Chapter 7); clay from village commons; and bamboo and cane from forests governed by laws that have not always recognised the rights of forest communities.

docs.title: 15.11.4 Knowledge and Its Ownership
docs.text: Traditional designs and techniques are easily copied by industrial producers in India and abroad, and existing intellectual property law protects them only partly. GIs protect names; design registration protects individual new designs; copyright protects individual works. Collective, inherited knowledge falls between these categories. Documentation by museums, design schools and craft organisations helps preserve knowledge of techniques and designs, but documentation cannot replace living transmission from one practitioner to another.

docs.title: 15.11.5 Health and Safety
docs.text: Many crafts carry occupational hazards: silicosis among stone-carvers and agate-workers, lung disease among glass and metal workers, injuries and eye strain among weavers and embroiderers, exposure to toxic dyes, mordants and metals among dyers, printers and jewellers. Child labour, once widespread in carpet weaving, glass-bangle making and other crafts, has been reduced but not eliminated. A craft revival that ignores these issues romanticises hardship.

docs.title: 15.11.6 Women Artisans
docs.text: Women make up a large part of the craft workforce, especially in embroidery, weaving in the North-East, basketry, pottery preparation, bead-work and the processing of fibres; yet they are often recorded as “helpers” rather than artisans, paid less, and excluded from the control of markets and from organisations dominated by men. Many of the most successful craft initiatives of recent decades, such as SEWA, the embroidery collectives of Kutch and Bihar and many self-help groups, have been organised by and for women. Their experience shows that income from craft can increase women’s independence and standing in their families, but also that the double burden of household and craft work can be heavy (Wilkinson-Weber 1999; Chakravarti 2003).

docs.title: 15.11.7 Caste and Dignity
docs.text: Many of the communities that practise crafts, especially those working with leather, bamboo, fibre and clay, are Dalit, Ādivāsī or “backward” castes, and the stigma attached to manual work and to their identities has not disappeared. Revival efforts that present crafts as timeless “heritage” can ignore this history, or even reinforce it by expecting artisans to remain in their hereditary occupations. Respect for craft must include the freedom of artisans’ children to choose other work, and the dignity of those who choose to stay.

docs.title: 15.12 Conclusion
docs.text: The crafts described in this volume embody one of the great bodies of practical knowledge in human history: the knowledge of how to transform cotton into muslin, iron into crucible steel, ore into zinc, clay into a temple’s terracotta skin, and threads into paṭolā whose patterns appear only when warp and weft meet. That knowledge was created and carried mostly by people whom the dominant texts ranked low and whose names were rarely recorded. To value Indian craft knowledge truly is to value its makers: to record their achievements accurately, without myth or exaggeration; to recognise the injustices of caste and colonial exploitation that shaped their lives; and to ensure that those who practise crafts today can do so with dignity and a fair reward.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For crafts region by region, Ranjan and Ranjan (2007); for the work of the post-independence revival, Chattopadhyay (1975); for the making of the idea of Indian craft, McGowan (2009); for the Fabric of India exhibition of 2015, Crill (2015); for the origins of the National Institute of Design, Eames and Eames (1958); for the Bauhaus exhibition in Calcutta, Mitter (2007).

docs.title: A Guide to Further Reading
docs.text: The short notes at the end of each chapter list the main sources for that chapter. This guide is selective and evaluative: it suggests where a reader should begin, what each work does best, and where its limits lie. Full details are given in the Select Bibliography.

docs.title: Where to Begin
docs.text:
For what is made where today, the indispensable work is Handmade in India, edited by M. P. and Aditi Ranjan (Ranjan and Ranjan 2007). It is a regional encyclopaedia, richly photographed and organised state by state, with descriptions of processes and products; it has little history and almost no social analysis, and is best used beside a historical account such as this one. For textiles as objects, Rosemary Crill’s catalogue The Fabric of India (Crill 2015) is the best single illustrated introduction, and Gillow and Barnard (1991) is a reliable practical survey of techniques. Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay’s Handicrafts of India (Chattopadhyay 1975) belongs to the revival it describes and should be read as a document of that movement as well as a survey.

On the idea of the Indian craftsman, the classic statements are Coomaraswamy’s The Indian Craftsman (Coomaraswamy 1909) and Kramrisch’s essay on the traditions of the Indian craftsman (Kramrisch 1958). Both are eloquent and both largely leave caste aside. George Birdwood’s The Industrial Arts of India (Birdwood 1880) is a Victorian source, valuable for what it records and for its attitudes. Abigail McGowan’s Crafting the Nation in Colonial India (McGowan 2009) is the best modern account of how the category of “Indian crafts” itself was made, and is the natural corrective to all three.

docs.title: Early History and Texts
docs.text: Kenoyer (1998) is the clearest introduction to Indus crafts by the archaeologist who has studied them most closely; Allchin and Allchin (1982) remains a sound general archaeology. For guilds and trade in early India, Chakravarti (2002) is concise and reliable, and Kosambi (1956) is still stimulating, though its model of post-Gupta decline is debated. The translations of the Arthaśāstra by Olivelle (2013) (with up-to-date notes and dating) and Kangle (1960–1965) (with fuller commentary), of Manu by Olivelle (2005), of the Periplus by Casson (1989) and of the Bṛhatsaṃhitā by Bhat (1981–1982) are the primary texts most often cited here. For Tamil literature, Ramanujan (1985) gives a selection of Caṅkam poetry in fine translations and Parthasarathy (1993) a complete translation of the Cilappatikāram. Irfan Habib’s Technology in Medieval India (Habib 2008) is a compact, well-documented account of the period from about 650 to 1750, the one most thinly covered in general surveys.

docs.title: Metals
docs.text: Metallurgy is treated in detail in Volume 14. Srinivasan and Ranganathan (2004) and Bronson (1986) are the best starting points on crucible steel, Balasubramaniam (2002) on the Delhi pillar and Craddock (2017) on zinc, lead and silver; all are written by specialists who also correct popular exaggerations. Verrier Elwin’s The Agaria (Elwin 1942) is a classic ethnography of iron-smelters made just before the craft disappeared.

docs.title: Textiles and Dress
docs.text: For the global trade, Riello (2013) is the most important recent synthesis, arguing that Indian cottons shaped European industrialisation; Parthasarathi (2011) makes a related case on comparative grounds, and Beckert (2014) sets both in a world history of cotton. The essays in Riello and Roy (2009) and Riello and Parthasarathi (2009) are uneven but cover markets from Japan to West Africa. Gittinger (1982) and Irwin and Brett (1970) remain the best accounts of the dyer’s technique; Guy (1998) and Barnes (2005) are essential for the Indian Ocean, and Barnes (1997) for the finds from Egypt. On weavers and the Company, Hossain (1988) and Parthasarathi (2001) are detailed and complementary; on medieval south Indian weavers, Ramaswamy (1985). Tirthankar Roy’s Artisans and Industrialization (Roy 1993) and Traditional Industry (Roy 1999) are the indispensable revisionist accounts of handloom weaving and other industries under colonial rule. For Africa, Machado (2014) and Prestholdt (2008) write from the side of the consumers. On dress, Goswamy (1993) is the best guide to surviving garments, Tarlo (1996) the best study of what clothing meant to those who wore it, and Cohn (1996) the classic essay on dress and colonial rule.

docs.title: Other Crafts
docs.text: On jewellery, Untracht (1997) is encyclopaedic and based on long fieldwork. On instruments and their makers, Deva (1978) describes the instruments, and Krishna (2020) shows, for the mṛdaṅgam, how much the makers’ history has been left out. On leather, there is still no full history; Roy (1999) covers the colonial industry, Lynch (1969) the shoe-makers of Agra and Rawat (2011) the history of the “leather-working” caste label. On painting as a craft, Goswamy (1997) reconstructs a family of hill painters with exceptional care, and Mitter (1994) traces the split between artist and craftsman in colonial India. Losty (1982) is a well-illustrated introduction to the arts of the book, and Topsfield (2006) to board and card games.

docs.title: Caste, Society and Economy
docs.text: Bayly (1999) is the best general history of caste in the eighteenth to twentieth centuries. Ambedkar’s Annihilation of Caste (Ambedkar 1936) is short and should be read whole; Chakravarti (2003) explains why caste and gender cannot be studied apart, and Omvedt (2008) and Zelliot (1992) trace the traditions of anti-caste thought and movement. On artisan communities, Brouwer (1995) presents a Viśvakarma world-view on its own terms and Mines (1984) a weaving caste’s long history. For the jajmānī debate, read Wiser (1936) with the critique in Fuller (1989). On the colonial economy, Dutt (1902) and Naoroji (1901) state the nationalist case, Bagchi (1976) and Morris (1963) the two sides of the deindustrialisation debate, and Haynes (2012) carries the story of artisans and merchants into the twentieth century. On Svadeśī and khādī, Sarkar (1973), Bayly (1986) and Trivedi (2007).

docs.title: Craft Knowledge and Design
docs.text: On tacit knowledge, Polanyi (1958) is the philosophical source; on the place of theory and practice in Sanskrit learning, Pollock (1985). Dharampal (1971) collects European accounts of Indian technology and should be read critically, Raj (2007) for the circulation of knowledge, and Venkatesan (2009) for what development programmes do to craft knowledge. On design and the crafts, the Eameses’ India Report (Eames and Eames 1958) is short and still worth reading, and Mitter (2007) covers the Bauhaus exhibition of 1922.

docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This is Volume 18 of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā: Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra: Polity and Law. It surveys Indian traditions of political thought and law from the Vedic period to the Constitution of the Republic of India: the Arthaśāstra and the later literature on polity; the theory of kingship in the śāstras and the epics; Buddhist and Jain ideas of the righteous ruler and the law of the monastic order; the Dharmaśāstra literature, from the Dharmasūtras and the Manusmṛti to the medieval commentaries and digests; courts, procedure, contract, property, inheritance, crime and the family in classical law; custom, caste and village institutions; the charters, scribes and statecraft of the medieval kingdoms; Islamic law and the Indo-Persian state of the Sultanate and the Mughals; the making of “Anglo-Hindu” and “Anglo-Muhammadan” law under British rule; and the Constitution’s encounter with this inheritance.

After an introduction, the chapters fall into four groups: the foundations of Indian political thought, the Arthaśāstra’s science of the state and the Buddhist and Jain alternatives to it (Chapters 2–8); the Dharmaśāstra literature (Chapters 9–11); the classical law of procedure, property, crime, the family and custom (Chapters 12–16); and the history of law and government from the medieval regional kingdoms and the Delhi Sultanate to the Republic (Chapters 17–20). Primary texts are quoted only where both the wording and the reference could be confirmed against a standard edition; elsewhere they are paraphrased, with the reference given. Dates follow current scholarship, with traditional dates labelled as such; in particular, the Arthaśāstra is treated as a composite text of c. 50 BCE–300 CE and the Manusmṛti as a work of about the second century CE, following Patrick Olivelle. The volume does not claim that the classical texts “anticipated” modern constitutions, welfare states or human rights; comparisons with other traditions are presented as comparisons.

The texts discussed here are, among other things, charters of social hierarchy, and the volume does not hide this. It sets out their provisions on varṇa, untouchability and women with references to the primary sources, and it gives space to the critics — from the Buddha to B. R. Ambedkar and modern feminist and Dalit scholars — who exposed and opposed them. It also tries to give due weight to the real intellectual achievements of the traditions: the Arthaśāstra’s analysis of the state, the Dharmaśāstras’ law of procedure and property, and the many forms of local self-government recorded in inscriptions.

References to standard editions, translations and studies — among others by P. V. Kane, Robert Lingat, J. D. M. Derrett, Ludo Rocher, Richard Lariviere, Patrick Olivelle, Donald Davis, R. P. Kangle, Thomas Trautmann, Mark McClish, R. S. Sharma, Romila Thapar, Upinder Singh, Uma Chakravarti, Muzaffar Alam and Marc Galanter — are given in the text and collected in the select bibliography, which is meant as a guide to further reading. A list of abbreviations follows the table of contents; a glossary, a chronology, brief notes on persons and a guide to the principal sources are provided at the end. No survey of this size can be exhaustive or free of error, and every quotation should, before scholarly use, be checked against a critical edition.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput Ramanujan College, University of Delhi Guru Pūrṇimā, 2026
